As summarized in Table 2-1, residential uses account for 36 percent of the City’s total acreage. The 
next largest percentage of land use is attributed to parks/open space (21.3 percent). In the City’s 
northeast corner, the South Morro Hills area contains most of the City’s agricultural land, which 
comprises approximately 11 percent of total land use. Commercial uses occupy just three percent of 
the City. Most commercial uses including retail, lodging, and offices are along the City’s commercial 
corridors, within the proposed SSCSP Planning Area.  
2.4 
Transit 
The Oceanside Transit Center (OTC) serves as a major regional transit hub, with Breeze Bus, Coaster, 
Sprinter, Amtrak, and Metrolink services all offered. It is the only location in the region where these 
services converge. The OTC is the northern terminus of the Coaster, western terminus of the Sprinter, 
and southern terminus of the Metrolink (City of Oceanside 2021b). The North County Transit District 
(NCTD) proposes to redevelop the OTC as a mixed-use complex featuring housing, commercial uses, 
and “mobility hub” elements (City of Oceanside 2021a). 


2.0 Environmental Setting 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 2-6 
The NCTD also maintains a number of bus routes throughout the City, which connect riders from 
the various residential, commercial, and industrial areas of the City to the railway stations. Bicycle 
facilities within the City consist of a network of Class I (Bike Path), Class II (Bike Lane) and Class III 
(Bike Route) designated bike facilities (City of Oceanside Circulation Element 2012). The San Luis Rey 
River Trail and the Coastal Rail Trail are important regional bicycle facilities. A third regional bicycle 
facility, the Inland Rail Trail, is being pursued by SANDAG. When completed, the Inland Rail Trail will 
connect the City with the cities of Vista, San Marcos, and Escondido. 
2.5 
Land Use and Planning Context 
Future development would be guided by the GPU and SSCSP, which is consistent with state, regional 
and local planning documents. A more detailed discussion of the planning context for various topics 
is provided within regulatory setting sections throughout this Recirculated Program Environmental 
Impact Report (RPEIR). As specifically discussed in Section 4.1, the project would be consistent with 
the California Coastal Act, state housing element law, San Diego Forward: The 2021 Regional Plan, 
draft Subarea Plan (SAP), Code of Ordinances, Local Coastal Plan, and Airport Land Use Consistency 
Plan.  
2.6 
Natural Environment 
2.6.1 
Biological Resources 
While the City is dominated by developed, disturbed, and agricultural operations, sensitive habitats 
and species are supported, particularly in proximity to wetland and riparian areas along the San Luis 
Rey River, its tributaries, and scattered canyons throughout the City. The City supports a variety of 
native and non-native vegetation communities of varying sensitivity, including uplands and wetland 
habitats and unvegetated areas, such as streams, lagoons, and beaches. The City prepared a habitat 
conservation plan (draft SAP) consistent with the North County Multiple Species Conservation 
Program. The draft SAP was never adopted, and in 2021, the City Council directed City staff to address 
habitat conservation in the GPU.  As such, habitat conservation has been addressed in the Vital and 
Sustainable Resources Element. 
A more detailed discussion of biological resources, including maps of potential occurrence areas for 
plant and wildlife species, and application of the goals of the draft SAP, is in Section 4.5 of this RPEIR. 
2.6.2 
Cultural and Tribal Cultural Resources 
The City has a long history of human occupation dating back approximately 10,000 years. The City is 
within the territory of the Luiseño Band and according to the South Coastal Information Center 
records, there are hundreds of historic and pre-historic sites within the City. The project provides an 
opportunity to develop policies focused on creating open space and other means of preserving 
known cultural resource areas, along with educational and historical context. A more detailed 
discussion of cultural resources is in Section 4.6 of this RPEIR. 


2.0 Environmental Setting 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 2-7 
2.6.3 
Climate, Air Quality, and Greenhouse Gas Emissions 
The project area, like the rest of San Diego County, has a Mediterranean climate characterized by 
warm, dry summers and mild winters. Long-term measurements at the Oceanside Marina indicate 
that winter low temperatures in the City average about 45 degrees Fahrenheit, and summer high 
temperatures average about 71 degrees Fahrenheit. The average annual precipitation is 10.5 inches, 
falling primarily from December to March (Western Regional Climate Center 2024). 
The City lies within the San Diego Air Basin, as identified by the California Air Resources Board (CARB). 
The region’s climate and air circulation patterns, combined with heavy traffic and urbanized land 
uses, contribute to the region being classified by the CARB as a non-attainment area for ozone and 
particulate matter standards. Air quality is discussed in greater detail in Section 4.4 of this RPEIR. 
A year 2018 greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory was conducted for the City as part of the CAP Update. 
Total communitywide emissions totaled 846,000 metric tons of CO2 equivalent. The CAP Update 
includes reduction measures to assist the City in reducing GHG to meet state targets. A detailed 
analysis of the project’s forecasted GHG emissions and future application of reduction measures is 
discussed in Section 4.9 of this RPEIR. 
2.6.4 
Geology and Landform 
City elevations range from zero along the coast to 940 feet above sea level, inland. The topography 
throughout the City can be characterized into three physiographic regions: low-lying coastal areas 
along the Pacific Ocean; the areas that comprise the City’s three principal waterways; and the foothills 
and higher elevations located along the eastern boundary of the City.  
The City is within the coastal sub province of the Peninsular Ranges Geomorphic Province. Geological 
formations underlying the City are largely composed of sedimentary rocks, identified as coarse-
grained, with alluvial formations along and fanning out from the San Luis Rey River, Loma Alta Creek, 
and Buena Vista Creek beds. Landslide susceptible areas are located adjacent to the alluvial planes, 
within Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) designated floodplains.  
Geological formations, including topography and major landforms located throughout the City 
throughout, are discussed in greater detail in Section 4.8 of this RPEIR. 
2.7 
Hydrology and Water Quality 
2.7.1 
Watersheds 
The City spans four watersheds: the San Luis Rey River Watershed includes the northern and 
northeast portion of the City, including a majority of the South Morro Hills area; the Loma Alta River 
Watershed includes the central portion of the City; the Buena Vista Creek Watershed includes 
southern portions of the City; and the Agua Hedionda Creek Watershed, which is mostly within the 
city of Carlsbad and includes the southernmost tip of the City. A detailed discussion of the City 


2.0 Environmental Setting 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 2-8 
watersheds and primary water bodies, as well as citywide draining is discussed in greater detail in 
Section 4.11 of this RPEIR. 
2.7.2 
Water Quality  
The City is home to a variety of waterbodies, such as rivers, creeks, lakes, lagoons, and the Pacific 
Ocean, all of which are popular destinations for fishing enthusiasts, boaters, skiers, bathers, and 
birdwatchers. Each of the watersheds have been identified as impaired for several pollutants under 
Section 303(d) of the Federal Clean Water Act. The identification of polluted waters is based on the 
total maximum daily loads of pollutants within the water body, as well as determining each 
waterbody's primary beneficial use. Water quality is discussed in greater detail in Section 4.11 of this 
RPEIR. 
2.7.3 
Flooding 
Several areas throughout the City are vulnerable to flooding including the coastal zones and 
designated Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA) located primarily along San Luis Rey River, Loma Alta 
Creek, and Buena Vista Creek. The SFHA is an area identified by the FEMA as an area with a special 
flood or mudflow, and/or flood related erosion hazard. Several portions of the Planning Area are 
subject to a 100-year flood. Details of the locations of the FEMA floodplains and floodways located 
throughout the City, constraints and permit requirements are discussed in greater detail in Section 
4.11 of this RPEIR. 
2.8 
Public Infrastructure 
Since the City is primarily developed, infrastructure, including roads, water, sewer, energy, and 
communication facilities, is available. Public utilities are discussed in greater detail in Section 4.17 of 
this RPEIR.  
2.8.1 
Water Systems 
The City of Oceanside Water Utilities Department is responsible for providing water service 
throughout the Oceanside Water District, which is contiguous with the City’s boundaries. Water 
supplies are purchased from the San Diego County Water Authority (SDCWA). The water supply and 
distribution system include connections to five SDCWA aqueducts and the City’s Mission Basin 
Groundwater Purification Facility. The City’s water distribution system facilities include 12 storage 
reservoirs, nine booster pump stations, two water supply stations, 54 pressure regulating stations, 
and seven altitude valves. The existing water pipeline network consists of 574 miles of pipe ranging 
from two to 42 inches in diameter, with most of the pipes being sized at eight inches and made of 
asbestos cement pipe. Additional details relating to water demand and supply and the adequacy of 
infrastructure are discussed in Sections 4.17.4 and 4.17.5 of this RPEIR.  


2.0 Environmental Setting 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 2-9 
2.8.2 
Wastewater Systems 
The Water Utilities Department is also responsible for the operation and maintenance of the City’s 
wastewater collection and treatment facilities. The department’s wastewater system contains over 
450 miles of pipelines, which collect and transport wastewater to two wastewater treatment plants, 
the San Luis Rey Water Reclamation Facility and the La Salina Wastewater Treatment Plant. The La 
Salina Wastewater Treatment Plant is scheduled to be decommissioned within the next five years, 
with wastewater treatment to be consolidated at the San Luis Rey facility, which has an overall 
treatment capacity of 13.5 million gallons per day (City of Oceanside 2020). Additional details relating 
to wastewater facilities and capacity are discussed in Sections 4.17.4 and 4.17.6 of this RPEIR. 
2.8.3 
Solid Waste 
The City provides solid waste collection and disposal services through its contractor, Waste 
Management of North County, Inc. The services consist of residential, commercial, and industrial 
solid waste and designated recyclables collection service. Solid waste is hauled to one of three 
landfills: Otay Landfill in the city of Chula Vista; El Sobrante Landfill in the city of Corona, and 
Sycamore Landfill in the city of San Diego. All landfills have remaining capacity to continue to serve 
the City. Additional details relating to reduction of waste and the City’s Zero Waste and recycling 
programs are discussed in Section 4.17 of this RPEIR.

Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR

Chapter 3.0 
Project Description 
Consistent with Section 15168 of the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines, this 
Recirculated Program Environmental Impact Report (RPEIR) provides a programmatic analysis of the 
potential environmental impacts associated with implementation of the goals, policies, actions, and 
projected buildout of the following planning documents: 
• 
General Plan Update (GPU) 
• 
Smart and Sustainable Corridor Specific Plan (SSCSP) 
• 
Climate Action Plan (CAP) Update 
These separate planning documents are part of a comprehensive planning effort collectively referred 
to as Onward Oceanside (project). As described in Section 15168 of the CEQA Guidelines, program 
level environmental review documents are appropriate when a project consists of a series of actions 
related to the issuance of rules, regulations, and other planning criteria. The project, which is the 
subject of this RPEIR, is pursued by the City of Oceanside (City) to develop broad and updated policy 
and regulatory documents to guide the future development of the City. 
3.1 
Project Background  
Per the State of California Government Code Section 65300, each city or county must adopt a long-
term General Plan “for the physical development of the county or city, and of any land outside its 
boundaries.” The General Plan reflects the development goals of the community and represents 
public policy relative to the distribution of both public and private land uses. Therefore, each city 
and county in California is required to adopt a comprehensive, long-term General Plan. The purpose 
of this planning exercise is to plan for important community issues, such as new growth, housing 
needs and environmental protection. A General Plan is also used to project future demand for 
services, such as sewer, water, roadways, parks, and emergency services.  
The City has never prepared a comprehensive update to its General Plan. Rather, the City has 
prepared and updated individual elements in response to evolving state planning law. Some of the 
City’s current General Plan elements were originally prepared in the 1970s and have not since been 
updated (Safety Element, Noise Element, Environmental Resources Management Element). The City 
prepared updates to the General Plan Circulation Element in 2012 and the Land Use Element was last 
updated in 1986. A Military Reservation Element was approved in 1981 and a Community Facilities 
Element and Hazardous Waste Management Element were approved in 1990.  
In 2017, the City commenced a Phase 1 GPU which introduced two new optional General Plan 
elements, namely an Economic Development Element (EDE) and an Energy and Climate Action 
Element (ECAP). These two General Plan elements were adopted along with a CAP on May 8, 2019. 
This Phase 1 GPU effort informs and provides important policy direction for the current effort as it 
pertains to economic development, achieving a balance between housing and employment, and 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-2 
encouraging economic growth in an environmentally sensitive manner that supports state and local 
goals for greenhouse gas emission reductions.  
In early 2020, the City started Phase 2 of its GPU with a comprehensive planning effort involving 
extensive stakeholder outreach including citywide workshops, neighborhood meetings, forums, 
community surveys, stakeholder interviews, ad hoc meetings, email correspondence, and City 
Council and Planning Commission workshops. This engagement resulted in the development of 
guiding principles that summarize the broad goals to be achieved through the GPU and its 
companion planning documents, the SSCSP and an updated CAP, collectively referred to as the 
project.  
As part of the comprehensive GPU, and in accordance with timeframes established by state law, the 
City previously prepared and adopted the 6th Cycle Housing Element Update. The 6th Cycle Housing 
Element, effective April 15, 2021 to April 15, 2029, was adopted by City Council on June 16, 2021 
(revised February 2022; City of Oceanside 2022a). The California Department of Housing and 
Community (HCD) certified the Housing Element on November 14, 2023. Generally, the Housing 
Element evaluates the City’s existing housing supply and analyzes the City’s population, employment, 
and household characteristics to address topics such as low-income housing needs, overpayment, 
and overcrowding. Specific programs are identified in the Housing Element that describe how the 
City would implement and achieve its housing goals and policies. The project would support 
implementation of Housing Programs 7 and 8, which address the City’s compliance with the state 
Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) goals assigned to the City, and Program 9, which 
establishes new zoning standards for properties identified as having the capacity to accommodate 
additional housing.  
3.2 
Project Objectives 
In accordance with CEQA Guidelines Section 15124, the following primary objectives support the 
purpose of the project, assist the lead agency in developing a reasonable range of alternatives to be 
evaluated in this RPEIR, and ultimately aid decision-makers in preparing findings and overriding 
considerations, if necessary. 
1. Create opportunities for residential growth and economic development throughout the City, 
supporting a balance between employment and housing opportunities. 
2. Address required rezoning to implement Programs 7, 8, and 9 of the 6th Cycle 2021-2029 
Housing Element providing for the opportunity for future residential development with a 
density range of at least 35 dwelling units per acre (du/ac) on selected sites. 
3. Channel the bulk of future housing and job growth into already urbanized areas to reduce 
urban sprawl, create synergies between residential and non-residential uses, and promote 
active transportation and transit ridership. 
4. Minimize potential land use compatibility conflicts associated with the proposed changes to 
existing land use designations and zoning. 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-3 
5. To the extent feasible, protect the integrity of existing single-family neighborhoods and 
provide appropriate transitions between these neighborhoods and adjacent areas 
accommodating more intensive land use and development. 
6. Facilitate the preservation and proper stewardship of passive and recreational open space, 
sensitive habitat, and other natural resources. 
7. Provide adequate community services and facilities to all community members and 
coordinate with other public agencies and the local non-profit sector to maintain and expand 
access to health care, educational opportunities, recreational activities, cultural and social 
experiences.  
8. Identify, protect, and enhance those characteristics that make the City a unique and 
interesting community. 
9. Promote water conservation, energy efficiency, renewable energy sourcing, and other 
sustainable practices. 
10. Minimize risks associated with natural hazards, including those exacerbated by climate 
change, and enhance the resiliency of historically under-resourced communities. 
3.3 
Project Component Parts 
The project consists of three separate but interrelated planning documents. 
• 
The GPU would recreate the policy framework and the associated land use designations of 
the existing General Plan and serve as the blueprint for physical development throughout 
the City. 
• 
The SSCSP would facilitate infill and redevelopment along the City’s major east-west 
commercial corridors: Mission Avenue, Oceanside Boulevard, and Vista Way. 
• 
The CAP Update would quantify and address greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated 
with changes in density and intensity of land uses implemented through the GPU and SSCSP.  
The GPU would result in increased density and intensity of land uses throughout the City, allowing 
for significantly expanded residential capacity and employment opportunities. Most of the growth 
and expanded development opportunities would be focused within the proposed SSCSP Planning 
Area; however, anticipated growth facilitated by the project would occur throughout the City. 
Potential impacts of the project are analyzed considering buildout of the City under new and/or 
redefined zoning, as well as overall policy implications of the GPU, SSCSP, and CAP Update. The 
project’s component parts are discussed below. 
3.4 
General Plan Update  
A General Plan is a set of policies and programs that serve as the blueprint for physical development. 
Its purpose is to establish a long-range vision for the community and to plan for important 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-4 
community issues, such as new growth, housing needs, public services, and environmental 
protection. A General Plan expresses broad community values and goals, outlines a vision of how 
the community should look in the future, and provides steps for achieving this vision. Overall, the 
City’s GPU has been guided by the following general principles: 
• 
Ensure opportunity and quality of life for future generations; 
• 
Create a distinct sense of place; 
• 
Promote environmental justice and social equity; 
• 
Preserve and enhance neighborhood character; 
• 
Promote a stable, diverse, and jobs-rich local economy; 
• 
Provide housing opportunities; 
• 
Establish inclusive and transparent decision-making processes; 
• 
Expand mobility options; 
• 
Protect public health and safety; 
• 
Enhance resilience and response to nature hazards and climate change; 
• 
Preserve and enhance natural resources; 
• 
Reduce greenhouse gas emissions; 
• 
Preserve cultural resources; and 
• 
Enhance recreational opportunities. 
The recently adopted General Plan elements, the EDE and ECAP, would continue to provide a policy 
framework for supporting economic growth and reducing energy use and GHG emissions within the 
City. For this GPU, the City has organized its updated General Plan elements around themes and 
guiding principles that reflect community input, the findings of technical studies, and state and 
regional priorities. The updated elements contain all state-mandated requirements, providing newly 
drafted goals, objectives, policies, and specific actions for future land use decision making. Table 3-1 
shows the updated elements included in this GPU with associated key topics and policy focus. Table 
3-1 also provides reference to the sections within this RPEIR where corresponding environmental 
issues are analyzed.

Proposed changes to land uses throughout the City fall into two general categories: (1) specific 
parcels would be subject to a redesignation of land use (i.e., a parcel previously designated 
commercial is changed to mixed-use); and (2) parcels remain as designated, but the land use 
designation would be redefined to allow greater density (i.e., a parcel assigned High Density is 
allowed 21.0-28.9 du/ac under the existing general plan, but would be allowed a maximum of 40 
du/ac under the GPU). 
The first category of land use changes would be primarily along the City’s three major transit 
corridors (Oceanside Boulevard, Mission Avenue, Vista Way) to support new housing growth, 
increased commercial opportunities, and mixed-use development. Additionally, the corridors would 
support new industrial land uses to encourage research and development. The proposed changes 
along the City’s corridors  would offer greater employment opportunities, and encourage the 
development of vibrant, walkable neighborhoods. The redesignation of a few industrial sites in 
proximity to transit would further allow for future mixed-use development. Development regulations 
and design criteria of the corridors would be governed by the SSCSP. The SSCSP Planning Area is 
shown in Figure 3-2; additional details of proposed uses within the SSCSP are discussed in 
Section 3.5.

and/or intensity of uses within existing land use designations would support anticipated growth.

3.4.2 
Updated General Plan Elements  
The following paragraphs provide a summary of the City’s organization and content of each updated 
element; specific policies are discussed throughout Chapter 4.0 of this RPEIR.  
3.4.2.1 Efficient and Compatible Land Use Element (ECLU) 
The ECLU guides the location, form, and character of new development throughout the City. It 
promulgates the principles of efficient use of limited resources, access to housing, and adequate 
land resources for employment-oriented uses. Goals and policies identified in the ECLU include 
promotion of efficient land uses to encourage walkable neighborhoods, neighborhood commercial 
developments, high density residential and mixed-use projects; and new development of compatible 
land uses especially within mixed-use areas. The ECLU provides direction for future development 
with respect to building scale and form, mixed-use design, parking, edge connections and buffers, 
nature in the built environment, and home occupations. Goals and policies support the following 
objectives: 
• 
Infill and redevelopment within the City’s major commercial corridors, at intensities and 
densities that support a broad mix of complementary uses, active transportation, and transit 
service; 
• 
New housing in commercial districts, primarily in conjunction with mixed-use development 
but also in the form of standalone residential uses where appropriate; and 
• 
Industrial areas reserved primarily for industrial uses, flexible commercial land use standards 
(e.g., providing for low-intensity, low-impact industrial uses), new housing that increases

3.4.2.2 Integrated Mobility Element (IM) 
This Integrated Mobility Element (IM) promulgates the principle of safe, convenient, affordable, and 
sustainable mobility options. With the City’s roadway network largely built out, and with few 
opportunities to add roadway capacity for automobiles, the IM focuses on improving the efficiency 
of the roadway network while encouraging alternative modes of transportation. Additionally, the IM 
promotes the transition to low and zero-emission vehicles, encouraging the expansion of electric 
and hydrogen vehicle charging facilities and exploring ways to motivate community members to 
choose vehicles powered by clean and renewable energy. Key topics in this element include roadway 
efficiency, active transportation improvements (including complete streets, transit access, pedestrian 
and bicycle facilities), transit service, transportation demand management (TDM), and zero-emission 
vehicles. Goals and policies support the following objectives:  
• 
Enhanced integration of different travel modes;  
• 
Complete streets; 
• 
Safe, accessible, and attractive transit facilities; 
• 
First-mile/last-mile connections (e.g., micro-mobility); and 
• 
Reduced vehicle miles traveled (VMT). 
3.4.2.3 Remarkable Community Element (RC) 
The Remarkable Community Element (RC) promulgates principles focused on strengthening the 
City’s sense of place, preserving and enhancing neighborhood character, protecting historic and 
tribal resources, and promoting Oceanside as a visitor destination. Key topics in this element focus 
on urban design, neighborhood character, public spaces, scenic views, historic and tribal resources, 
and visitor-oriented amenities and activities. Goals and policies support the following objectives: 
• 
Strengthen the City’s sense of place; 
• 
Preserve and enhance neighborhood character;  
• 
Protect cultural and tribal resources; and 
• 
Promote the City as a visitor destination. 
3.4.2.4 Vital and Sustainable Resources Element (VSR) 
The Vital and Sustainable Resources Element (VSR) addresses the preservation of resources including 
biological, cultural, historic, tribal cultural, visual resources, and agriculture. Key topics in this element 
include sensitive habitat and wildlife, soils, farmland, water resources, air quality, and GHG emissions. 
Goals and policies support the following objectives: 
• 
Conserve natural resources; 
• 
Conserve open space; 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-12 
• 
Protect air/water quality; and 
• 
Reduce GHG emissions. 
3.4.2.5 Safe and Resilient Environment Element (SRE) 
The Safe and Resilient Environment Element (SRE) addresses the state requirement to assess and 
minimize the community’s vulnerability to natural and manmade hazards. Key topics in this element 
include natural hazards, human-induced hazards (e.g., crime, terrorism, and cyber threats, climate 
adaptation. Goals and policies support the following objectives: 
• 
Understand risks associated with both natural and human-induced hazards; 
• 
Build resilience against wildfire, flooding, landslides, drought, seismic activity, tsunamis, 
contagions, sea-level rise, and climate change; 
• 
Ensure appropriate and adequate emergency response; 
• 
Manage the production, distribution, and use of hazardous materials; and 
• 
Create safe and secure public spaces. 
3.4.2.6 Healthy and Livable Community Element (HLC) 
The Healthy and Livable Community Element (HLC) provides an update to the City’s Community 
Facilities Element. Key topics in this element include public health and wellness, educational and 
recreational opportunities, access to goods and services, community facilities and services, access to 
technology, environmental justice, and social equity. Goals and policies support the following 
objectives: 
• 
Create an environment conducive to healthy living; 
• 
Minimize noise impacts; 
• 
Ensure adequate community facilities and services; 
• 
Enhance community engagement in the decision-making process; 
• 
Utilize technology to bring efficiency to municipal operations; and 
• 
Promote personal growth, social interaction, and inclusiveness.  
3.4.2.7 
6th Cycle Housing Element 
As stated above, the City has adopted, and HCD certified, the 6th Cycle Housing Element. The 6th Cycle 
Housing Element is part of the City’s GPU but is being processed separately and is therefore not one 
of the thematic elements evaluated in this RPEIR. 
This project would, however, result in land use changes that support implementation of Housing 
Element programs focused on the City’s RHNA obligation of 5,443 dwelling units (composed of 
multiple types of residential units at multiple income levels). The Housing Element specifically 
identifies an inventory of Candidate Rezone Sites (comprised of vacant and underutilized sites) along 
Vista Way, Oceanside Boulevard, and Mission Avenue. With the changes in land use designation to 
accommodate greater density within the SSCSP, the City estimates an additional 4,851 residential 
dwelling units would be accommodated within the City (City of Oceanside 2022a).

3.4.3 Citywide Mobility  
Implementation of the GPU would encourage multimodal mobility improvements, especially along 
the City’s major commercial corridors, improving safety and accessibility for transit riders, 
pedestrians, and bicyclists. IM Goals direct the City and future development to complete a safe and 
accessible pedestrian and bicycle network. Examples of GPU goals include the following: 
• 
Goal 4-A: Oceanside will be one of the most pedestrian and bicycle friendly communities in 
the San Diego region, with complete pedestrian and bicycle networks providing continuous 
and convenient access to transit, employment and retail centers, neighborhoods, schools, 
beaches, parks, public places, and other destinations. 
• 
Goal 4-B: The City’s active transportation networks will be free of physical barriers and 
hazards, providing for safe and efficient travel, and accommodating travelers of all abilities. 
• 
Goal 4-C: The City’s active transportation facilities will be comfortable and inviting, while 
contributing positively to the City’s visual quality.  
• 
Goal 4-D: The City’s active transportation networks will be located and designed to provide 
viable alternatives to driving, linking travelers to a wide range of destinations, including 
commercial venues, public services, recreational opportunities, and transit. 
3.4.3.1 Pedestrian Network 
The IM includes recommendations for a pedestrian route type classification system developed to 
focus and prioritize investment in the City’s pedestrian network and ensure that pedestrian 
improvements occur at the most appropriate locations. Pedestrian route type designations include 
Districts, Corridors, and Connectors. These routes are as shown in Figure 3-3 and defined as follows: 
• 
District Routes: Meant to accommodate the highest level of pedestrian activity and could 
include significant streetscape amenities, wide sidewalks, enhanced crosswalks, lighting, 
street trees, and street furniture. The District Routes are proposed to be located within urban 
core and mixed-use areas.  
• 
Corridor Routes: These pedestrian areas anticipate moderate levels of pedestrian activities 
and are designated along roadways that support commercial businesses, shopping districts, 
schools, and parks. Corridor Route features may include wider sidewalks with landscape 
buffer or street trees, pedestrian countdown signal heads with lead pedestrian intervals at 
signalized intersections, and high visibility crosswalks. 
• 
Connector Routes: Connector Routes are designated for roadways with low pedestrian 
activity and moderate to high levels of vehicular traffic. This designation makes up the 
greatest portion of the pedestrian route type system. The Connector Route type is intended 
to consist of standard sidewalks with accessible curb ramps and marked crosswalks with 
advance stop bars at signalized intersections.

The IM provides recommendations for the design and enhancement of pedestrian routes (see GPU 
IM Figure 4-2).  
The GPU also introduces Pedestrian Priority Zones along specific streets and general areas where 
the highest pedestrian activity is anticipated, including commercial corridors and near major transit 
stops. They should have wider than minimum sidewalks, pedestrian-oriented street furniture, 
pedestrian-scale lighting, shade-producing landscaping, wider separation between sidewalks and 
vehicular travel lanes, and crossing enhancements. As shown in Figure 3-3, the proposed Pedestrian 
Priority Zones are within the SSCSP, and discussed in greater detail in Section 3.5.3.  
3.4.3.2 Bicycle Alignments 
As shown in Figure 3-4, the IM recommends bicycle alignments and classifications throughout the 
City consisting of Class I bike paths, Class II bicycle lanes, Class III bicycle routes, and Class IV cycle 
tracks. Three regional Class I bike paths are identified including the San Luis Rey River Bike Path, 
Coastal Rail Trail, and Inland Rail Trail. Bicycle classifications are defined and summarized as follows: 
• 
Class I Bike Path: Provides a completely separated right-of-way designed for the exclusive 
use of bicycles and pedestrians with crossflows by motorists minimized. Bike paths can 
provide connections where roadways are non-existent or unable to support bicycle travel. 
The minimum paved width for a two-way bike path is eight feet (ten feet preferred), with a 
two-foot-wide graded area adjacent to each side of the pavement. 
• 
Class II Bike Lane: Provides a striped lane designated for the exclusive or semi-exclusive use 
of bicycles with through travel by motor vehicles or pedestrians prohibited. Bike lanes are 
one-way facilities located on either side of a roadway. The minimum bike lane width is five-
feet when adjacent to on-street parking, or six feet when posted speeds are greater than 
40 miles per hour. 
• 
Class III Bike Route: Provides shared use of traffic lanes with cyclists and motor vehicles, 
identified by signage and/or street markings known as “sharrows.”  Bike routes are best suited 
for low-speed, low-volume roadways as they do not provide a dedicated space for bicyclists. 
• 
Class IV Cycle Track, also referred to as a separated or protected bikeway, provides a right-
of-way designated exclusively for bicycle travel within the roadway and physically protected 
from vehicular traffic. 
The construction and improvement of the City’s bicycle network would result in greater mobility 
options, an opportunity to reduce traffic congestion, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

3.4.3.3 Transit 
Expansion of transit service is an integral component to the GPU’s land use plan which proposes the 
highest density development near existing and planned transit. Improved transit would support 
ridership and reduced automobile dependency. The GPU policies generally support planned 
improvements identified in the San Diego Association of Governments Regional Transportation Plan 
(RTP), including conversion of several City-serving North County Transit District (NCTD) bus routes 
to Rapid services by 2035. Examples of goals relating to the enhancement and improvement of transit 
throughout the City include IM goals, as follows: 
• 
Goal 4-I: Transit will become an increasingly viable and efficient mode of transportation to 
destinations throughout Oceanside and the greater region. 
• 
Goal 4-J: Community members will enjoy comfortable and convenient access to public 
transportation services. 
• 
Goal 4-K: In partnership with NCTD and other stakeholders, the City will leverage its position 
as a regional transit hub to encourage commuters and visitors to access Oceanside via rail 
and bus. 
• 
Goal 4-L: Infill and redevelopment within already urbanized areas will increase transit 
ridership and thereby generate demand for more frequent headways. 
The GPU’s regional transit recommendations for the City is depicted in Figure 3-5.

Pedestrian Priority Zones. Planned modifications to roadway classifications are summarized in

3.4.4 
Streetscape Improvements 
Implementation of the GPU would encourage the construction of streetscape amenities along 
pedestrian routes and activity areas. Enhancements may include the following: wider sidewalks; 
enhanced paving; pedestrian-scaled lighting; landscaped buffers, or street trees; street furniture; 
outdoor cafes and/or wayfinding. The RC provides guidance for enhancing streetscape including 
goals and policies to increase tree canopy coverage, include improved pedestrian access in building 
design, promote public amenities and landscape features. Examples of goals relating to citywide 
streetscape improvements include RC goals, as follows: 
• 
Goal 2-A:  Oceanside’s built environment will be easy to navigate, visually appealing, and 
accommodating of social engagement, community building, physical activity, and cultural 
enrichment. 
• 
Goal 2-B: Public spaces will be designed to welcome and safely accommodate all community 
members, including pedestrians, bicyclists, children, the elderly, and the disabled. 
• 
Goal 2-F: New development will contribute to the functionality, coherence, accessibility, visual 
quality, and unique character of the City’s built environment. 
Streetscape improvements as they specifically relate to each corridor are addressed in the SSCSP. 
3.4.5 
Parks and Recreation Facilities 
Implementation of the GPU would support the improvement and expansion of the City’s parks and 
community facilities. Examples of goals relating to the enhancement and improvement of parks and 
recreation throughout the City include HLC goals, as follows: 
• 
Goal 7-G: Adequate and accessible public parks, recreational facilities, and community 
centers will be provided, designed, and maintained to meet the active and passive 
recreational needs of the entire Oceanside community. 
• 
Goal 7-J: The City will have adequate, inclusive, and well-funded community facilities to serve 
the needs of Oceanside residents, including for formal and informal public gatherings, 
government and administration, and public safety.  
• 
Goal 7-K: The provision of new public facilities and services will be equitably distributed 
throughout the City, with a particular focus on ensuring access to community facilities for 
historically disadvantaged communities and providing parkland in locations where new 
growth is anticipated. 
The HLC supports the City’s 2019 Parks and Recreation Master Plan which identifies community needs 
and priorities and provides a development plan for the future of the City’s parks and recreation 
system. Specifically, the GPU identifies the City’s 2019 Parks and Recreation Master Plan as the vehicle 
to plan and locate new parks. As most new developments would be infill, the GPU provides guidance 
for additional park land to take the form of small parks, plazas, and linear parks that are integrated 
into new development. Generally, the GPU sets a standard to ensure that parks are evenly distributed 
throughout the City by maintaining parkland accessibility standard of 10-minute walk for 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-21 
Neighborhood Parks and 20-minute walk for Community and Special Use Parks (see Section 7.4 of 
the HLC for definitions of park types). Additionally, the GPU encourages the placement of new 
community parks and recreation facilities in areas that are currently underserved and/or that are 
expected to see higher density development. 
3.4.6 
Preservation of Biological Resources 
The GPU focuses on ensuring the continued support and enhancement of biological open space, 
sensitive vegetation, and wildlife. The VSR focuses on the protection and management of functional 
ecological communities, rather than preservation of individual species or isolated areas of habitat. 
At the same time, the VSR emphasizes coastal sage scrub and freshwater wetlands as key sanctuaries 
for sensitive species. To serve these two outcomes, the VSR goals and supporting policies provide 
the basis for an overall program to preserve open space, vegetation, and wildlife. Examples of goals 
relating to the protection of biological resources throughout the City include VSR goals, as follows: 
• 
Goal 5-A:  Conserve the full range of sensitive natural communities, threatened, endangered, 
or rare plant and wildlife corridors through the protection and enhancement of natural 
habitats and special status species populations. 
• 
Goal 5-B:  Revise and maintain over the long term a comprehensive assessment of the City’s 
conserved lands/hardline preserves, all conservation areas identified in the Draft Subarea 
Plan (SAP) (e.g., softline preserves, Pre-Approved Mitigation Areas [PAMAs], off-site 
mitigation zones, the Wildlife Corridor Planning Zone [WCPZ], and priority habitat restoration 
sites), and existing vegetation/habitat mapping to ensure the conservation framework for 
Oceanside reflects current conditions and supports the achievement of the City’s 
conservation goals. 
• 
Goal 5-C:  Develop and periodically revise as needed a Biological Resource Protection 
Ordinance (BRPO) that will codify the biological resource policy directives within this General 
Plan Update. The BRPO will specify the requirements that new developments must meet in 
order to receive City approval. At a minimum, new developments proposed on any parcel 
that may support special-status species or sensitive vegetation communities should assess 
the impacts to sensitive biological resources from the project and include measures to avoid 
or mitigate impacts to protected vegetation communities, consistent with mitigation ratios 
that will be codified in the BRPO, which are generally those outlined in the Draft SAP. The 
BRPO will serve to assist new development in assessing project impacts consistent with CEQA 
thresholds. The BRPO will also address land use adjacency standards for development 
adjacent to conserved lands, minimize impacts on species and habitats, and requirements 
for conservation land monitoring, management and endowment funding, to minimize 
impacts on species and habitats, and requirements for conservation land monitoring, 
management and endowment funding. 
• 
Goal 5-F: Design human access to, and use of, the natural environment to avoid adverse 
impacts to ecological health and diversity. 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-22 
3.4.6.1 
BRPO 
The GPU includes Action Item VSR-4, which directs the City to create a BRPO. The BRPO would 
establish standards applicable to development approvals, including habitat mitigation ratios, land 
use adjacency guidelines, long-term management and monitoring requirements for conserved lands, 
development standards for the WCPZ, and habitat preservation and buffer requirements. 
Preparation and adoption of the BRPO would occur through a future action within two years of 
adoption of the GPU but is not part of the proposed project. However, the GPU incorporates goals 
and policies that lay the foundation for identifying existing and potential preserves and for outlining 
strategies to avoid, restore, and reduce impacts on wildlife corridors and planned preserve areas. 
Several of the GPU’s concepts reflect material from the draft SAP and would be carried forward 
through GPU and SSCSP policy implementation. 
3.4.6.2 Conservation Framework 
The GPU includes a Conservation Framework composed of three primary components: the WCPZ; 
Focused Planning Areas consisting of hardline and softline preserves; and Priority Habitat Restoration 
Sites. Future development would be reviewed for consistency with this framework, including 
identification of existing and potential preserves and the application of procedures related to wildlife 
corridors and planned preserve areas. 
The GPU includes provisions related to wildlife crossings and habitat linkages associated with a 
north–south wildlife corridor. The WCPZ encompasses properties that contribute to the regional 
gnatcatcher stepping-stone corridor. Action Item VSR-14 identifies the commissioning of a wildlife 
movement study. This study would be completed through a future action separate from the 
proposed project and would examine local and regional corridors to inform potential improvements 
to connectivity. 
The GPU maintains the hardline preserve areas identified in the draft SAP. These areas consist of 
habitat that has already been conserved and is managed by land trusts, generally supported by non-
wasting endowments. The GPU includes policies that address management of these areas and the 
City’s role in maintaining conserved lands. Development within hardline preserves would be limited. 
The GPU also continues the designation of softline preserves (referred to as PAMAs in the draft SAP). 
These areas contain natural vegetation communities and areas that currently or potentially support 
wildlife movement or habitat linkages. These areas are intended to be conserved wholly or partially 
in conjunction with future development or capital improvement program projects. Development may 
occur within softline preserves subject to applicable GPU policies. 
The GPU identifies Priority Habitat Restoration Sites within the WCPZ, originally listed in the draft 
SAP and included in Table 5-1 of the VSR. Refinement of these sites will occur in a future preserve 
assessment, separate from the proposed project. 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-23 
3.4.6.3 Mitigation Standards 
The GPU includes mitigation ratios for impacts on vegetation communities, consistent with those 
identified in the draft SAP (see VSR Table 5-2). The mitigation requirements differ depending on the 
type and location of habitat affected.  
3.4.6.4 Environmentally Sensitive Habitat Areas  
The GPU reaffirms the requirement to protect Environmentally Sensitive Habitat Areas (ESHAs) within 
the coastal zone consistent with Section 30240 of the California Coastal Act. Development standards 
and biological resource protections within the coastal zone are governed by the City’s Local Coastal 
Land Use Plan and implemented through the Local Coastal Program. The GPU also includes policies 
that encourage restoration of degraded habitat within the coastal zone. 
3.4.7 
Agricultural District Policy Framework  
The GPU recognizes the importance of agricultural resources within its Agricultural District, 
specifically within the South Morro Hills community. Acknowledging the interplay between 
preservation and development, the GPU incorporates goals and policies that would guide a future 
Community Plan Amendment within South Morro Hills. Examples of goals relating to the protection 
and enhancement of agricultural resources throughout the City include VSR goals, as follows: 
• 
Goal 5-M: Agriculture in South Morro Hills and nearby areas will remain a viable economic 
enterprise, conserving farmland, containing urban sprawl, providing employment, and 
creating opportunities for local food sourcing. 
• 
Goal 5-N: The City will collaborate with the local agricultural community to promote farming 
methods and land management practices that improve soil health, reduce negative impacts 
to public health and the environment, and ensure the long term economic and environmental 
viability of farming.  
• 
Goal 5-O: South Morro Hills will continue to be designated primarily for agriculture use and 
ancillary commercial activity.  
• 
Goal 5-P: South Morro Hills will become a unique and engaging visitor destination featuring 
agritourism uses that provide supplemental revenue for local farms, generate jobs, and 
bolster the City’s hospitality sector. 
The City’s vision is to provide a balance of agricultural preservation, while allowing development that 
is compatible with agriculture. To do this, the VSR includes several policies focusing on strengthening 
the City’s active agricultural areas including the continued support for Tier 1 agritourism uses and 
establishing means to promote other visitor oriented agricultural programs. 
3.5 
Smart and Sustainable Corridors Specific Plan 
The SSCSP is a regulatory document, consistent with the ECLU that outlines strategies, standards, 
and processes meant to foster the revitalization of the Mission Avenue, Oceanside Boulevard, and 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-24 
Vista Way commercial corridors in the City. These corridors are envisioned as vibrant community 
spines benefitting from infill and redevelopment on currently vacant and underutilized sites. New 
housing and non-residential uses in these corridors would leverage existing urban infrastructure and 
capitalize on accessibility to transit and trails. As infill and redevelopment occur, each corridor would 
continue to meet the immediate needs of current and future residents, retain and expand commerce 
and employment, and enhance mobility. The SSCSP recognizes the unique character of each 
corridor, providing specific design guidance to ensure each corridor optimizes its distinct sense of 
place (see Sections 3.5.1.1 through 3.5.1.3). 
The SSCSP is comprised of eight chapters: (1) Introduction; (2) Setting and Context; (3) Land Use; 
(4) Urban Design; (5) Mobility; (6) Environmental Quality; (7) Infrastructure and Utilities; and 
(8) Implementation and Financing. 
3.5.1 
Chapter 3: Land Use  
SSCSP Chapter 3: Land Use provides a land use framework for the future growth and development 
within the SSCSP Planning Area. This chapter complements land use designations and compatibility 
policies laid out in the ECLU. The proposed land use framework for the SSCSP Planning Area would 
offer an array of housing options for people at all income levels and stages of life; for non-residential 
uses, the framework aims to support an inclusive commercial environment that provides retail and 
services that cater to residents’ daily needs while simultaneously inviting visitors from across the 
region. 
As development occurs, each corridor is planned to meet the needs of current and future residents, 
retain and expand commerce and employment, and enhance mobility options. Nodes of activity are 
planned near transit stations and major intersections to provide opportunities for infill growth, 
consistent with state, regional, and local smart growth initiatives. The SSCSP land use framework 
provides opportunities for mixed-use development with high-density residential and ground-level 
commercial to create more walkable and integrated neighborhoods. The land use framework 
supports frequent, reliable transit, as more people would have easy access to Sprinter and bus lines. 
New housing in the corridors would accommodate different income levels and family types. Income-
restricted housing would be implemented through the City’s Inclusionary Housing Ordinance and 
state incentives for affordable housing. Affordability can also be achieved through design, with 
smaller units, unbundled parking, and shared amenities.  
SSCSP land use goals include the following: 
• 
Goal 1: Oceanside’s major corridors will be safe, attractive, and lively environments 
supporting a mix of synergistic uses.  
• 
Goal 2: These corridors will continue to provide for commerce and employment, maintaining 
a business-friendly environment that enables a wide variety of commercial and industrial uses 
to thrive.  
• 
Goal 3: These corridors will support housing that accommodates all Oceanside residents, 
including lower-income households and residents with special needs.  
• 
Goal 4: Obsolete uses will be replaced through redevelopment and adaptive reuse. 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-25 
• 
Goal 5: Auto-oriented uses within the corridors will be sited and designed to contribute to a 
walkable environment. 
Specific land uses proposed along Mission Avenue, Oceanside Boulevard, and Vista Way are shown 
in Figures 3-6, 3-7, and 3-8, respectively.  
3.5.1.1 
Mission Avenue 
Mission Avenue is envisioned as a dynamic and culturally diverse corridor that blends elements of 
Native American and Spanish colonial history with new opportunities for housing, commerce, 
enhanced streetscape design, active transportation, and better physical and visual connections to 
the San Luis Rey River. The proposed land uses along Mission Avenue focus on maintaining existing 
levels of commercial activity while offering more housing options through redevelopment of older 
shopping centers. Specific goals related to the development of Mission Avenue include the following: 
• 
Goal 6: A revitalized Mission Avenue corridor will retain and expand commercial uses that 
serve both residents and visitors  
• 
Goal 7: New housing in the corridor will support commercial uses and create a dynamic and 
diverse urban environment. 
• 
Goal 8: New development and associated public realm improvements will enhance 
walkability and encourage transit ridership.  
• 
Goal 9: Additional linkages between the corridor and the San Luis Rey River will be 
established, and the river will be a key ecological, recreational, and visual resource that 
contributes to the function and character of the corridor. 
3.5.1.2 
Oceanside Boulevard 
Oceanside Boulevard is envisioned as a dynamic corridor replete with a mix of shopping and dining 
venues, twenty-first century industrial operations, high-quality recreational and entertainment 
venues, and midrise mixed-use development oriented around the Sprinter stations. New 
development in this corridor would catalyze restoration of Loma Alta Creek, which would be 
embraced as the core of an open space and trail system. Bicycle and pedestrian facilities, including 
the Inland Rail Trail, would foster a connected urban environment and provide safe and convenient 
access to the Sprinter light rail stations and Loma Alta Creek. Land uses along Oceanside Boulevard 
promote housing while encouraging higher and better use and aesthetic upgrades in existing light 
industrial areas. Specific goals related to the development of Oceanside Boulevard include the 
following: 
• 
Goal 10: Many of the industrial properties in the corridor will be redeveloped with higher and 
better uses that provide more employment while minimizing potential adverse impacts and 
enhancing the visual quality of industrial areas. 
• 
Goal 11 The corridor will function as a dynamic transit-oriented environment with a mix of 
walkable shopping venues, restaurants, industry, and residential development oriented 
around NCTD’s Sprinter rail stations. 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-26 
• 
Goal 12: The corridor will continue to provide essential commercial goods and services to 
residents while drawing visitors to retail and dining venues that offer unique and interesting 
experiences. 
• 
Goal 13: Distinct and vibrant transit villages will materialize around each of the Sprinter 
stations, providing a range of housing opportunities, commercial good and services, and 
mobility hub amenities.  
• 
Goal 14: New land use and development will embrace Loma Alta Creek as a character-
defining open space amenity while facilitating habitat restoration, recreational access, and 
enhanced visual quality. 
3.5.1.3 
Vista Way 
The Vista Way Corridor is envisioned as the community and regional-serving commercial hub of the 
City, providing essential goods and services and contributing significantly to the City’s jobs base. As 
aging shopping centers are redeveloped, opportunities would be explored for higher-intensity 
commercial, residential, and/or mixed-use projects, along with improved streetscapes and enhanced 
architecture. Land uses along Vista Way focus on intensifying existing commercial areas while 
providing housing through mixed-use development. Specific goals related to the development of 
Vista Way include the following: 
• 
Goal 15: The corridor will remain a regional commercial destination, while providing 
opportunities for more efficient land use through infill and redevelopment of strip 
commercial centers and associated surface parking lots. There will be no net loss of 
commercial floor area within the corridor. 
• 
Goal 16: The corridor will continue to evolve as a sub-regional healthcare hub, with expansion 
of existing medical facilities and increasing synergy between medical office, retail, and dining 
establishments. 
• 
Goal 17: The corridor will accommodate new housing in mixed-use development, where 
feasible and appropriate.  
• 
Goal 18: Development adjacent to Buena Vista Creek and Lagoon will preserve and enhance 
the ecological, recreational, and aesthetic value of these natural resources.

3.5.1.4 
Land Use Designations 
The SSCSP land use designations allow for a range of activities and development types intended to 
advance revitalization of the three corridors. Proposed land use designations throughout the SSCSP 
Planning Area are detailed in Section 3.2 of SSCSP Chapter 3: Land Use, and summarized below. The 
following provides a summary of those Land Use designations, as established in the ECLU and 
applied throughout the SSCSP Planning Area. Details of specific permitted uses within each 
designation are detailed in the SSCSP. 
a. Residential 
There are two residential land uses proposed for the SSCSP Planning Area. 
• 
Medium Density Residential (MD-R): The MD-R designation is intended to foster a wide range 
of neighborhood-oriented housing types and supportive residential facilities. The MD-R 
designation has a maximum potential density of 30.0 dwelling units per acre. 
• 
High Density Residential (HD-R): The HD-R designation allows for a full range of high-density 
housing types. Most new development under the HD-R designation is expected to be low- 
to mid-rise (generally four stories or shorter) multifamily housing. The HD-R designation has 
a maximum potential density of 40.0 dwelling units per acre. 
b. Mixed Use 
The Corridor Mixed Use (CoMU) and Centers Mixed Use (CeMU) designations are intended to foster 
development of combined higher density residential with commercial uses. 
• 
The CoMU designation allows for a broad mix of uses that integrate residential and 
compatible retail, services, and office uses to create walkable places that serve the daily needs 
of residents. The maximum residential density in this designation is 40.0 dwelling units per 
acre. The maximum floor area ratio (FAR) for all uses, inclusive of residential, would be 2.5, 
with a minimum required non-residential FAR of 0.15.  
• 
The CeMU designation allows for more intensive development than CoMU and is applied in 
strategic nodal locations along corridors and in transit-accessible areas. The maximum 
permitted residential density in this designation is 55.0 dwelling units per acre. The maximum 
FAR for all uses, including residential, would be 3.0, with a minimum required non-residential 
FAR of 0.20 FAR.  
In addition to these mixed-use designations, portions of the SSCSP are within the existing Coast 
Highway Incentive District. The Coast Highway Incentive District provides a zoning program that 
outlines form-based development standards, and, in some segments for additional residential 
density and building height in exchange for specific public benefits (e.g., public parking, public open 
space, commercial floor area exceeding the minimum FAR).  


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-31 
c. Commercial 
Commercial land uses are designed to foster a mix of business uses and development types to 
encourage commercial growth throughout the SSCSP Planning Area. There are three commercial 
designations proposed for the SSCSP Planning Area which would permit mixed-use development 
with a maximum residential density of 29 dwelling units per acre.  
• 
General Commercial (CG): The CG designation provides for regional, community, and 
neighborhood-serving commercial uses.  
• 
Neighborhood Commercial (CN): The NC designation provides for lower-intensity 
commercial uses that are compatible with nearby residential areas. 
• 
Professional Commercial (CP): The PC designation is intended to foster commercial office 
spaces for professional work 
d. Industrial 
Industrial land use designations allow for a range of uses that provide employment opportunities 
and contribute to the City’s economic base. There are two industrial designations in the SSCSP 
Planning Area.  
• 
General Industrial (GI): The GI designation provides industrial lands that can accommodate a 
wide range of industrial uses, including those of relatively high intensity.  
• 
Research and Development (RD): The RD designation is intended to accommodate high 
technology and research and development industries that can be located near residential 
areas and other sensitive receptors with appropriate buffering and attenuation measures. 
e. Public 
The Public designation is intended to provide for a broad range of institutional, educational, religious, 
and community uses. No residential uses would be permitted. 
f. Open Space 
The Open Space designation provides for public parks, public and private outdoor recreation 
facilities, trails, flood channels, water recharge areas, and water bodies. 
3.5.1.5 
Projected New Development  
Projected new development within the SSCSP Planning Area is summarized in Table 3-4. As shown 
therein, buildout under the SSCSP would result in an increase of 8,300 new residential units, and 
4,024,000 square feet of non-residential new development, producing 14,500 new jobs.

3.5.2 
Chapter 4: Urban Design  
SSCSP Chapter 4: Urban Design provides guidance for the overall design of each of the three 
corridors, including goals and policies to address all elements of urban design. The SSCSP includes 
urban design strategies, the implementation of which would create distinct streetscapes, parks and 
public spaces, wayfinding, signage, and public art. The chapter includes site and building design 
standards intended to guide new development to create more walkable and bikeable community 
areas. Examples of SSCSP Urban Design goals include the following:  
• 
Goal 1: Attractive and visually unified streetscapes within the corridors will encourage 
pedestrian activity, create a strong sense of place, and contribute to the City’s visual quality.  
• 
Goal 2: An expanded tree canopy and robust native, historic, and drought-tolerant 
vegetation within the corridors will provide shade and comfort and contribute to a range of 
benefits, including refuge for wildlife, stormwater management, and reduced urban heat 
island effects.  
• 
Goal 3: Greenways and complete streets improvements will connect the corridors to trails, 
riparian areas, recreational facilities, and adjacent neighborhoods. 
• 
Goal 4: Each corridor will exhibit distinct visual themes that foster a unique identity and 
inspire a sense of ownership among residents and business owners.  
• 
Goal 5: Vehicle traffic will be buffered from pedestrian areas and vehicle speeds will be 
managed to enhance the safety and comfort of pedestrians and bicyclists. 
• 
Goal 8: New development and renovations of existing buildings within the corridors will 
create pedestrian-friendly “outdoor room” environments that activate the public realm and 
provide seamless transitions between buildings and the street frontage. 
Implementation of the SSCSP goals, supported by policies and standards, would provide all three 
corridors with the opportunities for developing public spaces as neighborhood amenities that 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-33 
support community character and cohesion. Specifically, each corridor would be enhanced with 
parks and public spaces compatible with their respective land use frameworks. 
• 
Mission Avenue: The framework identifies connections to existing parks and trails, including 
the San Luis Rey River Trail, Mission San Luis Rey, Joe Balderrama Recreation Center, Brooks 
Street Pool, Ron Ortega Recreation Park, and Prince Memorial Skatepark. The framework also 
supports the integration of new urban parks and public spaces in conjunction with new 
development and right-of-way improvements. 
• 
Oceanside Boulevard: Emphasizing development around transit centers, the framework seeks 
to integrate plazas, paseos, and landscaped pathways into new development and within the 
public right-of-way to provide connections between transit stations and surrounding 
commercial and residential areas. Additionally, new connections to Loma Alta Creek are 
proposed as part of an integrated open space and trail system.  
• 
Vista Way: Acknowledge this corridor as a center for regional-serving retail and medical office 
uses, the framework seeks to facilitate passive-use plazas and other pedestrian-oriented 
spaces to enhance the customer experience and allow for gathering and social interaction. 
These pedestrian-oriented spaces would accommodate public art, entertainment, and other 
interactive elements to create an engaging, vibrant, and comfortable environment. 
Additionally, enhanced connections to Buena Vista Creek are part of an integrated open 
space and trail system. 
The SSCSP Urban Design chapter provides directions for site and building design throughout the 
corridors (see SSCSP Chapter 4 Section 4.3 for detailed Development Standards). The intent is for 
new development within the corridors to be cohesive with its existing context, as well as with the 
surrounding area. Building massing and siting in any infill development would consider the scale and 
nature of adjacent uses and incorporate context-sensitive design throughout each corridor. At the 
same time, new development is expected to significantly transform both the ambience and function 
of these areas, creating more active and close-knit urban spaces.  
The SSCSP identifies Pedestrian Priority Zones throughout the SSCSP Planning Area. The Pedestrian 
Priority Zones are shown in Figures 3-6, 3-7, and 3-8, specific to each corridor plan. This zone 
represents a mixed-use area adjacent to transit that would provide opportunities for enhanced 
pedestrian environments. Improvements within the zone would include the following: wider 
sidewalks (where feasible); distinctive and highly visible paving at crosswalks; Americans with 
Disabilities Act (ADA) compliant curb cuts and sidewalk conditions; outdoor dining areas; benches 
and other street furnishings; and landscaped buffers between roadways and sidewalks, planted with 
trees and drought-tolerant native or naturalized shrubs and groundcover (see Figure 4.2-7).  
The Urban Design chapter of the SSCSP sets up the framework for the restoration and creation of a 
new pedestrian pathway along Loma Alta Creek. The vision is to create areas along the creek for 
dining, recreation, and community amenities. The SSCSP calls for future development adjacent to 
the creek to include enhancement measures to improve the vitality of the creek while developing 
the pedestrian pathway.  


3.0 Project Description

Page 3-34 
3.5.3 
Chapter 5: Mobility  
SSCSP Chapter 5: Urban Design provides guidance for the SSCSP Planning Area to transition to a 
mixed-use use pedestrian-oriented environment that includes a significant amount of new housing. 
The SSCSP includes measures to enhance roadway efficiency, complete street improvements, 
improved access to transit, and site design elements in private development that accommodate all 
modes of travel. The Mobility Chapter furthers the overall vision for land use and transportation as 
outlined in the IM. Examples of SSCSP Mobility goals include the following: 
• 
Goal 1: The corridors will provide sufficient capacity within the Planning Area roadway 
network to serve local traffic needs as safely and efficiently as possible. 
• 
Goal 2: The corridors will serve as multimodal “Mobility Boulevards” that balance the needs 
of motorists with those of pedestrians, bicyclists, and transit service. 
• 
Goal 4: The corridors will provide safe and pleasant pedestrian environments with continuous 
sidewalks, safe crossings, and ADA-compliant design.  
• 
Goal 5: Pedestrian facilities in the corridors will link to nearby trails, parks, transit, and other 
public amenities. 
• 
Goal 7: Bicycle facilities along the corridors will be safe, comfortable, and accessible for 
bicyclists of all ages and abilities and should provide strong connectivity throughout the City. 
• 
Goal 9: Transit service along the corridors will become increasingly accessible, convenient, 
and comfortable, with improved frequencies, operating speeds, security features, and 
supportive amenities. 
The existing road network throughout the SSCSP Planning Area is proposed to remain the same with 
the following two exceptions: Oceanside Boulevard, from El Camino Real to Arroyo Avenue (five- to 
six-lane Arterial); and Mission Avenue, from Coast Highway to Clementine Street (two-lane one-way 
Collector). 
The SSCSP implements the IM Pedestrian Priority Zones and other pedestrian routes that extend 
through the corridors. As shown in Figure 3-3, each corridor supports Pedestrian Priority Zones, 
Corridors, and Connectors for pedestrian movement. Examples of recommended amenities and 
design features for each type of pedestrian route is detailed in SSCSP Chapter 5: Mobility, Section 5.2. 
As shown in Figure 3-4, several GPU designated bicycle routes traverse the SSCSP Planning Area. 
The SSCSP includes goals and policies to support the construction and enhancement of both 
pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure. In addition to pedestrian and bicycle improvements, the SSCSP 
encourages completion of the Inland Rail Trail which would provide an enhanced and extended 
bicycle route along the Oceanside Boulevard corridor. The Inland Rail Trail alignment would likely 
follow the Sprinter rail corridor. However, where this is not feasible, segments of the Inland Rail Trail 
may shift to parallel roadways such as Oceanside Boulevard. 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-35 
The following summarizes the proposed roadway configurations for each of the corridors: 
• 
Mission Avenue design is envisioned to include a four-lane Major Roadway with sidewalks, 
planted landscaping strips, buffered bike lane (or cycle track), and a raised, landscaped center 
median. 
• 
Proposed recommendations for the Oceanside Boulevard corridor include construction of a 
Class IV cycle track between El Camino Real and the City’s eastern boundary near Melrose 
Drive. The existing roadway geometry of Oceanside Avenue is planned to remain. Planted 
landscaping strips along the corridor, as well as high visibility crossing treatments at 
intersections are proposed to improve the pedestrian experience. 
• 
The Vista Way corridor runs adjacent to State Route 78 (SR-78) and is more constrained than 
the other corridors. Vista Way would remain a 4-lane roadway in the future with buffers 
added to the bike lanes. This enhancement would require converting the existing two-way 
left-turn lane to a narrow-striped median, where feasible, consolidating access to properties 
as the area redevelops to create the space needed for the buffers. Sidewalks would be built 
out the entire length of the corridor with shade trees and pedestrian and bicycle crossing 
treatments at the intersections, except where the corridor runs adjacent to SR-78 (where 
there are no fronting land use). 
3.5.4 
Chapter 6: Environmental Quality 
SSCSP Chapter 6: Environmental Quality addresses issues related to biological resources, geologic 
and seismic hazards, hazardous materials, hydrology and water quality, and noise as they relate to 
the SSCSP Planning Area. Examples of SSCSP Environmental Quality goals include the following: 
• 
Goal 1: Oceanside’s rich biological resources will be protected, enhanced, and expanded 
within the corridors. 
• 
Goal 2: Wildlife will safely move through and beyond the Planning Area via restored wetland 
and riparian corridors, conserved upland habitat, wildlife crossings, and dense tree canopy 
coverage. 
• 
Goal 3: Geologic and seismic risks will be minimized through thoughtful construction 
practices. 
• 
Goal 4: Thorough remediation and abatement practices consistent with federal, state and 
local standards will minimize exposure to hazardous materials throughout the Planning Area. 
• 
Goal 5: Proactive stormwater planning and installation of green infrastructure will reduce 
flooding risks along the corridors. 
• 
Goal 6: The streams, rivers, and water systems that run through and near the corridors will 
be restored to support healthy and well-balanced ecosystems. 
• 
Goal 7: Residents, workers, and visitors will not be impacted by excessive noise. 
The goals and policies complement those in the GPU and other local, State, and federal regulations 
and guidelines. Implementation of the goals and policies would guide the City to further the 
following: protect biological resources including the establishment of wildlife crossings and 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-36 
enhanced habitat connectivity; minimize seismic risks; reduce exposure to hazardous materials; 
reduce flood risk and stormwater runoff; and encourage noise reduction measures especially 
associated with development in proximity to high volume roadways and the Sprinter line.  
3.5.5 
Chapter 7: Infrastructure and Utilities  
SSCSP Chapter 7: Infrastructure and Utilities is focused on the assurance that adequate infrastructure 
and utilities would be available for both current and future development throughout the corridors. 
Examples of SSCSP Infrastructure and Utilities goals include the following: 
• 
Goal 1: Through water source protection, treatment, and testing, the City’s potable water 
supply will remain safe and healthful.  
• 
Goal 2: Potable water service will be reliable and of sufficient capacity to serve existing and 
future development within the Planning Area. 
• 
Goal 3: The City will ensure that necessary potable water infrastructure upgrades are 
implemented in conjunction with new development.  
• 
Goal 4: Wastewater services will be reliable and of adequate capacity to serve existing and 
future development within the Planning Area. 
• 
Goal 7: Stormwater infrastructure will be reliable and be of adequate capacity to serve 
existing and future developments within the Planning Area. 
Implementation of the goals and policies would provide direction for the City to ensure adequate 
water, wastewater, and stormwater infrastructure are available to serve the needs of future 
development. The goals and policies in this chapter complement the GPU citywide policy direction 
as well as other local, State and federal regulations and guidelines that relate to infrastructure and 
utilities.  
3.5.6 
Chapter 8: Implementation  
SSCSP Chapter 8: Implementation details many of the actions that would be required for effective 
implementation of the SSCSP. Future development within the SSCSP Planning Area would require 
future rezone actions that would be governed by the development standards identified in the SSCSP. 
These supplemental regulations would replace and take precedence over the base zone regulations 
of the City for the subject property. Where the regulations of the SSCSP are silent, the comparable 
regulations of the City zoning ordinance, and all adopted ordinances, regulations, standards, and 
guidelines of the City would prevail, as deemed appropriate by the City. Where the development 
standards contained in the SSCSP conﬂict with development standards of the City’s Zoning 
Ordinance, the standards contained in the SSCSP would apply. 
3.6 
Climate Action Plan Update 
The project includes an update to the 2019 CAP (City of Oceanside 2019) to account for the increased 
housing and employment growth resulting from the GPU and SSCSP. The CAP Update provides a 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-37 
comprehensive plan for addressing GHG emissions within the City. The CAP Update was developed 
concurrently with the GPU and reflects that document’s proposed land use and transportation 
strategy. The CAP Update incorporates applicable GPU goals and policies that would affect future 
GHG emissions throughout the City. 
3.6.1 
Reduction Targets 
The CAP Update is intended to reinforce the City’s commitment to reducing GHG emissions and 
demonstrate how the City would comply with state GHG emission reduction standards set forth in 
Senate Bill (SB) 32 and Assembly Bill (AB) 1279. As a Qualified GHG Reduction Strategy under CEQA 
Guidelines Section 15183.5, the CAP Update would also enable streamlined environmental review of 
future development projects in accordance with CEQA. Specifically, the CAP Update quantifies 
existing and projected GHG emissions generated by activities within the City and the region through 
horizon year 2050, and it includes GHG emissions reduction targets for the years 2030, 2045, and 
2050 (see subsection 3.6.2.2).  
Under business-as-usual (BAU) conditions, emissions would continue to rise through 2050. When 
the effects of the City’s participation in the Clean Energy Alliance and other existing state and federal 
policies are included—referred to as the Adjusted BAU (ABAU) forecast—emissions are projected to 
decline below 2018 levels. However, the ABAU forecast still falls short of meeting the City’s updated 
GHG reduction targets. Table 3-5 compares the ABAU forecast to the targets and shows the 
remaining emissions gap. The reduction measures in the CAP Update are designed to close that gap 
through additional local action.
