The GHG reduction measures of the CAP Update primarily focus on increasing the accessibility and 
availability of renewable energy, promoting energy efficiency, providing alternative modes of 
transportation, supporting a transition to zero emission vehicles and equipment, improving water 
efficiency, and supporting increased carbon sequestration in the urban forest and natural lands.  
Detailed reduction measures and implementing actions are included in Chapter 4 of the CAP Update; 
however, a few examples include the following: 
• 
Increase renewable energy availability to residents and businesses by providing 100% 
renewable/zero-carbon electricity through the Clean Energy Alliance by 2030.  
• 
Increase solar photovoltaic capacity in the City through financial incentives and local building 
code updates.  
• 
Reduce emissions from organic solid waste by increasing citywide landfill diversion rates.  
• 
Updating local building codes to encourage electrification of the City’s building stock and 
reducing natural gas use.  
• 
Support policies in the City’s GPU and SSCSP to encourage infill development along existing 
transit corridors where active transportation and transit are most viable. 
3.6.2 
CAP Update Component Parts 
The CAP Update includes four key components that create a holistic strategy for the City to reduce 
GHGs associated with growth projected through the GPU. Generally, these include a baseline 
citywide GHG emissions inventory, setting GHG reduction targets aligned with state goals, 
developing GHG reduction measures and the associated actions for implementation, and procedures 
for monitoring and reporting progress on the implementation of GHG reduction measures. 
3.6.2.1 
GHG Emission Analysis 
The initial evaluation of GHG emissions is called a GHG emissions inventory, which establishes an 
understanding of how GHG emissions are generated within the City, leading to the development of 
policies to address individual GHG emissions sources. As part of the CAP Update, the City completed 
a 2018 communitywide GHG emissions inventory to establish a baseline for developing the GHG 
emissions forecast and setting associated reduction targets. The GHG emissions forecast was 
developed evaluating how GHG emissions may change in the future under two scenarios: BAU (how 
growth alone would influence future GHG emissions); and ABAU (how growth alone would influence 
future GHG emissions).  
3.6.2.2 
GHG Reduction Targets 
The CAP Update includes GHG emissions reduction targets for the years 2030, 2045, and 2050. The 
GHG reduction targets of the CAP Update for the years 2030 and 2045 align with the state's GHG 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-39 
emission targets; the City’s GHG reduction target for the year 2050 aligns with the GPU horizon year. 
The City’s GHG reduction targets in this CAP Update are:  
• 
Reducing emissions 27 percent below 2018 levels by 2030 (aligned with SB 32);   
• 
Reducing emissions 90 percent below 2018 levels by 2045 (aligned with AB 1279); and  
• 
Maintaining emissions 90 percent below 2018 levels through 2050 (General Plan Update 
horizon year). 
3.6.2.3 
GHG Reduction Measures and Actions 
The CAP Update includes a suite of policies focused on reducing local GHG emissions, which are 
called GHG reduction measures. Each GHG reduction measure is focused on reducing emissions 
from specific sources under the City’s jurisdictional authority, such as on-road transportation and 
land use within its borders. Measures are implemented through a discrete set of actions. The core 
GHG reduction measures focus on increasing the delivery of renewable energy, enhancing building 
energy efficiency, providing alternative modes of transportation, supporting a transition to zero-
emission vehicles and off-road equipment, improving water use efficiency, increased diversion of 
organic waste from landfills, and supporting increased carbon sequestration in the urban forest, 
natural lands, and working lands. In total, the CAP Update includes 17 GHG reduction measures with 
104 implementation actions to achieve the GHG reduction targets.  
3.6.2.4 Monitoring and Reporting 
The CAP Update includes monitoring procedures for measuring progress as GHG reduction 
measures and actions are implemented over time. City staff will annually evaluate the 
implementation status of each action by monitoring key performance indicators and reporting 
progress towards interim and final GHG goals in a CAP Annual Report. The CAP Update has been 
prepared and adopted as a “qualified” CAP consistent with the CEQA guidelines. Under the 
provisions of a qualified CAP, if a development project in the City aligns with the City's goals and 
reduces emissions consistent with the CAP Update, it can streamline the analysis of its GHG emissions 
under CEQA. Within one year of CAP adoption the City will develop and adopt guidelines for 
discretionary projects subject to CEQA to demonstrate consistency with the CAP during the standard 
development review process. 
3.6.3 
CAP Update Organization 
The chapters of the CAP Update are summarized as follows. 
• 
Executive Summary. This chapter provides a summary of the CAP Update, including the scope 
and purpose of the CAP Update, the planning process, findings from the GHG emissions 
forecast, and proposed GHG reduction strategies. 
• 
Chapter 1: Introduction. This chapter introduces the City, outlines the context and purpose of 
the CAP Update, and describes the development process of the CAP Update and the 
community outreach conducted. 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-40 
• 
Chapter 2: Background. This chapter provides a background to climate change science, local 
climate impacts, existing legislation and efforts aimed at addressing climate change, and local 
efforts focused on GHG mitigation from the previous CAP and other City-led efforts. 
• 
Chapter 3: Greenhouse Gas Emissions Inventory, Projections, and Targets. This chapter 
summarizes and identifies trends from the Oceanside’s GHG emissions inventory, forecast of 
future emissions, and GHG reduction targets. 
• 
Chapter 4: Greenhouse Gas Reduction Measures and Actions. This chapter provides a list of 
GHG reduction measures that are required to meet GHG reduction targets and to provide a 
Qualified GHG Reduction Strategy for the City. This chapter quantifies GHG reductions from 
each CAP Update measure and applies these reductions to the emissions forecast. 
• 
Chapter 5: Implementation and Monitoring. This chapter provides a framework for 
implementing and monitoring the CAP update and includes guidance for future climate 
action planning efforts. 
3.6.4 
CAP Update Implementation 
The implementation of the CAP Update would require that new developments are constructed with 
more sustainable, energy-efficient and low-carbon features than existing developments. New 
development projects consistent with the growth projections in the City’s GPU (incorporated into the 
CAP Update) and applicable GHG reduction measures would be eligible for CEQA streamlining of 
GHG analysis, per the provisions of State CEQA Guidelines Section 15183.5. Furthermore, a project’s 
incremental contribution to cumulative GHG emissions may be determined not to be cumulatively 
considerable in such cases.  
The CAP Update meets the requirements under Section 15183.5 of the State CEQA Guidelines as a 
qualified plan for the reduction of GHG emissions for use in cumulative impact analysis on new 
development projects. Pursuant to the CAP Update, within one year of adoption the City would 
develop and adopt guidelines for discretionary projects subject to CEQA to demonstrate consistency 
with the CAP Update during the standard development review process. The guidelines will be the 
mechanism used both by private development and future City capital projects to demonstrate 
consistency with the CAP Update. The guidelines will establish a threshold of significance and will 
identify how projects can align with the GHG reduction targets through various pathways. 
Consistency with the CAP Update may be demonstrated through a CAP consistency checklist that 
documents incorporation of all applicable GHG reduction measures into a project’s analysis, 
quantitative GHG thresholds, or some combination thereof. Measures will be enforced as conditions 
of approval or under existing or future development ordinances to ensure that compliance can be 
confirmed before the project can be implemented.

development would rely on each property owner’s initiative and market forces. However, estimated 
buildout potential was used to inform the GPU Land Use Plan to foresee and accommodate 
anticipated land use needs.

3.7.1 
Focused Areas of Growth 
While the City anticipates the GPU would trigger growth throughout the City, the majority of growth 
is focused to occur within  the SSCCP Planning Area (see Figure 3-2). The SSCSP has been designed 
to accommodate higher residential density and increased intensity of uses to support the goals of 
the GPU ECLU.  
In addition to the SSCSP Planning Area, the project would also support growth throughout the City 
based on planned or foreseeable increases in parcel utilization. Development potential within all 
potential growth areas have been included in the project’s anticipated buildout projections (and thus 
included in the environmental analyses throughout this RPEIR) shown in Tables 3-6 and 3-7. A 
summary of the City’s potential growth areas are defined below. 
3.7.1.1 
Opportunity Sites 
Throughout the GPU process, properties were identified by the City which presented the greatest 
potential for change in land use types or intensities. These Opportunity Sites were identified and 
refined through both data-driven analysis of citywide development potential and site-specific 
knowledge of existing conditions and potential and are made up of both parcels which would 
maintain their existing land use designation but are deemed underutilized, or where land use 
designations are proposed to be changed to accommodate greater intensity of use and/or 
residential density.  
While most Opportunity Sites are within the SSCSP Planning Area, some are parcels where while land 
use designations would remain the same, due to location or other factors, the City feels there would 
be potential for increased development.

Housing Element Sites 
The project would support growth and development within parcels identified in the City’s 2021-2029 
Housing Element. These parcels were included in the Housing Element Sites inventory as vacant 
and/or underutilized, or candidate rezone sites which could accommodate higher residential density.

3.7.1.4 
Accessory Dwelling Units 
Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) are attached or detached units that provide complete independent 
living facilities for one or more persons including permanent provisions for living, sleeping, cooking, 
and sanitation, located on the same lot as a primary structure. Consistent with City regulations and 
state legislation, development of ADUs is permitted within single-family and multi-family zoning 


3.0 Project Description 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 3-45 
districts. Program 5 of the City’s 2021-2029 Housing Element encourages the development of ADUs 
as a source of affordable housing opportunities.  
3.7.1.5 
Senate Bill 9 Additional Units 
SB 9, known as the California Opportunity and More Efficiency (HOME) Act, was enacted in 2021 to 
provide options to increase available housing throughout the state. Specifically, SB 9 facilitates the 
creation of up to four housing units in a single-family zones lot typically used for one single-family 
home.  
3.7.1.6 
South Morro Hills 
The GPU does not propose any land use change within South Morro Hills. However, development 
assumptions associated with the North River Farms project include up to a maximum of 395 dwelling 
units. 
Development potential within South Morro Hills remains as allowed under the existing General Plan: 
900 residential units, 30 hotel rooms, and 188,950 square feet of non-residential land uses. These 
buildout numbers are accounted for in the total new development that could occur under the GPU.

3.8 
Intended Uses of the RPEIR 
This RPEIR examines the potential environmental impacts of implementing the project. As no specific 
developments are proposed as part of the project, this PEIR provides a programmatic approach and 
does not evaluate the potential project-specific environmental impacts of individual development 
proposals that may be allowed under the project after its adoption. Subsequent projects would be 
reviewed by the City for consistency with the project and this RPEIR, and adequate project-level 
environmental review would be conducted, as required, under CEQA. The intention of this RPEIR is 
to provide a streamlined approach to future CEQA review by providing regulatory and policy 
direction, with opportunity for future development projects to tier1 from this RPEIR with limited 
additional environmental review. To assist in the streamlining process, this RPEIR includes a 
framework of relevant policies, standard conditions of approval, and an MMRP to guide future 
projects.

4.1 
Land Use and Planning 
This section addresses potential project impacts related to land use and planning that could result 
from implementation of the Onward Oceanside project which includes the City of Oceanside (City) 
General Plan Update (GPU), Smart and Sustainable Corridors Specific Plan (SSCSP), and Climate 
Action Plan (CAP) Update, collectively referred to as the project. The GPU would apply to the entire 
City, while the SSCSP would apply to land within the Specific Plan boundary, referred to as the SSCSP 
Planning Area. As discussed in Chapter 3.0, Project Description, the analysis of potential impacts 
focuses on parcels throughout the City where the project either (1) proposes changes to existing land 
use designations or (2) where no land use change is proposed, but growth is anticipated to occur. 
The majority of the proposed increased density and intensity of uses would be within the SSCSP 
Planning Area, as shown in Figure 3-2. 
4.1.1 
Existing Conditions 
4.1.1.1 
Existing Citywide Land Uses, Zoning, and Development Patterns  
The City encompasses a total of 27,012 acres (approximately 42 square miles). The City’s current 
population is estimated to be 177,335 (City of Oceanside 2025). City land uses are primarily regulated 
by the current General Plan, existing Specific Plans, and the City’s Code of Ordinances. A portion of 
the City lies within the state’s coastal zone. Land uses within the coastal zone are specifically 
governed by the City’s Coastal Zoning Ordinance (CZO) and the Local Coastal Program (LCP).  
Existing General Plan land uses throughout the City are shown on Figure 4.1-1. Existing zoning 
designations are shown on Figure 4.1-2. As illustrated in these figures, land uses throughout the City 
range from agricultural operations in the City’s northeastern corner, to high density residential and 
commercial development along the coastline, to varying types and scales of residential, commercial, 
and industrial development spread throughout the City.

Overall, the existing development throughout the City totals 66,592 residential units and 
approximately 28,152,000 square feet of non-residential uses supporting 48,199 jobs (City of 
Oceanside 2025).  
a. Residential Land Uses  
Residential makes up 36 percent of the City’s land uses. Single-family homes are the most common 
type of residential development, comprising approximately 70 percent of total residential use within 
Oceanside. Single-family neighborhoods are dispersed throughout the City. Multi-family residential 
units comprise 19 percent of residential uses, with multi-family developments clustered in areas 
bordering the east-west corridors of Highway 76, Highway 78, and Mesa Drive, as well as the north-


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.1  Land Use 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.1-5 
south corridors of El Camino Real, Rancho del Oro Drive, and Old Grove Road. Multi-family housing 
is also prevalent in portions of the coastal area.  
Rural residential uses make up 8 percent of residential uses and are primarily located in the 
northeastern portion of the City. Mobile homes make up 4 percent of residential land uses and are 
concentrated near Douglas Drive, west of Interstate 5 and Loma Alta Creek. 
b. Parks and Open Space  
Just over a fifth of the City (approximately 21 percent) accommodates recreational and natural open 
space. Park and open space areas throughout the City are shown in Section 4.2, Figure 4.2-2. The 
park areas provide active recreational activities. See Section 4.15.1.4 for a discussion of the City’s 
existing parkland. Preserves and open space areas provide passive recreational opportunities and 
conservation of native habitat. The largest open space areas are found near the City’s northwestern 
border, along its principal watersheds, including the San Luis Rey River, Loma Alta Creek, and Buena 
Vista Lagoon, as well as within Guajome Regional Park south of the South Morro Hills area. 
c. Agricultural Uses 
The South Morro Hills region encompasses a 5.4-square-mile (3,440 acres) area and contains most 
of the City’s agricultural land. The area has a rich history of farming and is known to produce 
avocados, tomatoes, strawberries, cut flowers, succulents, and coffee, and has wholesale nurseries. 
While the area’s existing Agricultural designation is primarily intended to support farming, the City’s 
Zoning Ordinance does allow for parcels to be subdivided into 2.5-acre lots and developed with one 
single-family residence per parcel if the residential development does not interfere with agricultural 
activities. Several parcels along Sleeping Indian Road have been subdivided into 2.5-acre parcels for 
single-family homes. Additionally, current City zoning allows lower-intensity (“Tier 1”) agritourism 
uses such as U-Pick operations, petting zoos, and farm stands.  
d. Public and Institutional Uses 
Public and institutional land uses make up 6 percent of the City’s existing land uses. Schools and 
educational facilities make up most of this land use type. Three public school districts operate in 
Oceanside: Oceanside Unified, Vista Unified, and Bonsall Elementary. Private schools in Oceanside 
include Coastal Academy, St. Mary Star of the Sea, and several Montessori schools. Mira Costa 
Community College maintains two campuses in the City and there are several vocational schools 
including UEI College, California Career College, and Media Tech Institute. 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.1  Land Use 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.1-6 
e. Industrial Land Uses 
Industrial land uses make up 3.5 percent of the City’s land uses (see Figure 4.1-1). The City’s industrial 
uses are mainly those defined as light industry including warehousing and distribution, 
biotechnology, sports equipment and apparel, and food processing.  
f. Commercial Land Uses 
Commercial uses occupy 3.3 percent of the City (see Figure 4.1-1). Most commercial uses, including 
retail, lodging, and offices, are located along the City’s major transit corridors, including the Coast 
Highway, Highways 76 and 78, and Oceanside Boulevard. Downtown Oceanside, which includes the 
blocks surrounding Mission Avenue and Coast Highway, contains a mixture of commercial uses, and 
include the City’s main clusters of hospitality uses. 
4.1.1.2 
South Morro Hills Planning Area 
The South Morro Hills region is designated for agricultural use. South Morro Hills encompasses a 
5.5-square-mile (3,500 acres) area of agriculturally zoned land in the northeast corner of the City. 
Existing zoning allows for parcels to be subdivided into lots with a minimum size of 2.5 acres, 
developed with one single-family residence per parcel. Additionally, 2018 amendments to the Zoning 
Ordinance allow for Tier 1 agritourism activities (see Section 4.1.2.3.d, Agritourism Strategic Plan). 
Under the City’s existing General Plan and Zoning Ordinance South Morro Hills is designated as 
Agricultural (A). However, there are mechanisms established by the City’s Zoning Ordinance that 
allow for the redesignation of agricultural land to accommodate other uses. In particular, Article 17 
of the City’s Zoning Ordinance provides for the planned development (PD) plan process, which 
allows property owners and developers to proposed alternative land use designations on properties 
at least four acres in size. There are currently more than 30 developed PD plans throughout the City. 
In 2019, the City Council approved the first PD plan proposed in South Morro Hills. Known as North 
River Farms, the approved PD plan allows open space, single-family and medium-density residential, 
commercial, and agricultural uses on a 215-acre property at the southwest corner of South Morro 
Hills. The North River Farms project is expected to bring nearly 400 new housing units that most 
recently supported a variety of row crops (City of Oceanside 2020).  
The South Morro Hills Planning Area contains about 180 housing units and 150 employed residents. 
In 2017, there were 280 jobs in the area, with the vast majority (96 percent) in the agricultural sector 
(City of Oceanside 2020). The area’s existing land use pattern reflects a rural character. Table 4.1-2 
shows the extent of existing land uses in the community.

4.1.1.3 
Existing Specific and Area Plans 
The City has a number of planned communities governed by Specific Plans and Area Plans, each 
with specific residential character and design requirements. These individual plans serve to guide 
land use decisions and physical development within each focused area. These areas include the 
coastal zone; Coast Highway Incentive District; El Corazon Specific Plan; Oceanside Boulevard Vision 
Statement; Downtown Oceanside Master Plan; and Rancho del Oro Specific Plan. Relevant portions 
of each plan are discussed under Section 4.1.2.4, below.  
4.1.2 
Regulatory Setting 
4.1.2.1 
State  
a. California Coastal Act 
The California Coastal Commission was established by voter initiative in 1972 later made permanent 
by the Legislature through adoption of the California Coastal Act of 1976. The Coastal Commission, 
in partnership with coastal cities and counties, plans and regulates the use of land and water in the 
coastal zone. Development activities, which are broadly defined by the Coastal Act to include (among 
others) construction of buildings, divisions of land, and activities that change the intensity of use of 
land or public access to coastal waters, generally require a coastal permit from either the Coastal 
Commission or the local government. 
The Coastal Act includes specific policies (see Division 20 of the Public Resources Code) that address 
issues such as shoreline public access and recreation, visitor accommodations, terrestrial and marine 
habitat protection, visual resources, landform alteration, agricultural lands, commercial fisheries, 
industrial uses, water quality, offshore oil and gas development, transportation, development design, 
power plants, ports, and public works. The policies of the Coastal Act constitute the statutory 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.1  Land Use 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.1-8 
standards applied to planning and regulatory decisions made by the Coastal Commission and by 
local governments, pursuant to the Coastal Act. 
b. State Housing Element Law 
State Housing Element law requires cities to regularly update their housing elements to identify and 
analyze housing needs, establish reasonable goals based on those needs, and set forth a 
comprehensive list of actions to achieve those goals. In the face of mounting housing costs and the 
lack of affordable housing throughout the state, the legislature has prioritized the provision of a 
decent home and suitable living environment to each Californian, with particular focus on housing 
affordable to low and very low-income households. State Housing Element law (Government Code 
Section 65583 et seq.) requires all incorporated cities and unincorporated counties to regularly 
update their General Plan Housing Element to ensure each city and county in the state provides its 
fair share of housing at all economic levels. For the 6th housing cycle, San Diego County has been 
assigned a Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA) of 171,685 housing units with the City 
receiving an allocation of 5,443 units at four income levels (Very Low, Low, Moderate, and Above 
Moderate).  
Local jurisdictions must demonstrate in their Housing Element that they maintain adequate land 
resources under appropriate zoning to accommodate their share of the regional housing growth. 
Moreover, in accordance with state law, the Housing Element must also identify specific programs 
that describe how each jurisdiction will implement and achieve its housing goals and policies. 
Programs are typically implemented by action items that must be completed during the eight-year 
housing cycle. The City has been allocated a RHNA of 5,443 units for the 6th cycle (City of Oceanside 
2022). As discussed in Chapter 3.0, Project Description, the project would result in the 
implementation of Housing Programs 7 and 8, which address the City’s compliance with the state 
RHNA goals assigned to the City, and Program 9, which establishes new zoning standards for 
properties identified as having the capacity to accommodate additional housing. 
c. Senate Bill 375 
Senate Bill (SB) 375, the 2008 Sustainable Communities and Climate Protection Act, requires the 
California Air Resources Board (CARB) to set regional targets for the reduction of greenhouse gas 
(GHG) emissions. SB 375 is intended to ensure that cities and counties are closely involved in 
developing an effective plan for the region to achieve the targets and relies on the regional 
transportation planning process to achieve targeted goals (see Sections 4.9 and 4.16). 
4.1.2.2 
Regional  
a.  San Diego Forward: The 2021 Regional Plan 
San Diego Forward was adopted by the San Diego Association of Governments (SANDAG) Board of 
Directors on December 10, 2021. The 2021 Regional Plan focuses on forecasted growth in the region 
to the year 2050. The vision of the 2021 Regional Plan is to develop an assessable transportation 
system guided by three primary goals: the efficient movement of people and goods; access to 
affordable, reliable, and safe mobility options; and healthier air and reduced GHG emissions. San 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.1  Land Use 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.1-9 
Diego Forward is intended to provide a plan for future growth through the year 2050 based on 
principles of sustainability and smart growth.  
Complete Corridors 
The Complete Corridors vision combines infrastructure improvements and advanced technology to 
provide communities surrounding major highways with more travel options. The SANDAG is 
planning a road network, the intent of which is to accommodate safe multi-modes of transportation.  
Transit Leap and Mobility Hubs 
The 2021 Regional Plan supports the creation of a network of fast, convenient, and reliable transit 
services to move people from where they live to where they want to go. Mobility hubs are vibrant 
activity centers where different travel options–walking, biking, transit, and shared mobility–come 
together to connect people with their destinations and businesses with their customers. The GPU 
includes policies that support creating connections with SANDAG and North County Transit District 
(NCTD) to expand access to transit. 
Sustainable Communities Strategy 
By law, the Regional Plan must include several elements, one of which is the Sustainable Communities 
Strategy (SCS). Developed in accordance with SB 375, the SCS identifies ways to achieve SANDAG’s 
regional share of statewide GHG reduction targets from cars and light-duty trucks. In 2018, CARB set 
targets for the SANDAG region of a 15 percent reduction in GHG emissions per capita from 
automobiles and light-duty trucks compared to 2005 levels by 2020 and a 19 percent reduction by 
2035. 
The SCS also focuses on housing and job growth in the urbanized areas where there is existing and 
planned infrastructure; protection of sensitive habitat and open space; investment in a network that 
gives residents and workers transportation options; the promotion of equity for all; and the 
implementation of the plan through incentives and collaboration.  
Smart Growth Opportunity Maps 
The 2021 Regional Plan incorporates Smart Growth Concept Maps that identify the location of 
existing, planned, and potential Smart Growth Opportunity Areas (SGOA). The term “smart growth” 
refers to a compact, efficient, and environmentally sensitive urban development pattern. Smart 
growth focuses on future growth and infill development close to employment, services, and public 
facilities to maximize the use of existing infrastructure and preserve open space and natural 
resources. Smart growth is characterized by more compact, higher density development in urbanized 
areas throughout the region. These areas are walkable, bike-friendly, near public transit, and 
promote good community design, resulting in housing and transportation choices for those who live 
and work in these areas. 
SANDAG SGOAs within the City as shown on Figure 4.1-3. The planned SGOAs are located within 
the SSCSP Planning Area.

Draft 2025 Regional Plan 
The 2025 Regional Plan (currently in draft form) updates and refines the 2021 Regional Plan to reflect 
new demographic forecasts, post-pandemic travel behavior, and fiscal constraints. The Draft 2025 
Regional Plan maintains the region’s commitment to multimodal, sustainable, and equitable mobility 
while expanding transit, updated regional growth forecasts (Series 15), advancing equity, health, and 
safety through improved access to jobs and essential services, and applying updated modeling tools 
and performance metrics to meet state GHG reduction targets (SANDAG 2025). The Draft 2025 
Regional Plan is anticipated to be approved in December 2025.  
4.1.2.3 
Local  
a. City of Oceanside Draft Subarea Habitat Conservation Plan 
The draft Oceanside Subarea Plan (SAP) was prepared per the state of California’s Natural 
Community Conservation Planning Act of 1991 and the Endangered Species Act. In 1996, the City 
began subarea planning to better define conservation priorities within the City and developed a draft 
SAP under the subregional umbrella of the Multiple Habitat Conservation Program (MHCP). The 
approach was to identify a citywide preserve system that met local and regional biological goals, 
while minimizing fiscal and economic impacts to the City and adverse effects on private property 
rights or property values. Although the draft SAP was circulated for public review in 2004 and revised 
in 2009, it has not been adopted by the Oceanside City Council. Nevertheless, the City utilizes the 
draft SAP as a guide for habitat preservation and restoration in conjunction with new private 
development and capital improvement program projects (see Section 4.5).  
b. City of Oceanside Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance (October 11, 2021) 
The City’s Zoning Ordinance is an implementation tool for the General Plan and provides permitted 
land uses and development standards for each land use category. The Zoning Ordinance establishes 
zoning designations or classifications, each with a list of permitted uses and standards for building 
setbacks, densities, heights, and other design considerations. Figure 4.1-2 maps the existing zoning 
designations throughout the City.

c. Coast Highway Vision and Strategic Plan  
The Coast Highway Vision and Strategic Plan (CHVSP) was adopted by the City as an advisory 
document intended to guide future development of the Coast Highway Corridor. The CHVSP outlines 
a series of design ideas and concepts to revitalize the Coast Highway corridor and surrounding 
neighborhood. The CHVSP transforms the Coast Highway from an auto-oriented thoroughfare into 
a mixed-use pedestrian-oriented environment that accommodates new residential uses and 
expanded commercial amenities for residents and visitors. The CHVSP identifies four nodes for 
concentrated development in the planning area, focusing on creating transit, pedestrian, and bicycle-
oriented development and siting higher density development adjacent to the two transit stations in 
the district. Suggested development densities range from 43+ dwelling units per acre (du/acre) in 
the nodes, where higher density residential development is paired with employment hubs and 
commercial venues. Parking is reconfigured to be sited away from street frontage and required 
parking ratios are reduced near transit stations. One of the Strategic Plan components includes 
creation of an Incentive District along the corridor, which provides an alternative to existing zoning 
standards that allows for additional building height and density in exchange for public benefits, 
standalone residential uses, and expedited permit processing supported by form-based 
development standards. The Incentive District was adopted in August 2019 and is discussed in 
greater detail under Specific and Area Plans, below. 
d. Agritourism Strategic Plan  
Completed in 2017, the Agritourism Strategic Plan outlines two tiers of new agritourism uses for 
South Morro Hills. Tier 1 strategies are comprised of lower-intensity and lower investment uses like 
U-Pick operations, petting zoos, farm stands, and small bed and breakfasts. This strategy does not 
require new major infrastructure and embodies existing capacity of the farmers. On October 3, 2018 
the City Council approved amendments to the Zoning Ordinance to introduce agritourism and Tier 1 
agritourism activities; the Tier 1 Agricultural Zone amendments were effective as of November 2018. 
Future Tier 2 strategies build from Tier 1 but involve increased capital investments by both the 
farming community and the City. Tier 2 strategies would include higher-intensity and higher-


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.1  Land Use 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.1-13 
investment uses that may require additional public infrastructure, like hotels, festivals, and larger 
retail operations to sell farm products. Tier 2 strategies require a community-based vision of South 
Morro Hills which is not part of this effort.  
e. Airport Land Use Consistency Plan 
The purpose of an Airport Land Use Consistency Plan (ALUCP) is to provide for the orderly growth 
of airports and the areas surrounding airports, and to safeguard the general welfare of inhabitants 
within an airport’s vicinity. An ALUCP addresses compatibility between airport operations and future 
land uses that surround them by providing policies and criteria for aircraft overflight, noise, safety, 
and airspace protection, to both minimize the public’s exposure to excessive noise and safety hazards 
within the Airport Influence Area (AIA) that could affect airspace and/or overflight concerns. Any 
proposed land use plan amendments or rezones within an AIA are required by state law to be 
submitted to the Airport Land Use Commission for a consistency determination with the ALUCP. 
Portions of the City fall within the AIA of three airports, described below.  
Oceanside Municipal Airport  
Portions of the City are within noise compatibility contours and AIA Review Areas 1 and 2, as defined 
by the Oceanside Municipal Airport ALUCP (see Section 4.10, Figure 4.10-2a). AIA Review Area 1 
consists of locations where noise and safety concerns may necessitate limitations on the types of 
land use actions. Within AIA Review Area 1, generally all land use actions are subject to Airport Land 
Use Commission (ALUC) review. Under the GPU, two land use designations. Research and 
Development and Neighborhood Commercial are proposed within Review Area 1.  
Marine Corps Air Station Camp Pendleton 
The City is outside of any noise or safety zones associated with the Marine Corps Air Station (MCAS) 
Camp Pendleton ALUCP. However, portions of the City are located within AIA Review Area 2 of the 
MCAS Camp Pendleton ALUCP (see Section 4.10, Figure 4.10-2b). The adoption or approval of a new 
General Plan that could affect land within the AIA could require review by the Airport Land Use 
Commission depending on height allowance, potential visual hazard to aircraft, or potential to cause 
an increase in the attraction of birds or other wildlife that can be hazardous to aircraft operations in 
the vicinity of the airport. 
McClellan-Palomar Airport 
The City is outside of any noise or safety hazard zone associated with the McClellan-Palomar ALUCP. 
However, a small part of the southern tip of the City is located within Airport Overflight Notification 
Area and AIA Review Area 2 (see Section 4.10, Figure 4.10-2b).

City of Oceanside Specific and Area Plans

decisions about physical development in a focused area.

a. Local Coastal Program (and Coastal Zoning Ordinance) 
The California Coastal Act requires that individual jurisdictions adopt an LCP to implement Coastal 
Act policies. The City’s 1986 LCP consists of a land use plan document (separate from the General 
Plan) containing land use policies and an implementing ordinance applicable to the City’s coastal 
zone. Land use designations and existing zoning for the coastal zone are shown in Figures 4.1-1 and 
4.1-2, respectively. The purpose of the LCP is to guide future development in the City’s coastal zone 
in a manner that protects and enhances coastal resources.  
The City is undertaking an update of its LCP, including an updated policy framework for the Coastal 
Land Use Plan. The updated LCP would incorporate a coastal hazard vulnerability assessment and 
adaptation planning to address potential impacts of sea level rise and associated coastal hazards. 
The updated plan would also address a variety of topic areas including public access, recreation and 
visitor-serving facilities, scenic resources, planning and locating new development, and water quality 
protection. 
b. Coast Highway Incentive District  
Implementation of the CHVSP (see Section 4.1.2.3d) included the establishment of an Incentive 
District located along the Coast Highway corridor from Seagaze Drive to the City’s southern 
boundary at Buena Vista Lagoon. The Incentive District was adopted in August 2019, providing an 
alternative to (not a replacement of) existing zoning standards, allowing additional building height 
and density, standalone residential use, and expedited permit processing in exchange for public 
benefits and adherence to form-based development standards.  
The proposed SSCSP is informed by the Incentive District and would serve to further implement the 
vision for increased density and intensity of uses along Coast Highway.  
c. El Corazon Specific Plan  
The El Corazon Specific Plan was adopted in November 2009. The plan encompasses an 
approximately 465-acre area located in the center of the City, between El Camino Real and Rancho 
del Oro Drive to the west and east, and Oceanside Boulevard and Mesa Drive to the south and north. 
The El Corazon Specific Plan area is divided into six districts, each with a particular vision for future 
development with development standards, customized allowable uses, and design guidelines: parks 
and recreation (212 acres), habitat (164 acres), civic services (34 acres), Oceanside Boulevard 
commercial (25 acres), village commercial (19 acres), and hotel (11 acres). Since 2009, there have been 
several notable amendments and/or approvals, including but not limited to: in August 2011, the City 
Council selected a developer for the long-term buildout of recreational amenities (sports fields), 
commercial and residential areas consistent with the Specific Plan; in May 2016, a Specific Plan 
amendment to allow ground floor residential within the two commercial zones on the property; and 
in December 2019, an amendment adjusting land use acreages, adding public arenas as an allowed 
use, approval of a subdivision tentative map for the eastern property area, and increases to the site’s 
habitat district acreage to ensure consistency with conservation goals of the Specific Plan. 
Development of the Specific Plan and future park sites is ongoing.

d. Oceanside Boulevard Vision Statement  
Based on direction from City Council on February 21, 2007, a vision and master planning effort 
commenced for the area of Oceanside Boulevard bound by I-5 and El Camino Real. A 15-member 
task force led a six-month, staff-driven, public-engagement process (meeting nine times April–mid-
November 2007 and running two public workshops), producing the Vision Statement in November 
2007. The integrated effort between City staff, and public resulted in a vision for a sustainable creek 
along a vibrant neighborhood. The Oceanside Boulevard Corridor Vision Statement which can be 
accessed from the Onward Oceanside website (https://onwardoceanside.com/references) outlines 
steps to achieve this vision, including development of a Master Plan; encouragement of economic 
development and redevelopment of areas to offer quality services and a mix of uses; creation of a 
continuous network of paths and open spaces to encourage bicycling and pedestrian activity; 
incorporation of natural landscaping, art, and placemaking components; implementation of traffic 
management techniques; and establishment of a revitalized Loma Alta creek as the “core” of the 
open space and trail system. The master planning process is not yet completed. 
e. Downtown Oceanside Master Plan (2000) 
The Downtown Oceanside Master Plan was prepared to implement the land use policies approved 
by the Coastal Commission as part of LCP-1-91, which encourages the development of visitor-serving 
commercial facilities and tourist and visitor-oriented accommodations. The Master Plan applies to a 
nine-block area bounded by The Strand, Cleveland Street, Seagaze Drive, and Civic Center Drive. 
The Master Plan consists of standards and guidelines and serves to implement existing City 
regulations (e.g., Zoning Ordinance, LCP) and Community Development Commission land use 
regulations and development criteria. Development in the nine-block area has either been 
completed or is underway. 
f. Rancho del Oro Specific Plan (1985) 
The Rancho del Oro Specific Plan area encompasses approximately 1,940 acres of land within the 
geographic center of the City. The plan was prepared to provide for the development of 
comprehensive planned community made up of several subdivisions or “villages,” each with its own 
master plan. Many of those villages are located near College Boulevard north of Oceanside 
Boulevard and others south of Mesa Drive between College and El Camino Real. The mixed land use 
plan provides for the phased development of the property with industrial and commercial uses as 
well as a variety of residential housing opportunities and includes provisions for implementing 
circulation system and public utility improvements. The Master Plans include the Planned Residential 
Development Mater Plan, Commercial Master Development Plan, and Industrial Master 
Development Plan, each containing supplemental zoning regulations (i.e., density, permitted,

4.1.3 
Proposed GPU and SSCSP Policies 
The proposed GPU and SSCSP include policies intended to reduce potential adverse environmental 
impacts resulting from buildout of the plans. As future development is proposed, development 
would be required to demonstrate consistency with the GPU and SSCSP policy framework, as 
applicable. The policy framework would be implemented by the City during future discretionary 
and/or ministerial project reviews to ensure impact minimization. The analysis of potential impacts 
considers how implementation of these policies at the project level would serve to reduce the 
significance of potential adverse impacts. 
4.1.3.1 
Policy Framework 
The following policies are examples of the policy framework intended to support land use 
consistency throughout the City, and do not intend to be exclusive of all additional relevant policies 
that may apply to future development. 
a. GPU Efficient and Compatible Land Use Element (ECLU) 
The ECLU provides direction for balanced and organized land uses. The City is striving to support 
both new development and protect and enhance the City’s natural environment, and conservation 
of farmland.  
• 
Goal 3-J: As the City’s commercial corridors and established neighborhoods accommodate 
additional housing and employment-oriented uses, land use compatibility will be maintained 
through land use and development standards, right-of-way public realm improvements, and 
code enforcement.  
• 
Goal 3-K: Transitional areas between districts characterized by different land use types and 
intensities will provide for landscape buffers, traffic management features, noise-attenuating 
features, and contrasting visual elements. 
Efficient Land Uses 
• 
Policy 3-3: Encourage the development of walkable neighborhoods. 
• 
Policy 3-4: Employ zoning incentives, streamlined project review, and strategic public realm 
improvements to channel the bulk of new housing and non-residential development into 
already-urbanized areas currently served by infrastructure and transit. 
Use Compatibility 
• 
Policy 3-20: Identify and consider adjacent and surrounding land uses and land divisions in 
any City action creating a legal division of land or real property, to ensure compatibility and 
proper integration.

b. GPU Integrated Mobility Element (IM) 
The IM promotes a citywide mobility network that effectively integrates all modes of travel, making 
it easier for travelers to both access and transition between a broad range of mobility modes. The 
IM includes goals and policies that align with the 2021 Regional Plan. 
• 
Goal 4-E: The City’s vehicular circulation network will provide for the safe movement of 
automobiles while accommodating sustainable alternative travel modes. 
• 
Goal 4-F: The City’s vehicular circulation network will provide for efficient traffic movement

• 
Goal 4-G: Through coordinated land use and transportation planning, enhanced 
transportation management systems, and expanded pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure, 
the City will facilitate a decrease in vehicle miles traveled (VMT) and associated greenhouse 
gas emissions. 
Safe and Accessible Facilities

•

require all roadway construction and maintenance projects to be reviewed for potential opportunities 
to incorporate complete street improvements (e.g., pedestrian facilities, bicycle facilities, transit 
amenities, stormwater runoff features, etc.).  
c. SSCSP Mobility  
The SSCSP Mobility chapter provides guidance for anticipated land uses to be supported and 
enhanced by mobility choices. The chapter aligns City goals and policies for the SSCSP Planning Area 
with the 2021 Regional Plan  
• 
Policy M-27: Mobility Hubs. Implement mobility hub sites within the Oceanside mobility hub 
coverage area boundaries recommended in the SANDAG Regional Plan. The boundary 
encompasses Oceanside west of El Camino Real. Mobility hub sites should be encouraged 
throughout the coverage area, though feature extensively along the SSCSP corridors at 
transit stops, activity centers and major developments. Mobility hub sites are places where 
different transportation options and amenities are configured in one physical location to 
provide a combination of amenities to facilitate multimodal trips and help address transit 
"first and last mile" access. Amenities may include long-term and short-term bicycle parking 
options, dedicated space for pick-up and drop-off, comfortable waiting areas, staging of 
flexible fleet equipment (e.g., shared vehicles, bicycles, and scooters), and trip planning 
information.

4.1.4.2 
Impact Analysis  
A significant percentage of the City’s land area supports single-family residential development. The 
project does not propose changes to existing land use and development standards for single-family 
development, and thus no significant physical changes to the City’s single-family neighborhoods are 
anticipated. The project seeks to catalyze change primarily within the City’s major commercial 
corridors by facilitating infill and redevelopment through increased residential density allowances, 
increased building height allowances, and a streamlined development review process. The project 
also seeks to facilitate higher and better use within some of the City’s industrial areas (e.g., Oceanside 
Business Park, Industry Street). A key objective of the project is to protect open space and farmland 
by channeling the bulk of future housing and employment growth into the City’s already urbanized 
commercial corridors and industrial areas.  
The GPU and SSCSP land use frameworks focus future development and redevelopment within 
already urbanized areas (ECLU Policy 3-4), especially those areas identified in SANDAG Smart Growth 
Opportunity Areas map. Although future infrastructure improvements are anticipated, the project 
does not include the construction of new roads that could physically divide an established 
community.  
4.1.4.3 
Significance of Impacts 
The City is urbanized with established roadways and the project does not include any project features 
that would have the potential to physically divide an established community. Indeed, the goals and 
policies of the GPU and SSCSP call for improvements that reduce existing physical barriers 
occasioned by roadways, railroads, and natural features like topography and watercourses. 
Therefore, impacts would be less than significant.  
4.1.4.4 
Mitigation 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required.

This subsection is intended to provide perspective on whether the proposed project fits into the 
framework of existing relevant goals and policies. Because the project is a comprehensive update of 
the City’s General Plan policies and introduction of new policies guiding development of the SSCSP

to guide future growth and development, as well as City plans other than the General Plan. 
Future development throughout the City would be required to adhere to the goals, policies and 
actions contained within the updated General Plan elements. Likewise, future development within 
the SSCSP Planning Area would be reviewed for consistency with goals and policies contained within 
the SSCSP. The application of the proposed goals and policies are discussed throughout Chapter 4.0 
of this RPEIR. However, any policies related specifically to land use consistency are discussed below.  
The project also includes an update to the City’s Climate Action Plan (CAP) to account for increased 
housing and employment growth resulting from the GPU and SSCSP. A detailed discussion of the 
CAP and the project’s role in implementation of updated GHG targets is included in Section 4.9.  
a. State Regulations and Plans 
California Coastal Act 
Development within the coastal zone requires uniformity with the California Coastal Act (see 
Section 4.1.2.1.a). Implementation of the goals and policies of the California Coastal Act are captured 
in the City’s LCP and applicable to development within the City’s coastal zone. The project could 
result in growth along the coast. Future development would adhere to the LCP as discussed below 
(see Section 4.1.5.2.c). Through LCP implementation, future development under the GPU and SSCSP 
would be consistent with the California Coastal Act.

b. Regional Regulations and Plans 
San Diego Forward: The 2021 Regional Plan 
The adopted 2021 Regional Plan includes three primary goals: the efficient movement of people and 
goods; access to affordable, reliable, and safe mobility options for everyone; and healthier air and 
reduced GHG emissions regionwide. Although the Draft 2025 Regional Plan is available for public 
review, it has yet to be adopted. Therefore, this analysis is focused on the adopted plan. 
Efficient Movement  
The GPU and SSCSP proposal to increase residential density, commercial and industrial intensity and 
increase jobs throughout the City would result in a greater need for the efficient movement of people 
and goods. The opportunities for growth would be within the SSCSP Planning Area where there is 
ample access to existing and planned transit. Implementation of the SSCSP land uses would 
redesignate industrial sites in proximity to transit to allow for future mixed-use development. 
Additionally, the IM promotes the 2021 Regional Plan’s goal of the efficient movement of people and 
good through the inclusion of strategies that create a comprehensive transportation system 
supporting complete corridors, transit leap, and mobility hubs. For example, IM Policy 4-14 supports 
complete streets principles to make streets equally accessible and comfortable for users.  


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.1  Land Use 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.1-21 
Mobility Options 
The proposed increase in density and intensity of uses would result in a greater need for access to 
affordable, reliable, and safe mobility options. There are existing and planned SANDAG SGOA 
throughout the City. The SGOAs support transit hubs which would provide expanded mobility 
options. The Oceanside Transit Center is one of the most robust transit hubs in southern California, 
accommodating four rail services (Amtrak Surfliner, Metrolink Orange County Line, NCTD Coaster, 
and NCTD Sprinter) and NCTD Breeze bus service. Consistent with the 2021 Regional Plan goal for 
improved mobility options, the City seeks to expand the existing transit resources through smart 
growth and improved active transportation infrastructure in proximity to rail stations and bus routes 
(City of Oceanside 2024a). The IM would be supported by an Active Transportation Plan and a Trails 
Master Plan both of which will promote improvements that connect pedestrians and bicyclists to 
commercial districts and community facilities. Overall, implementation of the GPU and SSCSP 
promotes a citywide mobility network that effectively integrates all modes of travel, including driving, 
walking, biking, transit use, ride-hailing services, and powered micro-mobility options (City of 
Oceanside 2024b).  
Reduced GHG Emissions 
Increased density and intensity of uses could result in the need for strategies for healthier air and 
reduced GHG emissions regionwide. It is the intent of the GPU and SSCSP that reliance on 
automobiles as a primary mode of transportation would be reduced, especially within the SSCSP 
Planning Area. Both the GPU and SSCSP include goals and policies to encourage growth and 
development within proximity to transit and improve alternative modes of transportation including 
the planning of pedestrian and bicycle friendly corridors. Through these measures, and as required 
by the CAP Update, per capita GHG emissions would be reduced. Details relating to the City’s CAP 
Update and the project’s inclusion of GHG reduction measures are analyzed in Section 4.9 of this 
RPEIR. 
Consistency with 2021 Regional Plan  
Overall, the 2021 Regional Plan serves as the blueprint for how the San Diego region will grow and 
how SANDAG will invest in transportation infrastructure to provide more transportation choices, 
strengthen the economy, promote a healthy environment, and support thriving communities. The 
proposed GPU and SSCSP would be consistent with and support implementation of the plan’s vision 
and primary goals. The ECLU and IM provide coordinated land use and transportation planning 
strategies and policies and would be consistent with the 2021 Regional Plan. 
c. Local Regulations and Plans 
Draft SAP 
The City’s draft SAP has not been formally adopted by the City Council; rather, in 2021 the City 
Council directed City staff to address habitat conservation in the GPU. However, it is used as a guide 
for habitat preservation and restoration in conjunction with new private development and capital 
improvement program projects. Future development throughout the City, especially within the 
SSCSP Planning Area, could result in encroachment on sensitive plants and wildlife, impede wildlife 
corridors, and undermine habitat conservation. Section 4.5.2.3.b includes a summary of proposed 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.1  Land Use 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.1-22 
GPU and SSCSP goals and policies framework intended to preserve and protect biological resources 
throughout the City. The City has incorporated many of the key principles and guidelines of the draft 
SAP into the VSR policy framework. Specifically, the VSR includes guidelines for identifying and 
updating existing and potential preserves and outlining strategies for avoiding, restoring, and 
reducing impacts to such areas as the Wildlife Corridor Planning Zone, agricultural exclusion zone, 
coastal zone, priority restoration sites, hardline preserve, and softline preserve (see Figure 4.5-6).  
Overall, GPU and SSCSP policies are informed by the draft SAP providing opportunities to ensure 
land use consistency between development and preserved areas, to improve land use adjacency, 
and avoid indirect impacts. Therefore, the project would be consistent with many policies of the City’s 
draft SAP. 
Code of Ordinances and Zoning Ordinance 
Updates to the Code of Ordinances and City’s Zoning ordinances would be required to fully 
implement the policies contained within the GPU and SSCSP. Future discretionary actions in the form 
of rezones and new or revised ordinances are expected to occur as stand-alone actions, or in 
cooperation with future development projects. Overall, future projects would be required to conform 
to all relevant design and development regulations consistent with applicable ordinances and City 
zoning.  
Local Coastal Plan 
Implementation of the GPU could result in increased growth within the City’s coastal zone. Future 
projects would be required to adhere to all LCP design and development standards. Prior to issuance 
of site-specific permits, development within the coastal zone would be required to show consistency 
with the City’s LCP including maintenance of beach access, and protection of marine habitat and 
visual resources.  
Coast Highway Vision and Strategic Plan 
The CHVSP identifies five key efforts the City should take to lay the groundwork for future 
development and revitalization of the area. Relevant to the GPU is the policy initiative that states, 
“Enable synergistic and economically sustainable mixed uses by zoning changes” (City of Oceanside 
2009). Key efforts associated with this policy include the following: creating a diversity of uses near 
one another; transit-oriented mixed-use development; prioritize non-residential uses on the ground 
floors of buildings within the new mixed-use districts; and allow a flexible mix of uses from building 
to building. The GPU furthers the initiative to place higher density, mixed-use and transit-oriented 
uses. Future development of sites within the CHVSP, consistent with the GPU, would further the plan’s 
initiatives for redevelopment and revitalization of the planning area.  
Airport Land Use Consistency Plan 
As stated in Section 4.1.2.3.e and shown in Figures 4.10-2a and 4.10-2b, portions of the City fall within 
the AIA for three airports: Oceanside Municipal Airport, MCAS Camp Pendleton, and McClellan-
Palomar Airport. Specifically, portions of the City are within each AIA as follows: 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.1  Land Use 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.1-23 
• 
Oceanside Municipal Airport: Airport Noise Contours, AIA Review Areas 1 and 2 
• 
MCAS Camp Pendleton Airport: AIA Review Area 2 
• 
McClellan-Palomar Airport: AIA Review Area 2 
 
AIA Review Area 1 consists of locations where noise and safety concerns may necessitate limitations 
on the types of land use actions. Specifically, Review Area 1 encompasses locations exposed to 
aircraft noise levels of 60 A-weighted decibels community noise equivalent level or greater together 
with the safety zones depicted on ALUCP maps. AIA Review Area 2 consists of locations beyond AIA 
Review Area 1 but within the airspace protection and/or notification overflight areas depicted on 
ALUCP maps. Limits on the heights of structures, particularly in areas of high terrain, are the only 
restriction on land uses within AIA Review Area 2. The recording of overflight notification documents 
is also required in locations within AIA Review Area 2. 
As discussed in detail in Section 4.10.5, the GPU would allow Industrial/Research and Development 
and Neighborhood Commercial uses within the Oceanside Municipal Airport Review Area 1. These 
are allowed uses within this AIA, subject to Oceanside Municipal Airport Safety Compatibility Criteria 
(see Table 4.10-5). Future development within this area would be required to conform to City’s airport 
zoning and the Safety Compatibility Criteria. Further, future development plans would be submitted 
to the ALUC for review. Future development proposed within Review Area 2 would not require ALUC 
review unless the project could: constitute a hazard or obstruction to air navigation; is within high 
terrain resulting heights greater than 35 feet; has the potential to create electrical or visual hazards 
to aircraft in flight; or has the potential to cause an increase in the attraction of birds or other wildlife 
that can be hazardous to aircraft operations (ALUC 2010). The City would be responsible for applying 
for a Consistency Determination to the ALUC prior to approval of future development. Additionally, 
future development within these areas would be required to adhere to SRE Policy 6-71 which ensures 
that land uses surrounding the Oceanside Municipal Airport are compatible with the operation of 
the airport and restrict development of potentially hazardous obstructions or other hazards to flight. 
Therefore, while it is possible that future development could be within AIA Review Areas, they would 
be required to show consistency with GPU policies as well as complete the consultation process with 
the ALUC. Therefore, the GPU and SSCSP would be consistent with relevant ALUCPs.  
Specific and Area Plans 
Future development consistent with GPU and SSCSP land use designations could occur within 
Specific and Area Plan Areas. Projects proposed within these sites would be required to show 
consistency with design guidelines and applicable regulations associated with individual relevant 
plans.  
4.1.5.3 
Significance of Impacts 
The GPU and SSCSP create a policy framework and associated land use designations to serve as the 
blueprint for future development throughout the City. Growth is anticipated primarily within the 
SSCSP Planning Area, but could occur throughout the City. Through compliance with existing plans 
and adherence to goals and policies of the proposed GPU and SSCSP, the project would not cause 
a significant environmental impact due to a conflict with any applicable plans, policies, or regulation

adopted for the purpose of avoiding or mitigating an environmental effect, and impacts would be 
less than significant. 
4.1.5.3 
Mitigation 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required. 
4.1.6 
Cumulative Analysis 
Development under the GPU and SSCSP would be reviewed for consistency with the proposed land 
use framework. Future projects would be subject to site-specific policy consistency analysis and 
compliance with applicable regulations such as the City’s Code of Ordinances, LCP, and any Area or 
Specific Plans, as applicable to the proposed project site. Application of regulations for each 
individual site-specific project would ensure that cumulative impacts related to land use consistency 
would be avoided. Additionally, future projects would be required to incorporate GPU and SSCSP 
policies to guide development to ensure land use compatibility and to avoid physical division of 
community. Therefore, through regulatory and policy compliance, the buildout under the project 
would not contribute to a cumulative impact related to land use.

4.2 
Aesthetics 
This section addresses potential project impacts related to visual resources that could result from 
implementation of the Onward Oceanside project which includes the City of Oceanside (City) General 
Plan Update (GPU), Smart and Sustainable Corridors Specific Plan (SSCSP), and Climate Action Plan 
(CAP) Update, collectively referred to as the project. The GPU would apply to the entire City while 
the SSCSP would apply to land within the Specific Plan boundary, referred to as the SSCSP Planning 
Area. As discussed in Chapter 3.0, Project Description, the analysis of potential impacts focuses on 
parcels throughout the City where the project either (1) proposes changes to existing land use 
designations or (2) where no land use change is proposed, but growth is anticipated to occur. The 
majority of the proposed increased density and intensity of uses would be within the SSCSP Planning 
Area, as shown in Figure 3-2.  
4.2.1 
Existing Conditions 
The City is comprised of visually diverse natural resources that include views of the Pacific Ocean, 
inland waterways, natural open space, distinct landforms, and mountain ranges. The topography of 
the City contributes to the overall character and quality of the existing visual setting. In general, the 
City’s visual setting can be characterized by three physiographic regions: the low-lying coastal area 
along the Pacific Ocean, the City’s three principal watersheds (San Luis Rey River, Buena Vista Creek 
and Lagoon, and Loma Alta Creek), and the foothills located along the eastern boundary of the City 
(Figure 4.2-1). City elevations range from zero along the coast to 940 feet above sea level inland. 
The built environment offers historic buildings, diverse architecture, landscaping, and public art 
dispersed throughout the City’s diverse neighborhoods. The residential, commercial, and public and 
semi-public developments scattered throughout the City offer varying degrees of visual appeal 
based on architectural design and site location. 
4.2.1.1 
Visual Landscape 
The western boundary of the City is the coastal area which includes extensive beaches, as well as the 
Oceanside Pier and Harbor. The coastal area provides expansive views of scenic resources in all 
directions, including distant mountain ranges to the east. Most of the coastal area within the City is 
developed with urban land uses, such as residential and commercial development. To the east of 
Interstate 5 (I-5), the City exhibits a much more suburban character, featuring large single-family 
subdivisions, strip commercial development, and large industrial parks. The foothills located along 
the eastern boundary of the City are characterized by rolling to hilly uplands that have been primarily 
used for agricultural purposes.

Approximately one-fifth of the City land uses (21 percent) accommodates recreational and natural 
open space (City of Oceanside 2021). Existing preserved areas located throughout the City are shown 
in Figure 4.2-2. These open space areas are located primarily adjacent to the City’s northern border 
with Marine Corps Air Station (MCAS) Camp Pendleton and the County of San Diego, and along the 
interior waterways, including the San Luis Rey River, Loma Alta Creek, and Buena Vista Lagoon, as 
well as within Guajome Regional Park south of the South Morro Hills area. Additional smaller swaths 
of open space have been preserved to retain natural landforms and vegetation. As shown in 
Figure 4.2-2, several designated preserve areas are located within or adjacent to the SSCSP Planning 
Area where most of the future increase in density and intensity of uses is proposed. 
The remainder of the City is characterized by urban development; vacant parcels comprise less than 
4 percent of the City. Interspersed within the City’s built environment are public parks, as well as 
semi-public resources such as Mission San Luis Rey and the Rosicrucian Fellowship. With landscaping 
and historic building design, these facilities contribute to the City’s visual quality (City of Oceanside 
2021).  
4.2.1.2 
Views and Scenic Resources 
Diverse views are supported throughout the City. Major scenic resources within the coastal areas 
include views of the Pacific Ocean, Oceanside Harbor and Pier, as well as Buena Vista Lagoon and 
the San Luis Rey River terminus. The City’s Local Coastal Plan (LCP) protects visual resources by 
maintaining existing view corridors through public rights-of-way and states that the City’s grid street 
system allows public views from several vantage points. Specifically, the east-west streets offer ocean 
views (City of Oceanside 1985). 
Within the western foothills, the visual resources include views out to the Pacific Ocean, as well as 
the San Luis Rey River and the open space habitat within MCAS Camp Pendleton to the north. The 
foothills provide an elevated view to the west, providing for extensive viewsheds that contribute to 
the overall aesthetic quality of the City. Views from the agricultural area of South Morro Hills extend 
north towards the open space and mountainous areas of MCAS Camp Pendleton and west to the 
Pacific Ocean and extend south overlooking the San Luis Rey River as well as the existing developed 
areas within the City (City of Oceanside 2019). 
The I-5 corridor is part of the California Scenic Highway System and is eligible for designation as an 
Official Scenic Highway (City of Oceanside 2021). As it passes through the City, I-5 provides visual 
access to the Pacific Ocean. While there is no citywide inventory of scenic views, the LCP states that 
the City’s important aesthetic resources include views of the Pacific Ocean, the San Luis Rey River, 
Buena Vista Lagoon, Oceanside Harbor, and Oceanside Pier (City of Oceanside 1985). 
There are a number of known historic structures within the City that add scenic value to surrounding 
communities, such as structures with historic architectural elements (see Section 4.2.4.2, below).

4.2.1.3 
Urban Form  
In addition to the natural features that define visual character, the City’s visual character is also 
defined by urban and suburban development patterns, diverse architecture, and streetscaping.  
The defining elements of a streetscape include roadway width, traffic control devices, paving, curb 
design, parking design, pedestrian and bicycle facilities, outdoor furnishings, landscaping, outdoor 
lighting, public art, signage, and building design and orientation. Streetscape design can contribute 
to a sense of place that invites outdoor activity, social gathering, and commerce. There is variation 
in streetscapes throughout the City; in some areas, streetscapes feature abundant landscaping, while 
in other areas streetscapes exhibit little to no landscaping (City of Oceanside 2021).  
There is no consistent, character-defining architectural theme in the City. To some degree, both 
residential and non-residential architecture is a product of its time, with older development generally 
reflecting more traditional styles and more recent development exhibiting a more contemporary 
aesthetic (City of Oceanside 2021). 
4.2.1.4 
Urban Forestry 
Urban forestry is defined as the planting, maintenance, care, and protection of tree populations in 
urban settings. The role of trees is an essential function of City planning and urban infrastructure. As 
shown in Figure 4.2-3, tree canopy varies greatly across the City. Overall, the City has an average 
tree canopy coverage of 15 percent. Specifically, within the proposed SSCSP Planning Area, Vista 
Way has the most canopy coverage at 12 percent, while Mission Avenue has 11 percent coverage 
and Oceanside Boulevard has 8 percent coverage. 
4.2.1.5 
Visual Character 
The visual character of the City cannot be singularly defined; different areas are defined by their land 
uses, urban design, and architectural elements. Residential neighborhoods and commercial districts 
reflect the eras in which they were developed. While some of the City is suburban and lower density, 
characterized by single-family neighborhoods and commercial strip centers, the City also includes 
pockets of higher-density attached housing, several industrial areas, a Downtown District with a 
major regional transit, farmland, and extensive open space. Additionally, the City’s coastal area is 
characterized by beach and coastal living.  
a. Neighborhood Planning Areas 
The City is comprised of 17 Neighborhood Planning Areas (NPAs), many of which are defined by 
specific community design factors and defining features. A number of NPAs are regulated by Specific 
Plans and/or Area Plans that provide supplemental development regulations and neighborhood 
focused policies (see Figure 4.1-5 and discussion in Section 4.1.2.4). Figure 4.2-4 shows the 
boundaries of the NPAs.

b. South Morro Hills 
South Morro Hills sits in the City’s northeast corner containing most of the City’s agricultural land, 
which comprises approximately 11 percent of the City’s total land use. South Morro Hills features 
distinctive landforms, including the Sleeping Indian rock formation, which can be seen from vantage 
points throughout the San Luis Rey Valley. The hillsides and glens of South Morro Hills support a 
wide variety of crops. Land holdings range from as much as 300 acres to 2.5-acre home sites with 
rural residential development largely concentrated along Sleeping Indian Road (City of Oceanside 
2021). South Morro Hills is the only non-urbanized portion of the City. As shown in Table 3-8, buildout 
under the GPU would not change the existing development potential of an increase of 900 residential 
units throughout the South Morro Hills area.  
South Morro Hills features rolling topography and panoramic views of the San Luis Rey Valley 
extending to the ocean.  
4.2.1.6 
City’s Commercial Corridors 
The City’s major east-west commercial corridors include Mission Avenue, Oceanside Boulevard, and 
Vista Way. Each of these corridors maintain a distinct character marked not only by surrounding 
geography, but also existing land uses and land use patterns. 
a. Mission Avenue 
Mission Avenue is a heavily travelled commuter roadway marked by commercial uses, primarily 
individual shopping centers, with architectural variation throughout. The corridor’s existing 
commercial centers are auto oriented with large parking lots and set back from the road with limited 
curb appeal. Some recent improvements have created outdoor dining and a more vibrant street 
scene. However, overall, Mission Avenue supports diffuse land patterns and limited cohesiveness in 
character. There are also smaller percentages of industrial, residential, and institutional land uses. 
Mission Avenue also supports Mission San Luis Rey de Francia, the largest of the California missions 
and a National Historic Landmark. There is parkland surrounding the Mission, but otherwise, park 
and open space areas along Mission Avenue are scarce. 
At Mesa Drive and Mission Avenue, where the character in the corridor changes to low intensity 
single-family homes and undeveloped parcels and the topography begins to transition to steeper 
slopes and hillsides, there are expansive views to the Cuyamaca and Laguna mountain ranges. 
Sidewalks do not extend through this portion of the corridor and the streetscape changes from 
ornamental planting to more naturalized planting throughout this stretch. Further east, the corridor 
is characterized by a more rustic and rural landscape. 
The San Luis Rey River extends through this corridor, providing contiguous open space and natural 
habitat.  


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.2 Aesthetics 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.2-9 
b. Oceanside Boulevard 
Oceanside Boulevard includes a mix of land uses, including commercial, industrial, office, residential, 
and recreational facilities. The City’s largest employment hub, a collection of business and technology 
parks, extends along the northern side of this corridor. The roadway parallels Loma Alta Creek, which 
has limited aesthetic value along the corridor.  
North County Transit District’s Sprinter rail line extends through this corridor with much designated 
as Smart Growth Opportunity Areas on the San Diego Association of Governments (SANDAG) Smart 
Growth Concept Map. There are park and recreation areas along Oceanside Boulevard including 
Goat Hill Park, SoCal Sports Complex, and other smaller park areas.  
Adjacent to the Sprinter station on the south side of the corridor there are views of the riparian 
corridor along Loma Alta Creek along with distant views of the mountains to the east. As Oceanside 
Boulevard crosses El Camino Real, the corridor is surrounded by open space including El Corazon 
Park which includes a series of undeveloped and developed open spaces such as the SoCal Sports 
Complex and a trails network through preserved habitat areas. Along the Loma Alta Creek riparian 
corridor, rolling hillsides are visible on the south side of the corridor. The corridor moves through 
the valley with steep slopes on both sides and distant views of the mountains.  
c. Vista Way 
There are a mixture of land uses along Vista Way, including retail, office, multi-family residential, and 
recreational facilities. The Vista Way corridor includes one of the City’s recent mixed-use 
development projects, Piazza D’Oro. Commercial uses occupy more than half of the corridor’s land 
area, including the El Camino County Club golf course, large shopping malls, and the Tri-City 
Hospital. There is limited parkland and open space. However, Buena Vista Creek flows through this 
corridor, opening into an expansive lagoon at its western boundary. 
4.2.1.7 
 Historic Resources  
The City is rich in historic resources, which can contribute to the visual character of certain areas. The 
City’s Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance (CZO) includes the deterrence and allowance of specific 
activities, and enforces development regulations to preserve the visual relationship between an 
historic resource and surrounding land uses (see Sections 4.2.2.2.a and 4.2.2.2.b, below). 
a. Historic Overlay District 
The Historic Overlay District (H) designation is applied to the 55 acres surrounding Mission San Luis 
Rey, as shown in Figure 4.2-5.
