b. Historic Resources 
A discussion of the criteria used by national and local preservation programs to designate historical 
resources is detailed in Section 4.6 of this Recirculated Program Environmental Impact Report 
(RPEIR). For the purposes of identifying historical resources in relationship to neighborhood and 
visual character, Figure 4.2-5 depicts those historic resources located throughout the City listed on 
the National Register of Historic Places, California Register of Historic Places, and the City’s locally 
designated resources.  
The Historical Overlay Zone lies within and adjacent to the Mission Avenue corridor within the SSCSP 
Planning Area.  
c. Coast Highway 
The Coast Highway Vision and Strategic Plan encompasses approximately three miles from Harbor 
Drive in the north to Buena Vista Lagoon in the south. The plan serves as a blueprint for the 
revitalization and enhancement of the Coast Highway corridor. It includes a series of implementation 
strategies and a set of design guidelines envisioning the maintenance of the historic value of the 
highway and its surroundings while also promoting the following:  environmentally and economically 
sustainable smart growth - transit, pedestrian, bicycle, multigenerational-friendly infill development; 
urban connectivity; and high quality urban and architectural design.  
4.2.1.8 
Parks and Open Space 
Existing citywide open space areas include recreational areas, playgrounds and school yards, and 
passive habitat preserve areas.  
a. Scenic Park Overlay District 
Areas with the “SP” designation are shown in Figure 4.2-6. As shown in Figure 4.2-6, the Scenic Park 
Overlay District lies within the northeast portion of the City, just south of South Morro Hills. At the 
center of the District is Guajome Regional Park, which supports 4.5 miles of multi-use, non-motorized 
trails through diverse biological habitats (County of San Diego Parks and Recreation 2014). The Scenic 
Park Scenic Overlay District seeks to ensure that land use and development in the vicinity of Guajome 
Regional Park complements and preserves the integrity of this important ecological, recreational, 
and scenic resource. The northern edge of Mission Avenue, within the proposed SSCSP Planning 
Area, is in the Scenic Park Overlay District.

4.2.2 
Regulatory Setting 
4.2.2.1 
State 
a. California Coastal Act  
The California Coastal Act (Public Resources Code Section 30000 et seq.) authorizes the state of 
California to regulate development within the state Coastal Zone, defined as the area between the 
seaward limits of the state’s jurisdiction and 1,000 yards landward from the mean high tide line. In 
Oceanside, the coastal zone boundary generally encompasses the area east of the Pacific Ocean to 
the Coast Highway. While scenic resources are not specifically mentioned, Public Resources Code 
Section 30001.5 calls to “protect, maintain, and, where feasible, enhance and restore the overall 
quality of the coastal zone environment and its natural and artificial resources.” 
b. California Building Standards Code 
Title 24 of the California Building Standards Code serves as the basis for the design and construction 
of buildings in California. In addition to safety, sustainability, new technology and reliability, the 
California Building Standards Code addresses light pollution and glare hazards through the 
establishment of maximum allowable backlight, up light, and glare (BUG) ratings. 
4.2.2.2 Local 
a. Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance (October 11, 2021) 
The City has utilized multiple zoning ordinances to regulate land use within its boundaries; these 
being the 1986 Zoning Ordinance for coastal areas, the 1992 Zoning Ordinance for Inland areas, and 
the Redevelopment Zoning Ordinance for the downtown area. City staff updated and consolidated 
the City’s zoning ordinances into the CZO. The 1986 Coastal Zoning Ordinance remains to provide 
specific regulatory standards and for development within the City’s Coastal Zone.  
Among the broad purposes of the CZO, it is intended to preserve the character and quality of 
residential neighborhoods, conserve and enhance the City's architectural and cultural resources, 
preserve the natural beauty of the topography of the City and ensure appropriate development with 
regard to these natural features and promote the maximum aesthetic values for all land, land uses, 
buildings and structures, and conserve and enhance key visual features (CZO Section 130). The CZO 
identifies Overlay Zoning Districts, which contain specific regulatory controls to preserve the nature 
of those districts. The Historic and Scenic Park Overlay Districts includes regulations aimed at the 
protection of visual resources.

Article 21, Historic Overlay District (“H”) 
The specific purposes of the “H” District, as it relates to visual resources and neighborhood character, 
includes the following: 
• 
Implement the City's General Plan and Chapter 14-A of the Oceanside City Code (see Sections 
4.2.2.2(b).  
• 
Deter demolition, destruction, alteration, misuse, or neglect of historic or architecturally 
significant buildings that form an important link to Oceanside's past. 
• 
Encourage development tailored to the character and significance of each historic district 
through a Conservation Plan that includes goals, objectives, and design guidelines and 
development criteria.  
Applications for demolition, new construction or alteration of property within the “H” District is 
subject to review by the City’s Historic Preservation Advisory Commission. Applications are reviewed 
in consideration of the visual relationship of proposed architectural design elements to the 
surrounding area, including scale, height, rhythm of spacing, pattern of windows and doorways, 
building siting and relationship to landscaping, roof pitch, architectural style, and structural details, 
materials, colors, and textures. 
Article 22, Scenic Park District (“SP”) 
The specific purposes of the “SP” District include the following: 
• 
Conserve and protect valuable natural resources of recreational and scenic areas in and 
adjacent to the Guajome Regional Park and other public parks. 
• 
Encourage the retention of natural slopes and waterways and minimize grading and 
alteration of drainage patterns.  
• 
Achieve a visually pleasing and compatible relationship between buildings and structures, 
parking areas, walkways and planting areas, and the natural environment. 
• 
Provide appropriate standards and criteria for reviewing proposals for new construction, 
exterior additions and alterations, relocation of buildings, and other development subject to 
the provisions of this Article. 
Land within the SP district is subject to development regulations to ensure grading does not degrade 
visual resources and views of the park are preserved. Regulations governing building height and 
building materials and finishes are also applied within this overlay to ensure structures are in 
reasonable architectural harmony with the character of the area. 
Section 3019 Landscaping, Irrigation and Hydroseeding 
The City requires minimum site landscaping to be applied to all projects, except single-family 
development consistent with the City of Oceanside Specifications and Guidelines for Landscape 
Development. Specifically, applications for development plan approval for projects subject to this 
section are required to include plans and written material showing how any applicable site

landscaping or planting area requirements are to be met. Additionally, requirements for projects 
within the Coastal Zone include both the necessity to screen undesirable views and not obstruct

Section 3021 Screening of Mechanical Equipment 
The City requires all exterior mechanical equipment, with some exceptions within some zones, to 
screen heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) and other equipment to protect views, 
especially within residential districts. 
Section 3039 Hillside Development Provisions 
The CZO contains development provisions to preserve and/or enhance the aesthetic qualities of 
natural hillsides and manufactured slopes. The specific purposes of the Hillside Development 
Provisions, as they relate to visual quality, include the following:  
• 
Maintain an environmental equilibrium consistent with existing vegetation, soils, geology, 
slopes, and drainage patterns, and to preserve the natural topography, including swales, 
canyons, knolls, ridgelines, and rock outcrops, wherever feasible. 
• 
Provide a mechanism for flexible design of residential development projects in hillside areas 
so that development may be concentrated in those areas with the greatest environmental 
carrying capacity and areas with low environmental carrying capacity developed at very low 
density or reserved as permanent open space. 
• 
Preserve the natural appearance of hillsides by assuring that development density and 
intensity relates to the slope of the land, and is compatible with hillside preservation. 
• 
Assure proper design is utilized in grading, landscaping, and in the development of structures 
and roadways to preserve the natural appearance of hillsides. 
• 
Encourage creatively designed hillside development requiring a minimal amount of grading. 
These regulations are applicable only to all residential development proposals on property, portions 
of which have a natural gradient in excess of 20 percent (20 feet of vertical distance for each 100 feet 
of horizontal distance) with a minimum elevation differential of 25 feet.  
b. City of Oceanside Code of Ordinances 
Chapter 14-A Historical Preservation  
This chapter of the Code of Ordinances is known as the Historical Preservation Ordinance (HPO). The 
HPO serves to safeguard the heritage of the City by providing for the protection of historical sites 
and areas representing significant elements of its history. The HPO regulations include enhancing 
the visual character of the City by encouraging and regulating the compatibility of architectural styles 
within historical areas reflecting significant architectural traditions (Code of Ordinances Section 
14A.2(b)). The HPO establishes the Historical Preservation and Advisory Commission; historical area 
and site designation criteria; historical area of site designation procedures; permits required to alter 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.2 Aesthetics 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.2-16 
or demolish historic structures; permit procedures; duty to keep in good repair; and penalties for 
non-enforcement. 
The Historic Preservation Advisory Commission adopts standards to be used by the commission in 
reviewing applications for permits to construct, change, alter, modify, remodel, remove, or 
significantly affect any historical area or site (Code of Ordinances Section 14A.5(k)) and is responsible 
for approval or disapproval of permits within the Historic Overlay District. 
Code of Ordinances Section 14A.6.2 contains the City’s Mills Act Program which allows the City to 
enter into voluntary agreements with owners of historic structures to incentivize the preservation of 
such structures.  
Chapter 39 Light Pollution Regulations 
Chapter 39 of the Code of Ordinances contains the City’s light pollution and light installation 
regulations, restricting the use of certain light fixtures emitting into the night sky that have 
detrimental effects on astronomical observation and research. This chapter details lighting standards, 
such as lamp types allowed, shielding requirements, and hours of operation for certain lighting types. 
c. Local Coastal Program 
The City’s LCP consists of a land use plan document (separate from the General Plan) containing 
land use policies and denotes some of the significant visual and aesthetically important areas, 
including the Pacific Ocean, Oceanside Harbor, the San Luis Rey River, the Buena Vista Lagoon, as 
well as the Oceanside Pier.  
The LCP addresses the San Luis Rey Specific Plan coastal objectives and policies. This includes the 
objective to ensure “new development is sited and planned in a manner which utilizes the San Luis 
Rey River environs to the fullest but retains the aesthetic and resource values present” (City of 
Oceanside 1985). The LCP seeks to enhance visual access to the river and regulate on-site signs that 
would detract from the visual quality of the area and cause excessive glare or annoyance to 
surrounding properties (City of Oceanside 2021). 
The LCP provides policy direction for the protection of visual resources, consistent with the California 
Coastal Act policy requiring that the visual qualities of the Coastal Zone be protected, and that new 
development be sited and designed to be visually compatible with the character of surrounding 
areas. The following objectives and most relevant policies that would apply to future coastal zone 
development, consistent with the project are as follows:  
Objectives: 
• 
The City shall protect, enhance and maximize public enjoyment of Coastal Zone scenic 
resources. 
• 
The City shall, through its land use and public works decisions, seek to protect, enhance, and 
restore visual quality of urban environment.

Policies:

Policy 1: In areas of significant natural aesthetic value, new developments shall be subordinate

d. Specific and Area Plans 
In addition to the City’s CZO, development within identified Specific Plans and Area Plans would be 
guided by the neighborhood characteristics, and/or specific supplemental development and design 
regulations related to visual standards.  
4.2.3 
Proposed GPU and SSCSP Policies  
The proposed GPU and SSCSP include policies intended to reduce potential adverse environmental 
impacts resulting from buildout of the plans. As future development is proposed, development 
would be required to demonstrate consistency with the GPU and SSCSP policy framework, as 
applicable. The policy framework would be implemented by the City during future discretionary 
and/or ministerial project reviews to ensure impact minimization. The analysis of potential impacts 
considers how implementation of these policies at the project level would serve to reduce the 
significance of potential adverse impacts.

Policy Framework 
The following goals and policies are examples of the broader policy framework and do not intend to 
be exclusive of all additional relevant policies that may apply to future development. 
a. GPU Remarkable Communities Element (RC) 
The RC proposes specific visual-related goals and policies focused on building design for all (all types 
of buildings), mixed-use, retail, commercial, and industrial buildings. Policies also provide design 
guidance related to architecture, streetscape, and neighborhood planning strategies that are specific 
to project level design.  
• 
Goal 2-D: The City’s natural environment and urban tree canopy will equitably enhance the 
city’s visual quality, mitigate the urban heat island effect, and improve the experience of the 
public realm. 
• 
Goal 2-F: New development will contribute to the functionality, coherence, accessibility, visual 
quality, and unique character of the City’s built environment. 
• 
Goal 2-O: The City will acknowledge and emphasize the unique identity of each of its 17 
Neighborhood Planning Areas (NPAs) and promote the preservation and enhancement of 
characteristics that make each NPA livable, resilient, and distinct. 
• 
Goal 2-Q: In the development review process, the City will consider how proposed projects 
impact the character and function of the surrounding NPA. 
• 
Policy 2-38: Enhance the appearance of alleys through landscaping, decorative lighting, open 
and/or low-profile fencing, and screening of waste receptacles, utilities, and other elements 
that detract from visual quality. 
• 
Policy 2-49: In partnership with adjacent property owners, improve the visual quality of alleys 
through enhanced paving, fencing, lighting, and landscape.  
• 
Policy 2-52: Design the public realm within urban corridors and Pedestrian Priority Zones to 
contribute to the vitality and visual quality of these areas in the following ways: 
o Accommodate all modes of transportation; 
o Provide ample landscaping and outdoor furnishings; 
o Provide wayfinding features that highlight transit options; and 
o Provide interactive and aesthetic elements (e.g., public art). 
• 
Policy 2.54: Build on Downtown’s existing character to enhance its vitality and visual quality, 
including through the following strategies: 
o Establish a rich tree canopy, with emphasis on shade trees; 
o Enhance access to the waterfront, through shared pathways, gathering spaces, 
wayfinding, and improved amenities;  
o Promote and manage City Hall, including the plazas, as gathering and event places;   
o Provide for outdoor dining where feasible, while ensuring adequate paths of travel;  
o Continue and build on the success of regular community events like Sunset Market and 
Farmer’s Market;

b. GPU Efficient and Compatible Land Use Element (ECLU) 
The ECLU purports to balance new development with protection and enhancement of environmental 
resources, including visual quality. Similar to the RC, this element proposes specific visual-related 
policies focused on contributing to visually appealing transition between land uses. The following 
policies are examples of the broader policy framework and do not intend to be exclusive of all 
additional relevant policies that may apply to future development. 
• 
Policy 3-31: As part of the Zoning Ordinance update, carefully consider development and 
design standards for transitional areas between higher and lower intensity uses, particularly 
where residential and non-residential uses abut. 
• 
Policy 3-32 Mitigate potential massing and shadowing impacts of higher-intensity and taller 
development through:

o High-quality, authentic architecture - i.e., composed of visually compatible elements that

structures, composed of high-quality, resilient materials. Fencing should not create significant 
massing or shadowing impacts on adjacent properties or the public right-of-way. 
• 
Policy 3-64: Encourage new residential development to approach maximum allowable 
densities, while minimizing potential impacts associated with building form and scale, parking 
demand, and on-site activities. 
• 
Policy 3-71: Design and operate commercial uses to complement and not conflict with 
adjoining residential areas. This shall be accomplished by:  
o Ensuring compliance with lighting and signage standards; 
o Requiring adequate landscaped buffers between commercial and residential uses; 
o Providing bicycle and pedestrian links between commercial centers and surrounding 
residential uses, and providing bicycle-parking racks; 
o Requiring articulated building façades and architectural details on elevations facing 
residential areas; 
o Ensuring that waste receptacles are enclosed and that adequate waste hauling is 
provided; 
o Requiring that truck bays be screened from view from residential areas; and 
o Prohibiting delivery and loading activities between the hours of 10:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. 
• 
Policy 3-97: Each industrial use shall provide adequate setbacks, attenuating structures, 
devices, and procedures to ensure that noise, vibration, odors, glare, heat, and other 
emissions do not interfere with neighboring industrial activities nor endanger the health, 
safety, peace, or general welfare of persons residing or working in the surrounding area.

c. SSCSP Land Use 
The Land Use chapter of the SSCSP provides policy direction to ensure compatible and cohesive land 
uses throughout the SSCSP Planning Areas, providing a framework for visually appealing 
development specific to each corridor. The following goals and policies represent examples of the 
broader policy framework and do not intend to be exclusive of all additional relevant policies that 
may apply to future development. The goals and policies also represent the City’s vision to improve 
visual quality and visual access to the City’s waterways. 
• 
Policy LU-25: Compatibility with Nearby Uses. Ensure that industrial development is designed 
and operated to minimize noise, heat, glare, dust, unscreened storage yards, air emissions, 
hazardous materials generation, and other negative effects, including by requiring screening, 
buffers, and landscaping, as necessary. 
• 
Policy LU-34: Compatibility with Adjacent Single-Family Neighborhoods. Promote site design 
and architecture that is sensitive to adjacent single-family neighborhoods – e.g., setbacks, 
screening and softening landscape, horizontal and vertical articulation, enclosed parking 
facilities, light pollution control, improvements to shared public space.  
Mission Avenue Corridor  
• 
Goal 9: Additional linkages between the corridor and the San Luis Rey River will be 
established, and the river will be a key ecological, recreational, and visual resource that 
contributes to the function and character of the corridor. 
• 
Policy LU-41: Linkages to the San Luis Rey River. Embrace the San Luis Rey River as a 
character-defining feature of the corridor and facilitate improved visual access and expanded 
pedestrian and bicycle connections to the river. 
• 
Policy LU-42: Scenic Views. Highlight and frame views of nearby mountain ranges and 
consider ways to incorporate these views into the branding of the corridor. 
Oceanside Boulevard Corridor 
• 
Goal 10: Many of the industrial properties in the corridor will be redeveloped with higher and 
better uses that provide more employment while minimizing potential adverse impacts and 
enhancing the visual quality of industrial areas. 
• 
Goal 14: New land use and development will embrace Loma Alta Creek as a character-
defining open space amenity while facilitating habitat restoration, recreational access, and 
enhanced visual quality.

d. SSCSP Urban Design 
The Urban Design chapter of the SSCSP focuses on overall design of each of the three corridors and 
lays out policies for the entire Planning Area that guide both private development and capital 
improvements. The following goals and policies represent examples of the broader policy framework 
and do not intend to be exclusive of all additional relevant policies that may apply to future 
development. The following policies are a sample of City guidance to promote visual appeal and 
develop a unique character for each of the corridors. Specific policies focus on the City’s vision to 
increase tree canopy and improve the visual appeal of the City’s waterway that traverse the corridors. 
• 
Goal 1: Attractive and visually-unified streetscapes within the corridors will encourage 
pedestrian activity, create a strong sense of place, and contribute to the City’s visual quality. 
• 
Goal 4: Each corridor will exhibit distinct visual themes that foster a unique identity and 
inspire a sense of ownership among residents and business owners. 
• 
Goal 9: Site design and architecture will complement visual themes meant to distinguish and 
organize each of the corridors. 
• 
Policy UD-1: Pedestrian-Oriented Streetscapes. Prioritize pedestrian-oriented streetscape 
improvements within pedestrian priority areas, as identified in Figure 4-1. Improvements 
should include the following: 
o Wider sidewalks (where feasible); 
o Distinctive and highly visible paving at crosswalks; 
o ADA compliant curb cuts and sidewalk conditions; 
o Outdoor dining areas; 
o Benches and other street furnishings; 
o Landscaped buffers between roadways and sidewalks, planted with trees and drought-
tolerant native or naturalized shrubs and groundcover. 
• 
Policy UD-5: Increase Tree Canopy. Plant shade street trees at intervals of a minimum of 30 
feet within Pedestrian Priority Zones and a maximum of 100 feet throughout the Planning 
Area. Seek opportunities to expand the street tree canopy further, including by planting a 
double row of trees around transit stations, planting large trees in existing and new median 
planters, and by maximizing tree planting in conjunction with new development and 
adaptative reuse of existing buildings. 
• 
Policy UD-10: Surface Parking. Surface parking is not permitted between the sidewalk and 
building façade within Pedestrian Priority Zones. 
• 
Policy UD-13: Establish Visually Unified Streetscapes. Establish a unified streetscape theme 
within each corridor by using consistent and distinct planting, lighting, street furniture, and 
signage along each corridor:

o Mission Avenue: Outside of the San Luis Rey Mission Historic District, the streetscape 
should feature visually contemporary streetscape elements to contrast with the character

o Oceanside Boulevard: Highlight the proximity to transit and industrial uses with visually

o Vista Way: Highlight the proximity to Buena Vista Creek and the State Route 78 with

Policy UD-26: Waterways and Riparian Habitats. The City shall facilitate visual access to

for passive recreational activities in proximity to waterways and riparian habitats through 
trails, viewing areas, and unprogrammed open space. 
• 
Policy UD-27: Compatibility with Adjacent Land Uses. Public open space design and 
programming should support and complement adjacent land uses by contributing to a safe 
and secure environment, avoiding excessive noise and glare, and maintaining visual quality. 
In some instances, buffers between open spaces and development may be necessary. 
Landscape buffers shall be prioritized. 
• 
Policy UD-60: Lighting Design. Building lighting fixtures shall be light pollution-reducing 
“dark sky compliant” fixtures that direct light downwards and should be selected to maximize 
energy efficiency.  
• 
Policy UD-61: Bulk and Massing. Require new development along the corridors to include 
architectural design features that create visual interest. 
Mission Avenue Corridor 
• 
Policy UD-14: Mission Avenue Tree Canopy. In order to provide a unique identity for Mission 
Avenue, street trees should consist of species that were of significance during the Mission 
Period in California. These include California peppers (Schinus molle), fruitless olives (Olea 
Europaea ‘Fruitless’), evergreen pear (Pyrus kawakamii), and cork oak (Quercus suber). Native 
California fan palms (Washingtonia filifera) can be utilized for median areas only, where they 
provide high clearance over roadways, but may not be used in pedestrian sidewalk areas.  
Oceanside Boulevard Corridor 
• 
Policy UD-15: Oceanside Boulevard Tree Canopy. Trees for Oceanside Boulevard shall include 
California sycamores (Platanus racemosa), coast live oak (Quercus agrifolia), Torrey pines 
(Pinus torreyana), white alder (Alnus rhombifolia), western redbud (Cercis occidentalis) and 
desert willow (Chilopsis linearis). Native California fan palms (Washingtonia filifera) or Medjool 
date palms (Phoenix dactylifera) can be utilized for median areas only, where they provide 
high clearance over roadways, but may not be used in pedestrian sidewalk areas.

Creek as part of the open space and trail system. 
4.2.4 
Scenic Vistas/Views and Scenic Resources 
4.2.4.1 
Thresholds of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to scenic resources are based on applicable 
criteria in the 2025 California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, 
would the project: 
• 
Have a substantial adverse effect on a scenic vista? 
• 
Substantially damage scenic resources, including, but not limited to, trees, rock outcroppings, 
and historic buildings within a state scenic highway? 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.2 Aesthetics 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.2-25 
4.2.4.2 Impact Analysis  
There are no designated State Scenic Highways within City limits. However, the City supports many 
diverse views and scenic resources including the Pacific Ocean and expansive beaches, inland 
waterways and open space, and distant mountain ranges to the east. The City places a high value on 
protecting these views as they create a sense of place that defines the City. The majority of increased 
density and intensity of uses proposed by the GPU would be within the SSCSP Planning Area. Future 
new development and redevelopment, especially within the SSCSP Planning Area, could detract from 
existing scenic vistas and views. 
As shown in Figure 4.2-2, future development within the SSCSP Planning Area, and throughout the 
City, could affect views of existing preserved areas, scenic views and vistas, due to potential increases 
in density and intensity in proximity to these areas. Future development would adhere to all relevant 
City regulations relating to avoidance and obstruction of views. Specifically, CZO Section 3039, 
Hillside Development Provisions, requires the preservation of hillsides to preserve visual integrity of 
the City’s natural environment. LCP policies, applied to new development and redevelopment within 
the Coastal Zone, require the maintenance of the natural aesthetic value of the areas and the 
protection of existing view corridors (LCP Policies 1 and 4).  
Parkland, open space, and historic sites and structures located throughout the City are considered 
scenic resources with significant aesthetic value. The City’s historic resources, including those 
designated on the National Register of Historic Places and the City’s locally designated resources, 
are depicted on Figure 4.2-5, and discussed in greater detail in Section 4.6 of this RPEIR. As shown 
in Figure 4.2-5, portions of the Historic Overlay District and known historic resources are within and 
adjacent to the SSCSP Planning Area. Increased development potential under the GPU and SSCSP 
could affect these scenic resources if project designs are not sensitive to the historic context for these 
existing resources. The City’s CZO and HPO currently provides protection against visual impacts to 
historic resources through additional development review processes, design requirements, and 
permit requirements. 
In addition to regulatory compliance, future development throughout the City would be required to 
implement GPU policies. The RC encourages the enhancement of scenic views through development 
policies focused on preservation and maintenance of existing views. Specifically, RC Policy 2-78 
encourages the preservation of scenic resources, including public views of the Pacific Ocean, habitat 
areas, and nearby mountain ranges. RC Policy 2-54 encourages the enhancement of the coastal area 
through establishment of tree canopies, waterfront access, streetscapes, and view corridors. The GPU 
also addresses the prevention of damage to scenic resources resulting from new development. GPU 
RC Policy 2-49 supports redevelopment and infill projects that enhance visual quality and encourages 
the improvement of the visual quality through enhanced paving, fencing, lighting, and landscape (. 
To protect historic resources in terms of their visual context, the GPU includes policy guidance for 
historic resource preservation, including ECLU Policy 3-33 which supports the development and 
implementation of design standards/guidelines for new development in proximity to historic 
structures to ensure visual compatibility. 
South Morro Hills maintains a rural agricultural character that represents a visual resource within the 
City. Although no land use change is proposed within this area of the City, Vital and Sustainable 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.2 Aesthetics 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.2-26 
Resources Element (VSR) policies provide a framework for future land use and zoning changes that 
could result in additional residential development. The GPU policy framework prioritizes protection 
of key open space views in South Morro Hills (see RC Policies 2-80 and 2-81) in Section 4.2.3.1.a. 
Development specifically within the SSCSP Planning Area could also result in the blockage of scenic 
views. As detailed in Section 4.2.1.6, the corridors have unique views of local riparian areas, open 
space, steep hills, and eastern mountain ranges. A primary goal of the SSCSP is the enhancement of, 
and restorative actions along the San Luis Rey River, Loma Alta Creek, and Buena Vista Creek, which 
would protect existing views and provide additional viewing opportunities. Future projects within the 
SSCSP Planning Area would adhere to relevant policies which are also focused on protecting views 
of mountain ranges (SSCSP Policy LU-42).  
4.2.4.3 Significance of Impacts 
Development throughout the City could adversely impact scenic vistas and views due to the increase 
in development potential and density. Future development would be required to comply with 
existing zoning and City regulations aimed at preserving and protecting scenic resources. 
Additionally, all future development and redevelopment would implement GPU and SSCSP goals 
and policies intended to guide the preservation and protection of scenic vistas, views, and aesthetic 
resources. Therefore, through regulatory and policy compliance, impacts to scenic views would be 
less than significant. 
4.2.4.4 Mitigation 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required. 
4.2.5 
Visual Quality and Character  
4.2.5.1 
Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to visual character and quality are based on 
applicable criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
In non-urbanized areas, substantially degrade the existing visual character or quality of public 
views of the site and its surroundings. If the project is an urbanized area, would the project 
conflict with applicable zoning and other regulations governing scenic quality? 
4.2.5.2 Impact Analysis 
a. Construction  
Implementation of the project would result in construction activities throughout the City. Temporary 
construction activities would involve grading and the use of heavy machinery that would be visible 
from the areas immediately surrounding the development sites. Therefore, construction activities 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.2 Aesthetics 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.2-27 
could degrade the existing visual character and quality of the respective development sites and their 
surroundings during the construction phase. 
All project-related construction activities would be temporary in nature and all construction 
equipment would ultimately be removed from individual project sites following completion of 
construction activities. Therefore, changes to local visual character and quality associated with 
construction of future development would be temporary and would not permanently affect the 
scenic quality of an area. 
b. Visual Quality  
As discussed in Section 4.14, Population and Housing, of this RPEIR, SANDAG has developed growth 
projections for the City through the year 2050 (see Table 4.14-1). To accommodate anticipated 
growth, the GPU proposes increased residential density and intensity of land uses primarily within 
the SSCSP Planning Area. Additionally, updated definitions of land use designations could trigger 
increased density and intensity of development throughout the City. Proposed changes in density 
and intensity of land uses, especially within the corridors, could conflict with regulations governing 
scenic quality and could result in changes to the visual quality in and around the project sites.  
New land use patterns established by the GPU and SSCSP would redefine the City’s visual 
appearance. As new and more intense land uses are introduced into the landscape, they become 
part of the visual environment. Like other physical resources, the visual environment can be subject 
to fragmentation. Loss of visual integrity can result in significant impacts on citywide visual quality.  
Urban Forestry 
Urban landscaping can add to the visual quality of landscaped boulevards, river and coastal 
promenades, greenways, and street-side tree boxes. The City’s vision includes increasing tree canopy 
as a means to improve the City’s visual appeal. The addition of large canopy trees throughout the 
City requires strategic planning and coordination with City departments and private developers. The 
City’s goal to establish an urban forestry program is also consistent with the City’s Climate Action 
Plan (see Section 4.9 of this RPEIR), which requires development projects to incorporate an annual 
average of 200 additional trees per year. Guidance for the increase in street tree canopy is included 
in both the RC and the SSCSP. For example, RC Policies 2-66 and 2-74, and ECLU Policy 3-106 require 
new development to contribute to increased tree canopy. Also, SSCSP Policy UD-5 provides general 
direction for the increase of tree canopy throughout the SSCSP Planning Area and specific guidance 
for the establishment of different tree palettes in each corridor (see SSCSP Policies UD-14, UD-15, 
and UD-21) to assist in the development of each corridor’s individual character and visual quality.  
Enhancement of Visual Quality 
New development and redevelopment within SSCSP Planning Area would be required to adhere to 
design guidelines embodied within the SSCSP Urban Design chapter. These design guidelines 
provide directions for the overall design of each of the three corridors. The Urban Design chapter 
addresses public realm and streetscapes, parks and public spaces, and wayfinding and public art. 
Additionally, the Urban Design chapter includes development standards providing specific and broad 
recommendations to create high-quality buildings and site plans intended to result in a high-quality 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.2 Aesthetics 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.2-28 
visual environment. Design guidelines and development standards would be applied to new 
development and infill development throughout the SSCSP Planning Area and includes measures 
focused on aesthetic improvements to alleys, project frontage, and site-specific landscaping. New 
development would be required to ensure architectural and structural consistency with surrounding 
existing development, landforms, and maintenance of view corridors. New development adjacent to 
waterways and riparian areas would be required to improve the visual quality of the waterways, 
potentially providing pedestrian walkways and public access to trails, especially along Loma Alta 
Creek. 
c. Visual Character  
The City is comprised of many neighborhoods with differing appeals, including small-town beach 
communities, suburban residential neighborhoods, bustling urban centers, and large lot agricultural 
areas. Important scenic resources throughout the City, such as neighborhood parks, natural open 
space, and inland waterways, add to the appeal and visual characterization. The GPU and SSCSP 
would increase density and accommodate growth throughout the City. Future growth has the 
potential to impact the visual environment through fundamental changes in land use and could 
change components of the landscape that contribute to the City’s existing visual character. For 
example, the City supports several NPAs which have their own appeal and character. Future land use 
changes could result in currently underdeveloped and vacant parcels to be developed with higher 
density residential and/or greater intensity commercial projects which could change the existing 
character of the surrounding neighborhood.  
Most changes would occur within the SSCSP Planning Area, which runs through several NPAs. 
Existing plans would continue to guide development within the NPAs; individual Specific Plans and 
Area Plans ensure maintenance of established character. Additionally, future development would be 
required to comply with citywide zoning and site regulations including screening of exterior 
mechanical equipment (CZO Section 3021) and all landscaping (CZO Sections 3019) and view 
protection standards.  
In addition to regulations and existing standards that serve to protect the City’s neighborhood 
character, the GPU and SSCSP propose goals and policies to promote and place a high priority on 
visual character including quality architecture, landscape, and site design.  
Urban Form 
As discussed above, the GPU creates a framework to enhance and maintain the visual character of 
the City through policy guidance focusing attention on fundamental urban design principles 
including pedestrian orientation, connectivity, transparency, legibility, indoor-outdoor space, urban 
greening, and a synergetic mix of uses. See Section 4.17 for details relating to pedestrian connectivity 
and support for multi-modalities throughout the City. The inclusion of pedestrian amenities as part 
of the new urban form assists in the development and maintenance of each visual appeal and 
character.  
Each of the City’s residential neighborhoods and commercial district reflect the eras in which they 
were developed and feature unique development patterns and distinct character. The GPU RC 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.2 Aesthetics 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.2-29 
Element Goal 2-F directs new development to contribute to the functionality, coherence, accessibility, 
visual quality, and unique character of the City’s built environment.  
South Morro Hills 
No changes to existing land use are proposed within South Morro Hills. Nonetheless, buildout of 
existing land uses would result in an additional 900 residential dwelling uses throughout the area. 
The GPU seeks to maintain the overall rural/agricultural character of the area, while promoting the 
introduction of agritourism uses to ensure continued viability of agricultural cultivation. It is further 
noted that the City Council directed staff to prepare an ordinance prohibiting further development 
in South Morro Hills beyond what is permitted under the existing General Plan and Zoning Ordinance 
until a community plan for South Morro Hills is prepared and approved by the City Council.  
Pedestrian Priority Zones 
Figures 3-6, 3-7, and 3-8 show the locations of proposed Pedestrian Priority Zones which are located 
throughout the SSCSP. This zone represents a mixed-use area adjacent to transit that would provide 
opportunities for enhanced pedestrian environments. An example of the vision for the Pedestrian 
Priority Zones is illustrated in Figure 4.2-7. As shown these areas would require adequate setbacks 
to support pedestrian activities including wider sidewalks with streetside amenities and buffering 
between walkway and streets. Development of the Pedestrian Priority Zones would be guided by 
SSCSP Policies including UD-1, which requires the prioritization of pedestrian-oriented streetscape 
improvements within pedestrian priority areas. Future development within or adjacent to designated 
Pedestrian Priority Zones would be required to prepare development plans that demonstrate 
consistency with the relevant SSCSP policies for Pedestrian Priority Zones. Enhanced pedestrian 
amenities and development standards in Pedestrian Priority Zones as envisioned by the City would 
provide consistency in visual character to the SSCSP Planning Area.  
SSCSP Design Guidelines 
The intention of the SSCSP is to improve the overall visual design, aesthetic cohesion, and character 
of the corridors. The plan includes design standards and a comprehensive strategy for the 
maintenance of visual quality to ensure that changes to the character of the corridor would be 
consistent with zoning and existing regulations. The SSCSP includes direction for the overall design 
of each of the three corridors and lays out policies for the entire Planning Area that would guide 
private development and capital improvements. In addition to structural development guidance, the 
SSCSP includes goals, policies, and standards addressing the elements of the public realm including, 
but not limited to, streetscapes, parks and gathering spaces, buildings, signage, lighting, and public 
art to promote aesthetically pleasing and consistent mixed-use corridors. The GPU policy framework 
would likewise enhance and maintain community and visual character throughout the SSCSP 
Planning Area. The GPU policies ensure compatibility with zoning and other City regulations includes 
overall building height and individual focused design standards for each corridor.

Building Height 
Increased building heights proposed to accommodate high density residential and mixed-uses 
within the SSCSP could result in a conflict with existing zoning. The SSCSP offers incentives to allow 
increased residential density and building height in exchange for the provision of privately owned 
and operated public spaces, reduced setbacks, and other deviations to base zoning standards. 
Deviations would be allowed based on a finding of public benefit and would result in the 
implementation of SSCSP policies. See Section 4.15.4.2.d for a discussion of allowances for increased 
building height in exchange for the integration of public spaces.

of the corridor, providing new urban parks and public spaces in conjunction with new development 
and right-of-way improvements. SSCSP policies guide future projects adjacent to the trail to improve 
the visual quality of the area, potentially providing pedestrian walkways and public access to trails.

•

space that interfaces with the public right-of-way (SSCSP Policy UD-41). 
• 
Improve open space opportunities (SSCSP Policies UD-42 and 43). 
Oceanside Boulevard 
The proposed land use plan for Oceanside Boulevard is shown in Figure 3-7. As shown therein, 
Pedestrian Priority Zones are proposed in four distinct locations adjacent to proposed mixed-use

opportunities for improvement of the City’s expanding trail system along Loma Alta Creek.

constructed with at least one pedestrian entrance facing the creek. Creekside development should 
embrace visual and physical access to the creek, including requiring improvements to the trail and 
thus visual quality surrounding the waterway. 
The general character of this corridor includes vibrant retail shops, restaurants, and new residential 
development. Examples of design guidelines specific to Oceanside Boulevard include the following:

Overall, new development and redevelopment projects would be required to adhere to GPU and 
SSCSP policies to both protect and enhance the aesthetic quality of future development and create 
visual continuity with surrounding land uses. Through site and building design standards,

design throughout each corridor. Future development within each corridor would adhere to the 
general and corridor specific SSCSP development regulations and design guidelines. Implementation 
of existing plans, City regulations, and adherence to proposed policies contained in the GPU and 
SSCSP would ensure consistent application of visual protection measures that support new density 
and intensity of uses under new land use designations, while ensuring protection of the City in 
general and individual neighborhood character.

unique neighborhoods and overall aesthetic due to the increase in development potential and 
density. Future development would be required to comply with existing zoning and ordinance 
regulations aimed at preserving and protecting visual qualities. Additionally, all future development 
and redevelopment would implement GPU and SSCSP goals and policies focused on the 
maintenance and improvement of the visual character of the City, especially within the SSCSP 
Planning Area. Therefore, through regulatory and policy compliance, impacts to visual quality and 
character would be less than significant. 
4.2.5.4 Mitigation 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required. 
4.2.6 
Light or Glare 
4.2.6.1 
Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to light and glare are based on applicable 
criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Create a new source of substantial light or glare which would adversely affect day or 
nighttime views in the area? 
4.2.6.2 Impact Analysis 
The main sources of daytime glare in the City is from sunlight reflecting from structures with reflective 
surfaces such as windows. A source of glare during the nighttime hours is artificial light from homes, 
buildings, and automobile headlights. Implementation of the project may introduce new sources of 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.2 Aesthetics 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.2-34 
daytime glare and may change nighttime lighting and illumination levels. Future development and 
redevelopment projects throughout the City would include residential and commercial uses 
containing structures and other potential sources of light and glare both during the day and at night. 
Building materials (i.e., reflective glass and polished surfaces) are the most substantial sources of 
glare. The amount of glare depends on the intensity and direction of sunlight, which is more acute 
at sunrise and sunset because the angle of the sun is lower during these times. The sources of new 
and increased nighttime lighting and illumination include, but are not limited to, new residential 
development, lighting from non-residential uses, lights associated with increased vehicular travel, 
street lighting, parking lot lights, and security related lighting for nonresidential uses. Increased 
nighttime lighting and illumination could result in adverse effects to adjacent land uses.  
Title 24 of the California Building Standards Code serves as the basis for the design and construction 
of buildings in California. In addition to safety, sustainability, new technology and reliability, the 
California Building Standards Code addresses light pollution and glare hazards through the 
establishment of maximum allowable standards. Future development would also be required to 
adhere to Code of Ordinances Chapter 39 which addresses citywide lighting standards.  
In addition to regulatory compliance future development would adhere to GPU and SSCSP goals 
and policies directed at protections against unwanted light and glare. RC Policy 2-84 enhances the 
City standards through encouragement to use dark-sky compliant outdoor light fixtures to minimize 
light pollution. Within the SSCSP Planning Area, SSCSP Policy UD-60 also supports City standards by 
requiring building lighting to be light pollution-reducing and dark sky compliant. Adherence to GPU 
and SSCSP policies would further ensure that future development would not create a new source of 
substantial light or glare that would adversely affect day or nighttime views in the area.  
4.2.6.3 Significance of Impacts 
Development throughout the City could increase light and glare due to the increase in development 
intensity and residential density. Through compliance with applicable state building standards and 
City regulations aimed at protecting against the effects of light and glare on day and nighttime views, 
coupled with GPU and SSCSP policies would ensure that any new sources of light or glare from 
development or redevelopment projects would be less than significant. 
4.2.6.4 Mitigation 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required.

of view corridors, view sheds, or scenic resources in the City. Future development would be reviewed 
for consistency with all relevant local plans, Code of Ordinance regulations, and proposed GPU and 
SSCSP policies. Specifically, design standards, landscape plans, and light regulations would be applied 
to all project-specific development.

to aesthetics.

4.3 
Agricultural and Forestry Resources 
This section addresses potential project impacts related to agricultural and forestry resources that 
could result from implementation of the Onward Oceanside project which includes the City of 
Oceanside (City) General Plan Update (GPU), Smart and Sustainable Corridors Specific Plan (SSCSP), 
and Climate Action Plan (CAP) Update, collectively referred to as the project. The GPU would apply 
to the entire City, while the SSCSP would apply to land within the Specific Plan boundary, referred to 
as the SSCSP Planning Area. As discussed in Chapter 3.0, Project Description, the analysis of potential 
impacts focuses on parcels throughout the City where the project either (1) proposes changes to 
existing land use designations or (2) where no land use change is proposed, but growth is anticipated 
to occur. The majority of the proposed increased density and intensity of uses would be within the 
SSCSP Planning Area, as shown in Figure 3-2.  
The analysis of agricultural and forestry impacts focuses on the potential loss of resources that could 
occur because of project implementation.  
4.3.1 
Existing Conditions 
4.3.1.1 
Agricultural Setting 
While the City is generally composed of urban/developed land, approximately 2,861 acres or 
10.6 percent of the City’s total land use, is designated as agriculture by the City’s existing General 
Plan (City of Oceanside 2021a). As previously stated in Section 4.1.1.c and shown in Figure 4.1-1, most 
agricultural land uses are concentrated within the City’s northeast corner within the South Morro 
Hills area. Specifically, as shown in Figure 4.1-2, except for a swath along the western border with 
Camp Pendleton, the City’s existing agricultural zoning is situated within South Morro Hills. The City 
has historically maintained policies supporting conservation of agriculture within the Agricultural 
District, e.g., agriculturally zoned lands, specifically within the inland portions of the City focused 
around South Morro Hills. Lot configurations within South Morro Hills are generally conducive to low 
intensity agricultural activity such as orchards, gardens, and limited animal husbandry. While single 
unit conventional residential development is permitted, the area is zoned to allow a maximum 
density of 0.4 dwelling units per acre, with minimum lot sizes of 2.5 acres. Although agricultural 
zoning is primarily located within South Morro Hills, agricultural land uses occupy areas of the City 
that are not within the Agricultural District. Approximately five percent of land within the SSCSP 
contains agricultural land uses such as nursery operations. These land uses are typically located 
within industrial zones and are considered interim land uses by the City until redevelopment occurs.

4.3.1.2 
Agritourism Strategic Plan/South Morro Hills 
Agritourism is generally defined as the operation of an agriculturally-related tourism business open 
to the public (Agricultural Marketing Resource Center 2023). Examples of agritourism activities 
include U-picks, on-farm markets, pumpkin patches, and vineyards and wineries with on-site tastings. 
Currently, a small part of the City’s tourism economy includes a winery, farmers’ markets and farm-
to-table dining events. However, to enhance the long-term economic viability of farming in South 
Morro Hills and broaden Oceanside’s appeal as a visitor destination, the City developed an 
Agritourism Strategic Plan. The Agritourism Strategic Plan involves a two-tiered strategy designed to 
establish a viable and successful agritourism program for the City. Tier 1 focuses on small-scale 
agritourism uses, value-add food processing operations, and “ag lab” activities that promote 
collaboration between the farming and academic communities. Tier 2 actions are more involved and 
require additional planning and a capital expenditure program to implement. Tier 2 actions include 
expanding the range of agritourism uses permitted in South Morro Hills, assessing the potential 
economic impact of agritourism, and preparing a Community Plan for South Morro Hills to better 
define a long-term vision for the area. See Section 4.3.2.2.a for additional information regarding the 
Agritourism Strategic Plan. 
Effective November 2018, the Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance (CZO) was amended to introduce 
agritourism and Tier 1 agritourism activities. The adoption of Tier 1 agritourism strategies allows low 
intensity and low investment agricultural activities in the South Morro Hills community.  
4.3.1.3 
North River Farms Project 
The City approved the North River Farms Planned Development Plan (North River Farms project) on 
January 17, 2020, ultimately allowing for the development of up to 395 residential units and other 
ancillary uses. The North River Farms project is therefore considered a pipeline project that was 
assumed in the overall growth assumptions for the City. Under the project evaluated herein, no land 
use changes are proposed in South Morro Hills and the anticipated buildout for the community is 
based on existing General Plan and zoning allowances. Following adoption of the GPU, a future 
South Morro Hills Community Plan would be developed and be subject to additional environmental 
review.  
The North River Farms project included a General Plan Amendment, Zone Amendment, Vesting 
Tentative Map, and Planned Development Plan. Approval of the project redesignated the site from 
Agriculture (A) to the following land use designations: Agricultural (A), Open Space (OS), Single 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.3 Agricultural and Forestry Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.3-7 
Family Residential (SFD-R), Medium Density Residential A (MDA-R), Medium Density Residential B 
(MDB-R), and Special Commercial (SC). The site was rezoned from Agriculture (A) to Planned 
Development (PD). The approved GPA and rezone are shown on Figures 4.1-1 and 4.2-1 (Existing 
General Plan Land Use Designations and Existing Zoning Designations, respectively).  
The 214.1-acre project site is located at the western entry of South Morro Hills, where it straddles 
North River Road and extends to the San Luis Rey River. While the project as originally approved 
allowed for as many of 525 dwelling units, the maximum unit count was reduced to just under 400 
as part of a legal settlement. North River Farms would also include parks, trails, fire house, retail, and 
commercial uses. Approximately 68.1 acres of the site would be dedicated to agricultural uses 
including a community garden, agricultural trails, production agriculture, and agritourism.  
Following approval of the North River Farms project, the City Council directed staff to prepare an 
ordinance prohibiting further development in South Morro Hills beyond what is permitted under the 
existing General Plan and Zoning Ordinance until a community plan for South Morro Hills is prepared 
and approved by the City Council. 
4.3.2 
Regulatory Setting 
4.3.2.1 
State 
a. California Department of Conservation 
The California DOC is the state agency that administers both the state FMMP and the California Land 
Conservation Act, more commonly known as The Williamson Act. The Important Farmland Mapping 
Program compiles information on the state’s important farmlands, including tracking farmland 
proposed for development and provides this information to state and local government agencies for 
use in planning and for decision makers and decision-making bodies. The FMMP Important Farmland 
Maps are based on a classification system that combines technical soil ratings and current land use. 
Important Farmland Categories include Prime Farmland, Farmland of Statewide Importance, Unique 
Farmland, Farmland of Local Importance, Grazing Land, Urban and Built-up Land, and Other Land. 
The FMMP’s Important Farmland Maps require that Prime Farmland meet the following criteria: 
(1) Prime Farmland must have been used for the production of irrigated crops at some time during 
the two update cycles prior to the mapping date, which equates to four years. Therefore, the land 
must have been used for irrigated agricultural production at some point in time during a four-year 
period of time prior to the most recent date of the Important Farmland Map date (DOC 2023a); and 
(2) the soil must meet the physical and chemical criteria for Prime Farmland or Farmland of Statewide 
Importance as determined by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) Natural Resources 
Conservation Service (NRCS). NRCS compiles lists of which soils in each survey area meet the quality 
criteria. Factors considered in qualification of a soil by NRCS (DOC 2017) include the following:  
• 
Water moisture regimes, available water capacity, and developed irrigation water supply  
• 
Soil temperature range  
• 
Acid-alkali balance  
• 
Water table  
• 
Soil sodium content  


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.3 Agricultural and Forestry Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.3-8 
• 
Flooding (uncontrolled runoff from natural precipitation) 
• 
Erodibility  
• 
Permeability rate  
• 
Rock fragment content  
• 
Soil rooting depth 
The California DOC, Division of Land Resource Protection, and the USDA NRCS both conduct regular 
and ongoing assessments of soil types and prepare detailed soil maps. Once soils are mapped, they 
are grouped into the following categories that have specific definitions. The categories and 
definitions are as follows:  
Prime Farmland. In California, the FMMP maps all statewide farmlands. The FMMP’s soils study area 
is contiguous with soil surveys developed by the USDA. The FMMP requires that any land designated 
as Prime must meet the criteria related to land use and soils. As such, farmland with the optimal 
combination of physical and chemical features to sustain long-term agriculture is described as Prime. 
The land has been determined to have the soil quality, growing season, and moisture supply needed 
to produce sustained high crop yields (DOC 2017). 
Farmland of Statewide Importance. As with Prime Farmland, Farmland of Statewide Importance must 
also meet both the criteria described above with respect to land use and soils and is similar to the 
Prime Farmland category. The difference is that Farmland of Statewide Importance tolerates greater 
shortcomings of the soil, such as greater slopes or less ability to store moisture (DOC 2017).  
Unique Farmland. This category of farmland is categorized as having lesser quality soils, but is still 
used for the production of leading agricultural crops. This farmland is typically irrigated, but can also 
include non-irrigated orchards or vineyards found in some climatic zones in the state. These lands 
must have been used for irrigated agricultural production at some time during the four years prior 
to the mapping date (DOC 2017).  
Farmland of Local Importance. Lands that have been determined by local jurisdictional authorities 
such as county boards of supervisors or local advisory committees to have a specific importance to 
the local agricultural economy are considered Farmland of Local Importance (DOC 2017).  
The FMMP has three other categories of land:  
1. Grazing Land. Land that is particularly suited to the grazing of livestock given existing 
vegetation. This particular designation was developed in concert with University of California 
Cooperative Extension, and a host of other groups with an interest in grazing and livestock 
(DOC 2017).  
2. Urban and Built-Up Land. This category refers to land that is occupied by structures with a 
building density of at least one unit to 1.5 acres or six structures to a 10-acre parcel. This 
category includes land uses such as residential, industrial, commercial, construction, 
institutional, public administration, railroad and other transportation yards, cemeteries, 
airports, golf courses, sanitary landfills, sewage treatment plants, water control structures, 
and other developed purposes (DOC 2017). 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.3 Agricultural and Forestry Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.3-9 
3. Other Land. All other lands that do not fall into the categories above are subsumed into this 
category. Examples of these lands include low-density rural developments, brush, timber 
wetland, riparian areas not suitable for livestock grazing, confined livestock poultry or 
aquaculture facilities, strip mines, borrow pits, and water bodies smaller than 40 acres. In 
addition, vacant and nonagricultural land surrounded on all sides by urban development and 
greater than 40 acres is mapped as Other Land (DOC 2017). 
b. Williamson Act Contracts and Agricultural Preserves 
The Williamson Act (California Administrative Code Section 51200 et seq.) was designed to incentivize 
landowners to retain prime agricultural land and open space in agricultural use, in order to slow the 
conversion of agricultural lands to urban and suburban development. The Williamson Act Program 
allows local governments and private landowners to enter into contracts for the purpose of 
restricting specific parcels of land to agricultural or related open space use. The minimum term for 
contracts is 10 years, and renewal of the contract is automatic unless the landowner or government 
initiates a process of term nonrenewal, thereby essentially rendering the contract indefinite. Once 
under contract, landowners receive substantially reduced property tax assessments, which are then 
based upon generated income as opposed to potential market value of the property (DOC 20123b. 
As discussed above, parcels within the City subject to a Williamson Act Contract are shown on 
Figure 4.3-2. 
c. Right to Farm Act 
California Civil Code Section 3482.5 established the Right to Farm Act, which is designed to protect 
commercial agricultural operations from nuisance complaints that may arise when the operation is 
conducting business in a “manner consistent with proper and accepted customs.” The code specifies 
established operations that have been in business for  
d. Sustainable Agricultural Lands Conservation Program 
The Sustainable Agricultural Lands Conservation Program (SALC) is an existing mechanism for 
agricultural preservation. The SALC utilizes statewide and state administered Cap-and-Trade 
proceeds to protect agricultural lands that are at risk of conversion to other uses. Protecting farmland 
avoids increased emissions associated with development and provides an opportunity to capture 
carbon in the land base. SALC’s mission is to support California’s need for agricultural conservation, 
economic growth, and sustainable development. SALC funds projects that protect at-risk agricultural 
lands from conversion to more pollution-heavy land uses such as urban or rural residential 
development. The program provides both Planning grants Agricultural Conservation Acquisition 
grants.  
4.3.2.2 Local 
a. Agritourism Strategic Plan  
Completed in 2017, the Agritourism Strategic Plan outlines two tiers of new agritourism uses for 
South Morro Hills. Tier 1 strategies are comprised of lower-intensity and lower investment uses like 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.3 Agricultural and Forestry Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.3-10 
U-Pick operations, petting zoos, farm stands, and small bed and breakfasts. Tier 1 strategies do not 
require new major infrastructure and embodies existing capacity of the farmers. In 2018, the City 
Council approved amendments to the Zoning Ordinance to allow agritourism and Tier 1 agritourism 
activities (see Section 4.3.2.2.b Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance). 
The Agritourism Strategic Plan identifies Tier 2 strategies that build from Tier 1 activities but would 
involve increased capital investments, and greater strategic and economic planning by both the farm 
community and the City. Tier 2 strategies would include higher-intensity and higher-investment uses 
such as hotels, festivals, and larger retail operations to sell farm products. Tier 2 strategies are not 
currently allowed by existing zoning allowances, would require additional public infrastructure 
investments, and require a community-based vision of South Morro Hills which is not part of this 
effort. 
The City also envisions the creation of a South Morro Hills Community Plan to facilitate the 
conservation of farmland and support farming as a commercial enterprise. In the future a South 
Morro Hills Community Plan would be developed and be subject to additional environmental review.  
b. Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance  
Article 14 of the Zoning Ordinance establishes an “A” Agricultural District which includes land use 
and development regulations applicable to inland portions of the City within this zone district. As 
shown in Figure 4.1-2, the Agricultural Zone as designated in the GPU coincides with the South Morro 
Hills.  
The purpose of the Agricultural District as specified in Zoning Ordinance Section 1410 is to: 
A. Provide a suitable classification for large-scale agricultural and mining operations and related 
open space uses.  
B. Allow agritourism uses incidental and compatible with agricultural operations. 
C. Limit non-agricultural uses to those incidental to agricultural operations. 
D. Permit only very low-density residential development, compatible with low-intensity 
agriculture and keeping of livestock. 
Section 1420 provides a schedule of land use regulations for the Agricultural District including those 
allowed, those requiring use, administrative, agricultural activity, or special event permits, those 
requiring administrative development plan, and those not allowed in the zone.  
Section 1450, Agricultural Activities, states the following:  
The specific purposes of the Agricultural Activities provisions are to: 
1. Provide for a quality working and business environment for agricultural businesses 
within the City. 
2. Recognize the potential for conflicts between agricultural uses and residential uses in 
the Agricultural District, and provide appropriate standards and criteria for activities 
associated with agriculture to avoid potential conflicts and promote compatibility 
between uses.

provide appropriate standards to avoid potential conflicts and promote compatibility 
between uses. 
4. Provide a streamlined approach to achieving compliance with specific development 
standards within the Agricultural District. 
4.3.3 
Proposed GPU and SSCSP Policies  
The proposed GPU and SSCSP include polices intended to reduce potential adverse environmental 
impacts resulting from buildout of the plans. As future development is proposed, development 
would be required to demonstrate consistency with the GPU and SSCSP policy framework, as 
applicable. The policy framework would be implemented by the City during future discretionary 
and/or ministerial project reviews to ensure impact minimization. The analysis of potential impacts 
considers how implementation of these policies at the project level would serve to reduce the 
significance of potential adverse impacts. 
4.3.3.1 
Policy Framework 
The following goals and policies are examples of the broader policy framework intended to minimize 
impacts to biological resources throughout the City, and do not intend to be exclusive of all 
additional relevant policies that may apply to future development. 
a. GPU Vital and Sustainable Resources Element (VSR)  
• 
Goal 5-M: Agriculture in South Morro Hills and nearby areas will remain a viable economic 
enterprise, by conserving farmland, minimizing urban sprawl, providing employment, and 
creating opportunities for local food sourcing. 
• 
Goal 5-O: South Morro Hills will continue to be designated primarily for agriculture use and 
ancillary commercial activity.  
• 
Policy 5-73: Promote activities and operations that expand the market for local agricultural 
products, both within Oceanside and throughout the San Diego region. 
• 
Policy 5-86: Require that new housing development on all agriculturally-zoned properties 
continue to provide a 100-foot buffer from wetlands and other sensitive habitat and at least 
a 50-foot buffer from any adjacent agricultural properties. 
b. GPU Efficient and Compatible Land Use Element (ECLU) 
• 
Policy 3-108: Leverage the CEQA process to promote infill and redevelopment, fully mitigate 
impacts on biological resources and farmland, and reduce vehicle miles traveled (VMT). 
c. SSCSP Environmental Quality 
No agricultural preservation policies are included in the SSCSP due to the lack of any Agriculture 
District lands and agricultural land uses being considered an interim land use.
