4.5.1.5 
Critical Habitats 
Figures 4.5-3 and 4.5-4 illustrate the location of USFWS designated critical habitat within the City 
that could support special status species plants and wildlife, respectively. As shown in Figures 4.5-3 
and 4.5-4, several critical habitats for both listed plants and wildlife are identified throughout the 
City. Most notable, the following critical habitats are identified: 
• 
Critical habitat for thread-leaved brodiaea (Brodiaea filifolia) is found in patches in the SSCSP 
Planning Area along Oceanside Boulevard.  
• 
Patches of critical habitat for least Bell’s vireo (Vireo bellii pusillus) and southwestern willow 
flycatcher (Empidonax traillii extimus) is found along the San Luis Rey River in the northern 
portion of the City. Additionally,  land north of State Route 76 is mapped within this critical 
habitat area. 
• 
Critical habitat is found for arroyo toad (Anaxyrus californicus) along the San Luis Rey in the 
upstream reaches within the City, just south of South Morro Hills. There are also parcels 
flanking North River Road that are mapped within this critical habitat area.  
• 
Critical habitat for coastal California gnatcatcher (Polioptila californica californica) is scattered 
within the western half of the City and this species is known to be present. These critical 
habitat areas are adjacent to portions of SSCSP Planning Area along Mission Avenue and 
Oceanside Boulevard. 
• 
Critical habitat for the tidewater goby (Eucyclogobius newberryi) is located within the mouth 
of the San Luis Rey River, in the coastal portion of the City. This species has not been 
identified in the area since 1958, with negative surveys in 2002 and 2003 (City of Oceanside 
2021). 
4.5.1.6 
Wildlife Crossings and Habitat Linkages 
A major barrier to north-south regional wildlife movement in the Wildlife Corridor Planning Zone 
(WCPZ) is State Route 76, which has few opportunities for wildlife crossings. Prioritizing an underpass 
at this location, as well as other crossing options would provide connections between the wild lands 
of Camp Pendleton to the north and the remainder of Oceanside, including the San Luis Rey River 
corridor to the south.

4.5.2 
Regulatory Setting 
4.5.2.1 
Federal  
a. Federal Endangered Species Act 
The United States Congress passed the Federal Endangered Species Act (FESA) in 1973 to provide a 
means for conserving endangered and threatened species in order to prevent species extinction, 
extirpation, etc. The FESA has four major components: the Section 4 provisions for listing species 
and designating critical habitat; the Section 7 requirement for federal agencies to consult with the 
USFWS to ensure that their actions are not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of species or 
result in the modification or destruction of critical habitat; the Section 9 prohibition against “taking” 
listed species; and the Section 10 provisions for permitting the incidental take of listed species. The 
term “take” is defined by the FESA to include the concept of “harm,” which agency regulations define 
to include death or injury that results from modification or destruction of a species habitat (50 Code 
of Federal Regulations [CFR] 17.3).  
Section 7 of the FESA 
Section 7 of the FESA provides that each federal agency undertaking a federal action which could 
significantly affect FESA species shall consult with the Secretary of Interior or Commerce, that any 
actions authorized, funded, or carried out by the agency are “not likely to jeopardize the continued 
existence of any endangered or threatened species or result in the destruction or adverse 
modification of lands determined to be critical habitat” (16 United States Code [USC] 1536(a)(2)). The 
term “agency action” is broadly defined in a manner that includes nearly all actions taken by federal 
agencies such as permitting or carrying out a project, as well as actions by private parties which 
require federal agency permits or approval (50 CFR 402.02). The consultation requirement of Section 
7 is triggered upon a determination that a proposed action “may affect” a listed species or designated 
Critical Habitat (50 CFR 402.14(a)). If the proposed action is a “major construction” activity, the federal 
agency proposing the action must prepare a biological assessment to include with its request for the 
initiation of Section 7 consultation.  
Included in the USFWS Biological Opinion is an Incidental Take Statement (ITS) that authorizes a 
specified level of take anticipated to result from the proposed action. The ITS contains “reasonable 
and prudent measures” that are designed to minimize the level of incidental take, adverse 
modification, or destruction to critical habitat, and that must be implemented as a condition of the 
take authorization (50 CFR 402.14(i)(5)).  
The issuance of a Biological Opinion concludes formal consultation, but consultation can be 
reinitiated if the amount or extent of incidental take authorized is exceeded, the action changes, new 
information reveals effects of the action not previously considered, or a new species is listed or 
Critical Habitat is designated (50 CFR 402.16). Once the Biological Opinion is issued, the project 
applicant must implement the terms and conditions, and conservation measures, mandated by the 
USFWS. Monitoring and reporting is required to be coordinated with the USFWS during the 
implementation of conservation measures.

Section 9 of the FESA 
Section 9 of the FESA prohibits any person from “taking” an endangered animal species. Regulations 
promulgated by USFWS and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration make the “take” 
prohibition generally applicable to threatened animal species as well (50 CFR 17.71). Section 9 thus 
prohibits the clearing of habitat that results in death or injury to members of a protected species.  
An authorization or permit to incidentally take listed species can be obtained either through the 
Section 7 consultation process or through the Section 10 incidental take permit process. In the 
context of Section 7, incidental take is authorized through an ITS that is issued consistent with a 
Biological Opinion. Measures required to conform to the ITS are contained in “reasonable and 
prudent measures,” as are the terms and conditions necessary to implement those measures. In the 
context of Section 10, incidental take is authorized through an ITP issued pursuant to 
Section 10(a)(1)(B). Measures contained in the ITP reflect the measures set out in a habitat 
conservation plan developed by the applicant in conjunction with the USFWS. 
Section 10 of the FESA 
Under Section 10(a)(1)(B) of the FESA, the USFWS may permit the incidental take of listed species that 
may occur as a result of an otherwise lawful activity. To obtain a Section 10(a)(1)(B) permit, an 
applicant must prepare a habitat conservation plan that meets the following five criteria: (1) the taking 
will be incidental to an otherwise lawful activity; (2) the applicant will, to the maximum extent 
practicable, minimize and mitigate the impacts of such taking; (3) the applicant will ensure that 
adequate funding for the plan will be provided; (4) the taking will not appreciably reduce the 
likelihood of the survival and recovery of the species in the wild; and (5) other measures, if any, that 
the USFWS requires as being necessary or appropriate for purposes of the plan will be met (16 USC 
1539(a)(2)(A)). 
b. Migratory Bird Treaty Act 
The Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA) (16 USC 703 et seq.) is a federal statute that implements treaties 
with several countries on the conservation and protection of migratory birds. The number of bird 
species covered by the MBTA is extensive and is listed at 50 CFR 10.13. The regulatory definition of 
“migratory bird” is broad and includes any mutation or hybrid of a listed species and any part, egg, 
or nest of such birds (50 CFR 10.12). The MBTA, which is enforced by USFWS, makes it unlawful “by 
any means or in any manner, to pursue, hunt, take, capture, [or] kill” any migratory bird, or attempt 
such actions, except as permitted by regulation. The take, possession, import, export, transport, sale, 
purchase, barter, or offering of these activities is prohibited, except under a valid permit or as 
permitted in the implementing regulations (50 CFR 21.11).  
c. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers 
The USACE has primary federal responsibility for administering regulations that concern waters and 
wetlands in the City. In this regard, the USACE acts under two statutory authorities, the Rivers and 
Harbors Act (33 USC 9 and 10), which governs specified activities in navigable waters, and the Clean 
Water Act (CWA; Section 404), which governs specified activities in waters of the U.S., including 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.5 Biological Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.5-13 
wetlands and special aquatic sites. Wetlands and non-wetland waters (e.g., rivers, streams, and 
natural ponds) are a subset of waters of the U.S. and receive protection under Section 404 of the 
CWA. The USACE has primary federal responsibility for administering regulations that concern waters 
and wetlands in the project area under statutory authority of the CWA (Section 404). In addition, the 
regulations and policies of various federal agencies mandate that the filling of wetlands be avoided 
to the maximum extent feasible. The USACE requires obtaining a permit if a project proposes placing 
structures within navigable waters and/or alteration of waters of the U.S. 
4.5.2.2 State  
a. California Endangered Species Act 
Like the FESA, the California Endangered Species Act (CESA) of 1970 provides protection to species 
considered threatened or endangered by the state of California (California Fish and Game Code, 
Section 2050 et seq.). The CESA recognizes the importance of threatened and endangered fish, 
wildlife, and plant species and their habitats, and prohibits the taking of any endangered, threatened, 
or rare plant and/or animal species unless specifically permitted for education or management 
purposes. 
The CESA declares that deserving plant or animal species would be given protection by the state 
because they are of ecological, educational, historical, recreational, aesthetic, economic, and 
scientific value to the people of the state. CESA establishes that it is state policy to conserve, protect, 
restore, and enhance endangered species and their habitats. Under state law, plant and animal 
species may be formally designated as rare, threatened, or endangered through official listing by the 
California Fish and Game Commission. Listed species are given greater attention during the land use 
planning process by local governments, public agencies, and landowners than are species that have 
not been listed. 
CESA authorizes that “[p]rivate entities may take plant or wildlife species listed as endangered or 
threatened under FESA and CESA, pursuant to a federal incidental take permit issued in accordance 
with Section 10 of the FESA, if the CDFW certifies that the incidental take statement or incidental take 
permit is consistent with CESA” (Fish and Game Code Section 2080.1(a)). 
Section 2081(b) and (c) of the CESA allows CDFW to issue an incidental take permit for a state-listed 
threatened and endangered species only if specific criteria are met. These criteria can be found in 
Title 14 California Code of Regulations (CCR), Sections 783.4(a) and (b). No Section 2081(b) permit 
may authorize the take of “fully protected” species and “specified birds.” If a project is planned in an 
area where a fully protected species or specified bird occurs, an applicant must design the project 
to avoid all take; the CDFW cannot provide take authorization under CESA. On private property, 
endangered plants may also be protected by the Native Plant Protection Act (NPPA) of 1977. 
Threatened plants are protected by CESA, and rare plants are protected by the NPPA. However, 
CESA authorizes that “Private entities may take plant species listed as endangered or threatened 
under the FESA and CESA through a federal ITP issued pursuant to Section 10 of the FESA, if the 
CDFW certifies that the ITS or ITP is consistent with CESA.” In addition, CEQA requires disclosure of 
any potential impacts on listed species and alternatives or mitigation that would reduce those 
impacts.

b. California Fish and Game Code - Sections 1601 to 1603  
Streambeds and other drainages that occur within the City are subject to regulation by the CDFW. 
The CDFW considers most drainages to be “streambeds” unless it can be demonstrated otherwise. 
A stream is defined as a body of water that flows at least periodically or intermittently through a bed 
or channel with banks and supports fish or other aquatic life. This includes watercourses having a 
surface or subsurface flow that supports, or has supported, riparian vegetation. CDFW jurisdiction 
typically extends to the edge of the blue-line streams, and therefore, usually encompasses a larger 
area than USACE jurisdiction. 
c. California Fish and Game Code - Sections 3503 and 3503.5  
Under Section 3503 of the California Fish and Game Code, it is unlawful to take, possess, or needlessly 
destroy the nest or eggs of any bird, except as otherwise provided by this code or any regulation 
made pursuant thereto. Section 3503.5 of the California Fish and Game Code prohibits take, 
possession, or destruction of any birds in the orders Falconiformes (raptors) or Strigiformes (owls) or 
of their nests and eggs. 
d. Regional Water Quality Control Board 
The federal Water Pollution Control Act (also known as the Clean Water Act) (33 USC 1251 et seq.), 
as amended by the Water Quality Act of 1987 (PL 1000-4), is the major federal legislation governing 
water quality. The purpose of the CWA is to “restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and 
biological integrity of the nation’s waters.” Discharges into waters of the U.S are regulated under 
Section 404. Waters of the U.S. include (1) all navigable waters (including all waters subject to the 
ebb and flow of tides); (2) all interstate waters and wetlands; (3) all other waters, such as intrastate 
lakes, rivers, streams (including intermittent streams), mudflats, sand flats, wetlands, sloughs, or 
natural ponds; (4) all impoundments of waters mentioned above; (5) all tributaries to waters 
mentioned above; (6) the territorial seas; and (7) all wetlands adjacent to waters mentioned above.  
e. California Natural Community Conservation Planning Act of 1991 
The Natural Community Conservation Planning (NCCP) Act is designed to conserve habitat-based 
natural communities at the ecosystem scale while accommodating compatible land uses in 
coordination with CESA. CDFW is the principal state agency implementing the NCCP program. The 
act established a process to allow for comprehensive, long-term, regional, multi-species, and habitat-
based planning in a manner that satisfies the requirements of the CESA and FESA (through a 
companion regional habitat conservation plan). The NCCP program has provided the framework for 
innovative efforts by the state, local governments, and private interests, to plan for the protection of 
regional biodiversity and the ecosystems upon which they depend. NCCPs seek to ensure the long-
term conservation of multiple species, while allowing for compatible and appropriate economic 
activity to proceed. Within the county of San Diego, the Final MSCP Plan (County of San Diego 1998) 
provides the framework for local agencies to prepare subarea plans and enter into implementing 
agreements with the Wildlife Agencies to obtain take authority under the NCCP.

f. California Coastal Act 
Enacted in 1976, the California Coastal Act (Coastal Act) aims to protect and enhance California's 
coastal resources, maximize public access to the shoreline, and balance coastal development with 
environmental protection. The Coastal Act requires local cities and counties within the designated 
coastal zone to prepare and implement a Local Coastal Program (LCP), which consists of a Land Use 
Plan and an Implementation Plan (zoning ordinances and maps). These LCPs must be certified by 
the California Coastal Commission as consistent with the policies and goals of the Coastal Act, such 
as protecting sensitive habitats, ensuring public access to beaches, preserving agricultural lands, and 
maintaining coastal water quality. Once an LCP is certified, the local government assumes primary 
responsibility for issuing Coastal Development Permits for development within its coastal zone, 
though the California Coastal Commission retains a critical oversight role through its appeal 
jurisdiction. 
4.5.2.3 Local  
a. North County Multiple Habitat Conservation Program 
The North County Multiple Habitat Conservation Program (MHCP) is a comprehensive, long-term 
regional habitat conservation plan established to protect sensitive species and habitats in northern 
San Diego County. The North County MHCP encompasses the City, as well at the cities of Carlsbad, 
Encinitas, Escondido, San Marcos, Solana Beach, and Vista. The program goals are to conserve 
approximately 19,000 acres of habitat, of which roughly 8,800 acres (46 percent) are already in public 
ownership and contribute toward the habitat preserve system for the protection of more than 80 
rare, threatened, or endangered species. The MHCP sets forth general and subarea conditions of 
coverage that must be met for each covered species for the cities to obtain take authorization. The 
MHCP Subregional Plan and Final Environmental Impact Statement/ Environmental Impact Report 
were adopted and certified by the SANDAG Board of Directors on March 28, 2003. Each MCHP-
encompassing cities must adopt subarea plans and implement agreements with the California 
Department of Fish and Game and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service before incidental take permits can 
be issued. The City has prepared a draft Subarea Habitat Conservation Plan, but does not have plans 
to finalize the effort.  
b. City of Oceanside Draft Subarea Habitat Conservation Plan/Natural 
Communities Conservation Plan 
The draft SAP was prepared per the NCCP Act and the CESA. The draft SAP, initially drafted in 2005 
and revised in 2010 and in 2016, addresses how the City will conserve and protect biological 
communities and species considered sensitive under the NCCP Act and CESA. Due to the prohibitive 
cost of management and implementation, which includes a lack of adequate implementation funding 
for land acquisition, maintenance and restoration, as well as staff resources, the City has decided not 
to pursue formal adoption of the draft SAP. Instead, many of the goals outlined in the draft SAP have 
been included in the City’s planning and biological conservation policies as detailed in the proposed 
VSR. The most critical draft SAP strategies captured in the VSR are summarized below.

Conservation Framework 
As a goal, the draft SAP was focused on conserving a minimum of 2,511 acres of existing native 
habitats through preservation and restoration. The draft SAP identifies Focused Planning Areas 
(FPAs) that generally correspond to those identified in the County of San Diego MHCP. The MHCP 
introduced this term to collectively refer to biological resources or lands that are either already 
conserved or are targeted to be wholly or partially conserved. The FPAs are based on biological core 
and linkage areas evaluated in the MHCP. For purposes of the City’s proposed VSR, the term FPA 
includes the hardline preserves, softline preserves, and pre-approved mitigation areas (PAMAs) from 
the draft SAP. It is inclusive of conservation banks, and some naturally vegetated lands within certain 
preserve planning zones targeted for conservation. A detailed discussion of the City’s hardline and 
softline preserve areas is included in Section 5.2 of the proposed VSR. It is noted that unlike the term 
“preserve,” the term “FPA” does not necessarily imply that all land within these properties will be, or 
needs to be, conserved.  
Wildlife Corridor Planning Zone 
A primary goal for the draft SAP was the identification and preservation/restoration of the north-
south “stepping stones” conservation area within an identified WCPZ, specifically identified to 
support habitat connection and dispersal zones for the coastal California gnatcatcher. Conservation 
of native habitats within the WCPZ would contribute to the conservation linkage between the City of 
Carlsbad’s MHCP Preserve to the south and the large intact coastal sage scrub stands to the north 
within Camp Pendleton.  
Priority Habitat Restoration Sites 
Priority Habitat Restoration Sites represent specific parcels within the WCPZ that are important for 
the enhancement of the north–south, regional coastal California gnatcatcher steppingstone corridor. 
These parcels, identified in Table 5-1 of the proposed VSR, were originally selected in the draft SAP 
based on conservation priority and restoration potential. Priority Habitat Restoration Sites identified 
in the draft SAP and the approximate net acreages are summarized in Table 5-1 of the proposed 
VSR. 
Mitigation Standards 
The draft SAP developed standards to apply to impacts to vegetation communities. These standards 
include both ratios for habitat-based mitigation, and guidance to ensure that off-site mitigation is 
directed to WCPZ and other PAMA. PAMA are defined as land outside the WCPZ that have significant 
resource values and would qualify for mitigation credit. The standards for mitigating impacts to 
upland habitats differ according to where the impacted habitat is located. Mitigation ratios for 
impacted vegetation communities is summarized in Table 5-2 of the proposed VSR. As noted therein, 
the City may periodically review and revise the mitigation ratios as needed. 
Consistent with the MHCP, the draft SAP includes no net loss of wetland vegetation communities.

c. San Luis Rey River Restrictive Covenants 
The City has been implementing a flood risk management project along the lower 7.2 river miles of 
the San Luis Rey River with their federal partner, USACE. The City was required to designate 
297.71 acres for conservation as mitigation for project impacts to riparian and riparian scrub habitat 
for the least Bell’s vireo, southwestern willow flycatcher, and other riparian bird and mammal species 
within the San Luis Rey River, pursuant to California ESA Incidental Take Permit No. 2081-2007-029-
05, between the City and CDFW dated February 1, 2008; the Agreement Regarding Proposed Stream 
or Lake Alteration Notification No. 1600-2007-0173-R5, executed by the City and CDFW dated 
February 5, 2008; and the Post Authorization Decision Document/Supplemental Environmental 
Impact Report/Post Authorization Change Report certified by the City, SCH 99061056, dated 
August 15, 2007. A Declaration of Restrictive Covenants was made by the City on September 22, 
2014, to ensure that the designated lands are maintained in a natural condition in perpetuity. These 
lands are subject to several conditions that identify allowable and restricted land uses to ensure that 
the permit requirements are maintained.  
4.5.3 
Proposed GPU and SSCSP Policies 
The proposed GPU and SSCSP include policies intended to reduce potential adverse environmental 
impacts resulting from buildout of the plans. As future development is proposed, development 
would be required to demonstrate consistency with the GPU and SSCSP policy framework, as 
applicable. The policy framework would be implemented by the City during future discretionary 
and/or ministerial project reviews to ensure impact minimization. The analysis of potential impacts 
considers how implementation of these policies at the project level would serve to reduce the 
significance of potential adverse impacts. 
4.5.3.1 
Policy Framework 
The following goals and policies are examples of the broader policy framework intended to minimize 
impacts to biological resources throughout the City, and do not intend to be exclusive of all 
additional relevant policies that may apply to future development. 
a. GPU VSR 
The VSR provides the framework for the protection, enhancement, and management of the City’s 
biological resources. The GPU envisions future growth to occur largely through infill and 
redevelopment in already urbanized areas, enabling open space conservation and the restoration 
and long-term management of sensitive habitat. The City has incorporated the key principles and 
guidelines of the draft SAP into the VSR policy framework. Specifically, action items VSR-1 through 
VSR-10 identify specific steps to be taken by the City to prioritize biological conservation measures. 
Also, the VSR provides specific mitigation ratios that would be applied to development which results 
in impacts to sensitive habitat. The proposed mitigation ratios are outlined in Table 4.5-4. Mitigation 
ratios differ depending on the location of project impacts, whether citywide or within the agricultural 
exclusion zone.

Goal 5-A: Conserve the full range of sensitive natural communities, threatened, endangered, 
or rare plant and animal species, and wildlife corridors through the protection and 
enhancement of natural habitats and special status species populations. 
• 
Goal 5-B:  Revise and maintain over the long term a comprehensive assessment of the City 
of Oceanside’s conserved lands/hardline preserves, conservation areas identified in the Draft 
SAP (e.g., softline preserves, PAMAs, off-site mitigation zones, the WCPZ, and priority habitat 
restoration sites), and existing vegetation/habitat mapping to ensure the conservation 
framework for Oceanside reflects current conditions and supports the achievement of the 
City’s conservation goals. 
• 
Goal 5-C:. Develop and periodically revise as needed a Biological Resource Protection 
Ordinance (BRPO) that will codify the biological resource policy directives within this General 
Plan Update. The BRPO will specify the requirements that new developments must meet in 
order to receive City approval. At a minimum, new developments proposed on any parcel 
that may support special-status species or sensitive vegetation communities should assess 
the impacts to sensitive biological resources from the project and include measures to avoid 
or mitigate impacts to protected vegetation communities, consistent with mitigation ratios 
that will be codified in the BRPO, which are generally those outlined in the Draft SAP. The 
BRPO will serve to assist new development in assessing project impacts consistent with CEQA. 
The BRPO will also address land use adjacency standards for development adjacent to 
conserved lands to minimize impacts on species and habitats, and requirements for 
conservation land monitoring, management and endowment funding, to minimize impacts 
on species and habitats, and requirements for conservation land monitoring, management, 
and endowment funding.

Policy 5-1: Upon codification of the City's BRPO, development shall adhere to all relevant 
aspects of the ordinance, including measures to avoid and/or mitigate impacts to sensitive 
natural communities, which include sensitive upland communities as well as aquatic 
resources such as wetlands, non-wetland waters, and riparian vegetation.

Policy 5-2: When determining boundaries for future conservation areas such as softline 
preserves and PAMAs, emphasis should be placed on preservation of softline preserves and

blocks of habitat with minimal edge effects, where possible.

contributes to habitat connectivity in areas covered by the North County Multiple Habitat 
Conservation Plan.

Policy 5-8: Ensure that the City has adequate resources to track and pursue the following

o Conserve 90-100 percent of all FPAs.

Policy 5-9: There shall be no-net-loss of coastal sage scrub, chaparral, or perennial native 
grassland within the coastal zone. Mitigation for impacts to any of these vegetation 
communities, when permitted, shall include a creation component that achieves the no-net-
loss standard. Substantial restoration of highly degraded habitat whose biological functions 
and values have been lost may be substituted for creation subject to consultation and 
concurrence of the Wildlife Agencies and the California Coastal Commission.

Policy 5-11: Wherever development or other discretionary actions are proposed in or adjacent 
to riparian habitats along the main stem San Luis Rey River, the riparian area and other 
wetlands or associated natural habitats should be designated as biological open space and 
incorporated into preserve land. In addition, where appropriate, continue requiring a 100-
foot biological buffer for upland habitats, beginning at the outer edge of riparian vegetation. 
Within the biological buffer, no new development shall be allowed. The area should be 
managed for natural biological values as part of the preserve system. In the event that natural 
habitats do not currently (at the time of proposed action) cover the buffer area, habitats 
appropriate to the location and soils should be restored as a condition for the proposed 
action. In most cases, coastal sage scrub vegetation shall be the preferred habitat to restore 
within the biological buffer. If natural habitats do not currently (at the time of proposed 
action) cover the 100-foot buffer area, habitats appropriate to the location and soils shall be

noise, glare, litter, and non-native/invasive species spread into conservation land. 
• 
Policy 5-35: Propose standard mitigation measure language within the new BRPO that aims 
to reduce inadvertent impacts to special-status species and habitats. Standard mitigation 
measures could include a nesting bird measure to prevent take of migratory birds protected 
under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act; or biological mitigation required during construction 
including duration, frequency, and reporting requirements. 
• 
Policy 5-36: Consider adoption of a habitat in-lieu fee to mitigate development impacts on 
disturbed land, agricultural land, and eucalyptus stands. 
Multi-benefit Open Spaces 
• 
Policy 5-43: Ensure that recreational opportunities along the San Luis Rey River, Loma Alta 
Creek, Buena Vista Lagoon, and other sensitive habitat areas comprising preserve lands in 
the City are compatible with habitat restoration and conservation efforts. Maintaining and 
enhancing biodiversity and meeting success criteria/conservation goals for restoration in 
these areas shall be prioritized over recreational use. 
• 
Policy 5-47: Encourage use of native plants for new development sites, particularly where 
sites abut habitat preserves and other open space and consider adoption of a landscape 
ordinance that discourages the planting of any species on the California Invasive Plant 
Council’s “Don’t Plant a Pest” list or similar list such as the San Diego County Invasive 
Ornamental Plant Guide. 
b. GPU Efficient and Compatible Land Use Element (ECLU) 
The ECLU focuses on the City’s facilitation of balanced land use to support new development while 
preserving and enhancing the natural environment and building appropriate connections and 
effective buffers between these two realms.

• 
Policy 3-22: Ensure land use compatibility around sensitive habitat areas and high impact 
uses such as agricultural areas, high intensity industrial uses, and the Camp Pendleton border 
by requiring adequate physical and visual buffers. 
c. SSCSP Environmental Quality 
• 
Goal 1: Oceanside’s rich biological resources will be protected, enhanced, and expanded 
within the corridors. 
• 
Goal 2: Wildlife will safely move through and beyond the planning area via restored wetland 
and riparian corridors, conserved upland habitat, wildlife crossings, and dense tree canopy 
coverage. 
• 
Policy EQ-1 Waterway Buffers: Consider a comprehensive study of opportunities to restore 
habitat and improve flood control within Loma Alta Creek as a basis for standard 
requirements for creek-adjacent development. In the absence of such a study, require that 
all new development maintain at least a 100-foot buffer from the riparian edge of Loma Alta 
Creek or  associated wetlands and restrict new development and lighting within the buffer 
to protect wildlife habitat and species diversity, facilitate movement of stream flows and 
ground water recharge, and improve the ability of wildlife to travel through riparian channels. 
Where feasible, allow public access in the form of open space or a multi-use trail within the 
waterway edge buffer, and incorporate interpretive signage for educational purposes in 
public access areas along waterways. 
• 
Policy EQ-2 Wetland and Riparian Habitat Connectivity: Maintain water-related features, 
including swales, detention basins, and seasonal waterways as open-air features and avoid 
undergrounding waterways whenever possible. Where feasible, consider daylighting 
undergrounded waterways, restoring earthen bottoms, integrating benched landscape areas, 
removing non-native vegetation, and other naturalizing strategies. 
• 
Policy EQ-3 Wildlife Crossings: Where appropriate and feasible, require that major road 
improvements to Mission Ave, Oceanside Blvd, and Vista Way within the Wildlife Corridor 
Planning Zone (as shown on Figure 5-1) incorporate wildlife road-crossing improvements such 
as bridged under-crossings, improved riparian connections, oversized culverts, and/or connected 
tree canopy, supporting wildlife connectivity and helping to preserve both special status species 
and access to critical habitat. High-priority wildlife should be identified by the City through further 
study as specified in the General Plan Action VSR-14. 
• 
Policy EQ-4 Planning and Funding: Collaborate with the development community, local 
conservation groups, SANDAG, Caltrans, and federal and state resource agencies for 
planning and funding.  
• 
Policy EQ-5 Roadway Improvements: Major roadway improvements shall be defined as 
projects that are not considered routine maintenance or pavement preservation projects 
(e.g., construction of new roads, widening of existing roads, construction of curbs and/or 
sidewalks; construction, replacement and repair of bridges).  
• 
Policy EQ-6 Bridge Spans: Where feasible design pedestrian and vehicle bridges over creeks 
and waterways to span the bed and bank of the creek and to avoid placing bridge piers or 
footings within the creek, within bridge safety limits. 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.5 Biological Resources

Page 4.5-23 
• 
Policy EQ-7 Bird-Friendly Design: Incorporate bird-friendly-building design features, 
consistent with the associated voluntary standards of the California Green Code, wherever 
feasible. 
• 
Policy EQ-8 Plant Selection: Require all new or renovated developments and streetscape 
designs to use planting palettes of native or naturalized low-water plant species that are 
climate appropriate, support local insects and animals, and require minimal irrigation. 
• 
Policy EQ-9 Limit Turf: Limit irrigated turf to areas intended for active recreation, such as 
picnic areas and playing fields, in order to reduce water use and increase the use of low-
water habitat-supporting landscape plants. Explore low-water alternatives, including drought 
tolerant varieties of turf-grasses and artificial turf, for all lawn areas. 
• 
Policy EQ-10 Urban Forestry: Improve the street tree canopy along Mission Avenue, 
Oceanside Boulevard, Vista Way, and all surrounding side streets by filling gaps in the existing 
street tree canopy with large canopy trees along the roadway and in landscaped medians, 
selecting low-water native or naturalized tree species with mature canopy sizes of at least 
30 feet in diameter. 
• 
Policy EQ-11 Tree Root Health: In areas with extensive paving or where limited space is 
available for street tree basins, and where tree basins are smaller than 16 square feet, require 
the use of suspended pavement, a structural cell system, and/or sidewalk tree grates to 
prevent soil compaction and support healthy root growth. 
• 
Policy EQ-12 Soil and Water Resource Monitoring: Require development applications to 
include a preliminary soils report and hydrologic and hydraulic analyses. 
4.5.4 
Sensitive Species and Habitat 
4.5.4.1 
Thresholds of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to sensitive species and habitat are based 
on applicable criteria in the 2025 California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines, 
Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Have substantial adverse effects, either directly or through habitat modifications, on any 
species identified as a candidate, sensitive, or special status species in local or regional plans, 
policies, or regulations, or by the CDFW or USFWS? 
• 
Result in a substantial adverse effect on any riparian habitat or other sensitive natural 
community identified in local or regional plans, policies, regulations, or by the CDFW or 
USFWS? 
4.5.4.2 Impact Analysis 
As shown in Figures 4.5-3 and 4.5-4, critical habitats which could support listed plants and wildlife 
are located throughout the City. Additionally, as detailed in Tables 4.5-2 and 4.5-3, habitats 
throughout the City have the potential to support special status plant and wildlife species. Future 
development could encroach upon USFWS designated critical habitats and would have the potential 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.5 Biological Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.5-24 
to adversely affect sensitive plant and wildlife species. Specifically, future development anticipated 
within the SSCSP Planning Area could be located within and adjacent to complex wetland, riparian, 
and upland ecosystems, that support a diverse array of habitat and wildlife resources. Undeveloped 
grasslands, coastal sage scrub, chaparral, marshes, and wetlands along the corridors accommodate 
many native and protected animals such as the least bell’s vireo, southwestern willow flycatcher, 
golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos), burrowing owl (Athene cunicularia), and southern california rufous 
crowned sparrow (Aimophila ruficeps canescens). Additionally, vegetation communities including 
spreading navarretia (Navarretia fossalis), California Orcutt grass (Orcuttia californica), and others 
listed in Table 4.5-3 could be affected by development within the SSCSP Planning Area and 
throughout the City. 
All future development would be required to adhere to the proposed goals and policies included in 
the VSR focused on minimizing adverse effects to sensitive habitat and species.  
The City has incorporated key principles and guidelines of the draft SAP into the VSR policy 
framework. Proposed VSR goals and policies in tandem with the GPU Conservation Framework, 
shown in Figure 4.5-5, provides guidance for future development by identifying existing and 
potential preserves and outlining strategies for avoiding, restoring, and reducing impacts to wildlife 
corridors and planned preserve areas.  
The VSR encourages the development and codification of a BRPO which would apply to removal 
and/or encroachment on sensitive habitat/species. The BRPO (see VSR Goals 5-C and Action VS-4) 
would establish standard rules to be met by development as part of project approvals. These 
standards would include: habitat mitigation ratios; land use adjacency guidelines; habitat 
conservation management and monitoring requirements; and directives relating to the WCPZ.  
The City’s WCPZ is intended to provide habitat connectivity via a north–south coastal California 
gnatcatcher steppingstone corridor, linking existing conserved lands north of the San Luis Rey River 
completing the connection to large intact coastal sage scrub stands to the north within Camp 
Pendleton. Specific goals and policies within the VSR address the avoidance, conservation, or 
enhancement of the WCPZ. Specifically, VSR Policy 5-27 promotes the development on properties 
within the WCPZ to enhance on-site habitat value and maintain connectivity to the greatest extent 
feasible. See Section 4.5.6 for additional discussion and analysis of the City’s wildlife corridors.

The VSR also provides the framework for the maintenance of established and creation of additional 
preserves. The VSR would establish both hardline and softline preserves where development would 
be restricted or limited and subject to compliance with the GPU and SSCSP policy frameworks. 
Hardline preserves are defined as high-quality habitat areas already formally conserved and 
managed by land trusts, as identified in the draft SAP. The GPU seeks to strengthen and unify the 
management structure for these open spaces and ensure ongoing conservation through 
development of a citywide management plan. The City’s FPAs, which include hardline and softline 
preserve areas, and Priority Restoration Sites are shown in Figure 4.5-5. In keeping with the goals of 
the draft SAP, the VSR promotes the conservation of 90 to 100 percent of FPAs (VSR Policy 5-8). The 
VSR supports the City’s preservation efforts through implementation policies, including but not 
limited to the following: codification of BRPO (VSR Policy 5-1); encourage the maintenance and 
enhancement of the biological values of lands within the softline preserves (VSR Policy 5-2); continue 
to require documentation of on-site habitat during discretionary approval process (VSR Policy 5-32); 
continue to require 100 feet of biological buffers to protect habitat function and values (VSR Policies 
5-11 and 5-12).  
Implementation of the Conservation Framework, including policies related to biological conservation 
and WCPZ, and the City’s focus on maintaining and establishing preserves would ensure the City 
implements an overall conservation strategy ensuring sufficient habitats remain conserved to 
support sensitive species. Additionally, the implementation of GPU policies would support 
conservation and restoration of sensitive habitat.  
Although GPU and SSCSP policies would support conservation of habitats in the City, until 
development and adoption of the BRPO, future development could directly and indirectly impact 
sensitive, or special status species during construction and operation of development projects. 
Therefore, in tandem with adoption of the GPU, the City would approve the following Standard 
Conditions of Approval (SCOA) to be applied to development projects as conditions of project 
approval: 
SCOA-BIO-1: Land Use Adjacency Guidelines 
All development adjacent to identified biologically sensitive areas, including but not limited to 
hardline and softline preserves, shall implement the following Land Use Adjacency Guidelines (LUAG) 
to ensure that the project would not result in any indirect impacts to the adjacent sensitive habitat. 
Overall, potential indirect effects from drainage, toxics, lighting, noise, barriers, invasives, and brush 
management from project construction and operation shall not adversely affect off-site adjacent 
habitat. Projects shall comply with all aspects of these LUAG. 
Drainage: All new and proposed projects in and adjacent to sensitive habitat must not drain directly 
into the off-site property. All developed and paved areas must prevent the release of toxins, 
chemicals, petroleum products, exotic plant materials, and other elements that might degrade or 
harm the natural environment or ecosystem processes within the adjacent land. This can be 
accomplished using a variety of methods including natural detention basins, grass swales or 
mechanical trapping devices. These systems should be maintained approximately once a year, or as 
often as needed, to ensure proper functioning. Maintenance should include dredging out sediments 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.5 Biological Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.5-27 
if needed, removing exotic plant materials, and adding chemical-neutralizing compounds (e.g., clay 
compounds) when necessary and appropriate. 
Toxins: Land uses that use chemicals or generate by-products are potentially toxic or impactive to 
wildlife, sensitive species, habitat, or water quality need to incorporate measures to reduce impacts 
caused by the application and/or drainage of such materials. Such measures should include 
drainage/detention basins, swales, or holding areas with non-invasive grasses or wetland-type native 
vegetation to filter out the toxic materials. Regular maintenance should be provided. Where 
applicable, this requirement should be incorporated into leases on publicly owned property as leases 
come up for renewal. 
Lighting: Lighting of all developed areas adjacent to sensitive habitat should be directed away from 
such land. Where necessary, development should provide adequate shielding with non-invasive 
plant materials (preferably native), berming, and/or other methods to protect the sensitive habitat 
and sensitive species from night lighting. 
Noise: Uses in or adjacent to sensitive habitat should be designed to minimize noise impacts. Berms 
or walls should be constructed adjacent to commercial areas, recreational areas, and any other use 
that may introduce noises that could impact or interfere with wildlife utilization of the area. 
Excessively noisy uses or activities adjacent to breeding areas must incorporate noise reduction 
measures and be curtailed during the breeding season of sensitive species. Adequate noise reduction 
measures should also be incorporated for the remainder of the year. 
Barriers: New development adjacent to sensitive habitat may be required to provide barriers (e.g., 
non-invasive vegetation, rocks/boulders, fences, walls, and/or signage) along the boundaries to 
direct public access to appropriate locations and reduce domestic animal predation. 
Invasives: No invasive non-native plant species shall be introduced into areas adjacent to sensitive 
habitat. 
Brush Management: New residential development located adjacent to sensitive habitat must be set 
back from the edge of the habitat to accommodate the City’s brush management requirements. 
Vegetation clearing shall be done consistent with City standards and shall avoid/minimize impacts 
to listed species to the maximum extent possible. For all new developments, regardless of the 
ownership, the brush management would be the responsibility of a homeowners association or other 
private party.  
SCOA-BIO-2: Construction Best Management Practices 
All development within or adjacent to identified biologically sensitive areas shall implement the 
following best management practices (BMPs) during construction activities:  
1. Prior to construction, temporary fencing (with silt barriers) shall be set along the limits of 
project impacts (including construction staging areas and access routes) to prevent 
additional habitat impacts and prevent the spread of silt from the construction zone into 
proposed on-site open space and/or adjacent native habitat. If work occurs beyond the 
fenced or demarcated limits of impact, all work shall cease until the problem has been 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.5 Biological Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.5-28 
remedied to the satisfaction of the City of Oceanside. Temporary construction fencing shall 
be removed upon project completion. 
2. Impacts from fugitive dust will be avoided and minimized through watering and other 
appropriate measures. 
3. The project applicant shall develop an educational pamphlet (in English and Spanish) for the 
identification of raptor nests and to guide tree pruning/removing activities during the 
breeding season. Trimming of trees containing raptor or migrating bird nests shall be 
prohibited during the raptor breeding season (January 15 to August 31).  
4. A monitoring biologist shall be onsite during (a) initial clearing and grubbing of all native 
habitats and (b) project construction within 500 feet of preserved habitat to ensure 
compliance with all conservation measures. The biologist must be knowledgeable of the 
covered species biology and ecology. 
5. All trash and debris shall be confined in enclosed bins located within staging areas.  
6. No pets will be allowed within the construction area.  
7. Any soil or other material stockpiled during construction that could be easily transported by 
wind or rain shall be covered when not actively in use.  
8. No materials shall be placed where they may enter sensitive habitat, receiving waters, or a 
storm drain, or be subject to wind or runoff erosion and dispersion.  
9. Appropriate washout, trackout, and dust control BMPs shall be implemented during 
construction.  
10. All vehicles and equipment scheduled for use in construction on the site shall be clean and 
free of mud or vegetation that could introduce plant pathogens or propagules of non-native 
plants. This includes equipment hauled into the site. The importance of this measure shall be 
discussed in the environmental awareness training materials.  
11. No construction vehicles or machinery shall be allowed outside of the delimited parking, 
staging, and work areas.  
12. All vehicles and equipment used on-site shall be well maintained and checked upon site entry 
for fuel, oil, and hydraulic fluid leaks or other problems that could result in spills of toxic 
materials. Drip pans will be used under all vehicles and equipment when not in active use.  
13. All vehicle fueling and maintenance activities will occur at least 100 feet away from any 
wetland, stream, or other water body unless in a designated area with appropriate berms to 
prevent spills from traveling beyond the upland work area.  
14. A Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan (SWPPP) shall be developed for the project and all 
measures included in the SWPPP shall be implemented during all phases of construction, as 
appropriate.  


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.5 Biological Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.5-29 
15. Temporary erosion control materials shall be inspected on a regular basis during construction 
consistent with the SWPPP, and any required repairs shall be implemented immediately.  
16. For any work within aquatic features or required setback around such features, the contractor 
shall be prepared to handle any localized hazardous waste spills (e.g., gas, oil, or pesticides). 
Spill control and cleanup materials (e.g., oil absorbent pads, fiber rolls) shall be kept on-site 
at all times in case a spill occurs. Any waste materials including, but not limited to, raw 
cement/concrete or washings thereof, asphalt, paint, construction waste, or other coating 
material, oil or other petroleum products, or any other substances which could be hazardous 
to aquatic life, should be prevented from contaminating the soil and/or entering any 
waterway or sanitary sewer system.  
17. All erosion control materials should use certified weed-free straw or other biodegradable, 
weed-free materials. No materials containing monofilament netting shall be used.  
SCOA-BIO-3: Biological Monitoring 
In order to prevent inadvertent disturbance to on-site sensitive habitat during construction, a 
qualified biologist shall be contracted to perform biological monitoring during all grading, clearing, 
grubbing, trenching, and construction activities. The following shall be completed:  
1. The qualified biologist shall perform the monitoring duties before, during and after 
construction.  
2. The applicant shall provide a copy of the biological monitoring contract, and cost estimate 
to the City of Oceanside.  
3. A Biological Monitoring Report shall be prepared and presented to the City of Oceanside to 
substantiate the supervision of the grading activities, and state that grading or construction 
activities did not impact any sensitive resources. 
4.5.4.3 Significance of Impacts 
Buildout under the GPU and SSCSP would result in increased development throughout the City. New 
development has the potential to impact sensitive plant and wildlife species either directly through 
the loss of habitat (including critical habitat) and/or direct take, or indirectly by placing development 
in or adjacent to sensitive habitat. Potential impacts to sensitive species and/or designated critical 
habitat of listed species would be reduced through regulatory compliance, implementation of 
proposed GPU and SSCSP policies, and application of SCOA. SCOA would be applied to ensure site-
specific conditions are evaluated to minimize adverse effects to sensitive species and habitats. 
Nonetheless, absent project-specific development plans, it is not possible to state whether impacts 
to sensitive species and/or habitat are adequately protected. Therefore, at this program level, without 
the benefit of project-specific design measures and development plans, impacts would be significant.  


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.5 Biological Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.5-30 
4.5.4.4 Mitigation 
BIO-1: Biological Assessment and Habitat Based Mitigation 
Prior to approval of development permits, where new development is proposed on land that may 
support special-status species or sensitive vegetation communities, the City shall require an 
assessment of potential impacts to existing biological resources. The assessment must be conducted 
by an independent, qualified biologist. The biological analysis shall include an evaluation of the 
project’s direct, indirect, and cumulative impacts to sensitive species, sensitive habitats and wetlands. 
Surveys shall follow guidelines established for state- and/or federally-listed species. The analysis shall 
evaluate how the project has been designated to minimize and avoid impacts to the extent feasible 
and demonstrate consistency with the GPU and SSCSP policy framework, as applicable. Any 
unavoidable impacts to sensitive habitats shall be mitigated following the ratios identified in the 
City’s VSR Table 5-1. The location of mitigation shall not be isolated and shall support overall buildout 
of the City’s preserve system. The biological analysis shall identify species present or with a potential 
to occur on-site and shall identify avoidance strategies to minimize or avoid impacts to special-status 
species. Any potential impacts to state- or federally-listed species or their habitats and/or to 
jurisdictional waters would require permitting under the appliable regulatory agency including but 
not limited to the USACE, USFWS, CDFW, and the Regional Water Quality Control Board. Any 
unavoidable wetland impacts shall be mitigated to ensure a no net loss of wetlands. The analysis 
shall identify mitigation to ensure adverse effects are minimized to the extent feasible, consistent 
with the City’s policy and conservation framework. A monitoring and reporting program that ensures 
long-term stewardship of sensitive habitats conserved as mitigation or avoidance shall be 
implemented. 
BIO-2: Conservation Requirements 
1. Prior to approval of development permits, require all mitigation sites to be designated as 
Preserve, protected by legally binding conservation easements,  managed in perpetuity by a 
qualified and adequately resourced entity (e.g., private land trust, government agency) and 
funded through a non-wasting endowment.  
2. Utilize City-owned habitat areas primarily to mitigate impacts associated with capital 
improvement projects and other City-initiated actions. 
3. Allow mitigation outside of Oceanside only as a last resort and only when such mitigation 
contributes to habitat connectivity in areas covered by the North County Multiple Habitat 
Conservation Plan. 
4.5.4.5 Significance after Mitigation  
Projects with the potential to impact sensitive species and/or sensitive habitats would be required to 
implement mitigation measures BIO-1 and BIO-2 which requires a project-specific biological 
assessment to inform required mitigation measures including avoidance, mitigation ratios, and 
monitoring. Through implementation of mitigation measures BIO-1 and BIO-2, potentially significant 
impacts to sensitive species/habitat would be reduced to less than significant levels.

4.5.5 
Jurisdictional Wetlands and Waters 
4.5.5.1 
Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to jurisdictional wetlands and waters are 
based on applicable criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Have a substantial adverse effect on state or federally protected wetlands (including, but not 
limited to, marsh, vernal pool, coastal, etc.) through direct removal, filling, hydrological 
interruption, or other means? 
4.5.5.2 Impact Analysis 
Figure 4.5-2 shows National Wetland Inventory mapped wetlands throughout the City. As shown, 
wetlands are supported along the City’s corridors which lie within complex wetland ecosystems. 
Projects within these areas could impact jurisdictional wetlands and waters. Future development is 
required to conform with federal and state regulations relating to the protection of wetlands. 
Additionally, projects would be reviewed for consistency with GPU and SSCSP policies, including but 
not limited to the following: VSR Policy 5-8 states the City’s goal of no net loss of wetland habitat 
and VSR Policies 5-11 and 5-12 support and encourage the preservation, restoration, or enhancement 
of 100-foot buffers of natural vegetation adjacent to existing wetland vegetation communities. Within 
the SSCSP Planning Area, all new developments are encouraged to maintain a 100-foot buffer from 
the riparian edge of Loma Alta Creek or associated wetlands (SSCSP Policy EQ-1).  
Application of GPU and SSCP policies would not, on their own, capture all potential direct and indirect 
adverse effects to wetland habitat during construction and operation of development projects. 
However, the policy framework would ensure project designs incorporate buffering and encourage 
restoration of degraded habitat adjacent to wetlands. In addition, future development adjacent to 
wetlands would be required to implement SCOA-BIO-1 through SCOA-BIO-3, in addition to SCOA 
BIO-4, which would ensure avoidance of indirect impacts to wetlands during construction.  
SCOA-BIO-4: Protection of Wetlands during Construction 
Prior to commencement of construction activities, all wetland/riparian areas are to be clearly 
identified on the site using flagging, lathe, pin flags, or other methods sufficient to ensure that 
construction equipment does not enter protected areas. Field demarcation of wetlands shall be in 
agreement with the findings of a jurisdictional wetland delineation or biological resources 
assessment produced by a qualified biologist with experience in wetland delineation. Exclusion 
markers will be removed after construction is complete. This measure is additive to any applicable 
state or federal permits issued for specific projects. 
4.5.5.3 Significance of Impacts 
Development under the GPU and SSCSP could encroach upon jurisdictional wetland and waters. 
Potential impacts to wetland areas would be reduced through regulatory compliance and adherence 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.5 Biological Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.5-32 
to proposed GPU and SSCSP policies and application of SCOA. As detailed in the SCOA new 
development and redevelopment projects identified as having wetlands on or adjacent to a project 
site, or in proximity to where an adverse effect to wetland habitat could occur, would be required to 
include project design measures to implement the LUAG, and during construction implement 
protective construction measures and biological monitoring. Nonetheless, absent project-specific 
development plans, it is not possible to state whether impacts to on- and off-site wetlands would be 
adequately protected. Therefore, at this program level, without the benefit of project-specific design 
measures and development plans, impacts would be significant. 
4.5.5.4 Mitigation 
Implementation of mitigation measures BIO-1 and BIO-2, detailed in Section 4.5.4.4, would be 
implemented. With implementation of mitigation measure BIO-1 and BIO-2, impacts to wetlands 
resources would be less than significant.  
4.5.5.5 Significance after Mitigation  
Projects with the potential to impact wetland habitat would be required to implement mitigation 
measures BIO-1 and BIO-2 which requires a project-specific biological assessment to inform required 
mitigation measures including avoidance, mitigation ratios, and monitoring. Through 
implementation of mitigation measures BIO-1 and BIO-2, potentially significant impacts to wetland 
habitat would be reduced to less than significant levels. 
4.5.6 
Wildlife Corridors  
4.5.6.1 
Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to wildlife corridors and nursery sites are 
based on applicable criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Interfere substantially with the movement of any native resident or migratory fish or wildlife 
species or with established native resident or migratory wildlife corridors, or impede the use 
of native wildlife nursery sites? 
4.5.6.2 Impact Analysis 
Under the GPU and SSCSP, most of the new density and intensity of development would be focused 
within the City’s corridors which are built-up and not conducive to supporting wildlife corridors. 
However,  future development within the SSCSP Planning Area and throughout the City could result 
in a significant impact to wildlife corridors. 
The City has developed strategies to enhance biological connectivity. As discussed in 
Section 4.5.3.1.a, proposed VSR policies support establishment of the WCPZ as the City’s main area 
of focus for habitat preservation. The WCPZ encourages the preservation/restoration of a north-
south “stepping stones” conservation area to protect coastal sage scrub habitat connection for the 
coastal California gnatcatcher. Habitat creation, restoration, and enhancement are key priorities 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.5 Biological Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.5-33 
within the WCPZ, and the VSR policies establish a framework for achieving this goal. For example, 
VSR Policies 5-3 and 5-4 provide guidance for long-term conservation and restoration efforts in the 
WCPZ. Additionally, restrictions on new, non-native landscaping would encourage establishment of 
plantings favorable to gnatcatcher use during dispersal and discourage non-native plantings that 
may inhibit gnatcatcher use.  
WCPZ are shown in Figure 4.5-5. In addition to the coastal California gnatcatcher’s needs, prioritizing 
an underpass at State Route 76 and Mission Avenue, as well as other locations, could facilitate wildlife 
crossings across other major roadway barriers. To further encourage the maintenance and 
establishment of wildlife corridors and crossings, future development within the SSCSP Planning Area 
would be required to adhere to applicable proposed goals and policies relating to wildlife corridor 
planning. SSCSP EQ Goal 2 encourages the restoration and conservation of land to support wildlife 
crossings, and dense tree canopy coverage. Implementation of SSCSP Policy EQ-3 requires road 
improvements to Mission Avenue, Oceanside Boulevard, and Vista Way within the WCPZ (as shown 
on Figure 4.5-5) incorporate wildlife road-crossing improvements such as bridged under-crossings, 
improved riparian connections, oversized culverts, and/or connected tree canopy, supporting wildlife 
connectivity and helping to preserve both special status species and access to critical habitat. High-
priority wildlife connection locations include the following: 
• 
Near the intersection of El Camino Real and Oceanside Boulevard; 
• 
Near the intersection of Mission Avenue and Mesa Drive; and  
• 
Mission Avenue near Ron Ortega Recreation Park and Goat Hill Park Golf Course. 
The City is also committed to the preservation and increased density of large canopy trees. In 
addition to providing shade, aesthetic value, and greenhouse gas benefits (see Sections 4.2 and 4.9), 
large canopy trees offer biological value to breeding and migrating birds. The SSCSP emphasizes 
maintenance of existing canopy trees and expanding the urban forest within the corridors. Future 
development that could impact existing trees impeding migratory travel and breeding. 
Application of GPU and SSCSP policies would not, on their own, capture all potential to impact to 
wildlife corridors and nesting sites during construction and operation of development projects. 
Therefore, future development throughout the City would be required to include the following SCOA 
to be carried out as conditions of project approval:  
SCOA-BIO-5: Protection of Raptors/Migratory Birds  
All development shall avoid any direct and indirect impacts to raptors and/or any migratory birds, 
grubbing and clearing of vegetation that may support active nests and construction activities 
adjacent to nesting habitat will occur outside of the breeding season (January 15 to August 31). If 
removal of habitat and/or construction activities is necessary adjacent to nesting habitat during the 
breeding season, the applicant shall retain a qualified biologist to conduct a pre-construction survey 
to determine the presence or absence of non-listed nesting migratory birds on or within 300 feet of 
the construction area, and federally- or state-listed birds and raptors on or within 500 feet of the 
construction area. The pre-construction survey must be conducted within 10 calendar days prior to 
the start of construction, the results of which must be submitted to the City for review and approval 
prior to initiating any construction activities. If nesting birds are detected by the qualified biologist, 
the following buffers shall be established: (1) no work within 300 feet of a non-listed nesting 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.5 Biological Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.5-34 
migratory bird nest and (2) no work within 500 feet of a listed bird or raptor nest. The City may 
reduce these buffer widths depending on site-specific conditions (e.g., the width and type of 
screening vegetation between the nest and proposed activity) or the existing ambient level of activity 
(e.g., existing level of human activity within the buffer distance). If construction must take place within 
the recommended buffer widths above, the project applicant shall submit a formal request prepared 
by a qualified biologist recommending a buffer reduction supported by evidence that the reduction 
would not adversely affect nesting birds. The  City would have the discretion to approve buffer width 
reductions provided adequate evidence is provided to support a reduction to the buffer. 
4.5.6.3 Significance of Impacts 
Future development under the GPU and SSCSP would increase residential density and intensity of 
land uses which could result in impacts to migratory wildlife including the use of wildlife movement 
areas. In addition, future construction activities may require vegetation removal and/or construction 
activity noise levels that could disturb nesting birds. While, adherence to federal and state 
regulations, City planning strategies, GPU policy compliance, and implementation of SCOAs would 
reduce significant impacts, absent project-specific development plans, it is not possible to state 
whether impacts to wildlife corridors and nursery sites would be reduced to less than significant 
levels. Therefore, at this program level, without the benefit of project-specific design measures and 
development plans, impacts would be significant.  
4.5.6.4 Mitigation 
Implementation of mitigation measures BIO-1 and BIO-2, detailed in Section 4.5.4.4, would be 
implemented. With implementation of mitigation measures BIO-1 and BIO-2, impacts to wildlife 
crossings would be less than significant.  
4.5.6.5 Significance after Mitigation  
Projects within the WCPZ or which have the potential to impact wildlife crossings and/or habitat 
linkages would be required to implement mitigation measures BIO-1 and BIO-2 which requires a 
project-specific biological assessment to inform required mitigation measures including avoidance, 
mitigation ratios, and monitoring. Through implementation of mitigation measures BIO-1 and BIO-2, 
potentially significant impacts to wildlife corridors and nursery sites would be reduced to less than 
significant levels.

4.5.7.2 
Impact Analysis 
Initially drafted in 2005 and revised in 2010 and in 2016, the City’s draft SAP was meant to contribute 
to regional habitat conservation as outlined in the MHCP. Due to the prohibitive cost of management 
and implementation, which includes a lack of adequate implementation funding for land acquisition, 
maintenance and restoration, as well as for staff resources, the City has decided not to pursue formal 
adoption of the draft SAP. Instead, the City has incorporated the key principles and guidelines of the 
draft SAP in the VSR. Future development would be required to implement relevant policies and 
SCOA to support biological preservation. Therefore, no conflict with habitat conservation plans 
would occur.  
4.5.7.3 
Significance of Impacts 
Compliance with proposed GPU and SSCSP policies and SCOA would result in the implementation 
of key principles and guidelines established in the City’s draft SAP. The project would not conflict 
with an adopted or approved habitat conservation plan. Impacts would be less than significant. 
4.5.7.4 Mitigation 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required. 
4.5.8 
Cumulative Analysis  
Cumulative impacts consider how a project may affect biological resources on a regional scale. The 
cumulative study area includes the localized habitat areas defined generally by topography and man-
made features that reduce wildlife movement and generally create a local wildlife ecoregion. This 
ecoregion includes the entirety of the City. Future development projects would result in potentially 
significant impacts to sensitive species and upland habitats and wetland habitats, which could include 
jurisdictional wetlands. The combined impacts of multiple projects could result in a cumulatively 
significant impact to these biological resources. Future development would adhere to regulations 
and proposed policies focused on the protection and preservation of biological resources. 
Additionally, future projects would apply SCOA and mitigation measures BIO-1 and BIO-2 which 
require the preparation of project-specific biological assessment to inform project-specific mitigation 
measures including avoidance, mitigation ratios, and monitoring. Implementation of these mitigation 
measures would ensure that project level impacts to biological resources would be less than 
significant. Therefore, the combined incremental contribution of individual projects to cumulative 
biological resources impacts would be less than significant.

Impacts related to wildlife corridors and habitat conservation plans, NCCP, or other approved local 
regional or state habitat conservation plan, or any local policies or ordinances would be less than 
significant and would not contribute to a cumulative impact for these issues. The project would not 
contribute to a cumulative biological impact. Cumulative impacts would be less than significant.
