To achieve the necessary GHG reductions, the CAP Update identifies reduction measures that are 
organized under six focus sectors that align with emissions sectors considered in the 2018 GHG 
emissions inventory, including: 
• 
Energy, which includes measures that reduce emissions in the natural gas and electricity GHG 
inventory sectors;  


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.9 Greenhouse Gas Emissions 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.9-16 
• 
Transportation, which includes measures that reduce emissions in the on-road transportation 
and off-road transportation GHG inventory sectors; 
• 
Solid Waste; which includes measures to reduce emissions from organic decay in landfills by 
increasing waste diversion and composting;  
• 
Water; which includes measures that reduce water consumption and electricity emissions 
associated with the City’s water supply; 
• 
Carbon Sequestration, which reduces the City’s overall GHG emissions contribution by 
protecting natural lands and expanding the urban forests; and  
• 
Local Green Economy, which is intended to reduce emissions from consumer products and 
support local job growth in emerging sectors.  
Each sector includes one or more GHG reduction measures, and each measure includes multiple 
implementation actions. Implementation actions are key strategies that drive quantifiable GHG 
reductions, and, in some cases, provide co-benefits such as public health benefits, promoting local 
economic growth and increased resiliency to natural hazards.  
Performance indicators are provided for measures that have quantifiable GHG reductions to allow 
the City to monitor progress towards meeting the GHG reduction goal of the measure as the actions 
of the measure are implemented. Implementation progress for reduction measures that do not 
include performance indicators can be monitored based on whether the implementation action has 
been started, is ongoing, or has been completed. GHG reductions associated with the measures were 
calculated in a stepwise manner for the future years 2030, 2045, and 2050. In other words, GHG 
reductions are assessed during a snapshot in time in years 2030, 2045, and 2050. Measures are 
quantified for a single year rather than adding cumulative reductions from prior years, which aligns 
with the methodology used to develop the City’s GHG reduction targets. Importantly, GHG emissions 
reductions were quantified for measures wherever substantial evidence and reasonable assumptions 
were available to support calculations. Some of the GHG reduction measures were identified as not 
quantifiable because of lack of available data or quantification methods but would still be expected 
to reduce GHG emissions. They can be monitored for potential quantification opportunities in the 
future if data and/or quantification methods become available.

summarized in Table 4.9-5. Detailed measure calculations and assumptions supporting the GHG 
reduction estimates are provided in the CAP Update.

As shown, implementation of the CAP Update would achieve the 2030 GHG reduction targets and 
would make substantial progress towards 2045 and 2050 targets. While the GHG reduction targets 
for 2045 and 2050 are not met with quantified measures alone, the measures presented here are 
intended to be feasible with current City resources and cost-effective for community members. The 
measures have been developed to set the City on a pathway that aligns with the statewide GHG 
reduction targets and demonstrate alignment with the state’s key priorities of building electrification, 
preserving natural lands, infill-focused development, and expanding zero-emission vehicle access. 
The quantified GHG reductions for measures have been developed to ensure that near-term 
implementation actions can be substantially supported. However, some measures include longer-
term actions that are supportive of the state’s priorities but have not been quantified due to a lack 
of data or the inability to define programs in sufficient detail at this time. The City will monitor 
progress towards meeting near- and long-term reduction targets and update the CAP regularly to 
evaluate how new technologies, funding opportunities, and state and federal actions may support 
the City in reaching long-term CAP goals. The City will also explore additional measures and 
expansion of programs as GHG reduction trends are monitored over time. Since the specific path to 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.9 Greenhouse Gas Emissions 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.9-19 
compliance for the state in regard to the long-term reduction targets will likely require development 
of technology (e.g., carbon capture and storage, direct air capture) or other changes that are not 
currently known or available, specific additional reduction measures in addition to the policies 
presented within the CAP Update would be speculative and cannot be identified at this time.   
Chapter 5 of the CAP Update establishes a monitoring program and implementation strategy for the 
CAP Update measures. Successful implementation of the CAP Update would require a coordinated 
effort between City departments, stakeholders, and the community as a whole. Each GHG reduction 
measure includes a suite of actions that are divided amongst City departments, with a timeline for 
implementation provided for each. Additionally, GHG reduction measures that have a quantified 
GHG reduction potential have key-performance indicators that are tied to GHG emissions reducing 
activities. Monitoring and reporting would consist of annual progress reports on implementation 
status of measures and actions, annual updates to City Council and Commissions on progress and 
upcoming priorities, biennial GHG inventory updates, and updates to the CAP every five years.  
As the City monitors implementation progress of the GHG reduction measures of the CAP Update, 
it may be necessary to revise or refine GHG reduction measures to more effectively and efficiently 
meet GHG reduction targets. Throughout the development of this CAP Update, the City considered 
a multitude of reduction measures to reach its GHG reduction targets. Achieving a 2045 reduction 
target is the most challenging for a local agency due to the transformative changes and scale of 
reductions needed. Two primary factors for this challenge include the availability of resources for the 
City to develop and implement new policies and programs, and the costs of these new requirements 
for residents and businesses. As such, there are potential GHG reduction measures that could result 
in additional GHG reductions that were not included in the CAP Update, but may be available for 
inclusion in future updates. Comprehensive updates to the CAP Update would occur at a minimum 
of every five years from adoption of the previous iteration.  
Future GHG emission reduction measures may be feasible beyond 2030, but are not feasible at this 
time due to limited City resources, funding, market technology, or regulatory implications. The City 
would consider these and other measures for future CAP Updates. Examples of such measures 
considered, but not included in the CAP Update due to such limiting factors include:   
• 
Develop a not-for-profit TDM agency to assist employers in the development and 
implementation of TDM plans for commute trips reductions. With development of this 
agency, require all existing and new employers that generate over 100 vehicle trips per day 
to join the agency, paying a membership fee that helps fund local TDM programs that are 
available to members. Establishing such an agency would require resources and funding not 
available to the City at this time.   
• 
Develop a nonresidential building energy benchmarking program that requires 
non-residential buildings over a certain size to annually report energy consumption to the 
City and reduce energy consumption to below a specified benchmark. Establishing, 
implementing, and monitoring such a program would require resources beyond the City’s 
limited resources at this time.   
• 
Implement a Building Energy reach code for new construction that sets a GHG emissions 
efficiency threshold, where buildings must meet a specified GHG emissions level through 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.9 Greenhouse Gas Emissions 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.9-20 
energy efficiency and energy source design features. Implications of developing a reach code 
need further legal evaluation given the passing of AB 130.   
Although additional reduction measures could be available in the future, they are deemed infeasible 
at this time for reasons identified above. Therefore, while the CAP Update would achieve the 2030 
GHG reduction target, the continued emission gap associated with 2045 and 2050 targets would 
remain, representing a significant impact. 
4.9.4.3 Significance of Impacts 
The quantification analysis demonstrated that the total estimated reductions from all GHG reduction 
measures would be sufficient to meet the 2030 GHG reduction targets consistent with state goals. 
While the CAP Update would make substantial progress towards 2045 and 2050 targets, the analysis 
shows that the quantified measures would not be sufficient to meet the 2045 and 2050 targets. The 
monitoring program and implementation strategy would allow the City to track progress towards 
these targets and make adjustments as needed. City staff will annually evaluate the implementation 
status and performance of each GHG reduction measure and its actions. The City will prepare a 
comprehensive update to the CAP every five years, with the next comprehensive update occurring 
five years from the City Council’s adoption of the CAP Update. Updates would reflect the findings 
and recommendations of the monitoring reports and GHG inventory updates.  However, long-term 
targets will likely require development of technology or other changes that are not currently known 
or available. Therefore, additional reduction measures in addition to the policies presented within 
the CAP Update would not be feasible at this time. Because at this time 2045 and 2050 targets would 
not be met, impacts would be significant.  
4.9.4.4 Mitigation 
 While the City would continue to implement and monitor the effectiveness of the CAP Update, there 
is no feasible mitigation available at this time to address the emissions gap associated with 2045 and 
2050 targets. 
4.9.4.5 Significance of Impacts after Mitigation  
Impacts would remain significant and unavoidable.

regulations are based on applicable criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, 
would the project:

4.9.5.2 Impact Analysis 
Applicable plans, policies, and regulations include statewide GHG emission targets established by 
AB 32, SB 32, and AB 1279; the 2017 Scoping Plan (which establishes a specific statewide plan to 
achieve the 2030 target); the 2022 Scoping Plan (which outlines a pathway towards  statewide carbon 
neutrality by 2045); SANDAG’s RTP/SCS; regulations regarding increased use of renewables for 
electricity production (RPS); and the California Energy Code.  
a. State Plans 
EO S-3-05 and EO B-30-15 established GHG emission reduction targets for the state, and AB 32 
launched the CARB Climate Change Scoping Plan that outlined the reduction measures needed to 
reach the 2020 target, which the state has achieved. As required by SB 32, CARB’s 2017 Climate 
Change Scoping Plan outlines reduction measures needed to achieve the 2030 target. AB 1279, the 
California Climate Crisis Act, codified the carbon neutrality target as well as a target for 
anthropogenic emissions of 85 percent below 1990 levels by 2045. The 2022 Scoping Plan was 
adopted in December 2022. The 2022 Scoping Plan lays out a path to achieve targets for carbon 
neutrality and reduce anthropogenic GHG emissions by 85 percent below 1990 levels no later than 
2045, as directed by AB 1279.

buildings have electric-only HVAC and water heating, while

ensure long-term cost savings for residents and businesses.

contractors, technicians, and construction workers with 
expertise in electrical systems by partnering with regional 
organizations and providing training to the local workforce. 
Additionally, all newly constructed City facilities will be all 
electric, starting in 2026.

to achieve the statewide GHG reduction targets consistent with SB 32 and AB 1279. However, even

4.9.6 
Cumulative Analysis 
The issue of global climate change is inherently a cumulative issue, as GHG emissions of individual 
projects cannot be shown to have a material effect on global climate change. Impacts would be 
cumulative in nature if they lead to a substantial increase in GHG emissions, when combined with 
other development. As discussed, the framework for assessing GHG emissions in the state has been 
created through AB 32, SB 32, EO S-3-05, AB 1279 and the 2017 and 2022 Scoping Plans. If a project 
demonstrates that it is sufficiently reducing its overall GHG emissions consistent with statewide 
targets, the project’s impact can be determined not to be cumulatively considerable as it would 
contribute to the state’s GHG emission reduction targets. As discussed in Section 4.9.5.1 above, with 
implementation of the CAP Update, the City would be consistent with the statewide 2030 reduction 
target. However, the analysis shows that the quantified measures would not be sufficient to meet the 
2045 and 2050 targets. Implementation of the CAP Update provides for updates to GHG inventories, 
evaluate the performance of individual strategies, evaluate progress toward the City’s reduction 
targets, and make revisions to strategies, as necessary, to ensure that the City will achieve its targets. 
However, because it is unknown at this time how 2045 and 2050 targets would be met, 
implementation of the CAP Update would result in a significant cumulative impact related to GHG.

4.10 
Hazards and Hazardous Materials 
This section addresses potential project impacts related to hazards and hazardous materials that 
could result from implementation of the Onward Oceanside project, which includes the City of 
Oceanside (City) General Plan Update (GPU), Smart and Sustainable Corridors Specific Plan (SSCSP), 
and Climate Action Plan (CAP) Update, collectively referred to as the project. The GPU would apply 
to the entire City, while the SSCSP would apply to land within the Specific Plan boundary, referred to 
as the SSCSP Planning Area. As discussed in Chapter 3.0, Project Description, the analysis of potential 
impacts focuses on parcels throughout the City where the project either (1) proposes changes to 
existing land use designations or (2) where no land use change is proposed, but growth is anticipated 
to occur. The majority of the proposed increased density and intensity of uses would be within the 
SSCSP Planning Area, as shown in Figure 3-2.  
4.10.1 
Existing Conditions 
4.10.1.1 Emergency Response 
Like all jurisdictions within the San Diego operational area, the City operates under the Standardized 
Emergency Management System (SEMS) and the National Incident Management System (NIMS). 
SEMS and NIMS are based on the Incident Command System (ICS), which is a management system 
designed to provide a structure for response to any emergency.  
The Oceanside Fire Department (OFD) is the primary emergency response service provider for the 
City, providing comprehensive strategies and training in fire prevention, fire suppression, emergency 
medical services, emergency preparedness, 911 services, marine safety, lifeguarding services, and 
community-based fire services (see Section 4.15.1.1 for details of OFD operations). The OFD also 
administers the Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) training program. The purpose of 
CERT is to create a team of trained volunteer emergency responders who can assist the City during 
an emergency. During emergencies, the City can activate CERT volunteers for additional operational 
support. 
a. San Diego County Emergency Operations Plan 
The 2018 San Diego County Emergency Operations Plan (County EOP; County of San Diego 2018) 
describes a comprehensive emergency management system that provides for a planned response 
to disaster situations associated with natural disasters, technological incidents, terrorism, and 
nuclear-related incidents. It delineates operational concepts relating to various emergency situations, 
identifies components of the Emergency Management Organization, and describes the overall 
responsibilities for protecting life and property and providing for the overall well-being of the 
population. The plan also identifies the sources of outside support that might be provided (through 
mutual aid and specific statutory authorities) by other jurisdictions, state and federal agencies, and 
the private sector. The EOP Annex-Q addresses evacuation and provides a template for development 
of other jurisdictional evacuation plans. 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.10 Hazards and Hazardous Materials 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.10-2 
b. City Emergency Operations Plan  
The City Emergency Operations Plan (City EOP; City of Oceanside 2017) provides guidance for the 
City’s response to emergencies associated with natural, manmade, and technological disasters. The 
EOP defines responsibilities, establishes an emergency organization, defines lines of 
communications, and is part of the statewide SEMS and the federal NIMS. 
4.10.1.2 Hazardous Materials 
Hazardous materials are used throughout the City for a variety of purposes including manufacturing, 
service industries, various small businesses, agriculture, medical uses, schools, and households. 
Accidents can occur in the production, use, transport, and disposal of these hazardous materials. The 
probability of accidental spills is exacerbated by the fact that the region is susceptible to earthquakes. 
4.10.1.3 Hazardous Materials Sites 
The Hazardous Waste and Substances Sites (Cortese) List is a planning document that provides 
information about the location of hazardous materials release sites in the state. California 
Government Code Section 65962.5 requires the California Environmental Protection Agency (CalEPA) 
to develop, at least annually, an updated Cortese List. The California Department of Toxic Substances 
Control (DTSC) is responsible for a portion of the information contained in the Cortese List that is 
contained in their Envirostor database (2024).  
The other main source of information for sites in the Cortese List is the California State Water 
Resources Control Board’s (State Water Board) Geotracker Database. “Geotracker” is the State Water 
Board’s Internet-accessible database system used by the state board, regional boards, and local 
agencies to track and archive compliance data from authorized or unauthorized discharges of waste 
to land, or unauthorized releases of hazardous substances from underground storage tanks. This 
system consists of a relational database, online compliance reporting features, a geographical 
information system (GIS) interface, and other features that are utilized by the state board, regional 
boards, local agencies, regulated industry and the public to input, manage, or access compliance 
and regulatory tracking data. 
Figure 4.10-1 depicts the location of active Envirostor and Geotracker hazardous materials sites. As 
shown on Figure 4.10-1, there are two active Envirostor sites and 17 active Geotracker hazardous 
materials sites throughout the City. Table 4.10-1 lists each site location and describes the site listing.

4.10.1.4 Airport Hazards 
The San Diego County Regional Airport Authority (Airport Authority), acting as the Airport Land Use 
Commission (ALUC), is responsible for preparing Airport Land Use Compatibility Plans (ALUCPs) for 
all 16 airports in San Diego County. The ALUCPs are prepared to protect and promote the safety and 
welfare of airport users and residents in the airport vicinity. Specifically, these plans seek to protect 
the public from the adverse effects of aircraft noise, to ensure that people and facilities are not 
concentrated in areas susceptible to aircraft accidents, and to ensure that no structures or activities 
encroach upon or adversely affect the use of navigable airspace. 
Risks associated with airport operations include risks to people and property located in the vicinity 
of an airport in the event of an accident, and risks to the safety of persons aboard an aircraft. Airspace 
protection policies may address the height of objects on the ground and activities that can cause 
electronic or visual impairment to navigation. The City is located within the Airport Influence Areas 
(AIA) of three airports, Oceanside Municipal Airport, Marine Corps Air Station (MCAS) Camp 
Pendleton Airport and McClellan-Palomar Airport. 
a. Oceanside Municipal Airport 
The Oceanside Municipal Airport is located on 70 acres near the northwest corner of the City. This 
airport is a general aviation airport featuring a dual runway and fuel services. Most aircraft operations 
consist of general aviation. The airport accommodates a private skydiving business and a heliport 
for the Oceanside Fire Department. The Airport Compatibility Zones associated with the airport are 
shown on Figure 4.10-2a. As shown, a large swath of the City is encompassed by AIA Review Area 2. 
Portions of the City designated as Review Area 2 are those outside of noise and safety concerns, but 
within the airspace protection and/or notification overflight areas depicted on the associated maps. 
Limits on the heights of structures, particularly in areas of high terrain, are the only restrictions on 
land uses within Review Area 2. The recordation of overflight notification documents is also required 
in locations within Review Area 2 (ALUC 2010). As also shown in Figure 4.10-2a, portions of the SSCSP, 
specifically along Mission Avenue, are located within or adjacent to more restrictive compatibility 
zones.  
b. MCAS Camp Pendleton Air Station 
MCAS Camp Pendleton Air Station (also known as Munn Field) is located approximately three miles 
northwest of the City. The air station consists of an airfield and helipads. The air station supports over 
180 helicopters and a variety of Marine Corps units and visiting aircraft from other branches of the 
Armed Forces. As shown in Figure 4.10-2b, the AIA Review Area 2 associated with Camp Pendleton 
reaches into the City along most of the northern border of the City and through the midsection.

c. McClelland-Palomar Airport 
The County of San Diego owns and operates the McClelland-Palomar Airport, which provides 
general aviation, corporate, and commercial services. McClelland-Palomar Airport is located 
approximately three miles southeast of the City, within the city of Carlsbad. It consists of 
approximately 466 acres and has one asphalt runway and one asphalt helipad. Most aircraft 
operations consist of general aviation. As shown in Figure 2.10-2b, a small portion of the southern 
most part of the City is within the AIA Review Area 2.  
4.10.1.5 Transportation of Hazardous Materials 
Hazardous materials pass through the City via the freeway, rail, and surface street system. Interstate 
5 (I-5) is along the western boundary of the City. The nearest railway is the Burlington Northern and 
Santa Fe railway which runs north-south near I-5. There are also several commuter rail lines in the 
City. While train derailments can occur at any time, it is during an earthquake that a derailment and 
hazardous materials release would pose the greatest risk. The major automotive transportation 
routes through the City include State Route 76 (SR-76), State Route 76 (SR-78), Oceanside Boulevard, 
El Camino Real, College Boulevard, and Santa Fe Avenue. 
The City has no direct authority to regulate the transport of hazardous materials on state highways 
or rail lines. Transportation of hazardous materials by truck and rail is regulated by the U.S. 
Department of Transportation (U.S. DOT). U.S. DOT regulations establish criteria for safe handling 
procedures. Federal safety standards are also included in the California Administrative Code. The 
California Health Services Department regulates the haulers of hazardous waste. 
4.10.1.6 Wildfire 
Threats from wildfire hazards are determined based on factors, including fuel loading (vegetation); 
topography; climatic conditions, such as wind, humidity, and temperature; and the proximity of 
structures and urban development to fire hazards. Wildland fire hazards are most pronounced in 
wildland-urban interface areas, or where urban development is located close to open space areas 
where vegetation can serve as fuel. Generally, the periods of greatest risk for wildland fire are the 
late summer and early fall when vegetation is at its driest. Human activity, including residential and 
agricultural burning, campfires, and the use of fireworks can all trigger fires. Natural causes such as 
lightning strikes may also start fires. 
The California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (CAL FIRE) has developed two datasets for 
fire threat and hazard mapping. The first CAL FIRE mapping dataset provides maps which show fire 
threat potential throughout California. CAL FIRE ranks fire threat based on the availability of fuel and 
the likelihood of an area burning (based on topography, fire history, and climate). These two factors 
are combined to create a five-point scale of fire threats ranging from low to extreme. The fire threat 
for the City is shown in Figure 4.10-3. As shown therein the majority of the City is unranked because

The second mapping dataset consists of Fire Hazard Severity Zones (FHSZ), which were developed 
for community planning and real estate disclosure purposes and are meant to help limit wildfire 
damage to structures through planning, prevention, and the application of risk reduction measures. 
The mapped areas, or zones, are based on factors such as fuel (e.g., flammable vegetation), slope, 
and fire weather. There are three zones, based on increasing fire hazard: moderate, high, and very 
high. As shown in Figure 4.10-4, the majority of the City is  in urban areas not mapped within a FHSZ. 
Two Very High FHSZ are mapped within the City: north of SR-76 between Capistrano Park and 
Fireside Park; and  running the southern border of the City adjacent to the city of Carlsbad.  
4.10.1.7 Evacuation  
a. Evacuation Routes 
The City’s existing Public Safety Element includes evacuation routes and refugee centers for people 
who are forced from their homes during a disaster. The major streets and highways within the City 
would provide primary evacuation routes, and schools would serve as refuge centers capable of 
providing food and shelter (City of Oceanside 2002). The City’s adopted Public Safety Element of the 
General Plan contains a map of existing emergency evacuation routes that includes the major streets 
running through the City:  
• 
North-South Roads: Coast Highway, I-5, El Camino Real, College Boulevard, and North Sante 
Avenue 
• 
East-West Roads: Mission Avenue, Oceanside Boulevard, Vista Way, and SR-76 
Although the GPU updates safety related goals and policies relating to emergency response and 
evacuation, the existing evacuation routes provide a baseline for the existing safety setting.

As shown in Figure 4.10-5, a majority of communities between SR-76 and the Camp Pendleton 
border and areas along the San Luis Rey River are limited to a single access for evacuation. This area 
is within designated high fire threat areas and VHFHSZ (see Figures 4.10-3 and 4.10-4) where 
flammable vegetation is densest. There are also a few residential parcels located along the coast in 
the south Oceanside area and near flood zones adjacent to creek channels where residents may 
have limited evacuation access. 
b. Evacuation Procedures and Alerts 
The City is committed to ensuring residents are aware of local evacuation procedures and systems 
available in case of an emergency. Various emergency warning systems are used by the City including 
mobile emergency vehicle sirens and loudspeakers, public amplification systems, local television and 
radio stations, social media, emergency preparedness applications for smartphones, and door-to-
door notification by CERT. Additionally, the City employs AlertSanDiego, a reverse 9-1-1 system used 
to notify residences and businesses they may be at risk during an emergency. 
4.10.2 Regulatory Setting  
4.10.2.1 Federal  
a. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA) is the primary federal agency regulating 
hazardous wastes and materials. U.S. EPA broadly defines a hazardous waste as one that is specifically 
listed in U.S. EPA regulations, has been tested and meets one of the four characteristics established 
by the U.S. EPA (toxicity, ignitability, corrosiveness, and reactivity), or that has been declared 
hazardous by the generator based on its knowledge of the waste. U.S. EPA defines hazardous 
materials as any item or chemical that can cause harm to people, plants, or animals when released 
by spilling, leaking, pumping, pouring, emptying, discharging, injecting, leaching, dumping, or 
disposing into the environment. Federal regulations pertaining to hazardous wastes and materials 
are generally contained in Titles 29, 40, and 49 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR).  
b. Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act 
Discovery of environmental health damage from disposal sites prompted the U.S. Congress to pass 
the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA or 
Superfund). The purpose of the CERCLA is to identify and clean up chemically contaminated sites 
that pose a significant environmental health threat. The Hazard Ranking System is used to determine 
whether a site should be placed on the National Priorities List for cleanup activities.

c. Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act 
The Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act (SARA) pertain primarily to emergency 
management of accidental releases. It requires formation of state and local emergency planning 
committees, responsible for collecting, material handling, and transportation data for use as a basis 
for planning. Chemical inventory data are made available to the community at large under the “right-
to-know” provision of the law. In addition, SARA also requires annual reporting of continuous 
emissions and accidental releases of specified compounds. These annual submissions are compiled 
into a nationwide Toxics Release Inventory (TRI). 
d. Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976 
The Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976 (42 United States Code Sections 6901–6987), 
including the Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments of 1984, protects human health and the 
environment, and imposes regulations on hazardous waste generators, transporters, and operators 
of treatment, storage, and disposal facilities. The Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments also 
require the U.S. EPA to establish a comprehensive regulatory program for underground storage 
tanks. The corresponding regulations in 40 CFR Parts 260–299 provide the general framework for 
managing hazardous waste, including requirements for entities that generate, store, transport, treat, 
and dispose of hazardous waste. 
e. Hazardous Materials Transportation Act  
The U.S. DOT regulates hazardous materials transportation under Title 49 of the United States Code 
(U.S.C.). State agencies with primary responsibility for enforcing federal and state regulations and 
responding to hazardous materials transportation emergencies are the California Highway Patrol 
and the California Department of Transportation. These agencies also govern permitting for 
hazardous materials transportation. Title 49 CFR reflects laws passed by Congress as of January 2, 
2006.  
f. Federal Response Plan  
The Federal Response Plan of 1999 is a signed agreement among 27 federal departments and 
agencies, including the America Red Cross, that (1) provides the mechanism for coordinating delivery 
of federal assistance and resources to augment efforts of state and local governments overwhelmed 
by a major disaster or emergency; (2) supports implementation of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster 
Relief and Emergency Act, as well as individual agency statutory authorities; and (3) supplements 
other federal emergency operations plans developed to address specific hazards. The Federal 
Response Plan is implemented in anticipation of a significant event likely to result in a need for 
federal assistance or in response to an actual event requiring federal assistance under a presidential 
declaration of a major disaster or emergency. 
g. Disaster Mitigation Act 
The Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000 requires that a state mitigation plan, as a condition of disaster 
assistance, add incentives for increased coordination and integration of mitigation activities at the 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.10 Hazards and Hazardous Materials 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.10-15 
state level through the establishment of requirements for two different levels of state plans: 
“Standard” and “Enhanced”. States that develop an approved Enhanced State Plan can increase the 
amount of funding available through the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program. The Disaster Mitigation 
Act also established a new requirement for local mitigation plans. 
4.10.2.2 State  
a. Environmental Health Standards for the Management of Hazardous Waste 
California Code of Regulations (CCR) Title 22, Division 4.5 provides standards applicable to 
generators and transporters of hazardous wastes, and standards for operators of hazardous waste 
transfer facilities, among other regulations. 
b. Hazardous Materials Release Response Plans and Inventory 
Two programs in the California Health and Safety Code (H&SC) Chapter 6.95 are directly applicable 
to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) issue of risk due to hazardous substance release. 
In San Diego County, these two programs are referred to as the Hazardous Materials Business Plan 
(HMBP) program and the California Accidental Release Prevention (CalARP) program. The County 
Department of Environmental Health and Quality (DEHQ) is responsible for the implementation of 
the HMBP program and the CalARP program in San Diego County. The HMBP and CalARP programs 
provide threshold quantities for regulated hazardous substances.  
All facilities subject to CalARP requirements must submit a Risk Management Plan (RMP). An RMP is 
a document prepared by the owner or operator of a stationary source containing detailed 
information including, but not limited to, the regulated substance being handled or processed, 
potential consequences of accidental release, accident history, emergency response procedures, and 
training. 
c. Senate Bill 1889, Accidental Release Prevention Law/Chemical Accident Release 
Prevention Program 
Senate Bill (SB) 1889 required California to implement a federally mandated program governing the 
accidental airborne release of chemicals listed under Section 112 of the Clean Air Act. Effective 
January 1, 1997, CalARP replaced the previous California Risk Management and Prevention Program 
and incorporated the mandatory federal requirements. CalARP addresses facilities containing 
specified hazardous materials that, if involved in an accidental release, could result in adverse off-
site consequences. CalARP defines regulated substances as chemicals that pose a threat to public 
health and safety or the environment because they are highly toxic, flammable, or explosive. 
d. Emergency Response to Hazardous Materials Incidents 
California has developed an emergency response plan to coordinate emergency services provided 
by federal, state, and local governments and private agencies. Response to hazardous material 
incidents is one part of this plan. The plan is managed by the California Emergency Management 
Agency, which coordinates the responses of other agencies, including the CalEPA, California Highway 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.10 Hazards and Hazardous Materials 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.10-16 
Patrol, California Department of Fish and Wildlife, and Regional Water Quality Control Board 
(RWQCB). 
e. Cortese List: Section 65962.5(a) 
The Cortese List refers to provisions in Government Code Section 65962.5, which requires that the 
California DTSC, State Department of Health Services, State Water Resources Control Board (SWRCB), 
and designated local enforcement agencies compile and update lists of hazardous materials sites 
under their purview as specified in the code. The “Cortese List” consists of the information provided 
by these agencies under the code. 
The DTSC Brownfields and Environmental Restoration Program EnviroStor database provides DTSC's 
component of the Cortese List data by identifying State Response, Federal Superfund, and Backlog 
sites listed under H&SC Section 25356, as well as Certified with Operation and Maintenance sites. 
The EnviroStor database identifies sites that have known contamination or potentially contaminated 
sites requiring further investigation, and facilities permitted to treat, store, or dispose of hazardous 
waste. The EnviroStor database includes lists of the following site types: federal Superfund; State 
Response, including military facilities and State Superfund; voluntary cleanup; and school sites.  
The SWRCB GeoTracker database tracks sites that impact groundwater or have the potential to 
impact groundwater. It includes sites that require groundwater cleanup such as Leaking 
Underground Storage Tanks, Department of Defense, and Site Cleanup Program sites, as well as 
permitted facilities that could impact groundwater such as operating Underground Storage Tanks 
(USTs), irrigated lands, oil and gas production sites, and land disposal sites.  
f. California Department of Toxic Substances Control 
Within the CalEPA, the DTSC has primary regulatory responsibility, with delegation of enforcement 
to local jurisdictions that enter into agreements with the state agency, for the management of 
hazardous materials and the generation, transport, and disposal of hazardous waste under the 
authority of the Hazardous Waste Control Law. Since August 1, 1992, the DTSC has been authorized 
to implement the state’s hazardous waste management program for the CalEPA. 
g. Local Enforcement Agency/Integrated Waste Management Board: Burn Ash 
Sites 
The Local Enforcement Agency covers the process for evaluating and remediating burn dump sites. 
The Local Enforcement Agency provides guidance on the appropriate procedures to follow in 
evaluating the risks to public health and safety and the environment posed by burn ash dump sites 
and identify the steps to take to control these risks. The Integrated Waste Management Board 
conducts site assessments to classify and regulate burn sites.  
h. State Water Resources Control Board 
The San Diego RWQCB is authorized by the SWRCB to enforce provisions of the Porter–Cologne 
Water Quality Control Act of 1969. This act gives the San Diego RWQCB authority to require 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.10 Hazards and Hazardous Materials 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.10-17 
groundwater investigations when the quality of groundwater or surface waters of the state is 
threatened and to require remediation of the site, if necessary. 
i. The California Department of Transportation 
The California Department of Transportation manages more than 50,000 miles of California's 
highway and freeway lanes, provides inter-city rail services, permits more than 400 public-use 
airports and special-use hospital heliports, and works with local agencies. The California Department 
of Transportation is also the first responder for hazardous material spills and releases that occur on 
highway and freeway lanes and inter-city rail services. 
j. State Hazard Mitigation Plan 
The State Hazard Mitigation Plan (SHMP) is the state’s hazard mitigation guidance document and 
provides a comprehensive description of California’s historical and current hazard analysis, mitigation 
strategies, goals, and objectives. The SHMP reflects the state’s commitment to reduce or eliminate 
potential risks and impacts of natural and human-caused disasters by making California’s families, 
homes, and communities better prepared and more disaster-resilient. The SHMP is also a federal 
requirement under the Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000 for the State of California to receive federal 
funds for disaster assistance grant programs. 
k. State Aeronautics Act  
Through the State Aeronautics Act, every county that contains a public airport must develop and 
comply with an ALUCP with a 20-year planning horizon. The purpose of an ALUCP is to protect 
public health, safety, and welfare by providing for the orderly growth and land use development of 
the area surrounding the airport. ALUCP policies generally set controls on land use and development 
standards that ensure safe and efficient airport and flight operations and minimize the public’s 
exposure to excessive noise and safety hazards within the airport’s vicinity. An ALUCP does not 
designate land uses but instead establishes criteria to encourage the development of compatible 
land uses. It also has no ability to alter existing non-conforming uses; the focus is on future 
development.  
The body responsible for creating and carrying out the ALUCP is each respective county’s ALUC or 
other designated agency. The Airport Authority serves as the ALUC for San Diego County.  
l. California Underground Storage Tank Regulations 
The California Underground Storage Tank Regulations (CCR Title 23, Chapter 16) includes guidelines 
and standards to protect waters from hazardous substance discharges from USTs. The regulations 
establish construction requirements for new USTs; establish separate monitoring requirements for 
new and existing USTs; establish uniform requirements for unauthorized release reporting and for 
the repair, upgrade, and closure of USTs; and specify variance request procedures. It requires 
responsible parties to remediate any unauthorized releases from USTs. 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.10 Hazards and Hazardous Materials 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.10-18 
m. California Fire Code 
The California Fire Code (CFC) provides regulatory direction for the maintenance of brush 
management zones (BMZs), access road standards, placement of fire hydrants, and numerous other 
design and maintenance requirements for development projects. With respect to construction and 
demolition activities, Chapter 33 of the CFC outlines general fire safety precautions for all structures 
and all occupancies during construction and demolition operations. In general, these requirements 
seek to maintain required levels of fire protection, limit fire spread, establish the appropriate 
operation of equipment, and promote prompt response to fire emergencies. Features regulated 
include fire protection systems, fire fighter access to the site and building, means of egress, 
hazardous materials storage, and use and temporary heating equipment and other ignition sources. 
Chapter 7A of the CFC addresses structural ignition resistance and reducing ember penetration into 
homes. The CFC focuses on mitigating structural vulnerabilities through construction techniques and 
materials so that the buildings are resistant to ignitions from direct flames, heat, and embers, as 
indicated (Chapter 7-A, Section 701A Scope, Purpose, and Application). 
n. Attorney General Wildfire Guidance 
The California Office of the Attorney General issued guidance (Guidance) outlining best practices for 
analyzing and mitigating wildfire impacts of development projects under CEQA (State of California 
2022). The Guidance is intended to help local governments’ evaluation and approval considerations 
for development projects in fire-prone areas, and to help project design in a way that minimizes 
wildfire ignition and incorporates emergency access and evacuation measures. Importantly, the 
Guidance does not impose additional legal requirements on local governments, nor does it alter any 
applicable laws or regulations. The Guidance suggests best practices including establishing baseline 
conditions, guidance for local governments in establishing thresholds of significance, modeling fire 
behavior and risk, providing qualitative assessment of fire risk, and offering potential measures to 
mitigate fire risk. The Guidance additionally addresses wildfire evacuation analysis best practices. 
o. California Division of Occupational Safety and Health  
The California H&SC is the collection of state laws that govern the handling of hazardous waste, 
corrective action (remediation), and permitted facilities. The California Division of Occupational 
Safety and Health, or Cal/OSHA, defines and enforces worker safety standards and requires proper 
handling and disposal of hazardous materials including asbestos containing materials and lead 
containing surfaces according to the Occupational Safety and Health Act and federal and state EPA 
regulations. The Occupational Safety and Health Act/EPA Occupational Chemical Database compiles 
information from several government agencies and organizations. This database provides reports 
on physical properties, exposure guidelines, and emergency response information, including the 
U.S. DOT emergency response guide.

4.10.2.3 Regional  
a. Certified Unified Program Agency 
In 1993, SB 1082 gave the CalEPA the authority and responsibility to establish a unified hazardous 
waste and hazardous materials management and regulatory program, commonly referred to as the 
Unified Program. This program consolidates and coordinates six different hazardous materials and 
hazardous waste programs, and to ensure that they are consistently implemented throughout the 
state. The six programs include the following: Aboveground Petroleum Storage Ace Program; 
California Accidental Release Prevention Program; Hazardous Materials Business Plan Program; 
Hazardous Materials Management and Inventory Program; Hazardous Waste and Hazardous Waste 
Treatment Program; and Underground Storage Tank Program. The CalEPA oversees the Unified 
Program with support from DTSC, the RWQCBs, Office of Emergency Services, and the state Fire 
Marshal. 
State law requires the County and local agencies to implement the Unified Program. The agency in 
charge of implementing the program is called the Certified Unified Program Agency. The Hazardous 
Materials Division (HMD) of the County’s DEHQ is the Certified Unified Program Agency for San 
Diego County. 
b. County of San Diego Department of Environmental Health and Quality 
The HMD of the County’s DEHQ regulates hazardous waste and tiered permitting, USTs, 
aboveground petroleum storage and risk management plans, hazardous materials business plans 
and chemical inventory, and medical waste. The HMD’s goal is to protect human health and the 
environment by ensuring that hazardous materials, hazardous waste, medical waste, and 
underground storage tanks are properly managed. 
The County’s DEHQ HMD offers a Voluntary Assistance Program (VAP) that provides staff 
consultation, project oversight, and technical and environmental report evaluation on projects 
proposed on properties suspected or known to be contaminated with hazardous substances. This 
program allows for oversight of environmental assessment, cleanup, and risk evaluation to facilitate 
the rapid and cost-effective resolution of soil and groundwater contamination problems. A “No 
Further Action” letter or "Concurrence" letter is issued when the technical information, findings, and 
recommendations in the reports submitted demonstrate that human health and the environment 
are adequately protected. 
c. San Diego County Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan 
On February 7, 2023, the Board of Supervisors of the County of San Diego adopted the revised 2023 
Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan (MJHMP). The MJHMP is a countywide plan that identifies 
risks and ways to minimize damage by natural and manmade disasters. The MJHMP is a 
comprehensive document that serves many purposes, including creating a decision tool for 
management, promoting compliance with state and federal program requirements, enhancing local 
policies for hazard mitigation capability, and providing inter-jurisdictional coordination. The MJHMP 
includes potential mitigation actions related to wildfires and release of hazardous materials.

Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.10-20 
Specifically related to the City, wildfire and associated evacuation are included as potential hazards. 
The City has developed the following objectives and action items to assist in the reduction of hazards 
related to wildfire: 
• 
Objective 7.A: Develop a comprehensive approach to reducing the possibility of damage and 
losses due to wildfires. 
o Action 7.A.1 Utilize aggressive vegetation management programs to provide buffer zones 
between unimproved wildland and development. 
o Action 7.A.2 Adopt local building ordinances which improve building standards in 
urban/wildland interface (UWI) areas including defensible space, noncombustible 
fencing, boxed eaves, extruded metal window frames, Class-A non-combustible roofs 
and exterior wall coverings, and protected attic venting. 
o Action 7.A.3 Coordinate with federal, state and local wildlife agency representatives to 
develop regulations regarding brush management within sensitive areas and incorporate 
the regulations into the City’s Subarea Plan. 
d. San Diego County Emergency Operations Plan 
The County EOP describes a comprehensive emergency management system that provides for a 
planned response to disaster situations associated with natural disasters, technological incidents, 
terrorism, and nuclear-related incidents. It delineates operational concepts relating to various 
emergency situations, identifies components of the Emergency Management Organization, and 
describes the overall responsibilities for protecting life and property and providing for the overall 
well-being of the population. The plan also identifies the sources of outside support that might be 
provided (through mutual aid and specific statutory authorities) by other jurisdictions, state and 
federal agencies, and the private sector. 
4.10.2.4 Local  
a. City of Oceanside Emergency Operations Plan  
The City EOP forms the basis for the conduct and coordination of emergency operations within the 
City. The City EOP provides a system for the effective management of emergency situations; identifies 
lines of authority and relationships; assigns tasks and responsibilities; ensures adequate facilities, 
services, and resources; and provides a framework for adequate resources for recovery operations. 
b. City of Oceanside Code of Ordinances 
Chapter 3B Airport 
Article II of Chapter 3B is the City’s Airport Zoning Ordinance which was created for the purpose of 
preventing the creation or establishment of airport hazards to protect the lives and property of the 
occupants of the land located in the vicinity of airport landing areas. The regulations apply to the 
Oceanside Municipal Airport and surrounding zones are divided into the following: approach zones, 
transition zones, horizontal and conical surfaces. The Airport Zoning Ordinance includes height limits 
and use restrictions.

Chapter 14 Health and Sanitation 
The City adopted the County of San Diego Code of Regulations Sections 68.801 through 68.814 
related to the release of and response to hazardous material release incidents. Additional sections 
throughout the chapter include regulations relating to accumulation of hazardous materials, and 
liability for unauthorized disposal and/or release.  
Chapter 11 Fire Prevention 
The City adopts the California Fire Code as the governing regulations for the safeguarding of life and 
property from fire and explosion hazards arising from the storage, handling, and use of hazardous 
substances, materials and devices, and from conditions hazardous to life or property in the 
occupancy of buildings and premises and in the erection, construction, enlargement, alteration, 
repair, moving, removal, conversion, demolition, equipment use, and maintenance of buildings and 
structures.  
4.10.3 Proposed GPU and SSCSP Policies  
The proposed GPU and SSCSP include policies intended to reduce potential adverse environmental 
impacts resulting from buildout of the plans. As future development is proposed, development 
would be required to demonstrate consistency with the GPU and SSCSP policy framework, as 
applicable. The policy framework would be implemented by the City during future discretionary 
and/or ministerial project reviews to ensure impact minimization. The analysis of potential impacts 
considers how implementation of these policies at the project level would serve to reduce the 
significance of potential adverse impacts. 
4.10.3.1 Policy Framework  
The following policies are examples of the policy framework intended to minimize hazards 
throughout the City, and do not intend to be exclusive of all additional relevant policies that may 
apply to future development. 
a. GPU Safe and Resilient Environment Element (SRE) 
The SRE assesses the City’s exposure to natural and human-induced hazards and outlines goals, 
policies, and actions designed to mitigate the risk of injury and property damage associated with 
these hazards.  
Fire Hazards 
• 
Policy 6-23: Provide adequate staffing, equipment, technology, and funding for the 
Oceanside Fire Department to meet existing and projected service demands and response 
times. 
• 
Policy 6-25: Manage vegetation and the urban forest to reduce combustible load, erosion, 
and other terrain factors that influence fire likelihood and fire behavior. As such, the City’s 
Fire Department will conduct inspections to identify and mitigate existing non-conforming 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.10 Hazards and Hazardous Materials 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.10-22 
development to contemporary fire safe standards, in terms of road standards and vegetative 
hazard.  
• 
Policy 6-26: The City’s Fire Department will establish long-term ongoing maintenance for 
vegetation management and defensible space along city-maintained roads, open space 
areas, and fuel breaks. 
• 
Policy 6-28: Assess ways to minimize fire threats in the Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone 
(VHFHSZ) around and north of the Municipal Airport and along the Camp Pendleton border, 
including through reducing fire load, removing combustible invasive species, and creating 
fuel breaks and buffers. 
• 
Policy 6-29: Require all new development or redevelopment in the VHFHZ to incorporate 
fire-resistant building materials and design features, such as visible signage, consistent with 
the adopted Municipal Code and the most current versions of the California Code of 
Regulations, California Building Code, and California Fire Code.  
• 
Policy 6-30: New residential development should be avoided or minimized within the 
VHFHSZ and along the Camp Pendleton border. Following a large fire, development or 
redevelopment in the area should be evaluated.  
• 
Policy 6-31: In consultation with property owners, maintain practices to minimize fire risk in 
the VHFHSZ. These practices could include:  
o Incorporating fuel modification and defensible space techniques in accordance with 
applicable fire safety requirements and carried out in a manner which reduces impacts 
to environmentally sensitive habitat to the maximum feasible extent; 
o Conducting annual vegetation inspections by the City’s Fire Department of all properties; 
o Requiring annual self-reports by properties to the City that all installed fire alarms and 
sprinklers are functioning; 
o Using fire-retardant, native plant species in landscaping; 
o Complying with established standards and specifications for fuel modification, defensible 
space, access, and water facilities; and 
o Banning generators and fuel storage (e.g., for generators) in VHFHSZ. 
• 
Policy 6-32: Maintain fuel breaks where feasible and prioritize development in areas with 
existing adequate road networks, evacuation routes, and water infrastructure. Require any 
new development on sites of more than two acres in the VHFHSZ to comply with 
requirements in Policy 6-27 and prepare a Fire Protection Plan that minimizes risks by:  
o Assessing site-specific characteristics such as topography, slope, vegetation type, wind 
patterns, etc.; 
o Siting and designing development to avoid hazardous locations to the extent feasible; 
o Requiring street improvements to comply with minimum fire road access standards; and 
o Disallowing new subdivisions in areas with less than two evacuation routes (as shown in 
Figure 6-9) unless a development were to be able to provide additional connections to 
ameliorate this condition. 
• 
Policy 6-34: Continue to review development proposals to ensure that they incorporate 
required and appropriate fire-mitigation measures, including adequate provisions for 
occupant evacuation as well as access by fire-fighting personnel and equipment.

Policy 6-36: Ensure community access to up-to-date fire risk mapping, evacuation route

Policy 6-39: Maintain mutual aid agreements with adjoining jurisdictions, including Camp

Policy 6-40: In partnership with SDCWA, plan for the ongoing maintenance and long-term

Hazardous Materials 
• 
Goal 6-L: The City will minimize health and safety impacts related to the use, storage, 
manufacture, and transport of hazardous materials. 
• 
Policy 6-63: Review proposed facilities that would produce or store hazardous materials –
including gas, natural gas, or other fuels – to identify and require feasible mitigation of any 
significant risks. The review shall consider, at a minimum, the following: 
o Presence of seismic or geologic hazards;  
o Presence of other hazardous materials;  
o Proximity to residential development, sensitive receptors, and areas in which substantial 
concentrations of people exist, particularly communities already overburdened by 
pollution; and   
o Nature and level of risk and hazard associated with the proposed project.  
• 
Policy 6-64: Continue to ensure buildings and sites are or have been investigated for the 
presence of hazardous materials and/or waste contamination before development or if there 
is reason to believe an existing building or site may contain hazardous materials that pose a 
threat to possible users. Continue to require remediation and construction techniques for 
adequate protection of construction workers, future occupants, adjacent residents, and the 
environment. 
• 
Policy 6-65: Continue to coordinate with the County of San Diego’s HMD, the unified-
program agency responsible for issuing permits for and inspection of certain industrial 
facilities, monitoring the filing of disclosure forms and risk-management plans, and preparing 
hazardous materials assessment reports, remediation plans, and closure plans for such 
facilities. 
• 
Policy 6-66: Seek to prevent industrial and transportation accidents involving release of 
hazardous materials and enhance the City’s capacity to respond to such incidents through 
coordination with the California Highway Patrol, California Department of Transportation, 
and LOSSAN Rail Corridor Agency.  
• 
Policy 6-67: Supply the public with up-to-date information on existing hazardous materials 
sites and any known releases of hazardous materials in the City.  
• 
Policy 6-68: Assist residents in identifying and mitigating potential household hazards and 
encourage residents to dispose of hazardous household materials at the Household 
Hazardous Waste Facility operated by the City’s contracted waste hauler.

Policy 6-69: Ensure that operations involving hazardous materials are generally contained 
within enclosed buildings and that outdoor handling of such materials occurs in areas

Airport Hazards 
• 
Goal 6-M: Oceanside Municipal Airport will operate in accordance with all applicable 
standards established by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the San Diego 
Regional Airport Authority (SDRAA). Implementation of the Airport Land Use Compatibility 
Plan will ensure that land use and development in proximity to the airport does not create 
unacceptable levels of risk to aviation operations or people and property in the vicinity. 
• 
Policy 6-71: Periodically review and coordinate with the SDRAA staff on updates and 
modifications to the Oceanside Municipal Airport Airport Land Use Compatibility Plan 
(ALUCP). 
• 
Policy 6-72: Require land uses surrounding the Oceanside Municipal Airport to be consistent 
with the adopted ALUCP and restrict development of potentially hazardous obstructions or 
other hazards to flight. Discourage uses that may impact airport operations or do not meet 
Federal or State aviation standards. 
• 
Policy 6-76: Consider incentives to encourage contracted airport operators to address 
potential safety hazards and implement state-of-the-art safety protocols and technologies.  
Evacuation and Emergency Response 
• 
Goal 6-P: The health, safety, and welfare of people and property will be protected through 
the provision of adequate fire protection services, marine safety protocols, flood hazard 
mitigation, enforcement of building and fire codes, training and safety education, and 
emergency medical and rescue services. 
• 
Goal 6-Q: The City will ensure adequate evacuation access, fire prevention activities, and 
emergency response for all residents and visitors. 
• 
Goal 6-R: The City will coordinate across all municipal operations to provide comprehensive 
services during emergencies, including hazard mitigation, rescue efforts, public information, 
emergency medical care, temporary shelter, and sustenance. 
• 
Policy 6-79: Require that new residential development be served by more than one 
evacuation route, where feasible.  
• 
Policy 6-80: As part of the City’s Vegetation Management Plan, provide vegetation clearance 
on all public and private roads and maintain a higher level of tree and vegetation 
maintenance along Regional and Primary evacuation routes as shown on Figure 6-10, and 
remove flammable trees that could fall and block these routes. 
• 
Policy 6-81: Partner with Caltrans and neighboring jurisdictions on measures to protect critical 
evacuation routes and work with local agencies to develop contingency plans that address 
disconnected routes and explore roadway improvements that can provide better emergency 
access under emergency evacuation scenarios.

Policy 6-82: In partnership with the North County Transit District (NCTD), Oceanside Unified 
School District (OUSD), Emergency Operations Center (EOC) Transportation Unit, and law

designated shelter facilities during times of emergency.

• 
Policy 6-87: Prioritize capital improvements and maintenance of public facilities such as fire

free air filtration mask distribution, food and vaccine distribution, clean water, testing centers, 
evacuation/disaster shelters, etc.).  
• 
Policy 6-88: Locate critical facilities, such as hospitals and health care facilities, emergency 
shelters, fire stations, police stations, emergency command centers, and other emergency 
service facilities and utilities so as to minimize exposure to flooding, seismic, geologic, 
wildfire, and other hazards, except those facilities that provide frontline access, such as fire 
stations in areas of fire hazard. If critical facilities must be located in hazard zones, require 
building construction and materials that minimize hazard, safe access for emergency 
response vehicles, visible street signs, and adequate infrastructure for emergency scenarios, 
such as flooding, backup power and water supplies. 
• 
Policy 6-92: Continue to offer community training on emergency prevention, preparedness 
and response as part of the CERT program. Partner with community organizations to target 
harder-to-reach populations, such as the unhoused or linguistically isolated populations.  
b. GPU Efficient and Compatible Land Use Element (ECLU)  
The ECLU strives to strike a balance between accommodating new development, which provides for 
housing, employment, and essential services, and the protection against natural and man-made 
hazards. 
• 
Policy 3-24: Site and design new development to mitigate risk associated with earthquakes, 
landslides, fire, flooding, and other natural hazards.

The SSCSP Environmental Quality chapter addresses natural and man-made hazards including 
prevention and remediation measures supportive of federal, state and local regulations.

Hazardous Materials 
• 
Goal 4: Thorough remediation and abatement practices consistent with federal, state, and

• 
Policy EQ-15: Prevention of Exposure. Require proponents of projects within 100 feet of

documentation of assessment be submitted to City staff prior to issuance of development 
permits. 
•

been identified, require that documentation of site investigations and any required cleanup 
activities to be submitted to City staff during the development review process. Remediation 
and clean up of any contaminated sites in the Planning Area shall be in accordance with 
federal and State standards. 
d. SSCSP Land Use 
• 
Policy LU-45: Compatibility of Industrial Uses. Promote new industrial uses with higher 
employment densities in industrial areas within the corridor and ensure that such uses are 
compatible with surrounding land uses and do not negatively impact Loma Alta Creek. Site 
and building design shall minimize impacts, including but limited to noise, odors, traffic and 
aesthetics. 
4.10.4 Hazardous Materials  
4.10.4.1 Thresholds of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to hazardous materials are based on 
applicable criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Create a significant hazard to the public or the environment through the routine transport, 
use, or disposal of hazardous materials? 
• 
Create a significant hazard to the public or the environment through reasonably foreseeable 
upset and accident conditions involving the release of hazardous materials into the 
environment? 
• 
Emit hazardous emissions or handle hazardous or acutely hazardous materials, substances, 
or waste within one-quarter mile of an existing or proposed school? 
• 
Be located on a site which is included on a list of hazardous materials sites compiled pursuant 
to Government Code Section 65962.5 and, as a result, create a significant hazard to the public 
or environment? 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.10 Hazards and Hazardous Materials 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.10-27 
4.10.4.2 Impact Analysis 
Hazardous materials are any substance or combination of substances that may pose a risk to human 
health and safety or to the environment. Hazardous materials include toxic, corrosive, infectious, 
flammable, explosive and radioactive materials. Businesses, public or private institutions and private 
households all use or generate hazardous materials to some extent. Hazardous materials are 
routinely manufactured, used, stored or transported in nearly every community and therefore the 
risk of upset or discharge could occur within the City. 
a. Routine Use, Transport, and Disposal  
The City has no direct authority to regulate the transport of hazardous materials on state highways. 
This activity is governed by the U.S. DOT, as described in Title 49 of the CFR and by Title 13 of the 
CCRs. The state Office of Hazardous Materials Safety enforces regulations for the safe transportation 
of hazardous materials. New development or redevelopment under the GPU and SSCSP could result 
in the need to transport hazardous materials to and from specific project sites. Future projects would 
be required to ascertain appropriate documentation for all hazardous waste that is transported in 
connection with project site activities and would be provided as required by hazardous materials 
regulations. Hazardous waste produced on-site would be subject to regulatory requirements 
associated with accumulation, time limits, proper storage locations and containers, and proper 
labeling. Additionally, for removal of hazardous waste from a particular site, hazardous waste 
generators would be required to use a certified hazardous waste transportation company, which 
must ship hazardous waste to a permitted facility for treatment, storage, recycling, or disposal. 
Specifically, the California Hazardous Materials Management Act requires that businesses handling 
or storing certain amounts of hazardous materials prepare a Hazardous Materials Business 
Emergency Plan, which includes an inventory of hazardous materials stored on-site (above specified 
quantities), an emergency response plan, and an employee training program.  
With respect to construction, activities would involve temporary transport, management, handling, 
use, and storage of hazardous materials such as diesel fuels, lubricants, petroleum products, paints, 
solvents, and other typical chemicals required during construction. These activities could potentially 
expose workers, the public, and/or the environment to hazardous materials. Any potential exposure 
to hazardous materials would be handled in accordance with current and applicable federal, state, 
and local laws regarding safe transport, handling, and management. Such laws include the Cal/OSHA 
program, which would require the enforcement of worker safety standards and requires proper 
handling and disposal of hazardous materials. Additionally, the DTSC implements the state’s 
hazardous waste management program which ensures local regulatory agencies consistently apply 
statewide standards when they issue permits, conduct inspections, and engage in enforcement 
activities. 
Additionally, future development would be reviewed for consistency with relevant GPU and SSCSP 
goals and policies related to hazardous materials. Specifically, SRE Policy 6-64 would ensure that 
prior to development project sites are investigated for the presence of hazardous materials and/or 
waste contamination. Supplemental to regulations and GPU policies, projects within the SSCSP 
Planning Area would comply with SSCSP Environmental Quality Policies EQ-15 and EQ-16 ensuring 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.10 Hazards and Hazardous Materials 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.10-28 
that future development within 100 feet of existing hazardous sites or TAC sources to assess health 
risks, and if necessary document of site investigations and any required cleanup activities required. 
Overall, compliance with existing regulations and proposed policies relating to the use or disposal 
of hazardous materials and wastes would ensure a significant hazard to the public or the 
environment would not occur.  
b. Accidental Release 
An accidental release of hazardous materials could occur during: (1) the routine use, transport, and 
disposal of materials during project operation (as discussed above); or (2) through the accidental 
upset of hazardous materials – either known or unknown – during excavation and construction of 
future development. Exposure to hazardous materials could occur through contact with 
contaminated soil or groundwater, skin contact, or the inhalation of vapors or dust.  
Accidental releases would most likely occur in commercial and industrial areas. As shown in 
Figures 3-6, 3-7, and 3-8, and summarized in Table 3-4, the SSCSP proposes increased potential for 
commercial and industrial uses along the corridors. Future development and redevelopment projects 
would be required to adhere to applicable federal, state, regional, and local regulations focused on 
preventing release of hazardous materials. Specifically, any project that proposes a stationary source 
(business) would be regulated by the CalARP Program. If required, the proposed project would be 
required to submit an RMP under the CalARP Program. The RMP would be reviewed by HMD to 
ensure it adequately addresses all necessary information to ensure safe handling and emergency 
release procedures. Thereafter, RMPs are required to be reviewed and updated every five years.  
The MJHMP requires local jurisdictions to develop strategies for the prevention and reduction of 
hazards from accidental release of hazardous emissions. The City includes Action 9.A.3 of its Local 
Hazards Mitigation Plan to reduce possible damage from hazardous release. Action 9.A.3 requires 
the ongoing agreement with San Diego Hazardous Incident Response Team for continued support 
in emergency situations. Additionally, the City’s EOP provides guidance for hazardous materials 
releases including responsibilities of the OFD to respond, secure, and protect in the event of a 
hazardous material release situation. Other City branches would activate their emergency operations 
to support the Fire Department and provide evacuation notices and/or containment of hazardous 
locations.  
All future development throughout the City would be required to adhere to goals and policies within 
the GPU and SSCSP related to accidental release. These policies require both prevention and 
remediation of hazardous materials release. SRE Policy 6-66 seeks to prevent accidents involving 
release of hazardous materials and enhance the City’s capacity to respond to such incidents through 
coordination with federal, state, and local agencies. Also, where hazardous materials have been 
identified, SSCSP Policy EQ-16 requires documentation of site investigations and any required 
cleanup activities to be submitted to City staff during the development review process. 
Overall, compliance with existing regulations and proposed policies would ensure hazards to the 
public or the environment resulting from the accident release of hazardous materials would be 
minimized and not create a significant hazard.

c. Emissions near a School 
Schools are currently located throughout the City and could be located within a one-quarter mile of 
businesses utilizing, storing, or transporting hazardous materials. Implementation of the GPU and 
SSCSP would result in an increase in commercial and industrial uses, especially along the City’s 
corridors, in proximity to existing schools. 
As discussed above, all businesses which qualify would be required to submit a RMP under the 
CalARP Program. Each RMP would include the required information necessary to minimize potential 
release of hazardous materials. Furthermore, the City’s EOP provides direction for responding to 
hazardous release. Therefore, adherence with applicable federal, state, regional, and local plans and 
regulations, as well as proposed GPU and SSCSP policies, would ensure that accidental releases of 
hazardous materials or near existing or proposed schools would be minimized and not create a 
significant hazard. 
d. Hazardous Materials Site 
There are a total of 19 hazardous materials sites located throughout the City primarily within the 
SSCSP Planning Area (see Figure 4.10-1 and Table 4.10-1). In accordance with federal, state, regional, 
and local requirements, any new development, or redevelopment that involves contaminated 
property would necessitate the cleanup and/or remediation of the property in accordance with 
applicable requirements and regulations. No construction would be permitted at such locations until 
a “no further action” clearance letter from the responsible agency. Compliance with proposed GPU 
and SSCSP policies would likewise minimize hazards associated with hazardous material sites. 
Specifically, SRE Policy 6-64 supports actions to investigate the presence of hazardous materials 
and/or waste contamination before development. The City also commits to providing the public with 
information on existing hazardous materials sites and any known releases of hazardous materials in 
the City (SRE Policy 6-67). Within the SSCSP Planning Area, proponents of future projects within 100 
feet of existing hazardous sites or TAC sources would be required to assess health risks at the location 
in question as well as potential feasible design-related measures to minimize risks (SSCSP Policy 
EQ-15).  
Therefore, adherence to applicable cleanup and/or remediation requirements and regulations, 
coupled with compliance with City policies and COA would ensure that the project would not create 
a significant hazard associated with known hazardous materials sites. 
4.10.4.3 Significance of Impacts 
Adherence with applicable federal, state, regional, and local plans and regulations, as well as 
compliance with GPU and SSCSP policies would ensure that impacts associated with hazardous 
materials would be less than significant.  
4.10.4.4 Mitigation 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required.

4.10.5 Airport Hazards 
4.10.5.1 Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to airport hazards are based on applicable 
criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, for a project located within an airport 
land use plan or, where such a plan has not been adopted, within two miles of a public airport or 
public use airport would the project: 
• 
Result in a safety hazard or excessive noise for people residing or working in the project 
area? 
4.10.5.2 Impact Analysis 
As shown in Figures 4.10-2a and 4.10-2b, the City is located within AIA Review Area 2 of three airports, 
Oceanside Municipal Airport, MCAS Camp Pendleton Airport, and McClellan-Palomar Airport (see 
Section 4.10.1.4).  
Buildout under the GPU and SSCSP would result in greater residential density which could place 
additional residential uses within the AIAs. Future development would be required to adhere to the 
City’s Code of Ordinances Chapter 3B as well as each airport ALUCPs which sets forth policies to 
identify compatibility criteria for land uses within the airports AIAs. As shown in Figure 4.10-2a, 
portions of the City are located within Oceanside Municipal Airport AIA Review Area 1. AIA Review 
Area 1 includes six safety zones established for the purpose of evaluating the safety compatibility of 
land use development: Zone 1 comprises the immediate runway protection zone, Zone 2 the inner 
approach/departure zone, Zone 3 the inner turning zone, Zone 4 the outer approach/departure 
zone, Zone 5 the sideline zone, and Zone 6 the traffic pattern zone. Portions of the SSCSP, along 
Mission Avenue, are specifically within the Outer Approach/Departure Zone (Zone 2), and Traffic 
Pattern Zone (Zone 6). As shown in Figure 3-1, the two locations within Review Area 1 are proposed 
to support Research and Development (Zone 2) and Neighborhood Commercial (Zone 6).  
Oceanside Municipal Airport Safety Compatibility Criteria for Industrial/Research and development 
and Commercial land use types is summarized in Table 4.10-3. Future development would be 
required to adhere to safety compatibility criteria pursuant to the SRE Table 6-1.  
Additional land use compatibility criteria can be reviewed in Table III-2 of the Oceanside Municipal 
Airport ALUCP.
