Most of the airport compatibility zones that affect the City are within AIA Review Area 2. Generally, 
there are no development restrictions within Review Area 2 other than  height limits, related airspace 
protection policies, and overflight notification requirements. Within Review Area 2, only the following 
land use actions require ALUC review: 
• 
Any project which has received a final notice of determination from the FAA that the project 
will constitute a hazard or obstruction to air navigation, to the extent applicable. 
• 
Any proposed object in a High Terrain Zone or in an area of terrain penetration to airspace 
surfaces which has a height greater than 35 feet above ground level. 
• 
Any project having the potential to create electrical or visual hazards to aircraft in flight, 
including: electrical interference with radio communications or navigational signals; lighting 
which could be mistaken for airport lighting; glare or bright lights (including laser lights) in 
the eyes of pilots or aircraft using the Airport; certain colors of neon lights – especially red 
and white – that can interfere with night vision goggles; and impaired visibility near the 
airport. The local agency should coordinate with the airport operator in making this 
determination. 
• 
Any project having the potential to cause an increase in the attraction of birds or other wildlife 
that can be hazardous to aircraft operations in the vicinity of the airport (ALUC 2010).  
Future development within the airports’ AIA would also be required to adhere to proposed GPU 
policies. SRE Policy 6-72 ensures that land uses surrounding the Oceanside Municipal Airport is 
compatible with the operation of the airport and restrict development of potentially hazardous 
obstructions or other hazards to flight.  
Project sites that could support new development or redevelopment consistent with the GPU and 
SSCSP would be subject to development standards and restrictions as set forth in the City’s Airport 
Zoning Ordinance, and regulations stated in the ALUC compatibility zones. Regulatory compliance 
coupled with GPU policy consistency would ensure that the GPU and SSCSP would not result in any 
airport related safety hazards. 
4.10.5.3 Significance of Impacts 
Consistency with federal, state, and local regulations, along with consistency with GPU policies, would 
require future development to show compatibility with the zoning, ALUCPs, and associated FAA 
requirements. Impacts would be less than significant.

Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required.

restrict vehicular traffic would be required to implement appropriate measures to facilitate the 
passage of persons and vehicles through/around any required road closures.

4.10.7 Wildfires 
4.10.7.1 Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to wildfires are based on applicable criteria 
in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
 
Expose people or structures, either directly or indirectly, to a significant risk of loss, injury or 
death involving wildland fires? 
4.10.7.2 Impact Analysis 
As shown in Figures 4.10-3 and 4.10-4 and detailed in Table 4.10-2, portions of the City are within 
CAL FIRE’s Very High Fire Threat Areas and VHFHSZ as delineated by the state. Placing additional 
residential land uses adjacent to or within fire hazard areas can result in increased fire related risk to 
people and structures. While development within these higher risk areas are not precluded, it would 
require specific fire protection features be included in project designs. 
Consistent with the City’s Code of Ordinances, future development would be required to adhere to 
fire prevention regulations as detailed in the California Fire Code, as adopted by the City (Chapter 11, 
Article II, Section 11.15, City’s adoption of the CFC). Adherence to fire regulations includes adopting 
safety measures during construction activities, and installation and maintenance of fire preventive 
and protective features including fire sprinklers and landscape restrictions prior to occupancy. 
Future projects would be reviewed for consistency with proposed GPU policies focused on wildland 
fire prevention and protection. SRE Policies 6-25 and 6-26 support the removal of combustible 
invasive species and for all development to create fire fuel breaks and fuel buffers. Additionally, 
future projects encompassing greater than two acres would prepare a project-specific Fire Protection 
Plan to include an assessment of fire hazard potential, site design and safety measures to minimize 
fire hazards, ensure adequate access for fire apparatus, and providing evacuation routes (SRE Policy 
6-32). Pursuant to SRE Policy 6-29, all new development or redevelopment in the VHFHZ would 
incorporate fire-resistant building materials and design features consistent with the City’s adopted 
code and the most current versions of CBC and CFC. Management of landscape materials would also 
help prevent or reduce the spread of wildfire. Specifically, SRE Policy 6-31 encourages new 
development in the VHFHSZ to use fire-retardant, native plant species in landscaping.  


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.10 Hazards and Hazardous Materials 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.10-37 
All future projects would be designed to minimize potential hazards from wildfire through 
incorporation of site design features including construction materials, site access and fire apparatus 
support, Fuel Modification Zones, and water systems. Implementation of these measures would 
ensure future projects would not result in hazards related to wildfire. 
4.10.7.3 Significance of Impacts 
While development consistent with the GPU and SSCSP has the potential to increase fire hazards 
due to increased density and intensity of uses within higher risk fire areas, all development would be 
subject to state, and local fire safety regulations aimed at fire prevention and response. Additionally, 
new development and redevelopment would adhere to GPU policies associated with fire safety. 
Therefore, future development would not expose people or structures, to a significant risk of loss, 
injury or death involving wildland fires, and impacts would be less than significant. 
4.10.7.4 Mitigation 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required. 
4.10.8 Cumulative Analysis 
Future development could result in increased commercial and industrial uses which require the 
transport, use, and disposal of hazardous materials. New commercial and industrial could also result 
in an increase in the amount of truck traffic in the area, as well as the number of trucks potentially 
transporting hazardous materials. Therefore, the project could contribute to a cumulatively 
significant impact associated with hazardous materials. However, future development and 
redevelopment would be required to adhere to all relevant federal, state, regional, and local plans, 
regulations, and proposed GPU policies related to hazardous materials. Specifically, future projects 
would be required to provide all required information necessary to ensure that the proposed 
business is minimizing the potential for accidental release of hazardous materials. Similarly, future 
development and redevelopment would be required to adhere to applicable regulations relating to 
clean-up and/or remediation of hazardous materials, emergency access, and airport hazards. 
Furthermore, future development and redevelopment would be required to adhere to regulations 
related to wildfire, including the provision of fire prevention and emergency response services that 
minimize fire risks and protect life and property. Therefore, the project would not contribute to a 
cumulative impact related to hazards and hazardous materials.

4.11 
Hydrology and Water Quality 
This section addresses potential project impacts related to hydrology and water quality that could 
result from implementation of the Onward Oceanside project which includes the City of Oceanside 
(City) General Plan Update (GPU), Smart and Sustainable Corridors Specific Plan (SSCSP), and Climate 
Action Plan (CAP) Update, collectively referred to as the project. The GPU would apply to the entire 
City, while the SSCSP would apply to land within the Specific Plan boundary, referred to as the SSCSP 
Planning Area. As discussed in Chapter 3.0, Project Description, the analysis of potential impacts 
focuses on parcels throughout the City where the project either (1) proposes changes to existing land 
use designations or (2) where no land use change is proposed, but growth is anticipated to occur. 
The majority of the proposed increased density and intensity of uses would be within the SSCSP 
Planning Area, as shown in Figure 3-2.  
This analysis relies on secondary source information including, but not limited to, watershed, 
flooding, and hydrological conditions from geographic information systems (GIS) databases. The 
analysis also considered City programs and plans, and data available from the State Water Resources 
Control Board (SWRCB) and San Diego Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB). A discussion 
of sea level rise is also included in subsection 4.11.7(d). 
4.11.1 
Existing Conditions 
4.11.1.1 
Watershed Management Areas  
The SWRCB and RWQCB are responsible for protecting California’s water resources. California is 
divided into nine regions, also referred to as basins, based on major watersheds. The City is located 
within Region 9, San Diego Basin. The San Diego Basin encompasses approximately 3,900 square 
miles, including most of San Diego County and portions of southwestern Riverside and Orange 
counties. The basin is composed of 11 major hydrologic units, 54 hydrologic areas or units, and 
147 hydrologic subareas, extending from Laguna Beach southerly to the U.S./Mexico border (Basin 
Plan; RWQCB 2021). The Basin Plan subdivides the region into watersheds or hydrologic units (HUs), 
hydrologic areas (HAs), and hydrologic subareas (HSAs). A HU is defined as the entire watershed of 
one or more major streams. HAs consist of watersheds of major tributaries and/or major 
groundwater basins within a hydrologic unit. HSAs are major subdivisions of hydrologic areas 
including both water-bearing and non-water-bearing formations. 
As shown in Figure 4.11-1, the City is within two watersheds, also referred to as Watershed 
Management Areas (WMAs): San Luis Rey and Carlsbad watersheds.

4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-3 
The following provides a brief description of each WMA, including hydrologic data and the beneficial 
uses and impaired water bodies (water body segments not meeting water quality standards) as 
defined by the Clean Water Act (CWA) Section 303(d). 
a. San Luis Rey Watershed Management Area 
The San Luis Rey WMA encompasses a land area of about 560 square miles throughout the northern 
portion of the County of San Diego. The Lower San Luis Rey HA (903.1) portion of the San Luis Rey 
WMA comprises nearly 16,000 acres of the City. Pursuant to the CWA 303(d) list, the Lower San Luis 
Rey River, which drains into the Pacific Ocean, is listed as impaired for chloride, indicator bacteria, 
phosphorus, total dissolved solids (TDS), total nitrogen, benthic community effects and toxicity. 
Additionally, the Pacific Ocean shoreline at the San Luis Rey River outlet in Oceanside is impaired for 
indicator bacteria and is included as a regulated waterway under the regional Bacterial total 
maximum daily load (TMDL). Under the TMDL, the Pacific Ocean waters at the river's outlet is subject 
to additional regulatory requirements to reduce the frequency of public health advisories for 
bacterial contamination and is a significant driver of watershed management programs implemented 
by the City. 
b. Carlsbad Watershed Management Area 
The Carlsbad WMA comprises six distinct HAs covering a land area of 211 square miles. Three HAs 
including Loma Alta HA (904.1), Buena Vista Creek HA (904.2), and Agua Hedionda HA (904.3) are 
all within the City. The majority of surface runoff within these HAs drain into the Pacific Ocean. All 
but the Agua Hedionda HA are listed on the 303(d) list for heightened bacterial levels and 
concentrations of nutrients, sediment, toxicity, benthic community effects, pesticides and 
eutrophication. The Agua Hedionda Lagoon, which had previously been listed as impaired, has seen 
significant improvements in overall water quality over the last few years that inevitably warranted 
removal from the 303(d) list of impaired water bodies. 
4.11.1.2 Groundwater 
The City lies within the San Luis Rey Valley Groundwater Basin. Beneficial groundwater uses include 
municipal and domestic supply, agricultural supply, industrial service supply, water recreation, and 
the support of freshwater and wildlife habitat (RWQCB 2021). The City utilizes groundwater from the 
Mission Basin of the San Luis Rey Valley Groundwater Basin. Although the San Luis Rey Valley 
Groundwater Basin has been designated a medium priority basin under the California Statewide 
Groundwater Elevation Monitoring program, meaning that the state considers it a priority basin for 
monitoring, the Mission Basin is classified as a “Very Low” priority basin, per the California State 
Department of Water Resources Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA; see 
Section 4.11.2.2.d). As such, the Mission Basin is not required to have a Groundwater Sustainability 
Plan (GSP).  
The City’s potable water sources are generated from a blend of imported and desalinated seawater 
from San Diego County Water Authority and local groundwater from the Mission Basin. Local 
groundwater is pumped from eight City-owned wells within the Mission Basin and treated at the 
Mission Basin Groundwater Purification Facility, providing approximately 11 percent of the City’s 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-4 
water supply. The primary Mission Basin Groundwater Purification Facility treatment process utilizes 
reverse osmosis membranes to reduce salt concentrations present in the groundwater. 
4.11.1.3 Flooding  
The City is exposed to two general types of flooding: Riverine and Coastal. Riverine flooding is usually 
the result of heavy or prolonged rainfall occurring in main creeks and rivers in the city, especially the 
largest, San Luis Rey River. Portions of the City, including the coastal boundary, are located within 
Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) floodplains and floodways. Figure 4.11-2 shows the 
FEMA floodplains/floodways throughout the City and Table 4-11-1 provides a summary of the 
acreage within each FEMA flood designation.

4.11.1.4 Tsunami Areas 
A tsunami is a series of high-energy waves that radiate outward like pond ripples from an area where 
a generating event occurs, arriving at shorelines over an extended period. According to the 2023 
Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan (MJHMP), tsunamis as a hazard are given an “unlikely” 
probability to occur. However, they are assigned a “medium” overall significance ranking (County of 
San Diego 2023). The highest risk zones in San Diego County are located within the coastal zone. As 
shown in Figure 14 of the 2023 MJHMP, the entire City’s coastline is designated as a VE Zone, which 
is defined by FEMA as the coastal area subject to a velocity hazard (wave action). Further, maximum 
tsunami runup is projected to extend up the San Luis Rey River to the vicinity of the Oceanside 
Municipal Airport, landward of Coast Highway where this roadway crosses Loma Alta Creek and 
Buena Vista Lagoon.

4.11.1.5 Dam Failure and Inundation 
Dam failures can result in severe flood events. When a dam fails, a large quantity of water is suddenly 
released with a great potential to cause human casualties, economic loss, lifeline disruption, and 
environmental damage. A dam failure is usually the result of age, poor design, or structural damage 
caused by a major event such as an earthquake or flood (County of San Diego 2023). Pursuant to 
the 2023 MJHMP there have been no reported dam failures in the County of San Diego within the 
past five years. There are no dams in the City; Lake Henshaw Dam is outside the City, at the southeast 
base of Mount Palomar at the headwaters of the San Luis Rey River, and has the potential to flood 
several portions of the City as shown in Figure 4.11.3. If the dam was to fail, 4,775 acres of the City 
could be flooded (City of Oceanside 2021), including 292 acres of the Mission Avenue Corridor in the 
SSCSP Planning Area. 
4.11.1.6 Stormwater Drainage Facilities  
The existing drainage system throughout the City is a combination of storm drains, improved 
channels, and detention basins, which in many areas discharge to natural drainage paths. Many 
existing projects, as they were mapped and constructed, were required to dedicate portions of the 
properties to the City as drainage easements or flood water storage easements as a condition of 
project approval (i.e., development permits, tentative maps). 
a. Citywide 
The Master Plan of Drainage Update 2013 (see Section 4.11.2.4.c) analyzed existing drainage facilities, 
30 inches and larger, based on severity of inadequate pipe segments. Those facilities that overflowed 
during the 10- and -25 year storm events were upsized to convey the 25- and 100-year flows, and 
facilities that overflowed during the 100-year storm event were up-sized to convey the maximum 
100-year flows. Recommended facility sizes were provided based on hydraulic analysis only. In total, 
over 40,000 linear feet, or approximately 10 percent of the analyzed storm drain facilities, were 
identified to have inadequate capacity, and recommended for upsizing. 
b.  SSCSP Planning Area 
The SSCSP Planning Area roughly follows main drainage routes that convey stormwater runoff to 
the ocean. The Mission Avenue corridor is adjacent to the San Luis Rey River, Oceanside Boulevard 
follows Loma Alta Creek, and Vista Way is along Buena Vista Creek. 
The Master Plan of Drainage identified storm drains within each corridor with inadequacies to convey 
either the 10-year, 25-year, or 100-year storm events. All storm drains considered in the model have 
the capacity to convey the 2-year storm event. Storm drains that cannot convey the 10-year storm 
event are considered higher priority to facilities that cannot convey the 100-year storm event. 
Within the SSCSP Planning Area, multiple storm drain facilities were found to be inadequate. Along 
the Mission Avenue corridor, inadequate facilities are mostly due to limited capacity for the 100-year 
storm and are thus considered lower priority. Along Oceanside Boulevard and Vista Way, there are 
more areas with 25-year and even 10-year inadequate facilities.

4.11.2 
Regulatory Setting 
4.11.2.1 Federal  
a. Clean Water Act 
The federal Water Pollution Control Act (CWA) establishes a broad national program for protecting 
water quality and regulating discharges of waste and pollutants into waters of the United States 
(Title 33, United States Code, Section 1251 et seq.). It provides authority for the establishment of 
water quality standards and waste discharge limits for point source discharges (such as those from 
industrial facilities, sewage treatment plants, and stormwater). The key sections pertaining to water 
quality regulation are Sections 303, 401, 402, and 404. The act also prohibits discharges of pollutants 
without a permit or other authorization and allows authorized states to implement provisions of the 
act in lieu of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA). 
Section 303(d) 
Under CWA Section 303(d), states are required to identify “impaired water bodies” (those not 
meeting established water quality standards), identify the pollutants causing the impairment, 
establish priority rankings for waters on the list, and develop a schedule for development of control 
plans to improve water quality. The U.S. EPA then approves the state’s recommended list of impaired 
waters, or adds to or removes water bodies from the list. Each RWQCB must update the CWA Section 
303(d) list every 2 years, with the most recent 2024 California Integrated Report adopted in 2024. 
The CWA Section 303(d) list identifies priorities for development of pollution control plans for each 
listed water body and pollutant. The pollution control plans triggered by the CWA Section 303(d) list 
are called TMDLs. The TMDL is a “pollution budget” designed to restore the health of a polluted 
body of water and ensure the protection of beneficial uses. The TMDL also contains the target 
reductions needed to meet water quality standards and allocates those reductions among the 
pollutant sources in the watershed (point sources, nonpoint sources, and natural sources) (40 Code 
of Federal Regulations [CFR] 130.2). 
Section 401 Water Quality Certification 
Section 401 of the CWA requires that any applicant for a federal permit to conduct any activity, 
including the construction or operation of a facility, which may result in the discharge of any 
pollutant, must obtain certification from the state. This process is known as the Water Quality 
Certification. 
Section 402 National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System  
Section 402 of the CWA establishes the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) 
permit program to regulate the discharge of pollutants from point sources and discharge pollutants 
into waters of the United States. In California, the EPA has authorized the SWRCB and its nine 
RWQCBs to implement the NPDES program and issue permits, develop waste discharge 
requirements, administer 401 certifications and provide enforcement. The CWA regulation calls for 
the implementation of best management practices (BMPs) to reduce or prevent the discharge of 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-9 
pollutants from municipal separate storm sewer systems (MS4s) to the Maximum Extent Practicable 
and meeting the Best Available Technology Economically Achievable and Best Conventional 
Pollutant Control Technology standards for construction stormwater. Regulations and permits have 
been implemented at the federal, state, and local level to form a comprehensive regulatory 
framework to serve and protect the quality of the nation’s surface water resources. 
Section 404 
Section 404 of the CWA regulates the discharge of dredged and fill materials into waters of the 
United States, which include all navigable waters, their tributaries, as well as some wetlands adjacent 
to the aforementioned waters (33 CFR Part 328.3).  
Areas meeting the regulatory definition of waters of the United States are subject to the jurisdiction 
of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers under provisions of Section 404. Construction activities involving 
placement of fill into jurisdictional waters of the United States are regulated by the U.S. Army Corps 
of Engineers through permit requirements. No U.S. Army Corps of Engineers permit is effective in 
the absence of the state water quality certification pursuant to Section 401. 
b. Federal Emergency Management Agency 
FEMA is the primary agency in charge of administering programs and coordinating with communities 
to establish effective floodplain management standards. FEMA is responsible for delineating areas 
of flood hazards. It is then the responsibility of state and local agencies to implement FEMA 
requirements. Projects located within the mapped FEMA floodplains may require a Letter of Map 
Amendment (LOMA) before development potential.  
4.11.2.2 State 
a. Porter–Cologne Water Quality Control Act, as amended  
The Porter–Cologne Water Quality Control Act was established to protect the water quality and 
beneficial uses of waters of the State (California Water Code, Division 7, Section 13000 et seq.). The 
law gives broad authority to the SWRCB and nine RWQCBs to establish water quality standards and 
discharge prohibitions, issue waste discharge requirements, and implement provisions of the federal 
CWA. Under the Porter-Cologne Act, waters of the State include both surface and groundwater. Any 
entity or person proposing to discharge waste within any region of the state must file a Report of 
Waste Discharge with the appropriate regional board. 
b. National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System Permit Program  
In California, the SWRCB and local RWQCBs have assumed the responsibility of implementing the 
EPA’s NPDES program. In addition to its permitting programs, the SWRCB, through its nine RWQCBs, 
developed Regional Water Quality Control Plans (or Basin Plans) that designate beneficial uses and 
water quality objectives for California’s surface waters and groundwater basins, as mandated by both 
the CWA and the state’s Porter-Cologne Act. Water quality standards are thus established in these 
Basin Plans and provide the foundation for the regulatory programs implemented by the state.  


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-10 
Additionally, municipalities are required to develop and implement a Jurisdictional Runoff 
Management Plan (JRMP) to address activities to reduce pollutants in urban runoff and stormwater 
discharges that were contributing a substantial pollutant load to their systems.  
c. State General Construction Stormwater Permit 
Stormwater runoff from construction activity that results in soil disturbances of at least 1 acre of total 
land area (and projects that meet other specific criteria) is governed by the SWRCB under Water 
Quality Order 2022-0057-DWQ, NPDES Permit No. CAS000002. This permit regulates discharges of 
stormwater and non-stormwater from construction projects. The nine individual RWQCBs enforce 
the General Construction Stormwater Permit for projects within their region. 
It is the construction site owner or landowner’s responsibility to obtain coverage under this General 
Permit prior to commencement of construction activities. To obtain coverage, the operator or owner 
must file a Notice of Intent with a vicinity map and pay the appropriate fee with the SWRCB. The 
General Permit outlines the requirements for preparation of a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan 
(SWPPP). The SWPPP is a temporary document created to define and control the handling of 
stormwater runoff from a construction site. The SWPPP identifies construction BMPs, which are 
implemented during the construction phase of development. All future projects that would be 
disturbed by development exceeding one acre would be required to comply with the General 
Construction Stormwater Permit. 
d. Sustainable Groundwater Management Act 
The SGMA, enacted in 2014, provides a framework to regulate groundwater. The intent of the law is 
to strengthen local groundwater management of basins most critical to the state’s water needs with 
an understanding that groundwater is most effectively managed at the local level. SGMA requires 
basins to be sustainably managed by local public agencies (e.g., counties, cities, and water agencies) 
who become groundwater sustainability agencies, or GSAs. The primary purpose of the GSAs is to 
develop and implement a GSP to achieve long-term groundwater sustainability. The act requires 
GSPs to be developed for high and medium priority basins. The City utilizes groundwater from the 
Mission Basin, which is classified as a “Very Low” priority basin. Therefore, consistent with the SGMA, 
it is not required to have a GSP. 
4.11.2.3 Regional 
a. Water Quality Control Plan for the San Diego Basin, Region 9 (Basin Plan) 
The Basin Plan sets forth water quality objectives for constituents that could potentially cause an 
adverse effect or impact on the beneficial uses of water. Specifically, the Basin Plan is designed to 
accomplish the following: 
• 
Designate beneficial uses for surface and groundwater; 
• 
Set the narrative and numerical objectives that must be attained or maintained to protect 
the designated beneficial uses and conform to the state’s antidegradation policy; 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-11 
• 
Describe implementation programs to protect the beneficial uses of all waters within the 
region; and 
• 
Describe surveillance and monitoring activities to evaluate the effectiveness of the Basin Plan. 
The Basin Plan also identifies specific narrative and numeric water quality objectives for several 
physical properties (e.g., temperature, turbidity, and suspended solids), biological constituents (e.g., 
coliform bacteria), and chemical conditions of concern, including inorganic parameters, trace metals, 
and organic compounds. Water quality objectives for toxic priority pollutants (i.e., select trace metals 
and synthetic organic compounds) also are identified in the Basin Plan. 
b. Water Quality Improvement Plan (WQIPs) for the San Luis Rey River and 
Carlsbad Watershed Management Areas 
WQIPs are watershed-based planning documents prepared to meet the requirements of the San 
Diego Regional MS4 Permit, issued by the San Diego RWQCB. The MS4 Permit requires each WMA 
in the region to develop a coordinated strategy to improve surface water quality, reduce stormwater 
pollution, and achieve applicable TMDL and beneficial-use standards under the federal CWA. Each 
WQIP is developed collaboratively by the watershed “Responsible Agencies,” which include the cities, 
the County of San Diego, and other MS4 permittees within that watershed. The process typically 
includes coordination among the permittees, technical staff, and the public, with guidance from the 
RWQCB. WQIPs identify the highest-priority water quality conditions in each watershed, establish 
numeric goals and schedules for improvement, and outline specific strategies, BMPs, monitoring 
programs, and adaptive-management actions to achieve compliance. The WQIPs provide a 
regulatory framework for long-term water quality improvement efforts; WQIPs are formally 
submitted to and accepted by the RWQCB. 
The City is part of two WMAs: San Luis Rey and Carlsbad. The WQIP for each of these watersheds is 
summarized as applicable to the City. 
San Luis Rey WQIP 
San Luis Rey watershed is located in northern San Diego County and is bordered to the north by the 
Santa Margarita River Watershed and to the south by the Carlsbad and San Dieguito River 
watersheds. The San Luis Rey River extends over 55 miles and has a watershed of approximately 
360,000 acres. The San Luis Rey River discharges to the Pacific Ocean in the City of Oceanside. 
Population in the watershed is mostly centered in the City and the City of Vista, and unincorporated 
communities of Fallbrook, Bonsall, and Valley Center. Over 54 percent of the land in the watershed 
is undeveloped; other land uses include residential, agricultural, parks and open space, 
commercial/industrial, freeways/roads, recreation, and schools (RWQCB 2016). The San Luis Rey 
WQIP was originally accepted by the RWQCB in 2016. More recently, the San Luis Rey WMA 
jurisdictions developed an update of the WQIP which was submitted to the San Diego RWQCB with 
the WQIP 2020-2021 Annual Report. After an iterative review, the RWQCB issued an acceptance letter 
for the revised San Luis Rey WQIP update on January 11, 2023. 
The 2020-2021 San Luis Rey WMA Annual Report/WQIP Update identifies the following priority water 
quality conditions relevant to the City: eutrophic conditions (i.e., nutrients; Guajome Lake), chloride,

Page 4.11-12 
phosphorus, nitrogen, TDS, toxicity, nutrients, and trash (Lower San Luis Rey River) (RWQCB 2023).

as-needed basis, consistent with the MS4 Permit’s adaptive-management framework.

c. Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System Permits 
The City is one of 21 public entities in the County of San Diego that is a copermittee currently 
operating under the NPDES Municipal Stormwater Permit (R9-2013-0001, as amended by R9-2015-
0001 and R9-2015-0100), which requires that stormwater BMPs be incorporated into the permanent 
design of public and private development projects. The regionwide NPDES permit (commonly 
referred to as the Regional MS4 Permit) sets the framework for responsible agencies to implement 
a collaborative watershed-based approach to restore and maintain the health of surface waters. The 
Regional MS4 Permit required development of WQIPs that will allow watershed stakeholders to 
prioritize and address pollutants through an appropriate suite of BMPs in each watershed.  
d. Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan and Local Hazard Mitigation Plan 
The 2023 MJHMP is a countywide plan that identifies risks and ways to minimize damage from 
different potential hazards. The City has developed a Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP), included 
as an annex to the MJHMP, that focuses on potential hazards specific to the City. Dam failure and 
flooding are included as potential hazard exposures: 
• 
Reduce the possibility of damage and losses to life, property, and the environment, 
particularly critical facilities or infrastructure and City of Oceanside owned facilities, due to 
flooding and sea level rise (Goal 6). 
To meet this goal, the City has developed broad objectives intended to assist in the implementation 
of Goal 6, and for each of these objectives, specific actions were developed that would assist in their 
implementation. 
• 
Objective 6.A: Protect existing assets with the highest relative vulnerability to the effects of 
floods within the 100-year floodplain and sea level rise.

4.11.2.4 Local  
a. City of Oceanside Jurisdictional Runoff Management Program 
The City's JRMP is the City's approach to prevent polluted stormwater and other waste from entering 
its storm drain system and to protect the beneficial uses of receiving waters within its jurisdiction. 
The JRMP document presents an integrated programmatic approach to reduce the discharge of 
pollutants from the City's storm drain system to the Maximum Extent Practicable, effectively prohibit 
non-storm water discharges, and protect and improve the quality of waterbodies within the City (City 
of Oceanside 2022a:ES-2). The JRMP is an implementation framework of watershed management 
strategies that integrates with the Carlsbad and San Luis Rey WQIPs to which the City is a responsible 
agency. It also serves as a regulatory compliance tool to satisfy the requirements of the San Diego 
Regional Phase 1 Municipal Stormwater Permit (Regional MS4 Permit) and establish the City's legal 
authority to control and prevent the discharge of pollutants in stormwater through its local 
ordinance. 
b. Master Plan of Drainage  
Since the City's Master Plan of Drainage was updated in 2013, various developments have affected 
storm runoff flow patterns, and new drainage facilities have been added to the City’s storm drainage 
system. The Master Plan details the hydrologic conditions of the City and hydraulic capacity of the 
storm drain system to convey design storm events (2-year, 10-year, 25-year, and 100-year storms). 
The objectives of the Master Plan are to map drainage facilities, and then identify deficiencies and 
recommended upgrades which could be constructed as future development occurs. See 
Section 4.11.1.6 which summarizes stormwater drainage deficiencies throughout the City and the 
SSCSP Planning Area as detailed in the Master Plan. 
c. Watershed Protection Program 
The Watershed Protection Program (a component of Green Oceanside) monitors and enforces 
compliance with the NPDES Permits and actively investigates reports of landscape irrigation runoff, 
illegal dumping, and other violations. The program ensures that new development meets stormwater 
treatment and flow control standards promulgated by the San Diego RWQCB and that construction 
activities adhere to BMPs for reducing pollutants in stormwater runoff. 
d. Oceanside Storm Water Management  
Best Management Practices for Development 
All development and redevelopment projects are obligated to comply with federal, state, and local 
stormwater regulations during the planning, construction, and post-construction phases of 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-16 
development. Projects entering the construction phase of development are regulated under City 
grading and erosion control ordinances, and, dependent on acreage, the SWRCB under the 
Construction General Stormwater Permit (Order 2022-0057-DWQ and any amendments or 
reissuances thereto). The City is responsible for local administration and enforcement of stormwater 
management requirements throughout the development planning and construction stages for each 
project. To ensure that new and redevelopment complies with City ordinances and the San Diego 
Phase 1 Municipal Stormwater Permit, the City has developed a BMP Design Manual which addresses 
on-site post construction storm water requirements for Standard Projects and Priority Development 
Projects (PDPs).The BMP Design Manual provides guidance and procedures for planning, design, 
selection, and construction of permanent post-construction stormwater BMPs. Based on a site-
specific analysis of a proposed new or redevelopment project, permanent post-construction 
structural/treatment control BMPs may be required to ensure that a project controls the discharge 
of pollutants in stormwater to the Maximum Extent Practicable and reduces the volume and flow 
rate of runoff due to increases in impervious surfaces (City of Oceanside 2022b). 
Storm Water Quality Assessment 
Prior to project submittal all development and redevelopment projects applying for discretionary or 
administrative permits are subject to a formal Storm Water Quality Assessment (SWQA) 
determination. The objective of the SWQA is to ensure that all new and redevelopment projects 
receive a consistent and thorough initial review, with the purpose of categorizing projects, 
determining applicable Storm Water Quality Management Plan (SWQMP) requirements, and serving 
as a mechanism for recordkeeping of approved projects. The SWQA determination also 
demonstrates to the RWQCB that each project receives a consistent review and enables the City to 
document project categorization and satisfy the MS4 Permit requirements. The SWQA is an integral 
part of the City BMP Design Manual. 
Operation and Maintenance Plan 
The San Diego Regional Phase 1 Municipal Stormwater Permit requires the City to annually verify 
that all permanent post-construction BMPs (such as structural/treatment control BMPs and flow-
control facilities) are correctly installed and adequately maintained. Implementation of a long-term 
Operation and Maintenance Plan (O&M) is required as part of the final engineering phase of any 
project within the City that qualifies as a PDP through the SWQA and BMP Design Manual process. 
Engineers Design and Processing Manual 
The City Engineering Design Manual serves to establish procedures and minimum standards for 
various plans and documents submitted to and processed by the Engineering Department. The 
standards presented in the manual govern the processing of subdivision maps and related 
documents as well as public and private improvement and grading plans. The Manual specifically 
addresses the standards for preparation of Erosion Control Plans.  
Storm Water Facilities Maintenance Agreement 
The City Standard Storm Water Facilities Maintenance Agreement with Access Rights and Covenants 
(SWFMA) is a recorded agreement for the access to maintenance and repair of storm water 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-17 
management facilities (i.e. permanent post-construction BMPs), entered into between the owner and 
the City. The SWFMA is the final step to ensure ongoing storm water management and is a recorded 
document that runs with the land upon which the stormwater management facilities are constructed.  
f. City of Oceanside Code of Ordinances 
Chapter 40 Urban Runoff Management and Discharge Control Ordinance 
The overall intent of this ordinance is to protect water resources and to improve water quality. 
Specifically, the ordinance promotes: 
• 
Prohibiting polluted or non-storm water discharges from entering the storm water 
conveyance system; 
• 
Establishing minimum requirements for urban runoff management, including source control 
requirements, to prevent and reduce pollution; 
• 
Establishing requirements for development project site design, to reduce urban runoff 
pollution and erosion; 
• 
Establishing requirements for the management of flows from development projects, both to 
prevent erosion and to protect and enhance existing water-dependent habitats; 
• 
Establishing standards for the use of off-site facilities for urban runoff management to 
supplement on-site practices at new development sites; and 
• 
Establishing notice procedures and standards for adjusting urban runoff management 
requirements where necessary. 
The Urban Management and Discharge Control Ordinance includes compliance with current and 
applicable RWQCB discharge permits, requirements for discretionary approvals subject to discharge 
control, development of Urban Runoff Standards Manuals, and designations for permitted use of 
collected stormwater. 
Chapter 32C Public Facility Fee Requirements 
The Code of Ordinances includes provisions for the assessment of public facility fees as a condition 
of issuing building permits. The public facility fees regulate community growth and ensure that new 
development pay impact fees for new public facilities.  
Article IX Floodplain Management Regulations 
The purpose of this article is to protect against damage and loss associated with flood conditions. 
Specifically, development within flood prone areas are subject to floodplain management regulations 
to provide standards for preventing and reducing flood loss and damage. Identified Special Flood 
Hazard Areas (SFHA) are those having special flood, mudslide, mudflow or flood-related erosion 
hazards, and shown on an flood boundary and floodway maps prepared by FEMA. As applicable, 
City regulations mandate all Letter of Map Revisions required for flood control projects are to be 
approved by FEMA prior to the issuance of building permits.

4.11.3 Proposed GPU and SSCSP Policies 
The proposed GPU and SSCSP include policies intended to reduce potential adverse environmental 
impacts resulting from buildout of the plans. As future development is proposed, development 
would be required to demonstrate consistency with the GPU and SSCSP policy framework, as 
applicable. The policy framework would be implemented by the City during future discretionary 
and/or ministerial project reviews to ensure impact minimization.  The analysis of potential impacts 
considers how implementation of these policies at the project level would serve to reduce the 
significance of potential adverse impacts. 
4.11.3.1  Policy Framework 
The following goals and policies are examples of the broader policy framework and do not intend to 
be exclusive of all additional relevant policies that may apply to future development. 
a. GPU Vital and Sustainable Resources Element (VSR) 
The VSR addresses surface water and groundwater quality in terms of federal, state, and local 
regulations. The VSR includes a policy framework promoting consistency with regulations and 
standards set forth in water quality plans and programs. Additional goals and policies development 
to comply with stormwater management and pollution prevention.  
• 
Goal 5-G: Consistent with applicable federal and state regulations and the Water Quality 
Objectives set forth in the San Diego Basin Plan to protect water body Beneficial Uses, the 
City will maintain water quality in rivers, streams, creeks, lakes, and groundwater to support 
public use and a healthy environment for current and future generations. 
• 
Goal 5-R: The City will work with regulatory and resource agencies to achieve a balance 
between natural resources, economic benefit, and recreational opportunities along the 
coastline, proactively planning for sea level rise, erosion, and other climate-related coastline 
changes under the guidance and requirements of the Coastal Commission and Ocean 
Protection Council. 
• 
Goal 5-T: The City will prioritize beach restoration and preservation in the near term while 
acknowledging that other coastal adaptation strategies will be necessary to effectively 
address sea level rise and other climate-related impacts.  
• 
Policy 5-53: Promoting the use of Low Impact Development (LID) strategies, BMPs, pervious 
paving materials, and on-site infiltration for treating and reducing stormwater runoff before 
it reaches the municipal stormwater system. Continue implementing LID regulatory 
requirements as set forth under Municipal Stormwater NPDES permits adopted by the San 
Diego RWQCB and codified under City Municipal Code.  
• 
Policy 5-54: Ensure that stormwater discharge from existing and new development complies

Control Board (SWRCB).

b. GPU Safe and Resilient Environment Element (SRE) 
The SRE addresses the City’s potential risks from natural and man-made hazards, including flooding. 
The SRE includes a policy framework focusing on reducing flood hazard potential especially along 
the City’s major waterways and coastal areas. The following goals and policies are examples of the 
broader policy framework and do not intend to be exclusive of all additional relevant policies that 
may apply to future development. 
• 
Policy 6-1: Balance the use of waterways and floodplains for multiple purposes, with emphasis 
on public safety and environmental protection. Potentially appropriate uses in the floodplains 
include: 
o Flood control  
o Groundwater recharge 
o Open space 
o Natural habitat  
o Nature study 
o Pedestrian, equestrian, and bicycle activity 
o Passive and active recreational activity 
• 
Policy 6-3: Update development standards to require flood-resilient design on properties 
subject to significant flood risk. 
• 
Policy 6-7: Ensure that new construction and major improvements to existing structures 
within flood zones are in compliance with federal requirements, in part to ensure ongoing 
participation in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). 
• 
Policy 6-8: Prohibit development in FEMA-delineated floodways; ensure that all new 
development in 100-year floodplains is elevated at least one foot above base flood elevation 
and ensure FEMA maps are updated with Letters of Map Revisions accordingly.  
• 
Policy 6-19: For new development in the tsunami evacuation zone, require use of low impact 
engineering techniques, such as elevating structures above projected water levels, to mitigate 
impacts to people and property.  
• 
Policy 6-45: Ensure that the siting, design, engineering, and construction of new development 
minimizes the potential for erosion. 
• 
Policy 6-49: Continue to enforce ordinances for grading, erosion control, and sediment 
management, including the provisions of the urban runoff and discharge control ordinance.

c. SCCSP Environmental Quality 
The Environmental Quality chapter of the SSCSP provides policy direction to avoid risks from 
hydrologic hazards throughout the SSCSP Planning Areas, providing a framework for new 
development to avoid risks pertaining to flooding, drainage and stormwater runoff.  
• 
Policy EQ-18: 100-Year Flood Zones. Ensure that new projects located in Special Flood Hazard 
Area (SFHA) on parcels inundated by the 100-year floodplain are designed to reduce flood 
risk in compliance with the City’s required Floodplain Plan Review. 
• 
Policy EQ-19: Green Stormwater Infrastructure. In concert with the City’s water quality 
standards and Jurisdictional Runoff Management Program, require new development in the 
Planning Area to implement green stormwater infrastructure projects, such as rain gardens 
and detention bioswales to support water quality, reduce stormwater runoff, and enhance 
natural habitat in the Planning Area. For new development, ensure that post-development 
runoff rates do not exceed predevelopment rates. 
• 
Policy EQ-20: Roadway Bioswales. In addition to maximizing tree canopy, install vegetated 
bioswales to capture and treat stormwater in existing and new roadway medians and parkway 
strips along Oceanside Boulevard, Vista Way, and Mission Avenue. 
• 
Policy EQ-21: Pervious Surfaces. Minimize impervious surfaces and use pervious pavements 
where possible, retaining and increasing pervious surfaces such as landscaped areas, crushed 
aggregate, turf block, unit pavers, pervious concrete, or pervious asphalt. New parking lots 
and non-primary access road paving areas are required to be surfaced with permeable 
paving to encourage stormwater infiltration, and should disperse runoff from roofs, rainwater 
catchment system overflow, or pavement to vegetated areas where possible. 
• 
Policy EQ-23: Trash Reduction in Waterways. Keep trash from reaching waterways by 
requiring new development to provide regular and convenient trash, recycling, compost, and 
cigarette butt disposal receptacles, as appropriate, as well as signage promoting proper 
waste disposal. Install trash screens in all stormwater inlets. During construction, require that 
developers take steps to ensure that trash and debris from construction does not reach 
waterways. 
d. SSCSP Infrastructure and Utilities 
The Infrastructure and Utilities chapter of the SSCSP provides policy direction for water quality related 
to storm water planning.  
• 
Goal 7: Stormwater infrastructure will be reliable and be of adequate capacity to serve 
existing and future developments within the Planning Area. 
• 
Policy I-12: Streetscape Improvements. Design new streetscape and landscaped areas in the 
public right-of-way for stormwater management and the efficient use of water through:  
o The installation of low-maintenance, drought-resistant plant palettes;  
o Use of low-flow irrigation systems; and  
o Use of bioswales and rain gardens in planting areas, curb extensions, and other green 
infrastructure to help manage stormwater flow.

The Urban Design chapter of the SSCSP provides design guidelines and policy direction for reduction

4.11.4 
Water Quality Standards 
4.11.4.1 Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to water quality standards are based on 
applicable criteria in the 2025 California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines, Appendix G. 
Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Violate any water quality standards or waste discharge requirements or otherwise 
substantially degrade surface or ground water quality? 
4.11.4.2 Impact Analysis 
Implementation of the project would result in the construction of new impervious surfaces 
throughout the City and specifically within the SSCSP Planning Area, including building roofs, 
driveways, streets, concrete sidewalks and walkways, parking areas, and other site-specific 
improvements. All runoff generated in the City flows through the WMAs to the Pacific Ocean, which 
is an impaired water body. The increase in impervious areas could lead to increased flows of 
stormwater runoff that could negatively affect water quality in downstream waterbodies during both 
construction and operation of the project.  
a. Construction-Related Water Quality Impacts 
Future construction would involve grading, paving, utility installation, building construction, and 
landscaping installation, which could result in the generation of pollutants such as silt, debris, 
chemicals, and paints, all with the potential to affect water quality. Future construction activity greater 
than one acre would require coverage under the NPDES General Construction Permit (GCP). The 
GCP requires preparation and implementation of a SWPPP identifying site specific temporary BMPs 
that could control the handling of stormwater runoff from a construction site. Additionally, activity 
would be monitored by the City’s Watershed Protection and Stormwater Management Programs 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-22 
which authorize enforcement of stormwater management requirements throughout the 
development planning and construction stages for all projects. Likewise, future development would 
be reviewed for compliance with proposed GPU and SSCSP policies which further support 
compliance with RWQCB and SWRCB regulations relating to avoiding construction-related water 
quality impacts. Within the SSCSP Planning Area, compliance with SSCSP Policy EQ-23 provides 
direction for developers to take steps to ensure that trash and debris from construction does not 
reach waterways. Project conformance with existing regulations, along with the proposed GPU and 
SSCSP framework, would ensure that development projects would not violate water quality standards 
during construction activities.  
b. Post-Development Water Quality Impacts  
Storm water pollutants commonly associated with the long-term operations of land uses proposed 
by the project include bacterial indicators, metals, nutrients, pesticides, toxic organic compounds, 
sediments, trash and debris, and oil and grease. Specifically, residential, commercial and industrial 
uses, could increase urban runoff containing oil, grease, metals, pathogens, TDS, sediments, or toxic 
chemicals. Also, agricultural operations (in the South Moro Hills area), have the potential to 
contribute pollutants such as fertilizers, herbicides, insecticides, or bacteria into surface water bodies. 
Increased development potential could include increased pervious surfaces that would result in great 
stormwater runoff.  
The City’s Urban Runoff Management and Discharge Control Ordinance requires future development 
to comply with current and applicable RWQCB discharge permits and establishes regulations for 
development projects to include site design measures to reduce runoff pollution, including source 
control BMPs, and stormwater flow management. Consistent with the City’s stormwater management 
programs, all future development and redevelopment projects are subject to SWQA determination 
which requires a standard showing of consistency with all state and federal requirements. 
Additionally, City permit regulations make it necessary for projects to demonstrate compliance with 
SWQMP requirements prior to project approval.  
All future development and redevelopment identified as Standard Development Projects or Priority 
Development Projects would be required to include requisite levels of permanent source control 
BMPs and Low Impact Development (LID) design features intended to provide stormwater flow 
control and reduce stormwater runoff. This requirement is further supported by proposed GPU and 
SSCSP policies promoting the use of LID strategies, BMPs, pervious paving materials, and on-site 
infiltration for treating and reducing stormwater runoff before it reaches the municipal stormwater 
system, and designing stormwater conveyance and treatment systems to maximize pollutant source 
control. Likewise, development within the SSCSP Planning Area would be reviewed for policy 
consistency including conformance with SSCSP Policies promoting the minimization of impervious 
surfaces. Future projects would also be required to implement Stormwater Mitigation Plans with 
adequate long term treatment facilities such as infiltration or biofiltration, as well as means for trash 
reduction.  
Future projects would be required to adhere to relevant plans and programs, including the City 
requirements for preparation of project specific construction SWPPs and long term SWQMP. The 
additional implementation of applicable policies would ensure that future development would not

Page 4.11-23 
violate any water quality standards or degrade surface or ground water quality during construction 
or in the long term.  
4.11.4.3 Significance of Impacts 
While future development throughout the City has the potential to increase pollutants discharged 
into surface waters, all future development, whether discretionary or by right, would be subject to 
federal, state, and local regulations aimed at controlling water quality impacts. Additionally, policy 
compliance with proposed GPU and SSCSP policies would ensure impacts to water quality would be 
less than significant. 
4.11.4.4 Mitigation Measures 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required. 
4.11.5 
Groundwater Supplies 
4.11.5.1 Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to groundwater supplies are based on 
applicable criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Substantially decrease groundwater supplies or interfere substantially with groundwater 
recharge such that the project may impede sustainable groundwater management of the 
basin? 
4.11.5.2 Impact Analysis 
Development consistent with the proposed GPU and SSCSP would result in redevelopment of 
existing underutilized sites and new development of vacant sites with higher density residential 
and/or greater intensity of uses. Future development would increase the amount of impervious 
surfaces throughout the City, which could reduce the amount of rainwater able to infiltrate the soil 
resulting in the incremental reduction of groundwater recharge rates over time. This, in turn, could 
affect that portion of the City’s water supply which relies on groundwater.  
The City promotes a healthy water table by coordinating with other agencies that oversee 
groundwater sustainability, and furthering local efforts to maintain the groundwater recharge 
process primarily through maintaining the floodplains, limiting impermeable surfaces, and by 
collecting runoff in detention basins and swales (City of Oceanside 2023). The GPU contains goals 
focused on the maintenance of groundwater recharge and the vital health of groundwater resources. 
Specifically, VSR Goal 5-G and associated policies promote the maintenance and improvement of 
groundwater recharge.  
Overall, implementing GPU goals, and adherence to relevant plans and programs would ensure that 
future development would not obstruct groundwater recharge or impede the sustainability of the 
City’s groundwater basin.

4.11.6 
Drainage Patterns 
4.11.6.1 Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to drainage patterns are based on 
applicable criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Substantially alter the existing drainage pattern of the site or area, including through the 
alteration of the course of a stream or river or through the addition of impervious surfaces, 
in a manner, which would: 
o Result in substantial erosion or siltation on- or off-site;  
o Substantially increase the rate or amount of surface runoff in a manner which would result 
in flooding on- or off-site;  
o Create or contribute runoff water which would exceed the capacity of existing or planned 
stormwater drainage systems or provide substantial additional sources of polluted runoff; 
or  
o Impede or redirect flood flows? 
4.11.6.2  Impact Analysis 
a. Erosion or Siltation/ Increase Surface Runoff  
Development consistent with the GPU and SSCSP could alter drainage patterns resulting in increased 
volume and/or velocity of runoff which in turn could increase erosion and siltation in surface waters.  
Future grading, excavation, and construction activities could increase the potential for erosion and 
siltation. All future development would be required to conform with the City’s Urban Runoff 
Management and Discharge Control Ordinance which requires preparation of project-specific 
Erosion Control Plans designed to minimize the accelerated erosion and sediment runoff at a site 
during construction activities. The City’s Engineering Design and Processing Manual provides specific 
requirements to ensure erosion control measures are consistent with JRMP objectives. Consistent 
with the Engineering Design and Processing Manual, future projects would be required to submit 
hydrology and hydraulic calculations with all erosion control plans to qualify avoidance of changes 
to drainage velocities during both construction and post-construction/operational phases of 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-25 
development. Code of Ordinances Section 40.2.6 further requires post-construction BMPs to ensure 
that pollutants and runoff from the development will be reduced to the maximum extent possible. 
Post-construction BMPs would be designed to retain volume and velocity of stormwater to ensure 
that runoff flows leaving future development sites would not carry substantial amounts of sediment 
to downstream waters.  
Consistent with the City’s BMP Design Manual and Urban Runoff ordinance, all new projects must 
determine the potential changes in onsite runoff due to increases in impervious surfaces and/or 
drainage area alterations, then install and manage BMPs that regulate off-site discharges to mimic 
pre-project conditions (City of Oceanside 2021). Implementation of applicable stormwater BMPs and 
erosion control measures would be required to keep flows on-site and minimize the velocity of 
stormwater runoff. Such BMPs could include on-site drainage swales, bioretention features, use of 
permeable pavers in parking areas and streets, or infiltration basins which also serve as a means for 
pollutant removal. As discussed above, future projects, whether discretionary or ministerial, would 
be required to submit SWQMPs that include LID strategies and design measures to treat polluted 
runoff prior to entering the public storm drain system. These project specific studies would ensure 
that volume-based treatment LID BMPs are properly sized to infiltrate, filter, or treat the remaining 
portion of the runoff volume that was not retained or treated by other BMPs to maintain flow volume 
and velocity.  
VSR policies support the promotion of BMPs that minimize soil erosion, including soil stabilization 
and sediment control measures outlined in the City’s Grading Regulations Manual, BMP Design 
Manual, and Landscape Development Manual. Additional erosion control related policies are found 
in the SRE which promotes siting, design, engineering, and construction of new development 
minimizes the potential for erosion and enforcement of City ordinances for grading, erosion control, 
and sediment management, including the provisions of the urban runoff and discharge control 
ordinance.  
Overall, consistency with federal, state, and local regulations, along with policy compliance, would 
maintain drainage patterns and protect soil erosion that could result from increased stormwater 
runoff.  
b. Exceed Capacity of Stormwater System 
Generally, drainage facilities including storm drains, culverts, inlets, channels, curbs, roads, or other 
such structures are designed to prevent flooding by collecting storm water runoff and directing flows 
to either the natural drainage course and/or away from urban development. Future development 
consistent with the GPU and SSCSP would contribute additional runoff to the existing stormwater 
drainage system through the allowance of greater density and intensity of uses. If drainage facilities 
are not adequately designed, built, or maintained, new runoff could exceed the capacity of the 
existing storm water system. As discussed under Section 4.11.6.2.a, future projects that result in the 
development of new impervious surfaces would adhere to state and local regulations, and GPU and 
SSCSP policies, to ensure that runoff volumes and velocity of storm water runoff would not increase. 
Likewise, future development would be required to comply with project specific SWPPPs, which 
would identify BMPs to be incorporated into development plans to ensure that near-term 
construction activities would not result in substantial amounts of polluted runoff. Future 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-26 
development would also be reviewed for compliance with GPU policies promote the use of LID 
strategies, BMPs, pervious paving materials, and on-site infiltration for treating and reducing 
stormwater runoff. 
The City strives to maintain existing public facilities to meet current and future demands. Future 
projects would be required to adhere to the Public Facility Fee Requirements to ensure adequate 
stormwater facilities are available to support individually proposed projects. With specific focus on 
the SSCSP Planning Area, SSCSP Infrastructure and Utilities Goal 7 commits to stormwater 
infrastructure being reliable and of adequate capacity to serve existing and future developments 
within the SSCSP Planning Area. 
Through regulatory and policy compliance, coupled with payment of the Public Facility Fee assessed 
for both discretionary and by-right projects, future projects would not exceed the capacity of existing 
or planned stormwater drainage facilities, nor substantial additional sources of polluted runoff.  
c. Flood Flows  
Future development consistent with the project could increase volumes of stormwater runoff 
resulting in the impediment or redirection of flood flows. As described in Sections 4.11.6.2.a and 
4.11.6.2.b, future development would be required to adhere to regional and local plans, programs 
and regulations relating to storm water runoff and volume flow. All future development would 
include BMPs to manage polluted runoff and minimize flow volume and velocity. Future 
development, especially within the SSCSP Planning Area, would also be reviewed for adherence to 
SSCSP focused on avoiding increases in stormwater flows. For example, SSCSP Policy EQ-19 requires 
new development to ensure that post-development runoff rates do not exceed predevelopment 
rates. Also, SSCSP Policy UD-11 focuses on the reduction of impervious surfaces as a means to reduce 
stormwater velocity. 
4.11.6.3 Significance of Impacts 
While future development throughout the City has the potential to alter drainage patterns or 
increase stormwater runoff resulting in increased erosion, and otherwise impact the existing drainage 
system, all future development would be subject to federal, state, and local regulations aimed at 
reducing polluted stormwater and avoiding overloading the City’s drainage system. Both ministerial 
and discretionary development would be required to adhere to regulatory requirements including 
applicable NPDES permits issued by the San Diego RWQCB, the City’s JRMP and Code of Ordinances 
which include requirements for the elimination, control, or reduction of stormwater runoff. 
Additionally, policy compliance with the proposed GPU and SSCSP, would ensure impacts associated 
with drainage patterns and stormwater runoff would be less than significant.  
4.11.6.4 Mitigation Measures 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required.

4.11.7 
Flood Hazard 
4.11.7.1 Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to flood hazards are based on applicable 
criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project, in a flood hazard, 
tsunami, or seiche zones: 
• 
Risk release of pollutants due to project inundation? 
4.11.7.2 Impact Analysis 
a. FEMA Flood Areas 
As shown in Figure 4.11-2, portions of the City, are located within or partially within flood hazard 
areas. As shown, most flood areas are within the SSCSP Planning Area, especially within the 
Oceanside Boulevard Corridor along the Loma Alta Creek. Any area that lies within the FEMA-
designated 100-year floodplain is designated as high risk. Through its LHMP, the City has prepared 
action items to assist in preparing for flood hazards including participation in federal and state 
programs and conformance with NFIP standards. Future development within these areas, as well as 
the rest of the City, would be required to comply with FEMA requirements and Code of Ordinances 
Article IX, which requires flood safe measures be included in development plans. The City's Master 
Drainage Plan proposes facility improvements to provide additional protection from a 100-year storm 
event, including new culverts and other infrastructure, and the City requires that all development 
projects on parcels that lie within a FEMA-designated 100-year zone undergo a Floodplain Plan 
Review. 
The GPU envisions the multi-use of floodplains to encompass both flood control and recreational 
activity. Proposed policies provide guidance to future development to explore shared buffers for 
flood management and pedestrian/bicycle use.  
The proposed SSCSP envisions pedestrian and bicycle trails with access to Buena Vista Creek within 
the Vista Way corridor and to the San Luis Rey River Trail within the Mission Avenue corridor. Trails, 
greenway connections, and pedestrian pathways are shown on Figure 3-6 (Mission Avenue) and 
Figure 3-8 (Vista Way). Chapter 4 of the SSCSP, Urban Design and the Public Realm, provides policy 
guidance for flood control options that would be implemented by future development within the 
flood zones adjacent to the proposed trails.  
Additionally, future projects within designated flood zones would be required to comply with flood 
resilient designs, including elevated building pads, and/or other compliance measures as specified 
by FEMA and could be required to secure a LOMA prior to development permits to demonstrate 
that proposed structures would be located outside of a 100-year flood hazard area. Similar 
requirements would be implemented through proposed GPU and SSCSP goals and policies focused 
on impacts associated with flooding. Relevant proposed policies are summarized below.  


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-28 
All development would be required to adhere to the City GPU and SSCSP policies including the 
assurance that potential flood damage would be minimized. Therefore, adherence to FEMA 
processes and Code of Ordinances requirements for flood safe measures, and GPU policies would 
ensure that future development would not be subject to flooding and therefore, pollutants would 
not be released due to project inundation. 
b. Dam Inundation 
As shown in Figure 4.11-3, portions of the City are within the Dam Inundation Zone associated with 
the Lake Henshaw Dam. On-site flooding could occur because of nearby dam failure. Dams typically 
fail due to overtopping by reservoir water during heavy rainfall episodes, structural damage, and 
earthquake-related hazards. If an area lies within a dam inundation zone, it is considered at high risk. 
A dam is characterized as high hazard if it stores more than 1,000 acre-feet of water, is higher than 
150 feet tall, has potential for downstream property damage, and potential for downstream 
evacuation (County of San Diego 2023). Lake Henshaw capacity is 51,832 acre feet and is currently 
48 percent full at 24,665 acre feet (Vista Irrigation District 2023). The lake is maintained at 
approximately 40 percent capacity due to it being on the Lake Elsinore Fault Line. Failure of Henshaw 
Dam is unlikely. However, its failure would expose people or structures to significant risk. Henshaw 
Dam is an earthfill dam that is not subject to sudden catastrophic failure usually associated with 
concrete arch-type dams. Even if failure did occur, it would be of a slower, erosive type, resulting in 
less severe peak flows, allowing ample time for evacuation (City of Oceanside 2002). Additionally, 
inundation due to dam failure is considered unlikely because of state requirements that large dams 
receive seismic upgrades and routine inspections for safety. In California, the supervision, regulation, 
and inspection of all large dams not federally owned is the responsibility of the Division of Safety of 
Dams. They conduct periodic inspections of dams to identify deficiencies.  
The Vista Irrigation District is responsible for assessing and maintaining Lake Henshaw Dam. 
According to a 2022 report from the California Department of Water Resources Division of Safety of 
Dams, the Lake Henshaw Dam is in ‘Satisfactory’ condition, meaning that no existing or potential 
dam safety deficiencies are recognized (State of California Department of Water Resources 2022). 
As part of Vista Irrigation District’s 2020 Urban Water Management Plan, the district developed goals 
and objectives to reduce the possibility of damage and losses from dam failure. Specific interventions 
include updating dam inundation plans regularly, identifying hazard-prone structures, constructing 
barriers around structures, encouraging structural retrofitting, and coordinating with the U.S. Army 
Corps of Engineers, U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, and the California Department of Water Resources 
to support existing efforts to minimize dam failure. 
Although a portion of the City is located within a dam inundation zone, the possibility for dam failure 
is minimal and the project would not introduce any significant source of pollutants on-site that would 
be released in the event of a dam failure.  
c. Tsunami 
As discussed in Section 4.11.1.4, portions of the City’s coastal area and extending along the lower San 
Luis Rey River are located within a tsunami inundation zone as defined by the 2023 MJHMP. These 
areas of inundation are outside the SSCSP Planning Area. Implementation of the GPU would have 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.11-29 
the potential to increase the density of development within tsunami inundation areas and would 
incentivize residential development in areas subject to potential inundation result in in potentially 
significant impacts related to tsunami risk. The City is a TsunamiReady Community, as designated by 
the National Weather Service. The City earned this designation by defining tsunami hazard zones, 
installing evacuation route signage, conducting outreach on tsunami risk, establishing alert systems, 
and preparing a formal tsunami operations plan. Early warning of an approaching tsunami and 
clearance of high-risk areas are essential to minimizing the likelihood of injury and loss of life. The 
City’s public safety departments have established protocols for alerting and evacuating community 
members from tsunami hazard zones (see Section 4.10.5 of this Recirculated Program Environmental 
Impact Report. 
Notwithstanding the City’s readiness for tsunami evacuation, future development within the tsunami 
zones would be required to comply with proposed SRE Policy 6-19 which requires use of low impact 
engineering techniques, such as elevating structures above projected water level to ensure 
protection against tsunami. Through City emergency planning and tsunami readiness, along with 
implementation of GPU policies future development would not be subject to risk of tsunami and 
therefore, pollutants would not be released due to project inundation.  
d. Sea Level Rise 
While the analysis of sea level rise is not captured as a threshold of significance pursuant to CEQA, 
it is a subject for discussion especially related to coastal features that could be vulnerable to more 
severe flooding conditions under continued climate change and sea level rise. For example, the City’s 
harbor is one of many coastal features that are vulnerable to coastal hazards, as well as beach sand 
loss and bluff erosion. The City is currently updating the Local Coastal Land Use Plan and Local 
Coastal Program to address issues of inundation of vulnerable areas and planning for future sea level 
rise. Additionally, the GPU includes goals focused on proactive planning for sea level rise, erosion, 
and other climate-related coastline changes and prioritizing beach restoration and preservation 
while developing other coastal adaptation strategies to effectively address sea level rise. 
4.11.7.3 Significance of Impacts 
The project could increase potential risks associated with flood hazards and dam inundation due to 
the increased potential for higher density and greater intensity of uses within these zones. Future 
development would be required to adhere to state and local regulations, along with proposed GPU 
and SSCSP policies to ensure development within FEMA flood zones are consistent with all standards 
to ensure safe and flood free development. Additionally, development within the City’s coastal 
area/tsunami zone is subject to emergency planning and evacuation measures. The proposed SRE 
includes policies to encourage additional tsunami safety measures to be implemented by the City 
and local enforcement agencies. Additionally, the City is actively focusing on developing programs, 
regulations, and policy documents to address potential damage related to sea level rise. Therefore, 
through adherence to FEMA processing, City Code of Ordinances, and emergency requirements for 
flood safe measures, impacts associated with flood hazards and potential pollutant release, would 
be less than significant.
