4.11.8 
Conflict with Water Quality Plans 
4.11.8.1 Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to water quality plans are based on 
applicable criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Conflict with or obstruct implementation of a water quality control plan or sustainable 
groundwater management plan? 
4.11.8.2 Impact Analysis 
The project would be consistent with all relevant water quality plans. A summary of project 
compliance is as follows: 
• 
The City lies within the San Luis Rey Valley Groundwater Basin, the use of which is governed 
by the SGMA. The primary purposes of the SGMA is to ensure that groundwater levels are 
maintained, reduction of groundwater storage is minimized, and that groundwater quality is 
maintained (Upper San Luis Rey Groundwater Management Authority 2023). As discussed in 
Section 4.11.5.2, the City works with local agencies to ensure groundwater sustainability, and 
maintenance of the groundwater recharge process. Additionally, implementation of 
proposed GPU and SSCSP policies as throughout would ensure maintenance of groundwater 
recharge and avoid any conflict with the SGMA. 
• 
The City is within RWQCB Region 9, San Diego Basin Area, which is subject to watershed 
management strategies in the San Luis Rey River and Carlsbad  WQIPs. The WQIPs prioritize 
and address basin-specific pollutants through an appropriate suite of BMPs intended to assist 
in the reduction of known impairments. The City’s WMAs are primarily impaired for chloride, 
indicator bacteria, phosphorus, TDS, total nitrogen, benthic community effects and toxicity. 
The project would be consistent with the WQIPs, as detailed in Section 4.12.3.2, future 
projects throughout the City would be required to includes a project-specific BMPs and water 
quality treatment features that would ensure the project does not contribute to the 
impairment of the watersheds. Additionally, implementation of proposed GPU and SSCSP 
policies as summarized throughout would ensure that specific conditions are evaluated and 
site appropriate BMPs are included in project SWPPPs and construction plans, as well as the 
inclusion of permanent BMPs. 
• 
The NPDES program establishes a comprehensive water quality program to manage urban 
stormwater and minimize pollution of the environment to the maximum extent practicable. 
As discussed in Sections 4.11.4.2.a and 4.11.6.2.a future projects would be required to prepare 
a SWPPP which would outline preliminary construction BMPs that would be implemented as 
project design features, to minimize disturbance, protect slopes, reduce erosion, and limit or 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.11 Hydrology and Water Quality

Page 4.11-31 
prevent various pollutants from entering surface water runoff. Implementation of these BMPs 
would ensure that construction activities would not result in polluted runoff from the project 
sites consistent with the requirements of NPDES permit.  
• 
The City’s JRMP presents strategies to reduce the discharge of pollutants into the storm drain 
system. As discussed in Section 4.11.6.2.a, future projects would be required to include BMPs 
that demonstrate compliance with the requirements outlined in the JRMP. These projects 
would include BMP plans that can prevent pollution discharge regardless of season. 
Therefore, the project would not conflict with a water quality control plan or a sustainable 
groundwater management plan.  
4.11.8.3 Significance of Impacts 
The project would be consistent with all relevant water quality control plans. Impacts related to 
conflicts or obstruction with such plans would be less than significant.

Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required. 
4.11.9 
Cumulative Analysis 
The geographic scope of the cumulative impact analysis for hydrology and water quality generally 
includes drainage basins, watersheds, water bodies or groundwater basins, depending on the 
location of the potential impact and its tributary area. The project’s cumulative study area is the City’s 
three WMAs. Future projects would be required to adhere to the federal, state, and local regulations 
for the design and implementation of site design, source control, treatment control best 
management practices to ensure all stormwater standards are met. Additionally, future development 
would adhere to all GPU and SSCSP goals and policies aimed at improving water quality, maintaining 
and improving groundwater recharge, preserving drainage patterns and avoiding flood hazards. 
Conformance with the applicable stormwater, drainage and flooding standards would preclude 
potentially significant water quality impacts from occurring and all project level impacts associated 
with hydrology and water quality would be less than significant. Future projects would implement 
project‑specific site design, source control, and structural pollutant control measures consistent with 
federal, regional, and local water quality standards to ensure adverse impacts to water quality 
resulting potential erosion of soils are minimized. Therefore, the combined effect of all future projects 
would not result in incremental contributions to a cumulative impact on water quality. Cumulative 
impacts would be less than significant.

4.12 
Mineral Resources 
This section addresses potential project impacts to mineral resources that could result from 
implementation of the Onward Oceanside project which includes the City of Oceanside (City) General 
Plan Update (GPU), Smart and Sustainable Corridors Specific Plan (SSCSP), and Climate Action Plan 
(CAP), collectively referred to as the project. The GPU would apply to the entire City, while the SSCSP 
would apply to land within the Specific Plan boundary, referred to as the SSCSP Planning Area. As 
discussed in Chapter 3.0, Project Description, the analysis of potential impacts focuses on parcels 
throughout the City where the project either (1) proposes changes to existing land use designations 
or (2) where no land use change is proposed, but growth is anticipated to occur. The majority of the 
proposed increased density and intensity of uses would be within the SSCSP Planning Area, as shown 
in Figure 3-2.    
This analysis relies on secondary sources including state and regional mineral mapping.  
4.12.1 
Existing Conditions 
As mandated by the Surface Mining and Reclamation Act (SMARA) of 1975 (California Public 
Resources Code, Section 2710 et seq.), the California State Minerals and Geology Board classifies 
California mineral resources with the Mineral Resource Zone (MRZ) system. The MRZ classification 
system categorizes lands based on their suitability as sources of sand, gravel, and stone deposits for 
construction aggregate (see Section 4.12.2.1 for definitions of MRZs). 
The City supports two major areas of mineral deposits (City of Oceanside 2002). One of these is the 
San Luis Rey River Basin, which contains landfill and beach sand (non-construction quality) and 
construction quality sand suitable for concrete and plaster. This deposit area is located along the 
lower San Luis Rey River south of Camino Real to the mouth of the Pacific Ocean. A second mineral 
deposit area, east of El Camino Real and north of Oceanside Boulevard, contains significant deposits 
of silica sand, primarily used in glass manufacturing (City of Oceanside 2002). This area was previously 
mined for silica sand but operations have been closed and portions of the area have been developed 
with housing, an aquatics center, a sports arena, and a senior center. Governed by the El Corazon 
Specific Plan, this area is slated for additional development. 
4.12.2 Regulatory Setting 
4.12.2.1 Federal  
a. Surface Mining and Reclamation Act of 1975 
SMARA established policies for the conservation, development, and reclamation of mineral lands. It 
also contained specific provisions for the California Geological Survey to classify the regional 
significance of mineral resources using MRZs. The objective of these zones is to identify the 
significance of mineral deposits and ensure that the mineral potential of land is recognized and 
considered by local government decision-makers before they make land use decisions that could 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.12 Mineral Resources 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.12-2 
preclude mining. The highest priority areas are those within the state that are subject to urban 
expansion or other irreversible land uses that would preclude mineral extraction. The following 
provides a description of the four different MRZs: 
• 
MRZ-1 designates areas where adequate geologic information indicates that no significant 
mineral deposits are present, or where it is judged that little likelihood exists for their 
presence.  
• 
MRZ-2 designates areas underlain by mineral deposits where geologic data indicates that 
significant measured or indicated mineral resources are present.  
• 
MRZ-3 designates areas that contain known mineral deposits, the significance of which 
cannot be evaluated from available data. 
• 
MRZ-4 designates areas where available information is inadequate for assignment to an MRZ 
zone. 
Figure 4.12-1 shows the distribution of each MRZ category throughout the City. Table 4.12-1 presents 
the approximate acreage of each MRZ category. Most of the City is designated as MRZ-3, land for 
which the significance of mineral resources cannot be determined. A small amount of land within the 
northeastern and northwestern portion of the City is designated as MRZ-4, land where available 
information is inadequate for assignment to an MRZ. Some land in the northern portion of the City is 
categorized as MRZ-2, areas underlain by mineral deposits where geologic data indicates that 
significant measured or indicated mineral resources are present.

the potential for loss of mineral resources is low because there is a lack of known mineral resources 
in the area, the feasibility of a mining operation within a highly developed urban environment is low 
due to land use conflicts, and there is little undeveloped land available for mining.

4.13 
Noise 
This section addresses potential project impacts related to noise that could result from 
implementation of the Onward Oceanside project which includes the City of Oceanside (City) General 
Plan Update (GPU), Smart and Sustainable Corridors Specific Plan (SSCSP), and Climate Action Plan 
(CAP), collectively referred to as the project. The GPU would apply to the entire City while the SSCSP 
would apply to land within the Specific Plan boundary, referred to as the SSCSP Planning Area. As 
discussed in Chapter 3.0, Project Description, the analysis of potential impacts focuses on parcels 
throughout the City where the project either (1) proposes changes to existing land use designations 
or (2) where no land use change is proposed, but growth is anticipated to occur. The majority of the 
proposed increased density and intensity of uses would be within the SSCSP Planning Area, as shown 
in Figure 3-2.  
4.13.1 
Existing Conditions 
4.13.1.1 Noise Descriptors and Terminology 
Sound levels are described in units called the decibel (dB). Decibels are measured on a logarithmic 
scale that quantifies sound intensity in a manner similar to the Richter scale used for earthquake 
magnitudes. Thus, a doubling of the energy of a noise source, such as doubling of traffic volume, 
would increase the noise level by 3 dB; a halving of the energy would result in a 3 dB decrease. 
However, human perception of noise has no simple correlation with acoustical energy. A change in 
noise levels is generally perceived as follows: 3 A-weighted dB [dB(A)] barely perceptible, 5 dB(A) 
readily perceptible, and 10 dB(A) perceived as a doubling or halving of noise (California Department 
of Transportation [Caltrans] 2013).   
In technical terms, sound levels are described as either a “sound power level” or a “sound pressure 
level”. Both share the same unit of measure, the dB. However, sound power is the energy converted 
into sound by the source. As sound energy travels through the air, it creates a sound wave in the air 
that exerts pressure on receivers such as an eardrum or microphone, the sound pressure level. Sound 
measurement instruments only measure sound pressure, and limits used in standards are generally 
sound pressure levels.  
The human ear is not equally sensitive to all frequencies within the sound spectrum. To 
accommodate this phenomenon, the A-scale, which approximates the frequency response of the 
average young ear when listening to most ordinary everyday sounds, was devised. When people 
make relative judgments of the loudness or annoyance of a sound, their judgments correlate well 
with the A-scale sound levels of those sounds. Therefore, the “A­weighted” noise scale is used for 
measurements and standards involving the human perception of noise. Noise levels using A-
weighted measurements are designated with the notation dB(A). 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.13 Noise 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.13-2 
a. Descriptors 
The impact of noise is not a function of loudness alone. The time of day when noise occurs and the 
duration of the noise are also important. In addition, most noise that lasts for more than a few 
seconds is variable in its intensity. Consequently, a variety of noise descriptors has been developed. 
The noise descriptors used for this study are the equivalent continuous noise level (Leq) and the 
community noise equivalent level (CNEL).  
The Leq is the equivalent steady-state noise level in a stated period of time that is calculated by 
averaging the acoustic energy over a time period; when no period is specified, a 1-hour period is 
assumed.  
The CNEL is a 24-hour equivalent sound level. The CNEL calculation applies an additional 5 dB(A) 
penalty to noise occurring during evening hours, between 7 p.m. and 10 p.m., and an additional 
10 dB(A) penalty is added to noise occurring during the night, between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. These 
increases for certain times are intended to account for the added sensitivity of humans to noise 
during the evening and night. 
b. Propagation 
Sound from a localized source (approximating a “point” source) radiates uniformly outward as it 
travels away from the source in a spherical pattern, known as geometric spreading. The sound level 
decreases or drops off at a rate of 6 dB(A) for each doubling of the distance. Vehicle traffic and 
railway noise are not a single, stationary point source of sound. When assessed over a period of time, 
the movement of vehicles and trains makes the source of the sound appear to emanate from a line 
(line source) rather than a point when viewed over some time interval. The drop-off rate for a line 
source is 3 dB(A) for each doubling of distance.  
The propagation of noise is also affected by the intervening ground, known as ground absorption. 
A hard site (such as parking lots or smooth bodies of water) receives no additional ground 
attenuation, and the changes in noise levels with distance (drop-off rate) are simply the geometric 
spreading of the source. A soft site (such as soft dirt, grass, or scattered bushes and trees) provides 
an additional ground attenuation value of 1.5 dB(A) per doubling of distance. Thus, a point source 
over a soft site would drop off at 7.5 dB(A) per doubling of distance and a line source over a soft site 
would drop off at 4.5 dB(A) per doubling of distance. 
c. Noise-Sensitive Receptors 
Noise-sensitive receptors are associated with land uses wherein indoor and/or outdoor human 
activities may be subject to stress and/or significant interference from noise. They include residential 
(single- and multi-family dwellings, mobile home parks, dormitories and similar uses); transient 
lodging (which are sensitive at night including hotels, motels and similar uses); hospitals, nursing 
homes, convalescent hospitals, and other facilities for long-term medical care; and public or private 
educational facilities, libraries, churches and other places of public gathering. In addition to buildings, 
exterior use areas may also be considered noise-sensitive receptors. Exterior use areas are areas 
where frequent human use for prolonged periods (at least an hour) may reasonably occur. Common 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.13 Noise 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.13-3 
examples of exterior use areas include residential backyards, multi-family communal areas, patios, 
picnic areas, recreation areas, playgrounds, and parks.  
4.13.1.2 Vibration Descriptors and Terminology 
Vibration consists of energy waves transmitted through solid material (Caltrans 2020). Ground borne 
vibration propagates from the source through the ground to adjacent buildings by surface waves. 
Vibration energy spreads out as it travels through the ground, causing the vibration amplitude to 
decrease with distance away from the source. Ground borne vibration is measured by its peak particle 
velocity (PPV). The PPV is normally described in inches per second (in/sec). Human reaction to 
vibration is dependent on the environment the receiver is in as well as individual sensitivity. As 
example, vibration outdoors is rarely noticeable and generally not considered annoying. Typically, 
humans must be inside a structure for vibrations to become noticeable and/or annoying. Based on 
several federal studies, the threshold of perception is 0.035 PPV, with 0.24 in/sec PPV being a 
distinctly perceptible (Caltrans 2020). 
The Federal Transit Administration (FTA) has identified the following three categories of vibration-
sensitive uses: 
Category 1 – High Sensitivity Uses: 
 Buildings where ambient vibration well below levels associated with human annoyance is essential 
for equipment or operations within the building. Typically uses covered in Category 1 include 
vibration-sensitive research and manufacturing facilities, hospitals, and university research 
operations.  
Category 2 – Residential Uses: 
 Buildings where people sleep. Typical uses covered in Category 2 include residential, hotels, and 
hospitals.  
Category 3 – Institutional Uses: 
 Buildings that do not have vibration-sensitive equipment, but still have the potential for activity 
interference. Typical uses covered in Category 3 include schools, churches, other institutions, and 
quiet offices.

measurement locations are shown in Figure 4.13-1.

4.13.2 Regulatory Setting 
4.13.2.1 Federal  
a. Construction 
The FTA Transit Noise and Vibration Impact Assessment Manual (FTA 2018) recommends a daytime 
construction noise level threshold of 80 dB(A) Leq(8) when detailed construction noise assessments 
are performed to evaluate potential impacts to community residences surrounding a project. 
Although this guidance is not a regulation, it can serve as a quantified standard in absence of such 
limits at the state and local jurisdiction levels. 
b. Vibration 
The FTA provides criteria for acceptable levels of groundborne vibration for various types of 
buildings. Structures amplify groundborne vibration; wood-frame buildings, such as typical 
residential structures, are more affected by ground vibration than heavier buildings. The level at 
which groundborne vibration is strong enough to cause architectural damage has not been 
determined conclusively, but the standards recommended by the FTA are shown in Table 4.13-2. 
Table 4.13-2

“Frequent Events” is defined as more than 70 vibration events per day. Most rapid transit projects fall into this category. 
“Occasional Events” is defined as 30 to 70 vibration events per day. Most commuter trunk links fall into this category 
“Infrequent Events” is defined as fewer than 30 vibration events per day. This category includes most commuter rail 
systems. 
 
For Category 1 uses such as vibration sensitive equipment, the screening distance from the right-of-
way is 600 feet. For Category 2 land uses such as residences and buildings where people would 
normally sleep, the screening distance is 200 feet. The screening distance for Category 3 land uses 
such as institutional land uses with primarily daytime uses, is 120 feet. 
4.13.2.2 State  
a. California Code of Regulations 
For residential uses, interior noise levels for habitable rooms are regulated also by Title 24 of the 
California Code of Regulations, California Noise Insulation Standards. Title 24, Chapter 12, 
Section 1206.4 of the 2022 California Building Code requires that interior noise levels attributable to 
exterior sources not exceed 45 CNEL in any habitable room within a residential structure. A habitable 
room is a room used for living, sleeping, eating, or cooking. Bathrooms, closets, hallways, utility 
spaces, and similar areas are not considered habitable rooms for this regulation.  
For non-residential structures, Title 24, Chapter 12, Section 1207.5 refers to 2022 California Green 
Building Standards, Chapter 5 – Nonresidential Mandatory Measures, Division 5.5 – Environmental 
Quality, Section 5.507 – Environmental Comfort, Subsection 5.507.4 – Acoustical Control. Pursuant 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.13 Noise 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.13-10 
to these standards, all non-residential building construction shall employ building assemblies and 
components that achieve a composite sound transmission class rating of at least 50 or shall otherwise 
demonstrate that exterior noise shall not result in interior noise environment where noise levels 
exceed 50 dB(A) Leq in occupied areas during any hour of operation. 
b. San Diego County Airport Land Use Commission 
The Oceanside Municipal Airport is located in the northwest portion of the Planning Area north of 
SR-76, south of the San Luis Rey River, and east of Benet Road. The San Diego County Airport Land 
Use Commission (ALUC) prepares airport land use compatibility plans (ALUCP) in order to promote 
compatibility between airports and the land uses surrounding them. ALUCPs set compatibility criteria 
applicable to local agencies in their preparation or amendment of land use plans and ordinances. 
The Oceanside Municipal Airport ALUCP was prepared in 2010 and provides noise level contours and 
noise compatibility criteria for various land uses (San Diego County ALUC 2010). The noise 
compatibility criteria are shown in Table 4.13-4. 
4.13.2.3 Local  
a. City of Oceanside Code of Ordinances  
Chapter 38 Noise Control Ordinance 
Section 38 of the City’s Code of Ordinances, known as the Noise Control Ordinance, establishes noise 
level limits for stationary sources. Noise level limits are specific to base district zones such as 
residential zones, commercial zones, etc. Except for exempted activities, it is unlawful for any person 
to cause or allow the creation of any noise in excess of applicable noise level limits at or beyond the 
property boundary. When property lines form the joint boundary of two zones, the sound level limit 
shall be the arithmetic mean of the limit applicable to each of the zones. Table 4.13-5 below 
summarizes noise level limits.

The Noise Control Ordinance has not established any upper limits for construction noise because it 
is temporary and will cease to occur after completion of the project construction. The Noise Control 
Ordinance regulates the timing of construction activities and includes special provisions for sensitive 
land uses. Section 38.17(h) of the Noise Control chapter prohibits construction between the hours of 
10:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. Monday through Saturday. No construction activities shall occur outside of 
these hours, on Sundays, or federal holidays.  
4.13.3 Proposed GPU and SSCSP Policies 
The proposed GPU and SSCSP include policies intended to reduce potential adverse environmental 
impacts resulting from buildout of the plans. As future development is proposed, development 
would be required to demonstrate consistency with the GPU and SSCSP policy framework, as 
applicable. The policy framework would be implemented by the City during future discretionary 
and/or ministerial project reviews to ensure impact minimization.  The analysis of potential impacts 
considers how implementation of these policies at the project level would serve to reduce the 
significance of potential adverse impacts. 
4.13.3.1 Policy Framework 
The following policies are examples of the policy framework associated with noise, and do not intend 
to be exclusive of all additional relevant policies that may apply to future development. 
a. GPU Healthy and Livable Communities Element (HLC) 
The HLC proposes noise-related policies that are specific to project level design.   


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.13 Noise 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.13-13 
• 
Goal 7-X: The City will consider existing and future noise levels when making land use 
planning decisions to minimize exposure to excessive noise, including from motor vehicle 
traffic, fixed rail, aircraft, industrial land uses, and other sources. 
• 
Goal 7-Y: The impact of noise on people will be minimized through noise reduction and 
suppression techniques.   
• 
Policy 7-158: Use the sound level limits matrix (Table 7-9) and Future Noise Contours Map 
(Figure 7-11) as criteria to determine acceptability of a proposed land use. Establish and 
enforce allowable noise limits for daytime levels and nighttime levels (Table 7-10).  
• 
Policy 7-159: Seek to limit new noise-sensitive uses – including schools, daycares, hospitals, 
places of worship, and homes – where noise levels are higher, if alternative locations are 
available for the uses in the City.  
• 
Policy 7-160: Ensure that new development does not generate noise in excess of the sound 
level limits outlined in Table 7-9, whenever feasible.  
• 
Policy 7-161: For all projects that have noise exposure levels that exceed the standards in 
Table 7-9, site planning and architecture should incorporate noise-attenuating features. With 
mitigation, development should meet allowable sound level limits in Table 7-9.  
• 
Policy 7-162: Discourage the use of berms and sound walls for noise mitigation; rather, 
encourage the use of project design techniques such as increasing the distance between the 
noise source and the noise sensitive receiver and use non-noise sensitive structures (e.g., a 
garage) to shield noise sensitive areas. If a berm or wall is determined necessary to mitigate 
noise, discourage exclusive use of walls in excess of six feet in height and encourage use of 
natural barriers such as site topography or constructed earthen berms. When walls are 
determined to be the only feasible solution to noise mitigation, then the walls shall be 
designed to limit aesthetic impacts. 
• 
Policy 7-163: Regularly monitor noise levels near sensitive uses to assess efficacy of, or 
additional need for, traffic calming measures. 
• 
Policy 7-164: Work with railroad service providers and the Federal Railroad Administration to 
establish Quiet Zones in the City where trains do not routinely sound their horns at grade 
crossings. 
• 
Policy 7-165: Address appropriate construction noise and vibration control measures, 
standards, and monitoring procedures for future development in the City’s Municipal Code 
to reduce impacts to nearby uses.

HLC Figure 7-10 is recreated herein as Figure 4.13-4.

of the receiving use. 
2Where it is not possible to reduce noise in outdoor activity areas to the allowable maximum, levels up to 5 dB higher 
may be allowed provided that available exterior noise level reduction measures have been implemented and interior 
noise levels are in compliance with this table. 
3dB(A) CNEL = A-weighted decibels community noise equivalent level. 
4An exterior noise exposure level of 65 dB(A) CNEL is allowable for residential uses in a mixed-use project and for 
residential uses within the Oceanside Municipal Airport Area of Influence, pursuant to the noise compatibility 
policies contained in the ALUCP. 
 
b. GPU Efficient and Compatible Land Use Element (ECLU) 
The ECLU provides policies that focus on land use compatibility between potentially conflicting uses such 
as noise. The element seeks to coordinate land uses to minimize noise on surrounding areas, especially 
where adjacent uses may not be compatible.  
Use Compatibility 
• 
Policy 3-18: Develop zoning standards that ensure compatibility where intensive or 
potentially noise and air quality impacting uses are proposed near areas with existing or 
proposed residential uses. 
• 
Policy 3-19: Require that high-impact land uses operate within enclosed buildings capable of 
containing emissions, and limit noise, glare, and odor to within the site perimeter and screen 
equipment, goods, and activities from public view. 
High Density Residential Development 
• 
Policy 3-61: Ensure proper noise attenuation for residential uses including insulation and 
noise attenuating window treatments where appropriate. 
o In determining the need for noise attenuation, the projected noise contour map 
(Figure 7-10), Tables 7-6 and 7-7 that outline noise standards should be used. In 
particular, for residential development located within a projected 65 dB or higher noise 
environment, noise attenuation practices—extending from intelligent site planning to 
insulation—are warranted. 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.13 Noise 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.13-17 
Allowable Uses 
• 
Policy 3-96: Each industrial use shall provide adequate setbacks, attenuating structures, 
devices, and procedures to ensure that noise, vibration, odors, glare, heat, and other 
emissions do not interfere with neighboring industrial activities nor endanger the health, 
safety, peace, or general welfare of persons residing or working in the surrounding area. 
c. SSCSP Environmental Quality 
The Environmental Quality chapter of the SSCSP provides policy direction to avoid risks to residents, 
workers, and visitors from excessive noise throughout the SSCSP Planning Areas.  
• 
Policy EQ-25: Site Design. Orient buildings away from noise sources, including highways, 
freeways, and the Sprinter line, to reduce noise nuisance. Bedrooms of residential buildings 
should be located on the opposite side of the building from the noise source unless an 
adequate sound barrier is in place. 
• 
Policy EQ-26: Noise-Attenuation. Require all residential and other noise-sensitive 
development within the 65 CNEL noise contour (as shown in Figure 6-8) to undertake 
development that is noise-rated in accordance with the California Code of Regulations. 
Require certification of such from a qualified acoustical engineer when so desirable. 
• 
Policy EQ-27: Loading Dock Orientation. To the extent feasible, locate commercial and 
industrial loading areas away from sensitive receptors. Loading areas can be sited within 
enclosed or covered spaces or oriented such that buildings and other site improvements 
serve to shield loading activities from adjacent properties and the public right-of-way. 
• 
Policy EQ-28: Excessive Vibration. Require that new development near the Sprinter rail line 
be limited as follows to avoid impact from excessive vibration, unless vibration isolation 
construction is undertaken: 
o No new buildings where low ambient vibration is essential for interior operations may be 
located within 225 feet of the railroad tracks. These uses may include but are not limited 
to vibration-sensitive research and manufacturing, hospital research areas, concert halls, 
and TV/recording studios. 
o New residences or other buildings where people sleep may be located within 100 feet of 
the railroad tracks only with the appropriate noise attenuation, including siting bedrooms 
or sleeping quarters away from the tracks, noise attenuating insulation and windows. 
These uses include multi-family dwellings, houses, hospital patient rooms, and hotels. 
o No schools may be located within 70 feet of the railroad tracks. 
d. SSCSP Land Use 
• 
The Land Use chapter of the SSCSP includes site design and construction measures to 
minimize noise impacts throughout the SSCSP Planning Area. Policy LU-19: Low-Intensity, 
Low-Impact Industrial Uses. Allow for low-intensity, low-impact industrial uses in commercial 
areas. Such uses shall maintain a storefront, occupy no more than 15,000 square feet of floor 
area, generate minimal truck traffic, and comply with all applicable noise and air emissions 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.13 Noise 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.13-18 
standards.  Associated activities shall be conducted entirely within enclosed and properly 
insulated spaces. 
• 
Policy LU-25: Compatibility with Nearby Uses. Ensure that industrial development is designed 
and operated to minimize noise, heat, glare, dust, unscreened storage yards, air emissions, 
hazardous materials generation, and other negative effects, including requiring screening, 
buffers, and landscaping, as necessary. 
• 
Policy LU-34: Compatibility with Adjacent Single-Family Neighborhoods. Promote site design 
and architecture that is sensitive to adjacent single-family neighborhoods – e.g., setbacks, 
screening and softening landscape, horizontal and vertical articulation, enclosed parking 
facilities, light pollution control, improvements to shared public space.   
4.13.4 Noise Level Increases 
4.13.4.1 Thresholds of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to noise level increases are based on 
applicable criteria in the 2025 California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines, Appendix G. 
Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Generate a substantial temporary or permanent increase in ambient noise levels in the vicinity 
of the project in excess of standards established in the local general plan or noise ordinance, 
or applicable standards of other agencies? 
4.13.4.2 Impact Analysis 
a. Vehicle Traffic Noise 
Traffic noise occurs adjacent to every roadway and is directly related to the traffic volume, speed, 
and mix of vehicles. Existing and future traffic volumes, speeds, and truck percentages for roadway 
segments, as well as the day/evening/nighttime traffic distribution, were obtained from the traffic 
engineer. The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) Traffic Noise Model algorithms were used to 
calculate distances to noise contours for each roadway. The FHWA model takes into account traffic 
mix, speed, and volume; roadway gradient; relative distances between sources, barriers, and sensitive 
receptors; and shielding provided by intervening terrain or structures. 
The analysis of the noise environment considered that the topography was flat with no intervening 
terrain between sensitive land uses and roadways. Because modeled predicted noise levels do not 
account for obstructions, they are higher than those which would actually occur. In actuality, 
buildings and other obstructions along the roadways would shield distant receivers from the traffic 
noise. Existing and future vehicle traffic noise calculations are provided in Appendix C. 
Increase in Ambient Noise 
Long-term traffic noise that affects sensitive land uses would be considered substantial and 
constitute a significant noise impact if the project would: 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.13 Noise 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.13-19 
• 
Increase noise levels by 5 dB or more where the no project noise level is less than 60 CNEL; 
• 
Increase noise levels by 3 dB or more where the no project noise level is 60 CNEL to 65 CNEL; 
or 
• 
Increase noise levels by 1.5 dB or more where the no project noise level is greater than 
65 CNEL. 
The noise analysis is based on the baseline (year 2016) and future (year 2050) traffic volume data. 
For purposes of the noise analysis, 178 roadway and freeway segments were analyzed. The change 
in noise level was calculated for buildout of the GPU as well as buildout of the existing General Plan. 
Noise impacts were determined by comparing the change in noise levels between the existing 
condition and buildout of the GPU to the criteria listed above. For informational purposes, this 
analysis also includes a discussion of the difference in impacts that would occur when compared to 
buildout of the existing General Plan. The existing and buildout noise levels are summarized in 
Table 4.13-8.

Except for the segments of Oceanside Boulevard between Rancho Del Oro Drive and College 
Boulevard, Marron Road between Western City Limit and College Boulevard, and Foussat Road 
between Alex Road and Mission Avenue, there are noise-sensitive residential uses located adjacent 
to each of these roadway segments. The GPU contains policies that would reduce impacts associated 
with vehicle traffic noise. For new noise-sensitive uses, HLC Goals 7-X and 7-Y require the City to 
consider noise levels when making land use decisions and minimize noise through noise reduction 
and suppression techniques. HLC Policies 7-158, 7-159, 7-160, 7-161, and SSCSP Policies EQ-25, and 
EQ-26 establish sound level limits and require noise reduction through site planning and 
architecture. Through implementation of these policies, noise levels at new noise-sensitive land uses 
would be evaluated and noise reduction techniques implemented to reduce noise exposure. For 
existing noise-sensitive land uses, HLC Policy 7-163 requires the City to regularly monitor noise levels 
near sensitive uses to assess efficacy of, or additional need for, traffic calming measures. However, 
the increase in ambient noise levels adjacent to the roadway segments listed above would likely 
remain at levels that would expose existing noise-sensitive receptors to a significant increase in 
ambient noise levels.

Land Use Compatibility 
Future vehicle traffic noise contours are shown in Figure 4.13-4. A significant impact would occur if 
implementation of the project resulted in an exposure of people to current or future motor vehicle 
traffic noise levels that exceed standards established in the HLC (see Table 4.13-6).  
The GPU land use plan proposes a variety of land uses, including residential, retail, office, industrial, 
and hotels. Most of the land use designations included in the GPU have been carried forward from 
the existing General Plan. The GPU primarily focuses future development and redevelopment within 
the City’s main corridors as further detailed in the SSCSP. As shown in Figure 4.13-4, the SSCSP 
Planning Area is located adjacent to freeways and other heavily traveled roadways. Noise-sensitive 
uses that are developed near higher-volume roadways could experience noise levels in excess of the 
proposed GPU noise standards.  
The GPU contains policies that would reduce impacts associated with land use compatibility. HLC 
Policy 7-158 requires the use of the sound level matrix and future noise contour map to determine 
acceptability of a proposed land use. HLC Policy 7-159 seeks to limit new noise-sensitive uses where 
noise levels are higher if alternative locations are available. HLC Policies 7-160 and 7-161 establishes 
exterior and interior noise level standards and requires noise-attenuation through site planning and 
architecture. For the SSCSP, Policy EQ-25 also requires site design measures and architecture to 
reduce noise exposure and Policy EQ-26 requires noise-rated development in accordance with the 
California Code of Regulations for residential development located within the 65 CNEL contour. 
Additionally, all future development located in areas where exterior noise levels exceed the land use 
compatibility standards, site-specific interior noise analyses demonstrating compliance with the 
interior noise standards of Title 24 would be required. These requirements for site-specific noise 
analyses would be implemented through submission of a Title 24 Compliance Report to demonstrate 
interior noise levels of 45 CNEL. Through implementation of this regulatory framework, exterior and 
interior traffic noise associated with new development would not expose existing noise-sensitive 
receptors to a significant increase in ambient noise levels.  
b. Railroad Noise 
Oceanside Transit Center accommodates four separate rail lines in the Planning Area – North County 
Transit District’s Coaster and Sprinter as well as Metrolink’s Orange County Line and Inland Empire–
Orange County Line and Amtrak’s Surfliner. The Coaster commuter rail service operates between the 
Oceanside Transit Center and the Santa Fe Depot in San Diego. The route follows the South Coast 
Highway within the City. The Sprinter hybrid-rail system connects Oceanside at the Oceanside Transit 
Center to Escondido via the SR-78 corridor. The Metrolink Orange County Line is a commuter rail 
line that runs from the Oceanside Transit Station through Orange County to Union Station in 
Downtown Los Angeles. The route alignment generally follows the I-5 corridor to Union Station. The 
Metrolink Inland Empire–Orange County Line is a commuter rail line that runs from the Oceanside 
Transit Center through Orange County to San Bernardino. The Pacific Surfliner is an intercity rail line 
that runs between the Santa Fe Depot in Downtown San Diego along the Highway 101 corridor to 
the Oceanside Transit Center and then to the north through Orange County, Los Angeles, and 
Ventura County, terminating in San Luis Obispo. Additionally, freight trains utilize the north-south 
railroad tracks during the nighttime hours. The number of Sprinter, Amtrak, and Metrolink trains that

As shown in Table 4.13-9, noise-sensitive receivers in the vicinity of the railroad tracks could be 
exposed to noise levels that exceed the compatibility standards (see Table 4.13-6). However, as 
previously discussed, the GPU contains policies that would reduce impacts associated with land use 
compatibility. The goals, policies, and noise reduction measures discussed in Section 4.13.4.2.a, Land 
Use Compatibility, also apply to noise levels generated by railroad operations. Additionally, HLC 
Policy 7-164 requires the City to work with railroad service providers and the Federal Railroad 
Administration to establish Quiet Zones in the City where trains do not routinely sound their horns 
at grade crossings. Implementation of these policies would ensure that new development located in 
the vicinity of the railroad tracks would be designed to reduce noise levels to the City’s compatibility 
standards and would reduce nuisance noise generated by train warning horns.  
c. Stationary Noise 
A significant impact would occur if implementation of the project resulted in the exposure of people 
to noise levels that violate the regulations contained in the City’s Code of Ordinances Chapter 38, 
Noise Control Ordinance. Stationary sources of noise include activities associated with a given land 
use. The City includes multiple land uses, including residential, commercial, industrial, and mixed-use 
land uses. Various land uses contain on-site stationary noise sources, including rooftop heating, 
ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) equipment; mechanical equipment; emergency electrical 
generators; parking lot activities; loading dock operations; and recreation activities. Noise sources 
from industrial uses would include mechanical equipment, generators, and trucks. Potential noise 
conflicts could occur in mixed-use areas where residential uses are located in close proximity to 
industrial, commercial, and retail uses. Stationary noise is considered a “point source” and attenuates 
over distance at a rate of 6 dB(A) for each doubling of distance. The exact location and nature of 
future stationary noise sources is not known at this time, and therefore cannot be calculated in this 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.13 Noise 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.13-27 
analysis. Impacts were assessed in this analysis by identifying potential types of stationary sources 
and locations of mixed-use land use interfaces and identifying applicable regulations and mitigation 
framework for addressing impacts. 
Noise levels within the City are currently dominated by vehicle traffic on freeways and heavily traveled 
area roadways, and would continue to be the primary source of noise under buildout of the GPU. 
The type of land uses proposed under the GPU would be similar to the land uses that currently exist. 
Therefore, future noise levels from stationary sources throughout the City would not be expected to 
increase the hourly or daily average sound level with respect to current conditions. While noise-
sensitive residential land uses would be exposed to noise associated with the operation of 
commercial and industrial uses, future development would be required to show compliance with the 
City’s Noise Control Ordinance. As detailed in Section 4.13.2.3, the City regulates specific noise level 
limits allowable between land uses including limits on hours of operation for various noise-
generating activities, guidance for measuring potential noise violations, and violation procedures. 
Additionally, HLC Policy 7-158 establishes and enforces allowable noise limits for daytime and 
nighttime levels (see Table 4.13-6). SSCSP Policy EQ-27 requires that commercial and industrial 
loading docks within the SSCSP Planning Area be oriented away from and shielded sensitive 
receptors. Enforcement of the Noise Control Ordinance of the City’s Code of Ordinances and GPU 
policies would ensure that future development would not result in a substantial permanent increase 
in ambient noise levels.  
d. Construction Noise 
Future development implemented under the GPU could result in a temporary ambient noise increase 
due to construction activities. Due to the developed nature of the City, there is a high likelihood that 
construction activities would take place adjacent to existing structures and that sensitive receptors 
would be located in proximity to construction activities.  
Construction noise typically occurs intermittently and varies depending upon the nature or phase of 
construction (e.g., demolition; land clearing, grading, and excavation; erection). Construction noise 
would be short term and would include noise from activities such as site preparation, truck hauling 
of material, pouring of concrete, and the use of power tools. Noise would also be generated by 
construction equipment use, including earthmovers, material handlers, and portable generators, and 
could reach high noise levels for brief periods. Noise levels generated by typical construction 
equipment are summarized in Table 4.13-10.

Construction equipment would generate maximum noise levels between 70 and 95 dB(A) Lmax at 
50 feet from the source when in operation. During excavation, grading, and paving operations, 
equipment moves to different locations and goes through varying load cycles, and there are breaks 
for the operators and for non-equipment tasks, such as measurement. Average construction noise 
levels were calculated for the simultaneous operation of three common pieces of construction 
equipment: backhoe, excavator, and loader. The usage factors were applied to the maximum noise 
level at 50 feet for each piece of equipment, and then noise levels were added logarithmically. Hourly 
average noise levels would be approximately 83 dB(A) Leq at 50 feet from the center of construction 
activity when assessing three pieces of common construction equipment working simultaneously. 
Construction noise levels of 83 dB(A) Leq at 50 feet would attenuate to 80 dB(A) Leq at 70 feet. Noise 
levels would vary depending on the nature of the construction including the duration of specific

The City regulates construction noise through Section 38.17(h) of the Noise Control Ordinance by 
limiting construction activities to 7:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. from Monday through Saturday. Additionally, 
HLC Policy 7-165 states that the City will “[a]ddress appropriate construction noise and vibration 
control measures, standards, and monitoring procedures for future development in the City’s 
Municipal Code to reduce impacts to nearby uses.” Through implementation of the Noise Control 
Ordinance and HLC 7-165, construction noise impacts associated with future development 
implemented under the GPU would not result in significant ambient noise levels.  
4.13.4.3 Significance of Impacts 
a. Vehicle Traffic Noise 
Increase in Ambient Noise 
GPU buildout would result in a significant noise increase over existing ambient noise levels at several 
roadway segments. With the exception of the segments of Oceanside Boulevard between Rancho 
Del Oro Drive and College Boulevard, Marron Road between Western City Limit and College 
Boulevard, and Foussat Road between Alex Road and Mission Avenue, there are noise-sensitive 
residential uses located adjacent to each of these roadway segments. The GPU contains goals and 
policies that would reduce noise levels at new noise-sensitive development. However, existing land 
uses would be exposed to significant increase in ambient noise. Impacts to existing noise-sensitive 
land uses would be significant. 
Land Use Compatibility 
The GPU contains policies that would reduce impacts associated with land use compatibility. Through 
implementation of this regulatory framework, along with site-specific noise analyses as required by 
Title 24 to demonstrate interior noise levels of 45 CNEL, exterior and interior traffic noise impacts 
associated with new development would be less than significant. 
b. Railroad Noise 
Noise-sensitive receivers in the vicinity of the railroad tracks could exceed the compatibility 
standards. However, as previously discussed, the GPU contains policies that would reduce impacts 
associated with land use compatibility. Through implementation of this regulatory framework, 
railroad noise impacts associated with new development would be less than significant. 
c. Stationary Noise 
Enforcement of the Noise Control Ordinance of the City’s Code of Ordinances and GPU policies 
would ensure that future development would not result in a substantial permanent increase in 
ambient noise levels, and impacts associated with stationary sources of noise would be less than 
significant.

4.13.4.4 Mitigation 
a. Traffic Noise 
Increase in Ambient Noise 
Impacts associated with the increase in ambient noise would be significant without mitigation. For 
existing noise sensitive land uses, possible noise-reduction measures would include retrofitting older 
structures with acoustically rated windows and doors featuring higher Sound Transmission Class 
ratings, which is a measure of exterior noise reduction performance. However, there is no mechanism 
in place for implementing such a retrofit program. Because the significant noise impacts would be 
to existing homes and other noise-sensitive uses in an already urbanized area, there is no feasible 
mitigation.

significant and unavoidable at this program level of review.

4.13.5 Groundborne Vibration and Noise 
4.13.5.1 Thresholds of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to groundborne vibration and noise are 
based on applicable criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Result in generation of excessive groundborne vibration or ground borne noise levels? 
4.13.5.2 Impact Analysis 
a. Construction 
Construction activities may include demolition of existing structures, site preparation work, 
excavation of parking and subfloors, foundation work, and building construction. Demolition of an 
individual site may last several weeks to months and may produce substantial vibration. Excavation 
for underground levels could also occur on some development sites, and vibratory pile driving could 
be used to stabilize the walls of excavated areas. Piles or drilled caissons may also be used to support 
building foundations.  
As with any type of construction, vibration levels during any phase may at times be perceptible. 
However, non-pile driving or foundation work construction phases that have the highest potential 
of producing vibration (such as jackhammering and other high power tools) would be intermittent 
and would only occur for short periods of time for any individual development site. By use of 
administrative controls, such as scheduling construction activities with the highest potential to 
produce perceptible vibration to hours with least potential to affect nearby properties, perceptible 
vibration can be kept to a minimum and as such would result in a less than significant impact with 
respect to perception.  
Pile driving has the potential to generate the highest groundborne vibration levels and is the primary 
concern for structural damage when it occurs within close proximity of structures. As shown in 
Table 4.13-10, vibration generated by construction equipment has the potential to be substantial, 
since it has the potential to exceed the FTA criteria for architectural damage (e.g., 0.12 PPV for fragile 
or historical resources, 0.2 PPV for non-engineered timber and masonry buildings, and 0.3 PPV for 
engineered concrete and masonry). Construction details and equipment for future project level 
development is not known at this time. However, the GPU contains Policy 7-H which requires the 
City to address appropriate construction noise and vibration control measures, standards, and 
monitoring procedures for future development in the City’s Code of Ordinances to reduce impacts 
to nearby uses. With implementation of this policy, future development would be required to 
implement vibration control measures during construction, thereby ensuring that construction 
vibration impacts would not be excessive.  
b. Railroad 
As discussed in Section 4.13.4, the Coaster, Sprinter, Amtrak Surfliner, Metrolink, and freight trains 
operate within the Planning Area. Construction of vibration-sensitive uses in close proximity to 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.13 Noise 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.13-32 
railroad tracks can cause rattling windows and vibration of floors. Train vibration depends upon a 
variety of factors. The weight of the train, the travel speed, the condition of the track, and the 
character of the subsoil all affect the observed vibration level. Vibration impacts due to the proximity 
of land uses to the rail corridor were analyzed using the FTA criteria shown in Table 4.13-3. Based on 
published schedules, 78 Sprinter trains operated on the east-west railroad tracks. These are 
considered frequent events (more than 70 per day). 52 Coaster and Amtrak Surfliner trains and 
occasional freight trains operate on the north-south railroad tracks south of the Oceanside Transit 
Center, and 35 Metrolink and Amtrak Surfliner trains and occasional freight trains operate on the 
north-south railroad tracks north of the Oceanside Transit Center. These are considered occasional 
events (30 to 70 per day). As shown in Table 4.13-3, a significant vibration impact may occur if 
Category 1, 2, and 3 land uses are exposed to vibration levels of 65, 72, and 75 vibration decibels 
(VdB), respectively, for frequent events, and 65, 75, and 78 VdB, respectively, for occasional events. 
Figure 4.13-5 shows the generalized ground surface vibration curves that are based on 
measurements of ground-borne vibration at representative North American transit systems (FTA 
2018). These curves can be used to represent vibration characteristics for standard transportation 
systems. Using these curves, it was determined that Category 1 land uses would be exposed to 
significant vibration levels within approximately 350 feet of the north-south railroad tracks and 140 
feet of the east-west Sprinter railroad tracks, Category 2 land uses would be exposed to significant 
vibration levels within approximately 140 feet of the north-west railroad tracks and 60 feet of the 
east-west Sprinter railroad tracks, and Category 3 land uses would be exposed to significant vibration 
levels within approximately 120 feet of the north-west railroad tracks and 40 feet of the east-west 
Sprinter railroad tracks. In order to reduce these impacts, the SSCSP contains Policy EQ-28 that would 
limit land uses within these screening distances unless vibration isolation construction is undertaken. 
Through implementation of this policy, railroad vibration impacts would not be excessive.  
c. Stationary Sources 
Industrial manufacturing operations occasionally utilize equipment or processes that have a potential 
to generate groundborne vibration. However, vibrations found to be excessive for human exposure 
that are the result of industrial machinery are generally addressed from an occupational health and 
safety perspective. The residual vibrations are typically of such low amplitude that they quickly 
dissipate into the surrounding soil and are rarely perceivable at the surrounding land uses. 
Residential and commercial uses do not typically generate vibration. Therefore, vibration impacts 
associated with stationary sources would not be excessive.  
4.13.5.3 Significance of Impacts 
a. Construction 
The GPU contains HLC Policy 7-165 which requires the City to address appropriate construction noise 
and vibration control measures, standards, and monitoring procedures for future development in 
the City’s Code of Ordinances to reduce impacts to nearby uses. With implementation of this policy, 
future development would be required to implement vibration control measures during construction, 
thereby reducing construction vibration impacts to a level less than significant.

4.13.6 Aircraft Noise 
4.13.6.1 Thresholds of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to aircraft noise are based on applicable 
criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Be located within the vicinity of a private airstrip or an airport land use plan, or, where such 
a plan has not been adopted, within two miles of a public airport or public use airport, and 
expose people residing or working in the area to excessive noise levels? 
4.13.6.2 Impact Analysis 
The Oceanside Municipal Airport is located in the northwest portion of the Planning Area north of SR-
76, south of the San Luis Rey River, and east of Benet Road. Airport noise contours are shown in 
Figure 4.13-3 and the San Diego County ALUC noise compatibility criteria is shown in Table 4.13-4. Based 
on these airport contours, no residential portions of the Planning Area are located within the modeled 
airport noise contours. The quietest modeled contour, 60 CNEL, is considered the maximum acceptable 
level in the ALUCP for new residential uses. Except for a few commercial parcels and open space areas, 
all Planning Area uses are outside of this contour and thus experience noise levels that are lower than 60 
CNEL from the Oceanside Municipal Airport. All commercial and industrial parcels are located outside 
the 65 CNEL noise contour, and all industrial uses are located outside the 70 CNEL. Therefore, these uses 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.13 Noise 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.13-35 
would also be compatible with ALUCP standards. Occasional aircraft overflight noise may be audible to 
people in the Planning Area. However, 24-hour average noise levels from airport operations in the 
Planning Area are compatible with the ALUCP.  
4.13.6.3 Significance of Impacts 
Land uses would not be exposed to airport noise levels that exceed the ALUCP noise compatibility 
criteria. Impacts associated with airport noise would be less than significant. 
4.13.6.4 Mitigation 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required. 
4.13.7 Cumulative Analysis 
The analysis of vehicle traffic noise is cumulative in nature because the analysis considers noise 
impacts associated with buildout of the City and the traffic assumptions used in the analysis include 
cumulative traffic associated with regional growth. Cumulatively, there would be a substantial 
amount of additional new future development and associated travel demand within the City and in 
the surrounding region. The residences and other sensitive land uses located along most of the City 
roadways are currently affected by the existing traffic noise, and cumulative growth would result in 
an increase in ambient noise. Therefore, noise impacts associated with ambient noise increase and 
land use compatibility would be cumulatively considerable. Because the significant noise impacts 
would be to existing homes and other noise-sensitive uses in an already urbanized area, there is no 
feasible mitigation. Cumulative impacts would remain significant and unavoidable. 
Stationary source of noise, construction noise, and vibration are generally localized impacts that do 
not have regional or cumulative considerations. Noise sources associated with past, present, and 
future development in the region include construction equipment, landscape and building 
maintenance activities, mechanical equipment, solid waste collection, parking lots, commercial, 
office, and industrial activities, and residential, school, and recreation activities and events. Noise 
sources that are adjacent to one another could combine to increase cumulative noise levels. 
However, through enforcement of the City’s Noise Ordinance, cumulative stationary, construction, 
and vibration noise impacts would be less than significant.

Population and Housing 
This section addresses potential project impacts related to population and housing that could result 
from implementation of the Onward Oceanside project which includes the City of Oceanside (City) 
General Plan Update (GPU), Smart and Sustainable Corridors Specific Plan (SSCSP), and Climate 
Action Plan (CAP) Update, collectively referred to as the project. The GPU would apply to the entire 
City, while the SSCSP would apply to land within the Specific Plan boundary, referred to as the SSCSP 
Planning Area. As discussed in Chapter 3.0, Project Description, the analysis of potential impacts 
focuses on parcels throughout the City where the project either (1) proposes changes to existing land 
use designations or (2) where no land use is proposed, but growth is anticipated to occur. The 
majority of the proposed increased density and intensity of uses would be within the SSCSP Planning 
Area, as shown in Figure 3-2. 
This section is based on data available from the California Department of Finance (DOF), San Diego 
Association of Governments (SANDAG), the City’s 2021-2029 Housing Element (HEU), and research 
performed in the preparation of the GPU.  
4.14.1 
Existing Conditions 
4.14.1.1 Population and Housing Trends 
SANDAG is the metropolitan planning organization responsible for developing demographic 
projections, including population, household, and employment projections, for the 19 jurisdictions in 
the County, including the City of Oceanside. Regional and City population and housing trends are 
discussed further below.  
a. Population 
Region 
SANDAG anticipates 3.7 million people will be living in the San Diego region, an increase of 
approximately 13 percent, by the year 2050. With this population growth, there is an expectation of 
a need for 440,000 more jobs and 274,000 more homes. To accommodate anticipated growth goals 
for healthier air and reduced greenhouse gas emissions, SANDAG seeks to focus growth and 
development in the region’s urbanized areas, where there are existing and planned infrastructure 
and transportation options (SANDAG 2021a). 
City of Oceanside 
SANDAG developed a set of regional projections for the year 2050 as part of its Series 14 Regional 
Growth Forecast. Table 4.14-1 presents SANDAG growth projections for population, households, and 
jobs within the City through 2050. These projections provide a gauge for City planning to 
accommodate forecasted population and housing, including the level of housing that would be 
needed to satisfy future Regional Housing Needs Assessments (RHNA) beyond the 2021-2029 HEU 
cycle. It is noted that SANDAG is currently working on Series 15 growth projections, which would

b. Housing 
Region 
As of 2016, there are 1,190,555 existing housing units in the San Diego region. Between 1950 and 
2019, the housing supply has not kept pace with the growing population of the San Diego region, 
resulting in rising housing prices. Consequently, the State of California faces a persistent housing 
crisis, and San Diego County is no exception. More affordable housing is needed for extremely low, 
very low-, low-, and middle-income households. Steps at the local, regional, and state level are being 
taken to address the availability and affordability of housing. By 2050, the regional housing supply is 
forecasted to increase by 208,744 to 1,471,299, which would be 23.6 percent growth above the 
current regional population (SANDAG 2021b).  
During the RHNA process, California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) 
determined that 171,685 housing units would need to be planned for in the San Diego region over 
the 2021-2029 Housing Element cycle (SANDAG 2021b). 
City of Oceanside 
Pursuant to the HEU, the City is estimated to currently accommodate 66,475 housing units, consisting 
of 43,164 single-family detached homes (65.0 percent), 20,156 multi-family dwelling units 
(31.0 percent), and 3,107 (5.0 percent) mobile homes. Compared to the region, the City has a higher 
percentage of single-family units and a similar percentage of multi-family units (City of Oceanside 
2022:Table 9). The current overall vacancy rate in Oceanside is estimated at 7.0 percent. Based on 
the number of occupied units and household populations, the number of people per household as 
estimated in the American Community Survey 2018 Census data is 2.83 persons (City of Oceanside 
2022:Table 4). According to the most recent American Community Survey (2020), people per 
household in the City is estimated to be 2.8 which is similar to the American Community Survey 2018 
Census data.

4.14.2 Regulatory Setting 
4.14.2.1 State  
a. Senate Bill 375 and Assembly Bill 1233 
Senate Bill (SB) 375, the Sustainable Communities and Climate Protection Act, was passed in 2008. 
SB 375 focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, as discussed further in Section 4.5. As a part 
of this effort, SB 375 requires that regional housing needs be addressed in conjunction with regional 
transportation in order to integrate housing, land use, and transportation planning together. In the 
San Diego region, this unified regional planning effort is completed by SANDAG via San Diego 
Forward.  
Assembly Bill (AB) 1233 (enacted in 2005), requires each city or county in California to draft and 
implement a housing element as part of the General Plan for their jurisdiction. The housing elements 
provide an assessment of housing needs and an inventory of resources and constraints relevant to 
the meeting of these needs.  
b. Regional Housing Needs Assessment 
To respond to state population and household growth, and to ensure the availability of decent 
affordable housing for all income groups, the state enacted a law that requires SANDAG and other 
councils of governments to periodically distribute the state-identified housing need for their regions. 
As discussed in Section 3.2, local jurisdictions are required by state law (Government Code Section 
65580 et seq.) to plan for their fair share of projected regional housing growth in their region over a 
specified planning period. Housing unit construction goals are set by the HCD and allocated to cities 
through regional planning agencies. HCD is responsible for determining this regional need, initiating 
the process by which each region must then distribute their share of statewide need to all 
jurisdictions within its region. See Table 4.14-2 for total RHNA allocations.  


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.14 Population and Housing  
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.14-4 
4.14.2.2 Regional  
a. San Diego Forward: 2021 Regional Plan 
The 2021 Regional Plan, adopted by the SANDAG Board of Directors on December 10, 2021, is a 
comprehensive regional planning document that sets the vision for the future of the San Diego 
region and includes various planning document components to guide future improvements to meet 
that vision. The Regional Plan is updated every four years and combines three planning documents 
that SANDAG must complete per state and federal laws: the Regional Transportation Plan, 
Sustainable Communities Strategy, and Regional Comprehensive Plan. In addition, San Diego 
Forward addresses regional growth and housing needs utilizing regional growth forecast and the 
RHNA.  
b. Draft 2025 Regional Plan 
The Draft 2025 Regional Plan updates and refines the 2021 plan to reflect new demographic 
forecasts, post-pandemic travel behavior, and fiscal constraints. The 2025 Draft Regional Plan 
maintains the region’s commitment to multimodal, sustainable, and equitable mobility but places 
greater emphasis on: 
• 
Expanding transit and active transportation networks rather than new freeway expansions; 
• 
Integrating updated regional growth forecasts (Series 15) and Sustainable Communities 
Strategy assumptions; 
• 
Advancing equity, health, and safety outcomes through improved access to jobs and 
essential services; and 
• 
Applying updated modeling tools and performance metrics to meet state greenhouse gas 
reduction targets (SANDAG 2025). 
4.14.2.3 Local 
a. City of Oceanside Housing Element 
Consistent with state law, the City recently updated the General Plan Housing Element to serve the 
planning period of 2021-2029. The Housing Element evaluates City demographics, housing 
resources, and constraints on development to provide a detailed inventory of potential sites to serve 
projected housing needs. The Housing Element includes a Housing Action Plan which contains goals 
and policies to address housing-related issues during the 2021-2029 planning period. The primary 
goal of the Housing Action Plan is to ensure that reasonable housing is available at a cost that is 
affordable to all current and future residents. 
4.14.3 Proposed GPU and SSCSP Policies 
The proposed GPU and SSCSP include policies intended to reduce potential adverse environmental 
impacts resulting from buildout of the plans. As future development is proposed, development 
would be required to demonstrate consistency with the GPU and SSCSP policy framework, as

applicable. The policy framework would be implemented by the City during future discretionary

4.14.3.1 Policy Framework 
The City’s policy framework is intended to minimize impacts associated with population and housing 
throughout the City, and do not intend to be exclusive of all additional relevant policies that may 
apply to future development.

4.14.4 Population Growth 
4.14.4.1 Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to population growth are based on 
applicable criteria in the 2025 California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines, Appendix G. 
Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Induce substantial unplanned population growth in an area, either directly (for example, by 
proposing new homes and businesses) or indirectly (for example, through extension of roads 
or other infrastructure)? 
4.14.4.2 Impact Analysis 
SANDAG forecasting estimated an increase in population growth of approximately 7,616 by the year 
2050. To accommodate this growth, HCD assigned a RHNA to the City of 5,443 units. The project 
would result in increased density throughout the City, primarily within the SSCSP Planning Area. 
Specifically, as summarized in Tables 3-5 and 3-8, implementation of the GPU and SSCSP would 
result in the development potential of approximately 16,875 new residential units, 8,300 of which 
would be within the SSCSP Planning Area. Buildout of all potential residential units would result in 
population growth of 45,100. This estimated increase in population growth is greater than the current 
Series 14 regional growth forecasted by SANDAG. Table 4.14-3 compares existing residential 
units, population, and employment with projected buildout under the GPU.

4.14.5 Displace Housing or People 
4.14.5.1 
Threshold of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to displacement of homes or people are 
based on applicable criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Displace substantial numbers of existing people or housing, necessitating the construction 
of replacement housing elsewhere? 
4.14.5.2 
Impact Analysis 
Future development and redevelopment throughout the City would be primarily located in 
commercial districts but would still have the potential to displace people and housing through 
demolition of existing residential structures. However, for each home that would be removed, more 
housing units would be provided in its place which would accommodate more people and ensure 
no net loss of housing. Further, per the provisions of Section 65590 of the State Government Code, 
referred to as the “Mello Act”, the conversion or demolition of existing residential units in the coastal 
zone which are occupied by persons and families of low or moderate income shall not be permitted 
unless provisions have been made for replacement of those dwelling units which result in no net loss 
of affordable housing.

4.14.6 Cumulative Analysis 
The study area considered for the population and housing cumulative impact analysis is defined as 
the region. Buildout of the project would respond to the City’s allocation under RHNA and would 
accommodate the projected population growth in the region, consistent with adopted plans and 
regional growth principles. The project would exceed SANDAG estimates allowing the City to meet 
RHNA allocations for this housing cycle, and through the year 2050. The City would have a buffer in 
all income categories to ensure the City can navigate the no net loss provisions of the state Housing 
Element law. Overall, the project would accommodate future housing and population demands. 
Therefore, the project would not contribute to a cumulative impact related to population and 
housing.

In addition to providing emergency response services to the community, OFD performs a number 
of non-emergency functions. These functions include fire investigations, plan checks for all new 
developments, fire prevention inspections, and public education and informational programs (OFD 
2023). 
The City participates in Automatic Aid Agreements within San Diego County and is a participant in 
the statewide Mutual Aid Agreement. This allows the OFD to provide and receive all-risk assistance 
across the state of California. With Automatic Aid, the OFD and its neighbors operate using the 
principle of closest available resource regardless of jurisdictional boundary. This improves response 
times and service to the community. Furthermore, participation in this program helps provide 
adequate fire station service area coverage and response times to all portions of the City.  
In 2005, the City Council adopted a resolution establishing an expectation that OFD respond to 
“Priority 1” level fire and emergency medical services calls within five minutes 90 percent of the time. 
The City has found that it increasingly difficult to meet this response time standard, especially within 
the downtown core and select portions of the City (City of Oceanside 2021b). 
4.15.1.2 Police Protection 
The Oceanside Police Department (OPD) provides services to the community with 219 sworn police 
officers and 115 professional staff members. The OPD handles approximately 110,000 calls for service 
each year (OPD 2023). The police department headquarters is located at 3855 Mission Avenue, 
Oceanside, California 92054 (see Figure 4.15-1). 
The OPD has a goal to maintain a response time standard of five minutes for all Priority I and II 
emergency service calls (City of Oceanside 2021a). Table 4.15-2 indicates that the OPD has been 
meeting these response time goals as of 2019 (City of Oceanside 2022).

4.15.1.3 Schools 
Students residing in the City in kindergarten through 12th grade are served by the Oceanside Unified 
School District (OUSD), the Vista Unified School District (VUSD), the Bonsall Unified School District 
(BUSD), the Carlsbad Unified School District (CUSD), and a variety of parochial and secular private 
schools. OUSD operates 23 schools: 16 elementary schools (three of which are located on Marine 
Corps Air Station Camp Pendleton), four middle schools, two comprehensive high schools, and one 
alternative high school. These facilities are shown in Figure 4.15-2. Oceanside students may also 
attend BUSD, CUSD, or VUSD just outside the City. The VUSD serves students at four elementary 
schools, two middle schools, and one high school. The BUSD operates one elementary school in the 
City. The CUSD does not have facilities in the City but does serve City residents in the Tri-City area. 
Both the OUSD and VUSD operate adult education programs (City of Oceanside 2021b). 
The OUSD has witnessed a steady decline in enrollment over the last several years, despite an 
increase in the City’s population. Specifically, total enrollment for the 2007-2008 school year was 
20,384 students; enrollment in the 2019-2020 school year decreased to 19,371 students. As of the 
2019-2020 school year, OUSD served a student body of 19,371 students. According to the State’s 
eligibility standards, OUSD has 747 permanent and 242 portable classrooms, with a total capacity 
for 23,852 students (City of Oceanside 2021b).  
4.15.1.4 Parks and Recreational Facilities 
The City’s Parks and Recreation Division provides park and recreation services throughout 
Oceanside. The City currently maintains approximately 871 acres of parkland including 155.6 acres of 
school park space available for public use via MOUs. As of 2020, the City’s parks and recreation 
facilities consist of 17 community parks, 16 neighborhood and pocket parks, one community garden, 
one regional park, three recreation centers (Junior Seau Community Center, Joe Balderrama 
Recreation Center, and Melba Bishop Recreation Center), a YMCA and Boys and Girls Club, two senior 
centers, five skate parks, and two community pools. Other facilities include Oceanside’s 3.5 miles of 
beach, the Oceanside Small Craft Harbor, and the Oceanside Municipal Pier.
