4.15.1.5 Other Public Facilities (Libraries) 
The Oceanside Public Library operates three branch libraries and one learning center:  
• 
Civic Center Library (330 North Coast Highway, measuring 36,315 square feet)  
• 
Mission Branch Library (3861 Mission Avenue, measuring 12,260 square feet) 
• 
John Landes Community Center Library (2855 Cedar Road, measuring 
• 
Oceanside READS Learning Center (804 Pier View Way, in leased space measuring 
2,295 square feet) 
These facilities provide study and community rooms, computers and printers, early learning services, 
workforce training programs, veterans resources, and a wide range of community events (e.g., author 
talks, concerts, cultural celebrations.) These facilities are shown in Figure 4.15-1.  
The Oceanside Public Library also provides two mobile libraries that deliver library services and 
materials to residents in underserved neighborhoods.  
The City’s current goal is to provide 0.55 square feet of library facilities per resident and three staff 
(one librarian and two clerical staff) per 6,000 residents. Currently, the library square footage is 
approximately half of what the General Plan recommends, and staff levels are approximately two-
thirds of the recommended level (City of Oceanside 2021b). The City recently adopted the Public 
Library Strategic Plan 2024-2028 to promote marketing, outreach, expansion, inclusivity, and growth 
as it relates to library services (see subsection 4.15.2.2(e).  
4.15.2 Regulatory Setting 
4.15.2.1 State Regulations 
a.  Assembly Bill 2926 
Assembly Bill (AB) 2926, passed in 1986, allows school districts to collect impact fees from developers 
of new residential and commercial/industrial building space to assist in providing school facilities for 
students. Development impact fees (DIFs) are also referenced in the 1987 Leroy Greene Lease-
Purchase Act, which requires school districts to contribute a matching share of costs for construction, 
modernization, and reconstruction projects. 
b. Senate Bill 50 (Statutes of 1998), State School Funding, Education Code Section 
17620  
Senate Bill (SB) 50, adopted in 1998, limits the power of cities and counties to require mitigation of 
school facilities impacts as a condition of approving new development. It also authorizes school 
districts to levy statutory developer fees at levels higher than previously allowed and according to 
new rules. California Education Code 17620 establishes the authority of any school district to levy a 
fee, charge, dedication, or other requirements against any development within the school district for 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.15 Public Services 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.15-9 
the purposes of funding the construction of school facilities, as long as the district can show 
justification for the fees. 
c.  Quimby Act and Assembly Bill 1359 
The Quimby Act, which is within the state’s Subdivision Map Act, authorizes the legislative body of a 
city or county to require the dedication of land or impose fees for park or recreational purposes as 
a condition to the approval of a tentative or parcel subdivision map, if specified requirements are 
met. One of these requirements is that the dedicated land or fees, or combination thereof, shall be 
used only for the purposes of developing or rehabilitating neighborhood or community park or 
recreational facilities to serve the subdivision for which the land was dedicated or fees were paid. 
The act provides that the dedication of land or the payment of fees, or both, shall not exceed the 
proportionate amount necessary to provide 3 acres of park area per 1,000 persons residing within a 
subdivision subject to the act, except as specified. 
d. California Education Code 
Section 17620 of the California Education Code authorizes school districts to require construction 
projects within the boundaries of the districts to pay a fee used for funding construction or 
reconstruction of school facilities. 
4.15.2.2 Local Regulations 
a. City of Oceanside Code of Ordinances 
Chapter 32B – Impact Fees  
Chapter 32B of the City’s Code of Ordinances covers all impact fees imposed by the City as a 
condition of development approval for the purpose of financing capital improvements, the need for 
which is attributable to such development, unless expressly exempted. Fees include: (d) Park fees 
imposed pursuant to Ordinance No. 91-10; and (e) Park fees imposed pursuant to article 40 of the 
Zoning Regulations. 
Chapter 32C – Public Facility Fee  
Chapter 32C of the City’s Code of Ordinances outlines provisions for assessing and collecting public 
facilities fees as a condition of issuing a building permit for the purpose of defraying the actual or 
estimated costs of constructing needed public facilities. 
Chapter 32D – Parkland Dedication and Payment of Fees  
Chapter 32D of the City’s Code of Ordinances outlines provisions that apply to all development 
within the City by which additional residential lots and/or dwelling units are created. Every owner, 
developer or subdivider who creates such lots and/or units is required to dedicate a portion of land, 
pay a fee, or do both for the purposes of providing open space, park and recreational facilities. In 
accordance with the standards of 5 acres of developed parkland for each 1,000 people, set forth in 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.15 Public Services 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.15-10 
the community facilities element1, a developer would dedicate land and/or pay a fee as required by 
this chapter.  
b.  Parks and Recreation Master Plan 
In 2019, the City adopted a new Parks and Recreation Master Plan (Master Plan). The Master Plan 
provides guidelines for the orderly development of future park, recreation, and open space facilities 
and programs to meet the community’s current and future needs. The Master Plan is intended to 
provide a realistic view of the City’s parks and recreation system and to develop a vision for the parks 
and recreation system through 2030. 
c.  Pedestrian Master Plan  
The Pedestrian Master Plan aims to guide how the City plans and implements pedestrian projects, 
including projects to enhance neighborhood quality or mobility options by providing pedestrian 
improvement projects. The Pedestrian Master Plan identifies and prioritizes pedestrian projects 
based on technical analyses and community input and provides a prioritized list of projects to 
improve the City’s ability to receive grant funding to implement the top priority projects. The 
Integrated Mobility Element (IM) includes goals and policies for development of a recreational 
pedestrian network (see Section 3.4.3.1 and Figure 3-3). 
d. Bicycle Master Plan  
The Bicycle Master Plan is a comprehensive update to the 1995 City of Oceanside Circulation Element 
and Recreational Trails Element and identifies points where the City’s bikeway system could be 
integrated with the San Diego County regional bikeway system. The Bicycle Master Plan evaluates 
the City’s existing bikeway facility system and its relationship with other systems, such as mass transit, 
and recommends improvements wherever appropriate. Additionally, the goal of the Bicycle Master 
Plan is to maximize the efficiencies offered by multi-modal connections between mass transit and 
bikeways as well as to promote a viable alternative to the automobile travel in a climate particularly 
conducive to bicycle transportation. The IM includes goals and policies for development of a 
recreational bicycle network (see Section 3.4.3.2 and Figure 3-4). 
e. Public Library Strategic Plan Update 2024-2028 
The Public Library Strategic Plan Update 2024-2028 (Strategic Plan) serves as a roadmap to align the 
library’s resources (staff, space, funding) with its mission and vision for the next five years. The 
updated plan represents a strategic shift from general library services to transforming the library’s 
role in the community. It emphasizes racial equity, aiming to make the library more inclusive, building 
a staff that reflects the City’s diversity. The Strategic Plan is structured to deepen the library’s 
engagement with the community, including its intention to offer multilingual and culturally relevant 
programming and expand educational and enrichment programs.

f. Proposition H 
In June 2008, City voters approved Proposition H, authorizing the OUSD to issue up to $195 million 
in general obligation bonds for school facility improvements, enabling the district to complete the 
repairs and modernization effort established under the Proposition G bond construction program to 
provide high-quality facilities to all students. Under Proposition H, City schools will receive repairs, 
modernization, upgrades, expansion, and new construction as warranted by enrollment and facility 
usage needs to provide equitable facilities for all students. 
4.15.3 Proposed GPU and SSCSP Policies 
The proposed GPU and SSCSP include policies intended to reduce potential adverse environmental 
impacts resulting from buildout of the plans. As future development is proposed, development 
would be required to demonstrate consistency with the GPU and SSCSP policy framework, as 
applicable. The policy framework would be implemented by the City during future discretionary 
and/or ministerial project reviews to ensure impact minimization. The analysis of potential impacts 
considers how implementation of these policies at the project level would serve to reduce the 
significance of potential adverse impacts. 
4.15.3.1 Policy Framework 
The following goals and policies are examples of the broader policy framework and do not intend to 
be exclusive of all additional relevant policies that may apply to future development. 
a. GPU Remarkable Communities Element (RC) 
The RC promotes Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) which uses building 
design to reduction fear of crime by decreasing a criminal’s ability to commit a crime and increasing 
the chances that the crime will be seen and reported.  
• 
Policy 2-40: Apply the principles of Crime Prevention through Environmental Design (CPTED) 
in the design of public realm improvements and ensure adequate lighting, natural 
surveillance, clear distinctions between public and private space, and the use of resilient 
materials that reduce maintenance requirements.  
• 
Policy 2-41: Continue to apply CPTED principles in the design of new development and 
encourage the provision of adequate public lighting,; windows overlooking streets or parking 
lots,; and paths to increase pedestrian activity within private development projects and public 
facilities in order to enhance public safety and reduce calls for service. 
b. GPU Healthy and Livable Communities Element (HLC) 
The HLC acknowledges the need for City public facilities to support anticipated growth. The City is 
committed to ensure equitable access to public services, and to park and recreational amenities. The 
following goals and policies are examples of the broader policy framework and do not intend to be 
exclusive of all additional relevant goals and policies that may apply to future development. 


4.0 Environmental Analysis

Page 4.15-12 
• 
Goal 7-G: Adequate and accessible public parks, recreational facilities, and community 
centers will be provided, designed, and maintained to meet the active and passive 
recreational needs of the entire Oceanside community.  
• 
Goal 7-H: A well-maintained and integrated system of parks and accessible open spaces will 
be seamlessly connected by a citywide network of clearly marked trails and pathways. 
• 
Goal 7-K: The provision of new public facilities and services will be equitably distributed 
throughout the City, with a particular focus on ensuring access to community facilities for 
historically disadvantaged communities and providing parkland in locations where new 
growth is anticipated. 
• 
Goal 7-N: The City library system will contribute to a high quality of life for residents through 
quality library collections, technologically improved services, well-staffed facilities and events, 
consistent and diverse programming, and welcoming environments. 
• 
Goal 7-O: Educational facilities will be equitable, safe, healthy, technologically equipped, 
aesthetically pleasing, sustainable, supportive of optimal teaching and learning, welcoming 
to parents and community members, and supportive of both neighborhood and Citywide 
school choices.

pocket parks shall be accomplished through homeowners’ association dues. Pocket parks

Also associated with trail improvements, the HLC includes Action Item HLC-8 for the development 
of a Trails Master Plan that would: (1) identify trails, trail access points, and public rights-of-way that 
lack sufficient wayfinding and signage; (2) create opportunities for improved connections between 
major trails and City assets; (3) recommend improvements to the public right of way; (4) develop a 
comprehensive suite of updated trail design guidelines that emphasize accessibility for all user types 
and connectivity to major destinations; and (5) prioritize a list of proposed trail facilities. The Trails 
Master Plan would be accompanied by recommendations for funding and implementation, trail 
maintenance guidelines, schedules, programs, and policies to support trails and amenities, an 
accessibility analysis of existing trails and trailheads, a prioritized list of existing trail/trailhead 
accessibility improvements; and trail accessibility guidelines. HLC-8 would be the responsibility of the 
City’s Planning Division and Parks and Recreation, with a time frame for completion by the year 2031.

Policy 7-65: Maintain an effective facilities financing program to ensure the impact of new

c. GPU Safe and Resilient Environment Element (SRE) 
The SRE provides guidance for enhanced public safety measures, especially in terms of fire and police 
protection. In addition to traditional policing, proposed policies provide direction for community 
oriented policing and CPTED. The following goals and policies are examples of the broader policy 
framework and do not intend to be exclusive of all additional relevant goals and policies that may 
apply to future development. 
• 
Goal 6-U: The Oceanside Police Department will continue to invest in crime prevention 
initiatives, including community policing programs, services for unhoused individuals, 
support for neighborhood watch groups, graffiti abatement, application of CPTED principles, 
and dissemination of information on home and business security, domestic violence, 
consumer fraud, etc. 
• 
Policy 6-94: Maintain adequate police staffing and material resources to ensure reasonable 
response times and the capacity to resolve law enforcement issues in a manner consistent 
with legal standards and best practices.  
• 
Policy 6-99: Coordinate with transit security entities to ensure adequate surveillance of areas 
in proximity to transit stops and stations. 
d. GPU Efficient and Compatible Land Use Element (ECLU) 
The ECLU promotes public safety through land use trends and CPTED, including secure 
developments and safe living spaces. The ECLU also promotes incentives for additional park and 
recreational amenities than otherwise required. 
Allowable Land Uses 
• 
Policy 3-35: Promote uses that provide for natural surveillance of the public realm including 
uses with visually transparent storefronts, outdoor seating or dining areas, and a 12 to 18-
hour presence. 
• 
Policy 3-63: Require that higher-density residential development include common areas that 
support health and wellness and social interaction, spaces for distraction-free working in 
larger developments, and adequate and secure bike parking areas.

Page 4.15-15 
e. GPU Integrated Mobility Element (IM) 
The IM will be supported by an Active Transportation Plan (ATP) and a Trails Master Plan, both of 
which would promote improvements that connect pedestrians and bicyclists to commercial districts 
and community facilities. The ATP will consolidate the City’s Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plans and 
identify priority projects that close gaps in the City’s active transportation infrastructure. The Trails 
Master Plan (see also HLC-8) will focus on dedicated trail connections between neighborhoods and 
nearby recreational facilities – a key objective of the City’s recently updated Parks and Recreation 
Master Plan–while also facilitating the completion of the Coastal Rail Trail and the Inland Rail Trail. 
As specifically detailed in Action Item IM-1, the preparation of the ATP would lie with the City’s 
Planning Division and Traffic Engineering Division, with an anticipated timeline for completion by the 
year 2028. 
f. SSCSP Urban Design  
The SSCSP Urban Design chapter addresses the interface between urban growth and parks and 
recreation. Through the SSCSP Urban Design policy framework, the SSCSP Planning Area features 
parks and public spaces to provide multiple opportunities to enhance the development of parkland 
and provide recreational amenities. The following goals and policies are examples of the broader 
policy framework and do not intend to be exclusive of all additional relevant policies that may apply 
to future development. 
• 
Goal 7: A robust and integrated system of parks, recreational facilities, and open spaces will 
provide visual relief, integrate elements of nature into the built environment, support 
stormwater management, reduce the heat island effect, and accommodate a wide range of 
activities, including passive and active recreation, informal gatherings and special events, and 
the general enjoyment of the outdoors.  
Public Realm and Streetscape 
• 
Policy UD-9: Greenway Connections. Enhance access to creeks and open spaces as well as 
neighborhood destinations through greenway connections, as shown in Figures 4-4, 4-5 and 
4-6. Allow nearby development to build greenway connections as part of a public benefits 
package. 
Parks and Public Spaces 
• 
Policy UD-24: Parks and Public Space Requirements. New developments are required to 
provide open space as specified in Table 4-2 in accordance with the guidelines presented in 
Table 4-1. Per-unit open space requirements in mixed use developments may be combined 
and provided either as privately-owned public spaces or dedicated public easements within 
the Planning Area as long as the space is visible from a public street or from on-site areas 
normally frequented by the public and publicly accessible during business hours. 
• 
Policy UD-25: Public Open Spaces as Focal Points. Public open spaces within the corridors 
should be integrated into new development and capital improvement projects as pedestrian-
oriented focal points that provide respite and visual relief while contributing to the spatial 
organization and legibility of the built environment. Each corridor should include a variety of 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.15 Public Services 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.15-16 
public open spaces – neighborhood parks, pocket parks, plazas, linear parks, paseos, and 
trails that provide connections between the built environment and natural areas. Public open 
spaces should be accessible to residents of surrounding neighborhoods, including those with 
special needs. Collectively, these public open spaces should accommodate a wide range of 
outdoor activities.  
• 
Policy UD-28: Connections to Other Open Spaces and Trails. Parks and public spaces should 
be designed to create an inter-connected park system accessible to the City’s residents, 
visitors, and workforce, including through the greenway connections identified in Figure 4-12. 
The City shall develop and employ consistent visual themes for wayfinding signage that 
identifies and highlights connections between public open spaces in the corridors.  
• 
Policies UD-30 through UD-34: Multiple policies direct the design of open space and parks, 
park land relationships with buildings and streets, public amenities, and public space 
attributes including shade trees, lighting, and art. Specific design guidelines are included in 
UD Table 4-1. 
• 
Policy UD-36: Sustainable Public Spaces. Incorporate sustainable elements into the design of 
new parks and public spaces including trees, drought-tolerant native or naturalized plants, 
bioswales, and pavements with a high solar reflectance index.  
Corridor Specific Open Space 
Mission Avenue 
•

Policy UD-41: Public Spaces: Projects involving five or more acres shall devote at least two

Policy UD-43: San Luis Rey River Flood Control Improvements. Collaborate with the Army

additional public open space and associated amenities in conjunction with flood control 
improvements within and adjacent to the San Luis Rey River. 
Oceanside Boulevard

Result in substantial adverse physical impacts associated with the provision of new or 
physically altered governmental facilities, need for new or physically altered governmental 
facilities, the construction of which could cause significant environmental impacts, in order 
to maintain acceptable service ratios, response times or other performance objectives for fire 
protection, police protection, schools, parks, or other public facilities? 
4.15.4.2 Impact Analysis 
a. Fire Protection 
The City is mostly developed with all areas receiving fire protection services from one of the eight 
existing fire stations. Additionally, the City has a mutual aid agreement with the neighboring cities of 
Carlsbad and Vista. Per the agreement, when an emergency call comes into dispatch, the nearest 
emergency responder is notified regardless of the jurisdictional boundaries. Nonetheless, increased 
intensity of uses and residential density throughout the City could result in a burden on the OFD and 
increase response times.  
OFD would be required to review and approve all final site plans for future development to ensure 
adequate site accessibility and response times, as well as project design features consistent with the 
City Fire Code (California Fire Code) relating to fire safety compliance. Buildout of the SSCSP would 
allow midrise buildings (between four to six floors) to be constructed within the SSCSP Planning Area. 
OFD would review project-specific building plans to ensure fire safety compliance requirements are 
part of construction plans including the following: delineated evacuation routes; use of fire-resistant 
construction material; and readily apparent fire safety equipment (smoke detectors, fire 
extinguishers. Additionally, the City has an established public facility development impact fee 
program (Code of Ordinances Chapters 32B and 32C) that requires new development to provide 
funds towards capital improvements for public services, including fire and emergency services. Under 
these regulations, future projects would be required to pay applicable developer impact fees in 
accordance with the City’s requirements to ensure that facilities are funded, and new facilities are 
constructed as needed. In addition to City code compliance, future development throughout the City 
would be reviewed for compliance HLC Policy 7-94, which supports future development to pay its 
proportionate share of the costs of the parks and public facilities necessitated by development 
through the payment of impact fees. 
Buildout under the GPU and SSCSP would increase the demand on fire protection services in 
comparison to existing conditions. Individual projects would be required to adhere to all applicable 
regulations and implement relevant GPU and SSCSP policies, including payment of public facility 
development impact fees. However, absent project-specific development plans, it is unknown at this 
time whether such new development could trigger the need for expanded or additional fire facilities 
to provide adequate fire and emergency services, including City-prescribed emergency response 
times. Construction of new fire stations in the future could result in environmental impacts, including 
disturbances or conversion of habitat, water pollution during construction, increased noise levels, 
and an increase in impermeable surfaces. At the time future fire stations are proposed, they would 
require a separate environmental review and regulations in existence at that time would address 
potential environmental impacts related to the construction and operation of new fire stations. 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.15 Public Services

Page 4.15-19 
Therefore, because the location and need for potential future fire stations cannot be determined, it 
is unknown whether impacts would occur.  
b. Police Protection 
The OPD provides police protection services to all areas of the City. As with fire services, increasing 
land use intensity and residential density throughout the City could increase demand for police 
protection services. Specifically, buildout of the project could result in development of as many as 
16,875 new residential units, 14,500 of which would be within the SSCSP Planning Area. Buildout of 
all potential new residential units could result in population growth of over 45,000 new residents. 
Because most of the anticipated growth would be within already urbanized areas (i.e., already 
serviced by the OPD), the City’s public safety service area would not be expanded.  
As detailed in Section 4.15.1.2, the City has adequate police protection services and has been meeting 
response time goals. Additionally, the OPD’s crime prevention efforts have provided local education 
and activities which have assisted in building safer communities. The Crime Prevention Unit works to 
provide awareness covering an array of topics including, but not limited to, home security, auto theft 
prevention, personal safety, consumer fraud (OPD 2024). Future development projects would be 
required to ensure adequate site access, emergency access, and maintain police department 
response times. Future development would also be guided by SRE Goal 6-U which provides direction 
for crime prevention through the application of CPTED. Application of additional policies promote 
CPTED principles including designing public realm improvements to ensure adequate lighting, 
windows overlooking streets, and paths to increase pedestrian activity within private development 
projects (RC Policies 2-40 and 2-41). Likewise, development under the GPU would be expected to 
implement ECLU Policy 3-35 which promotes the enhancement of natural surveillance of both private 
property and public spaces and thereby provide an organic defense against crime and uncivil 
behavior. The City has an established public facility development impact fee program (Code of 
Ordinance Chapters 32B and 32C) that requires new development to provide funds towards capital 
improvements for public services including police services. Future projects would be required to pay 
applicable developer impact fees in accordance with the City’s requirements. In addition to City code 
compliance, future development would be required to pay its proportionate share of the costs of the 
parks and public facilities necessitated by development through the payment of impact fees for 
police services (HLC Policy 7-94). 
Buildout of the GPU and SSCSP would increase the demand on police protection services in 
comparison to existing conditions. While policy compliance and payment of public facility 
development impact fees, would serve to promote adequate police protection services, including 
response times, absent project-specific development plans, it is unknown at this time whether new 
development could trigger the need for expanded or additional fire facilities. Construction of new 
police stations in the future could result in environmental impacts, including disturbances or 
conversion of habitat, water pollution during construction, increased noise levels, and an increase in 
impermeable surfaces. At the time future police stations are proposed, they would require a separate 
environmental review and regulations in existence at that time would address potential 
environmental impacts related to the construction and operation of new police stations. Therefore, 
because the location and need for potential future police stations cannot be determined, it is 
unknown at this program level of review whether impacts would occur.

Page 4.15-20 
c. Schools 
As the City grows under the GPU, citywide demand for educational facilities would increase, 
potentially putting a strain on existing school facilities. Changes in demand for school facilities would 
result not only from new population in new housing, but also from changes in population 
demographics and resulting changes in school-age population cohorts. While the City does not 
provide or manage schools, enrollment, or plans for future school facilities, the GPU does seek to 
ensure adequate educational facilities are available to serve the population.  
OUSD serves the largest student population in the City. However, parts of the City are served by 
VUSD, BUSD, and CUSD as shown in Figure 4.15-2. Despite increased population growth over the 
last few years, the City has experienced a steady decline in enrollment over the last several years as 
a result of an aging population. VUSD is experiencing a decline in enrollment with an annual loss of 
over 429 students a year projected through 2026. BUSD enrollment for the 2019-20 school year is 
also down slightly from the 2017-18 enrollment, but by an amount that may be within normal 
fluctuations. Contrastingly, CUSD enrollment has increased slightly in recent years, expanding from 
11,077 in the 2015-16 school year to 11,481 in the 2019-20 school year (City of Oceanside 2021b). 
Buildout of the GPU and SSCSP would result in an influx of new student-age population to be served 
by City serving schools. While there is currently school capacity, it is possible that future development 
could generate student population beyond available enrollment capacity. Future projects would be 
subject to City DIFs, as applicable, as well as applicable district development impact fees. As outlined 
in Section 4.15.2.1 state regulated developer fees allow school districts to impose mitigation fees on 
new development as a method of addressing increased enrollment. SB 50 states that the fees 
imposed by school districts constitute the exclusive method of considering and mitigating impacts 
on school facilities caused by a development project.  
In addition to state regulatory framework, and City public facility fees, future development would be 
required to adhere to HLC Goal 7-0 focusing on the improvement and equitable availability of 
schools for all OUSD students.  
Buildout of the GPU and SSCSP would increase the demand on the school districts service the City 
in comparison to existing conditions. However, through policy compliance and payment of state 
mitigation and City public facility development impact fees, it is ensured that student enrollment 
would be available prior to approval of building permits. Therefore, it is not anticipated that the 
project would require construction of new or the expansion of existing schools. Should construction 
of schools be proposed in the future, project specific CEQA compliance, including preparation and 
approval of adequate environmental documentation would be required. This, however, is outside 
the scope of the GPU and SSCSP.  
d. Parks and Recreation 
As discussed in Section 4.15.1.4, and shown in Table 4.15-3, the City is below its parkland 
requirements. The increase in population that would occur under the GPU and SSCSP could result in 
the overuse of existing parks and/or the need for increased parkland. Buildout of the GPU would 
result in a total population growth of 45,100 by the year 2050. The GPU would maintain the existing 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.15 Public Services 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.15-21 
standard of five acres per 1,000 residents; based on this standard, the City would require an additional 
need of 234.5 acres of parkland. To reach this goal, the GPU encourages new development to include 
publicly accessible parks and open spaces. As the City is largely built out and much of the anticipated 
new development would be infill, additional parkland will likely take the form of small parks, plazas, 
and linear parks that are integrated into new development. Where parkland cannot be created on-
site as a part of new developments, the City’s park impact fee funds (Code of Ordinances Chapter 
32D; HLC Policy 7-94) would be directed to areas lacking park access.  
The GPU also focuses on the construction and improvement of public parks, pedestrian routes (see 
Figure 3-3), bicycle paths (see Figure 3-4), and hiking trails. The ECLU includes policies focused on 
future development incentives in exchange for the construction of additional park and recreational 
amenities consistent with the SSCSP which would create opportunities for developing enhanced 
parks with connective trails, especially along the Loma Alta and Buena Vista Creeks. Future 
development would be reviewed for consistency with HLC policies focused on the assurance that 
new development provides pocket parks and community parkland (HLC Policy 7-39). Additionally, 
HLC Policies 7-43 and 7-44, support the maintenance of existing, and construction of new trails to 
serve as community parkland. As detailed in Section 4.2.5.2b, new development adjacent to 
waterways would be required to provide pedestrian walkways and public access to trails to create 
additional recreational activity.  
As detailed in GPU Action Items HLC-8 and IM-1, the City would prepare a Trails Master Plan that 
focuses on completing the City’s “spine” trails, including the San Luis Rey River Trail, Coastal Rail Trail, 
and Inland Rail Trail, and link these trails to parks and other key destinations through a secondary 
trails network. Improvement of these trails would also allow an increased feeling of safety along the 
trail, and enhancements to trail amenities could encourage more people to use the trail for 
recreational purposes. New development would implement HLC Policies 7-48 and 7-59 ensure 
connectivity enhancements along the trails are included in proximate project designs. HLC Policies 
7-49, 7-50, and 7-58 likewise assert the City’s dedication to trails and pedestrian connections and 
means to enhance recreational opportunities. 
The SSCSP encourages parks and open spaces to be designed as part of new development, creating 
a network of public spaces of various types and scales. Public spaces would provide opportunities 
for rest and recreation, contributing to each corridor’s positive identity and visual character (see 
Section 4.2.4.2.c for a discussion of the proposed visual character for each corridor). One way to 
further incentivize public spaces in new developments is to allow for additional building height, 
reduced setbacks, and other deviations from base zoning standards in exchange for the integration 
of public space. SSCSP Policies UD-30 through UD-36 provide detailed guidance on open space 
design based on adjacent building height; accommodation of age and abilities including American 
with Disability Act compliance; inclusion of amenities; and sustainable landscaping.  
The SSCSP identifies a vision for the corridors to parks and public spaces throughout the Planning 
Area. Examples of public space opportunities include the following: 
• 
Pocket Park: A pocket park is a small open space area that typically accommodates passive 
and small-scale, low-intensity active recreational activities. Pocket parks often provide open 
space in areas where development is highly constrained or undesirable. Pocket parks can be 
created on small or irregular pieces of land and serve as intimate focal points for gathering 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.15 Public Services 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.15-22 
and activity. Common elements of pocket parks may include benches and tables, 
playgrounds, art installations, barbecue pits, community gardens, and small-scale sports 
amenities like basketball courts. Although not required, many pocket parks may include small 
retail components such as coffee carts/shops to help activate the space. 
• 
Plaza: Plazas are visually engaging gathering spaces within community neighborhoods where 
outdoor events could be held. The incorporation of plazas around commercial areas creates 
an urban “living room,” where workers, residents, and visitors can gather and meet. The 
design of such spaces should consider the relationship of the plaza to other open spaces and 
amenities. Plazas work well in urban environments where open space is limited, such as 
around transit stations and retail centers. Plazas, therefore, represent a creative solution for 
providing publicly accessible open space within the built environment. 
• 
Linear Park: A linear park is a public open space that is considerably longer than it is wide, 
typically resulting from its adjacency to a physical feature such as a road, waterway, railway, 
trail or public utility lines. Linear parks typically connect to other open space to provide 
connectivity for walking, jogging, and biking, but can also include many other small-scale 
amenities that would be found in other parks, such as playgrounds, fitness equipment, picnic 
areas, overlooks, public art and picnic areas.  
• 
Paseo: Paseos serve as walkable “spines” that extend between developments and commonly 
provide direct pedestrian access to storefronts. These spaces do not accommodate 
automobiles and function as active linear public spaces that connect adjacent sites and 
provide for sitting, gathering, shopping, and creative activity. Paseos typically run 
perpendicular to streets and sidewalks, often linking them to alleys, parking, other 
commercial uses, and adjacent residential areas.  
• 
Parklet: A parklet is a temporary platform that replaces vehicle parking with an active 
pedestrian amenity. Parklets are typically located along an already active streetscape—often 
in front of businesses that draw pedestrian traffic. Parklets are a means of adding pedestrian 
improvements to the public realm without the need to expand right-of-way dimensions. 
Rimmed by portable planters, decorative fencing, and/or protective barriers, parklets often 
provide for outdoor dining. Due to safety concerns and limited curbside parking within the 
corridors, parklets would likely be limited to areas within the downtown or along side streets 
with lower traffic volumes and speeds. 
It is also critical to the design of the SSCSP Planning Area that each corridor should include a variety 
of public open spaces including neighborhood parks, pocket parks, plazas, linear parks, paseos, and 
trails. Corridor specific policies focus on individual standards for each corridor. 
New development within the SSCSP Planning Area would be required to provide open space as 
specified in Table 4.15-4. These requirements are included in the Urban Design Chapter of the SSCSP 
and would be required to be included as project design features to support the City’s adherence to 
parkland requirements.

Improving parks and trails is an integral part of the GPU and SSCP. The requirement for new 
development to assist the City in meeting its park standards through parkland dedication and/or 
payment of park impact fees would ensure that adequate parkland was available to accommodate 
increased population.  
Mission Avenue 
New development along the Mission Avenue corridor would be encouraged to meet open space 
standards related to connectivity with existing parks and trails and dedication of open space. New 
development would be required to implement public open space in conjunction with flood control 
improvements. The SSCSP includes policies specifically applicable to future projects proposed along 
the Mission Avenue corridor. Consistency with these policies would ensure parks, trails, and 
recreational amenities are included as project design features. Examples include:  
• 
SSCSP Policy UD-40: Connections to Existing Parks and Trails. Maximize pedestrian access to 
existing parks and trails through paths, sidewalks, paseos, and greenways, including to the 
San Luis Rey River Trail, Mission San Luis Rey, Joe Balderrama Recreation Center, Brooks 
Street Pool, Ron Ortega Recreation Park, Fireside Park, and Prince Memorial Skatepark. 
• 
SSCSP Policy UD-41: Public Spaces: Projects involving five or more acres shall devote at least 
two percent of total acreage to public space that interfaces with the public right-of-way. Such 
space shall have no dimension less than 20 feet.

Buildout of the GPU and SSCSP would increase the demand for existing parks and increase the City’s 
need to meet parkland ratio standards. Collectively, the GPU and SSCSP focus on improving and 
increasing parkland and open space throughout the City. Through policy compliance, and payment 
of park fees, future buildout of the GPU and SSCSP would provide adequate park and open space 
to accommodate City ratios and further the City’s vision for redesigned urban parks and additional 
open spaces, especially within the corridors. Parkland and/or open space proposed by future projects 
would be included as project specific design features requiring subsequent CEQA compliance, 
including preparation and approval of project specific environmental documentation.  
e. Other Public Facilities (Libraries) 
The increased population anticipated from the GPU and SSCSP would result in the need for increased 
library services to accommodate City residents and continue to meet City standards. Consistent with 
the goals of the Strategic Plan, the City continues to improve library services through identifying 
potential library locations (i.e., El Corazon) and expanding mobile library programs. Future 
development would be required to pay its proportionate share of the library’s costs of services 
necessitated by development through the payment of impact fees (HLC Policy 7-94).  
Buildout of the GPU and SSCSP would increase the demand on library services in comparison to 
existing conditions. However, through policy compliance and payment of public facility development 
impact fees, it is ensured that adequate library services, would be available prior to approval of 
building permits. Should construction of libraries be proposed in the future, project specific CEQA 
compliance, including preparation and approval of adequate environmental documentation would 
be required. This, however, is outside the scope of the GPU and SSCSP. 
4.15.4.3 Significance of Impacts 
a. Fire Protection 
While existing regulations and proposed GPU policies would reduce future development’s need to 
expand or construct new fire facilities to serve the project, absent specific development plans the 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.15 Public Services 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.15-26 
need for expanded or new future fire stations cannot be determined. Therefore, it cannot be ensured 
that all impacts associated with the construction and operation of potential future fire facilities 
associated with new development would be mitigated to a less than significant level. Impacts at this 
program level would be potentially significant. 
b. Police Protection 
While existing regulations and proposed GPU policies would reduce future development’s need to 
expand or construct new police facilities to serve the project, absent specific development plans the 
need for expanded or new future police facilities cannot be determined. Therefore, it cannot be 
ensured that all impacts associated with the construction and operation of potential future police 
facilities associated with new development would be mitigated to a less than significant level. Impacts 
at this program level would be potentially significant. 
c. Schools, Parks and Recreation, and Libraries 
Future buildout of the GPU and SSCSP would place an increased demand on public services including 
schools, parks, and libraries in comparison to existing conditions. Future projects would be required 
to pay DIFs and park fees prior to issuance of building permits to ensure projects pay their fair share 
of new public facilities as they are needed. Additionally, policy compliance would require new 
development projects to include parkland and/or open space design features, especially within the 
SSCSP Planning Area. Therefore, through regulatory compliance and future project-specific 
conditions of approval, impacts related to maintenance of acceptable ratios, and other performance 
objectives levels would be less than significant.

development cannot be determined at a program level of review, it is unknown what specific impacts 
may occur associated with the future construction and operation of such facilities. Thus, as it cannot

4.15.5 Recreation 
4.15.5.1 Thresholds of Significance 
Significance thresholds used to evaluate impacts related to recreation are based on applicable 
criteria in the 2025 CEQA Guidelines, Appendix G. Specifically, would the project: 
• 
Increase the use of existing neighborhood and regional parks or other recreational facilities 
such that substantial physical deterioration of the facility would occur or be accelerated? 
• 
Include recreational facilities or require the construction or expansion of recreational facilities 
which might have an adverse physical effect on the environment? 
4.15.5.2 Impact Analysis 
a. Increased Use of Parks/Recreational Facilities 
The GPU would result in the potential an increase of 16,975 new residential dwelling units and a total 
population growth of 45,100 by the year 2050. This increase would result in the potential for 
increased use of existing neighborhood and regional parks. As discussed in Section 4.15.4.2.d, future 
projects would be required to dedicate parkland and/or land for recreational purposes consistent 
with proposed GPU and SSCSP policies, and/or pay park impact fees (City Code of Ordinances 
Section 32D).  
The GPU maintains goals to meet the standards of providing a minimum of 5 acres of developed 
community parks per 1,000 residents. As discussed in Section 4.15.4.2.d, the City currently meets this 
standard and buildout of additional parkland as anticipated under the GPU would increase park and 
recreational facilities. The GPU and SSCSP include goals and policies, the implementation of which 
would result in further exceeding this standard. Through the requirement of including new or 
improved parkland, recreational amenities, and public spaces as features of new development, 
existing parkland and recreational facilities would not suffer substantial deterioration.  
The HLC supports construction of pedestrian and bicycle networks to provide additional recreational 
opportunities, as well as alternative modalities to connect existing parkland throughout the City. 
Specifically, the HLC requires future developments to provide the following: pocket parks and active 
recreational facilities (HLC Policy 7-39); construction or improvement of existing trails (HLC Policies 
7-43, 7-44, 7-48, and 7-50); and all new development would be required to pay its proportionate 
share of the costs of the parks and public facilities necessitated by development through the payment 
of impact fees for public rights of way, parks and recreation facilities, community facilities (HLC Policy 
7-94).  
Most of the new development would be focused within the SSCSP Planning Area. The addition of 
recreational opportunities within an urban setting is challenging. However, future development 


4.0 Environmental Analysis 
4.15 Public Services 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.15-28 
within the SSCSP Planning Area would be required to include public spaces (pocket parks, plazas, 
linear parks, paseos, and/or parklets) designed to provide opportunities for recreational activities 
(SSCSP Policy UD-24). Additionally, implementation of the SSCSP policies would create opportunities 
for developing connective trails, especially along the Loma Alta and Buena Vista Creeks (SSCSP Policy 
UD-28).  
As discussed above, new development within the SSCSP Planning Area would be required to provide 
open space as specified in Table 4.15-4. These requirements are included in the Urban Design 
Chapter of the SSCSP; new development would be reviewed for consistency to ensure required open 
space is included as part of project specific design features.  
b. Expansion of Recreational Facilities 
Buildout under the GPU and SSCAP would increase the City’s need for additional park and 
recreational land to accommodate the anticipated population. As described in Section 4.15.5.2.a, 
implementation of GPU and SSCSP policies would require new development to include public spaces 
for recreational uses. The SSCSP Planning Area is mostly built out; therefore, the proposed design of 
future recreational lands would be in-fill and urban parks, having minimal effects on the environment.  
4.15.5.3 Significance of Impacts 
Buildout of the GPU and SSCSP would increase population and thereby increase the need for additional 
park and recreational land. Future development would be required to include public spaces for 
recreational purposes as set forth in the HLC and SSCSP Urban Design policies. Future development 
projects would be reviewed for consistency with the design guidelines and SSCSP policies to ensure 
adequate recreational opportunities and facilities are provided. Additionally, Chapter 32D of the Code 
of Ordinances provides for payment of applicable developer and park impact fees. Therefore, the 
project’s impact on recreational facilities would be less than significant impact. 
4.15.5.4 Mitigation 
Impacts would be less than significant. No mitigation is required.  
4.15.6 Cumulative Analysis 
The impact analysis presented in Sections 4.15.4 and 4.15.5 above was cumulative in nature because 
it considers the need for future facilities to serve the entire City. As described therein, impacts 
associated with the expansion or construction of fire and police facilities would be significant and 
unavoidable at this program level of review. Therefore, impacts associated with future fire and police 
facilities would result in a potentially significant cumulative impact.

Transportation 
This section addresses potential project impacts related to transportation and circulation facilities 
that could result from implementation of the Onward Oceanside project which includes the City of 
Oceanside (City) General Plan Update (GPU), Smart and Sustainable Corridors Specific Plan (SSCSP), 
and Climate Action Plan (CAP) Update, collectively referred to as the project. The GPU would apply 
to the entire City, while the SSCSP would apply to land within the Specific Plan boundary, referred to 
as the SSCSP Planning Area. As discussed in Chapter 3.0, Project Description, the analysis of potential 
impacts focuses on parcels throughout the City where the project either (1) proposes changes to 
existing land use designations or (2) where no land use change is proposed, but growth is anticipated 
to occur. The majority of the proposed increased density and intensity of uses would be within the 
SSCSP Planning Area, as shown in Figure 3-2. 
Portions of the transportation analysis is based on the Transportation Impact Study (TIS)/Traffic 
Operations Analysis (TOA) prepared for the project by CR Associates (Appendix D). 
4.16.1 
Existing Conditions 
4.16.1.1 Existing Circulation Systems 
The City’s current Circulation Element was adopted in 1995 and updated in 2021. Transportation 
within the City consists of a multimodal system, which includes roadways, public transit, pedestrian 
paths, and bicycle facilities.  
a. Roadway Classifications 
The City utilizes a system of six classifications to identify the type of service each facility is intended 
to provide. The classifications are supported by design guidelines that indicate the characteristics of 
each facility. The City’s existing roadway system is shown in Figure 4.16-1. 
Expressway 
An Expressway is designed to provide express direct travel through a city with several lanes of travel 
in each direction. Expressways are divided highways with raised medians and fully controlled access 
at intersections. Grade separation of intersections can help improve multimodal safety and optimize 
Expressway operations. Expressways are constructed and maintained by the California Department 
of Transportation (Caltrans).

Prime Arterial  
A Prime Arterial is designed to provide regional, subregional, and intra-city travel. It includes high 
design standards with six lanes of travel, raised and landscaped medians, shoulders for emergency 
parking and bike facilities, and restricted access (e.g., fewer intersections, no driveways). On-street 
parking is prohibited.  
Major Arterial 
A Major Arterial is designed to provide intra-city and subregional connectivity and provide some 
property access in select areas. Driveways interfacing with these roads may have certain restrictions 
to ensure proper roadway functions. They typically have four or six lanes of travel, raised, landscaped, 
and striped medians, and shoulders for emergency parking and bike facilities. Left-turn movements 
are typically protected along Major Arterials. 
Secondary Collector  
A Secondary Collector is designed for intra-city travel as a link between arterial and collector 
roadways. They are commonly lined with driveways providing direct access to abutting properties. 
However, that is not its primary purpose. The typical design features include four travel lanes with a 
center two-way left-turn lane or left-turn pockets, and bike facilities. On-street parking may be 
present.  
Collector Street  
A Collector Street is designed to connect local streets with the adjacent arterial street network. These 
are usually two travel lanes with or without a center two-way left-turn lane and may include bicycle 
facilities. On-street parking may be present. Collector streets frequently have driveways, which 
provide direct access to abutting properties (although the desire is to limit access where possible to 
reduce potential conflicts). A Collector can also be a two-lane one-way street, such as the one-way 
couplet on Mission Avenue between Coast Highway and Clementine Street and Seagaze Drive 
between Coast Highway and Clementine Street.  
Local Street  
Local Streets are low capacity, low speed streets whose main purpose is to provide direct access to 
abutting properties. Local Streets typically do not provide or encourage vehicular connectivity 
beyond providing access to the nearest intersecting higher capacity roadway (most often, these are 
Collectors). The typical design standards include the provision of two travel lanes, parking lanes on 
both sides of the street, and direct driveway access.  
Table 4.16-1 provides a summary of the City’s street design criteria for each type of road classification.

b. Master Transportation Road Network 
The Master Transportation Plan serves as the vehicular chapter of the currently adopted Circulation 
Element. The Master Transportation Plan presents changes to the circulation network identified in 
the Circulation Element (see City of Oceanside 2012:Appendix E). 
c. Roadway Operations 
Operational performance of roadway segment and intersection vehicular operations is described in 
terms of Level of Service (LOS), a measure for vehicular operations based on traffic flow 
characteristics. While LOS is no longer the metric for analysis of traffic impacts under the California 
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), the City uses LOS as a means to measure adequacy of operations 
as detailed in the City’s Traffic Impact Analysis Guidelines for Vehicle Miles Traveled and Level of 
Service Assessment (TIAG; City of Oceanside 2020). Table 4.16-2 describes the characteristics of each 
LOS category, which range from LOS A – approximating free flow conditions to LOS F – 
approximating the most congested flow. Existing (and proposed) policy encourages maintenance of 
LOS D or better on City roads. 
Table 4.16-2 
Vehicular Level of Service Definitions 
LOS 
Characteristics 
A 
Represents the best operating conditions and is considered free flow. Individual users are virtually 
unaffected by the presence of others in the traffic stream. 
B 
Represents reasonably free-flowing conditions, but with some influence by others. 
C 
Represents constrained constant flow below speed limits, with additional attention required by the 
drivers to maintain safe operations. Comfort and convenience levels of the driver decline noticeably 
D 
Represents traffic operations approaching unstable flow with high passing demand and passing 
capacity near zero, characterized by drivers being severely restricted in maneuverability. 
E 
Represents unstable flow near capacity. LOS E often changes to LOS F very quickly because of 
disturbances (road conditions, accidents, etc.) in traffic flow. 
F 
Represents the worst conditions with heavily congested flow and traffic demand exceeding capacity, 
characterized by stop-and-go waves, poor travel time, low comfort and convenience, and increased 
accident exposure 
SOURCE:  Appendix D.

d. Vehicular Safety 
Traffic collision data was obtained from the San Diego Association of Governments (SANDAG) for 
the five-year period of 2018 to 2022. The number of collisions per year were as follows: 2018 
(1,556 collisions); 2019 (1,287 collisions); 2020 (1,116 collisions); 2021 (1,423 collisions); and 2022 
(1,375 collisions) (SANDAG 2024). Collisions have been largely concentrated at intersections along 
major roads, such as State Route 76 (SR-76), Oceanside Boulevard, El Camino Real, and College 
Boulevard. As previously shown in Figure 4.16-2, these corridors carry the City’s greatest volumes of 
vehicular traffic (City of Oceanside 2021).   
4.16.1.2 Main Streets and Highways 
The regional vehicular transportation facilities in the City consist of I-5, SR-76, and SR-78. I-5 is a 
north-south freeway that provides regional transportation access to the city of San Diego to the 
south and to Orange County and the city of Los Angeles to the north. The major thoroughfares of 
the City’s circulation network consist of Oceanside Boulevard, Mission Avenue, Melrose Drive, Coast 
Highway, Rancho Del Oro Drive, College Boulevard, and El Camino Real.  
The SSCSP Planning Area is primarily comprised of inland segments of Mission Avenue, Oceanside 
Boulevard, and Vista Way/Plaza Drive. These roadways serve as the City’s principal east-west 
transportation corridors. The operation of each roadway are as follows: 
• 
Mission Avenue operates as a four-lane major arterial with a raised central median.  
• 
Oceanside Boulevard operates as a four-lane arterial between I-5 and El Camino Real, a six-
lane prime arterial between El Camino Real and College Boulevard, and a four-lane major 
arterial between College Boulevard and the City’s eastern boundary.  
• 
The majority of Vista Way operates as four-lane secondary collectors with two-way left-turn 
lanes.  
4.16.1.3 Public Transit 
Figure 4.16-3 shows the existing public transportation routes and stops throughout the City. As 
shown, the North County Transit District (NCTD) maintains a number of bus routes throughout the 
City and the bus service is referred to as the Breeze service. Additional transit in the City includes 
Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) paratransit service, the Coaster commuter rail, and Amtrak rail 
service. The City is home to five railway stations along the NCTD Sprinter rail line, which runs parallel 
to Oceanside Boulevard. The NCTD Coaster railway line makes one stop in the City at the Oceanside 
Transit Center (OTC). The OTC provides access to Breeze bus service, Coaster rail service, Metrolink 
rail service, Amtrak rail service, and ADA paratransit service. The OTC is a major transportation hub 
located in the San Diego segment of the Los Angeles-San Diego-San Luis Obispo coastal rail corridor 
that serves more than 1.2 million passengers each year and is in the midst of a $23.6 million platform 
improvement project that will increase the number of trains that can board passengers 
simultaneously and allow freight trains to move through the station while passenger trains are 
boarding.

The SSCSP Planning Areas currently support public transit operations as follows: 
• 
The Mission Avenue corridor is served by NCTD’s 303 Breeze bus route. NCTD operates 
Monday through Sunday, excluding holidays. The hours of operation for the 303 bus route 
are approximately 4:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m., Monday through Friday, and 6:00 a.m. through 
10:00 p.m., Saturday and Sunday. The 303 bus has 43 stops departing from the Vista Transit 
Center and ending in the OTC.  The San Luis Rey River Trail is an important active 
transportation facility within this corridor. 
• 
The Oceanside corridor is served by NCTD’s Sprinter rail line, which spans 22 miles, east to 
west, connecting the City, Vista, San Marcos, and Escondido, serving 15 stations along the 
Highway 78 corridor. The Sprinter runs every 30 minutes in each direction Monday through 
Friday, from approximately 4:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. Friday. Weekend trains operate every 30 
minutes between 10:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. and hourly before 10:00 a.m. and after 6:00 p.m. 
The City is working to align and implement the western reach of the Inland Rail Trail within 
this corridor; completing this segment of the Inland Rail Trail would create a contiguous 
pedestrian and bicycle trail between Oceanside and Escondido. 
• 
The Vista Way corridor is served by NCTD’s 302, 315, and 325 bus routes. The 302 bus line 
has 42 stops departing from Vista Transit Center and ending at OTC. The 315 bus has 52 stops 
departing from Carlsbad Village Station and ending at Vandegrift Boulevard & 16th Street. 
The 325 bus line has 43 stops departing from Oceanside Boulevard & Avenida del Oro and 
ending at Carlsbad Village Station.  
4.16.1.4 Pedestrian Mobility 
Pedestrian mobility in the City is largely guided by the Pedestrian Master Plan (City of Oceanside 
2009; see 4.16.2.3.b) The goal of the City’s Pedestrian Master Plan is to establish future planning and 
design standards for development within the City that focuses on creating an accessible and safe 
physical network for pedestrians. The City’s existing pedestrian infrastructure generally consists of 
sidewalks and pathways, crosswalks, and curb ramps. An inventory of existing infrastructure identified 
locations of deficiencies where sidewalks and curb ramps are missing along public roads 
(Figures 4.16-4 and 4.16-5).  
Vehicle-pedestrian collision data was obtained from the SANDAG for the five-year period of 2018 to 
2022. The number of collisions involving the pedestrians per year were as follows: 2018 (53 collisions); 
2019 (47 collisions); 2020 (46 collisions); 2021 (37 collisions); and 2022 (60 collisions) (SANDAG 2024). 
As seen, during the years 2018-2021, total collisions decreased. However, in 2022 the City 
experienced a high increase in the number of pedestrian-involved collisions.

4.16.1.5 Bicycle Mobility 
Bicycle facilities within the City consist of a network of Class I (Bike Path), Class II (Bike Lane), and 
Class III (Bike Route) designated bike facilities, generally described as follows: 
• 
Class I – Bike Path: Also referred to as a multi-use path or shared-use paths, a Class I facility 
provides a completely separated right-of-way designed for the exclusive use of bicycles and 
pedestrians with crossflows by motorists minimized. A bike paths can provide connections 
where roadways are non-existent or unable to support bicycle travel. The minimum paved 
width for a two-way bike path is eight feet, with a two-foot-wide graded area adjacent to the 
pavement. 
• 
Class II – Bike Lane: This class of bike facility provides a striped lane designated for bicycle 
use, prohibiting motor vehicles or pedestrians. A Class II bike lane is a one-way facility located 
on either side of a roadway. Pedestrian and motorist crossflows are permitted at locations 
such as intersections or vehicles preparing to make a right turn. Additional enhancements 
such as painted buffers and signage may be applied. The minimum bike lane width is five 
feet, or six feet when posted speeds are greater than 40 miles per hour. 
• 
Class III – Bike Route: This classification provides for shared use of traffic lanes with cyclists 
and motor vehicles. A bike routes can be identified by signage and/or lane pavement 
markings called “sharrows.” Such routes are best suited for low-speed, low-volume roadways 
with an outside lane of 14 feet or greater. Bike routes provide network continuity or designate 
preferred routes through corridors with high demand. Traffic calming features such as speed 
humps, traffic circles, and curb extensions can be used to help keep traffic speeds and 
volumes low, enhancing the comfort along these shared use facilities. 
• 
Class IV – Separated Bikeway: Also referred to as a cycle track, a Class IV facility provides a 
right-of-way designated exclusively for bicycle travel within the roadway that is physically 
separated from vehicular traffic. A cycle track can be designed for one- or two-way travel. 
Examples of physical separation include vertical separation (e.g., sidewalk level), flexible posts, 
railings, planters, or with on-street parking. 
The location of the City’s existing bicycle facilities is shown in Figure 4.16-6. Total mileage of the City’s 
bicycle network is 106 miles, providing connectivity to all Sprinter stations, OTC, and San Luis Rey 
Transit Center.

The City’s Bicycle Master Plan (City of Oceanside 2017; see Section 4.16.2.3.a) identifies the gaps in 
the existing regional bikeway facilities.  There are a few bike lanes that do not continue to the 
upcoming intersection due to roadway narrowing as they approach the intersection. Intersections 
where bike lanes are incomplete include: 
• 
Melrose Drive at Santa Fe Avenue 
• 
Oceanside Boulevard at Coast Highway 101 
• 
Oceanside Boulevard at I-5 Northbound Ramps 
• 
Oceanside Boulevard at Crouch Street 
• 
Oceanside Boulevard at El Camino Real 
• 
Oceanside Boulevard at College Boulevard 
Additional gaps include the following, pursuant to the 2017 update of the Bicycle Master Plan: 
• 
The San Luis Rey River Trail currently ends at North Santa Fe Avenue, but plans are in place 
to extend the trail southeast through Guajome Park and eventually connect with the 
Oceanside-Escondido Rail Trail.  
• 
Bike lanes are non-existent on El Camino Real between Mission Avenue and Mesa Drive. This 
stretch of road continues as bike lanes north past Mission Avenue and south past Mesa Drive. 
Due to the topography and lack of shoulder width, bike lanes have been excluded on this 
section of El Camino Real, although it is programmed to have bike lanes. 
• 
Bike lanes on westbound Mission Avenue do not continue west of I-5, except for a Class II 
bike route is provided on Mission Avenue from Horne Street to Pacific Street.  
• 
There are no bike lanes on Mission Avenue/SR-76 between Saddleridge Road and the City 
limit. 
• 
There are no east-west bicycle facilities connecting I-5 and the coast between Oceanside 
Boulevard and the San Luis Rey River Trail, except a Class III bike route on Civic Center 
Drive/Bush Street currently provides an east-west connection between the coast and areas 
east of I-5. 
Vehicle-bicycle collision data was obtained from the SANDAG Traffic and Safety Dashboard for the 
five-year period of 2018 to 2022. The number of collisions involving bicycles per year were as follows: 
2018 (51 collisions); 2019 (32 collisions); 2020 (36 collisions); 2021 (58 collisions); and 2022 
(66 collisions) (SANDAG 2024). As seen, during the years 2018-2021, total collisions fluctuated. 
However, in 2022 the City experienced a high increase in the number of bicycle-involved collisions.

4.16.2 
Regulatory Setting 
4.16.2.1 State 
a. California Complete Streets Act of 2008 
The Complete Streets Act (Assembly Bill [AB] 1358) was passed in 2008. As required by this act, upon 
any substantial revision to a General Plan, jurisdictions must incorporate revisions to the Circulation 
Element that plan for a balanced multimodal transportation network that meets the needs of all users 
including motorists, pedestrians, bicyclists, and users of public transportation. The act is intended to 
move the focus away from vehicular transportation to multimodal transportation, and, in part, to 
reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and promote physical activity and public health. In 
December 2010, the Governor’s Office of Planning and Research (OPR) refined its General Plan 
guidelines to provide direction on how local jurisdictions may prepare plans to safely and 
conveniently accommodate alternative modes of transportation in various urban and rural contexts.  
b. Senate Bill 375: Sustainable Communities and Climate Protection Act 
Senate Bill (SB) 375, the Sustainable Communities and Climate Protection Act, was signed into law in 
September 2008. SB 375 required the California Air Resources Board to set regional targets for 
reducing GHG emissions from passenger vehicles in accordance with the California Climate Change 
Scoping Plan (see Recirculated PEIR Section 4.5). The act is intended to align regional transportation 
planning efforts, regional GHG reduction targets, and fair-share housing allocations under state 
housing law. SB 375 requires Metropolitan Planning Organizations such as SANDAG to adopt a 
Sustainable Communities Strategy or Alternative Planning Strategy to address GHG reduction targets 
from cars and light-duty trucks in the context of that Metropolitan Planning Organizations’ Regional 
Transportation Plan. 
c. Senate Bill 743: California Environmental Quality Act Transportation Analysis 
Changes 
SB 743 (2013) created a process to change the way projects analyze transportation impacts pursuant 
to CEQA. Under SB 743, the focus of transportation analysis will shift from driver delay to reduction 
of vehicle miles traveled, and the associated reductions in GHG emissions, creation of multimodal 
networks, and promotion of a mix of land uses. SB 743 requires the OPR to amend the CEQA 
Guidelines to provide an alternative to level of service (LOS) for evaluating transportation impacts. 
According to the legislative intent contained in SB 743, these changes to current practice were 
necessary to more appropriately balance the needs of congestion management with statewide goals 
related to infill development, promotion of public health through active transportation, and 
reduction of GHG emissions.

4.16.2.2 Regional 
a. San Diego Forward: The Regional Plan  
SANDAG is the regional authority and Metropolitan Planning Organization that creates region-
specific documents to provide guidance to local agencies, as SANDAG does not have land use 
authority. SANDAG’s Regional Plan (SANDAG 2021) is a long-range planning document developed 
to address the region’s housing, economic, transportation, environmental, and overall quality-of-life 
needs. The purpose of the Regional Plan is to provide direction and guidance on future regional 
growth (i.e., the location of new residential and non-residential land uses) and transportation 
patterns throughout San Diego County as stipulated under SB 375. The Regional Plan establishes a 
planning framework and implementation actions that increase the region’s sustainability and 
encourage “smart growth while preserving natural resources and limiting urban sprawl.” The 
Regional Plan encourages an increase in residential and employment concentrations in areas with 
the best existing and future transit connections, and preservation of important open spaces. The 
focus is on implementation of basic smart growth principles designed to strengthen the integration 
of land use and transportation. 
The Regional Plan also addresses border issues, providing an important guideline for communities 
bordering Mexico. In this case, the goal is to create a regional community where San Diego, its 
neighboring counties, tribal governments, and northern Baja California mutually benefit from San 
Diego’s varied resources and international location. 
The 2025 Regional Plan (currently in draft form) updates and refines the 2021 Regional Plan to reflect 
new demographic forecasts, post-pandemic travel behavior, and fiscal constraints. The 2025 Draft 
Plan maintains the region’s commitment to multimodal, sustainable, and equitable mobility while 
expanding transit, updating regional growth forecasts (Series 15), advancing equity, health, and safety 
through improved access to jobs and essential services, and applying updated modeling tools and 
performance metrics to meet state GHG reduction targets (SANDAG 2025). The 2025 Draft Regional 
Plan is anticipated to be approved in December 2025. 
b. SANDAG Regional Bike Plan 
The Riding to 2050, the San Diego Regional Bike Plan adopted by SANDAG supports implementation 
of the Regional Plan. It provides a regional strategy to make riding a bike a useful form of 
transportation for everyday travel. The plan will help San Diego meet its goals to reduce GHG 
emissions and improve mobility. The goals of the Regional Bike Plan includes increasing levels of 
bicycling; improving bicycling safety; encouraging the development of Complete Streets; supporting 
reductions in emissions; and increasing community support. In September 2013, the SANDAG Board 
of Directors approved funding to implement the Regional Bike Plan Early Action Program, which 
focuses on the region’s highest-priority projects. Priority is chosen in part based on proximity to 
smart growth areas, taking into account that bikeways would be used more often if they connect 
high-density activity hubs within a short distance of each other, and on whether a project would fill 
key gaps in the regional bike networks. The Regional Bike Plan is currently being updated as part of 
SANDAG’s Active Transportation Program. 


4.0 Environmental Impact Analysis 
4.16 Transportation 
Onward Oceanside Recirculated PEIR 
Page 4.16-17 
c. North County Comprehensive Multimodal Corridor Plan  
The North County Comprehensive Multimodal Corridor Plan (CMCP) identifies all three SSCSP 
corridors (Mission Avenue, Oceanside Boulevard, and Vista Way excluding the Plaza Boulevard 
extents of that SSCSP corridor) as “Mobility Boulevards.” In the CMCP, mobility boulevards are one 
of the strategic anchors of North County’s mobility system, linking local activity centers to regional 
networks while also providing subregional connectivity. They emphasize multimodal design, safety 
and comfort for all modes of travel, and “person throughput” over vehicle throughput. Key strategies 
for mobility boulevards include “smart” arterials which use technology to optimize traffic conditions, 
space to accommodate higher quality active transportation facilities, high frequency transit services, 
and traffic signals equipped with Transportation System Management and Operations technology 
to provide coordination between travel modes. Elements of these strategies are envisioned for all 
three SSCSP corridors. To the extent feasible, SSCSP recommendations for each corridor observe the 
CMCP’s recommendations.  
4.16.2.3 Local  
a. 2008 Bicycle Master Plan (2017 Update) 
The 2008 Bicycle Master Plan was approved by City Council on December 17, 2008. The Bicycle 
Master Plan was updated in 2017 to reflect projects completed since the plan was approved. The 
City’s Bicycle Master Plan identifies the location and types of bicycle facilities within the City in a 
manner that promotes multimodal connections and provides alternatives to vehicular travel. The 
plan identifies top priority projects and estimated costs to complete each identified project segment. 
Financing programs and funding sources are also identified. The plan also provides design guidelines 
intended to guide development of all bikeway facility types in the City.  
b. 2009 Pedestrian Master Plan 
The purpose of the Pedestrian Master Plan is to provide policies and guidelines for pedestrian 
improvements within the City to make walking safer, accessible, easier, and more attractive for 
pedestrians. The plan serves as a framework for implementation of City plans and policies that relate 
to pedestrian infrastructure. Major goals of the plan focus around safety, walkability, connectivity, 
accessibility, and alternative transportation. The City’s Pedestrian Master Plan identifies design 
standards, the installation and maintenance of pedestrian facilities, and the provision of safe 
pedestrian circulation throughout the City. 
c. Thoroughfare and Traffic Signal Fee Program 
The City has adopted a Thoroughfare and Traffic Signal Fee Program, with the most recent update 
to the fees being July 1, 2017. This is based on Resolution No. 16-R0324-1, adopted May 18, 2016. The 
traffic signal fee was established by Ordinance No. 87-19, while the thoroughfare fee was established 
by Ordinance No. 83-01. The purpose of the Thoroughfare and Traffic Signal Fee Program is to 
finance the construction of roads, bridges, and traffic signals.
